questions.explanation: Mean results from a sample estimate the true mean in the larger population. Confidence intervals (CIs) account for some of the variability. The 95% CI of the mean is calculated by the following formula: 95% CI of mean = mean ± 1.96*standard error of mean where standard error (SE) is calculated by dividing the standard deviation (SD) by the square root of the sample size (N). Therefore, as the SD (numerator) increases, the SE and CI also increase; conversely, as N (denominator) increases, the SE and CI decrease. A larger (wider) CI indicates that there is a wider range of possible effects; a smaller (narrower) CI indicates that there is a narrower range of possible effects. The 95% CI for the groups in the study are as follows: Group A (drug X): 95% CI = 85.4 − 84.6 = 0.8 Group B (drug Y): 95% CI = 87.5 − 86.5 = 1.0 Group C (drug Z): 95% CI = 83.7 − 82.3 = 1.4 Drug Z has the widest CI, which suggests that, if this drug is used in a population of patients with diabetes mellitus, it will have the widest range of effects on glucose levels (compared to drugs X and Y). In this particular example, it is difficult to comment on the clinical significance of this finding, as the mean serum glucose values for all 3 groups – including the group taking drug Z – suggest relatively well-controlled diabetes; the study also compares the 3 drugs to one another with no control group. Although the 95% CI is given in the table, it is possible to calculate it manually for all 3 groups using the mean values and SD (with N = 100). A 99% CI would be calculated using the same formula but with 1.96 (Z-score corresponding to 95% of a normal distribution) replaced by 2.58 (Z-score corresponding to 99% of a normal distribution). (Choices A and B) This study does not give any information about the drugs' relative potencies (amount required to produce a given effect), which are usually determined by log-dose response curves. Comments about mortality cannot be made, as mortality rates are not mentioned. (Choice D) The researcher has selected patients with diabetes mellitus from the same county hospital and randomized them into 3 equal groups; this likely reflects adequate sampling and should help account for any differences between the groups. (Choice E) Because the CIs of groups A and C are nonoverlapping (the intervals 84.6-85.4 and 82.3-83.7 do not overlap), this suggests that there is a statistically significant difference between these 2 groups. Educational objective: The 95% confidence interval (CI) of the mean is calculated by the following formula: 95% CI of mean = mean ± 1.96*standard error of mean

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company researcher is working on drugs X, Y, and Z proposed for the treatment of diabetes mellitus. She selects a group of 300 patients with diabetes mellitus from a county hospital in Jackson, TN. She randomizes them into 3 groups of 100 patients each (groups A, B, and C). Patients in group A receive drug X, those in group B receive drug Y, and those in group C receive drug Z. questions.explanation: Intrauterine device Type Levonorgestrel Copper Duration of efficacy Up to 7 years Up to 10 years Mechanism Thickens cervical mucus Impairs implantation Cytotoxic endometrial inflammation Impairs sperm function Impairs implantation Benefits Decreases menstrual flow Can be used as emergency contraception Nonhormonal Can be used as emergency contraception Contraindications Active liver disease Current breast cancer Severe uterine cavity distortion Acute pelvic infection Wilson disease Copper allergy Severe uterine cavity distortion Heavy menstrual bleeding Acute pelvic infection The intrauterine device (IUD) is a highly effective method of long-acting, reversible contraception and a first-line option in adolescents because its efficacy is not user dependent. The copper-containing IUD prevents pregnancy by inducing a foreign body reaction in the uterus that impairs sperm function. The progestin-releasing IUD impairs pregnancy implantation and causes cervical mucus to thicken, which impedes sperm entry. Although IUDs have few adverse effects, irregular menstrual bleeding typically occurs the first few months after insertion. After 3-6 months, menstrual bleeding usually becomes regular. Some progestin-releasing IUD users may experience lighter and shorter menstrual bleeding compared to baseline. In contrast, menstrual bleeding may become longer and heavier and associated with increased cramping (dysmenorrhea) in copper-containing IUD users. This patient's menstrual history is notable for heavy menstrual bleeding and associated anemia, which are relative contraindications to the copper-containing IUD because the copper-containing IUD may exacerbate these conditions. The progestin-releasing IUD would effectively decrease menstrual blood loss and improve anemia in this patient. (Choice A) IUDs can be placed at any point during the menstrual cycle. Current menstruation is not a contraindication to placement and may facilitate insertion through the cervical os. (Choice B) IUDs are made from a nonlatex frame to which either copper or levonorgestrel is affixed. A copper allergy or history of Wilson disease is a contraindication, but a latex allergy is not. (Choice D) IUDs have very few contraindications and are safe and effective for use in all women regardless of age, gravidity, or parity. (Choice E) Recent unprotected intercourse is a risk factor for pelvic infection and pregnancy, which are contraindications to IUD placement. However, these have been excluded in this patient by pelvic examination and negative laboratory testing. In addition, both the copper-containing and progestin-releasing IUDs are highly effective forms of emergency contraception if inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse and may be offered to the patient for this indication. Educational objective: An intrauterine device (IUD) is a highly effective, long-acting, reversible contraceptive method and a first-line option for adolescents. Heavy menstrual bleeding with associated anemia is a relative contraindication for the copper-containing IUD; in these patients, a progestin-releasing IUD is preferable because it decreases menstrual bleeding.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old nulligravid girl is brought to the office by her mother for discussion about contraception. The patient recently started having sexual intercourse with her boyfriend, and both she and her mother agree that she needs reliable contraception. The patient is a competitive swimmer and hopes to obtain an athletic scholarship for college. She is interested in the intrauterine device because her mother has one and she was told that it is one of the most effective forms of contraception. The patient is currently on day 3 of menstruation, and her last episode of unprotected intercourse was yesterday. Menarche was at age 12; periods usually last 7-8 days with heavy bleeding and cramping. She takes naproxen for dysmenorrhea and iron for anemia. The patient has a latex allergy for which she carries an epinephrine pen. Physical examination is normal. Urine pregnancy and cervical nucleic acid amplification tests are negative. Which of the following is a contraindication to the copper-containing intrauterine device in this patient?

questions.explanation: Osteosarcoma vs Ewing sarcoma Osteosarcoma Ewing sarcoma Epidemiology Most common pediatric bone malignancy Bimodal distribution (age <25 & >50) Second-most common pediatric bone malignancy Highest incidence between age 10-15 Clinical features Chronic, localized pain & swelling Metaphyses of long bone (eg, femur, tibia, humerus) Rare: systemic findings & metastases Chronic, localized pain & swelling Diaphyses of long bone; pelvis, axial skeleton (eg, spine, ribs) Common: systemic findings (eg, fever, leukocytosis) & metastases (eg, lung) X-ray findings* Ill-defined osteolytic/osteoblastic lesion Sunburst periosteal reaction Ill-defined lytic lesion (moth-eaten appearance) Lamellated periosteal reaction ("onion skinning") *Periosteal elevation (ie, Codman triangle) is a nonspecific finding related to aggressive bone growth but is most commonly associated with osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone malignancy, typically occurs at sites of rapid bone growth. The metaphyseal long bone is the most common location, particularly in the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus. Classic presentation includes chronic, localized pain and a soft-tissue mass in adolescent boys. Minor trauma may incidentally call attention to the lesion, as in this case. Systemic symptoms (eg, fever, weight loss) are rare. Classic x-ray findings include bony destruction and a spiculated "sunburst" pattern of ossified fibers. Periosteal elevation, or Codman triangle, caused by aggressive underlying tumor growth, can also be seen. Alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase are often elevated due to turnover of damaged osteocytes. Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy, and treatment includes surgical resection and chemotherapy. (Choice A) Acute osteomyelitis typically presents with bone pain, limited mobility, and signs of systemic inflammation. In this patient, the lack of fever or leukocytosis in addition to the lytic lesion on x-ray make acute infection less likely. (Choice B) Ewing sarcoma is the second most common primary bone malignancy and is typically located in the pelvis or long-bone diaphyses. Localized bone pain and swelling are often accompanied by systemic findings (eg, leukocytosis). X-ray shows a lytic lesion surrounded by layers of reactive bone (ie, "onion skinning"). (Choice C) Osteoclastoma (giant cell tumor of bone) is a benign but locally aggressive tumor in long-bone epiphyses. Imaging typically reveals a "soap bubble" appearance due to bony trabeculae within the lesion. (Choice E) Stress fracture presents with focal pain that is worse with activity. X-ray may show cortical thickening and sclerosis or a fracture line. Educational objective: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone malignancy and typically affects the metaphyses of long bones in adolescent boys. Presentation includes pain and soft-tissue swelling, and radiographs show periosteal elevation (Codman triangle) and a "sunburst" pattern of ossification.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the office due to progressive right leg pain and swelling. He first noticed the pain a month ago after scraping his knee on the ground. The patient has used ibuprofen and ice every day, which have not controlled the pain or the swelling. He has no chronic medical conditions or previous surgeries. The patient takes no other daily medications and has no allergies. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F), blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 16/min. The right distal thigh is swollen and firm. There are no wounds or erythema of the overlying skin. All extremities exhibit full range of motion. Weight bearing and gait are normal. The remainder of the physical examination is normal. Laboratory studies reveal an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and a normal leukocyte count. X-ray shows periosteal elevation adjacent to an osteolytic lesion in the distal metaphysis of the right femur. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

questions.explanation: Features of fetal alcohol syndrome Facial dysmorphisms Smooth philtrum Thin vermillion border Small palpebral fissures Growth Height, weight & head circumference <10th percentile Neurobehavioral Developmental delay Cognitive impairment Behavioral issues (eg, ADHD, poor social skills) Seizures ADHD = attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. All pregnant patients should be screened for alcohol use. Alcohol is teratogenic, and cessation is recommended for all pregnant patients. There is no dose-response relationship between the quantity of alcohol consumed and the severity of fetal disease. However, fetal effects appear to be dependent on maternal metabolism and the pattern of consumption (eg, binge versus daily). A safe level of alcohol consumption in pregnancy has not been established. Complications of alcohol use in pregnancy include intrauterine fetal demise and fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS). FAS presents with fetal growth restriction, microcephaly, and facial dysmorphology. Typical facial findings include midfacial hypoplasia, micrognathia, flattened (smooth) philtrum, microphthalmia, short palpebral fissures, and thin upper lip. Central nervous system manifestations of FAS include irritability, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, learning disabilities, and intellectual disability. Patients who consume alcohol during pregnancy are at increased risk for FAS if they are also of advanced maternal age, of high parity, or have children with FAS. (Choice A) Congenital syphilis presents with hepatosplenomegaly, condyloma lata, and jaundice. The placenta is typically enlarged with an edematous umbilical cord. Infants with congenital syphilis are frequently asymptomatic at birth but become symptomatic at age 1-3 months. (Choice C) Opioids do not cause congenital defects. Maternal opioid abuse can cause neonatal opioid withdrawal (eg, irritability, tremors, vomiting, diarrhea, excessive salivation), referred to as neonatal abstinence syndrome. (Choice D) Maternal cigarette use is typically associated with isolated anomalies (eg, cleft lip, anal atresia, gastroschisis). This infant's presentation with multiple anomalies is more suggestive of a syndromic etiology, specifically FAS. (Choice E) Craniofacial abnormalities in trisomy 18 include microcephaly and micrognathia. However, trisomy 18 also presents with cardiac malformations, pulmonary hypoplasia, and a characteristic clenched fist with overlapping fingers, none of which are present in this infant. (Choice F) Uncontrolled hypothyroidism is a risk factor for obstetrical complications (eg, severe preeclampsia, preterm delivery) and may cause cognitive impairment in offspring. It does not cause physical congenital defects. Educational objective: Alcohol is a teratogen and there is no established safe level of use in pregnancy. Fetal alcohol syndrome is characterized by fetal growth restriction, smooth philtrum, short palpebral fissures, thin upper lip, and central nervous system abnormalities.

questions.stem: A male infant is born to a 37-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 4, at 39 weeks gestation by a precipitous spontaneous vaginal delivery. The mother did not receive prenatal care during this pregnancy but reports no complications during her previous pregnancies. Apgar scores are 6 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Weight is 2.35 kg (5 lb 2 oz). The infant has small eye openings, low-set ears, a sunken nasal bridge, and a thin upper lip. The placenta is small and has a thin umbilical cord. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this infant's condition?

questions.explanation: Functional adrenal masses Clinical features Hormone levels Cortisol-producing adenoma (most common) Central obesity, moon facies, enlarged dorsocervical fat pad Hypertension Proximal muscle weakness Hyperglycemia, hypokalemia Elevated cortisol (urine, salivary) Decreased ACTH & DHEAS No suppression by dexamethasone Aldosterone-producing adenoma Hypertension Hypokalemia (muscle cramps, weakness) Elevated plasma aldosterone-to-plasma renin activity ratio Pheochromocytoma Paroxysmal tachycardia, headache, tremor Hypertension Elevated urine metanephrines & catecholamines Elevated plasma metanephrines DHEAS = dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate. Adrenal masses can be functional (ie, metabolically active) or nonfunctional. Among functional tumors, cortisol-producing adenomas are the most common. This patient has several signs of hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome), including hypertension, hyperglycemia, obesity, facial plethora, striae, and dorsocervical fat accumulation (buffalo hump). In light of her CT scan findings, these clinical features are most likely due to a cortisol-producing adrenal adenoma. A cortisol-producing adenoma causes elevated levels of cortisol in urine and (late-night) saliva. Pituitary ACTH secretion is suppressed due to feedback inhibition. Because adrenal production of dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) is ACTH dependent, low ACTH levels lead to low DHEAS levels. Finally, as cortisol production by such tumors is autonomous (ACTH independent), cortisol levels are not suppressed following low-dose dexamethasone administration. (Choice A) ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome is characterized by an elevated (or inappropriately normal) ACTH level, cortisol production that is nonsuppressible following low-dose dexamethasone administration, and a high DHEAS level. Most cases are due to pituitary ACTH secretion (eg, pituitary adenoma), which would be suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone administration; some cases are due to ectopic ACTH production (eg, ACTH-producing small cell lung cancer), which would not be suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone administration. (Choice C) A normal hormonal profile would be characterized by normal ACTH and DHEAS levels with suppressible cortisol following low-dose dexamethasone administration. (Choice D) Elevated DHEAS levels with normal ACTH and cortisol profiles can be seen in patients with androgen-secreting tumors and certain subtypes of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. (Choice E) Dexamethasone-suppressible cortisol production with low ACTH and DHEAS occur in Cushing syndrome due to exogenous corticosteroid administration. Educational objective: Cortisol-producing adenomas are the most common functional adrenal tumors. Urine and salivary cortisol levels are elevated and ACTH levels are suppressed. Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate secretion is stimulated by ACTH and is low. Administration of dexamethasone (which normally suppresses the release of ACTH and production of cortisol) does not affect cortisol production by the adenoma.

Educational objective:
Cortisol-producing adenomas are the most common functional adrenal tumors.  Urine and salivary cortisol levels are elevated and ACTH levels are suppressed.  Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate secretion is stimulated by ACTH and is low.  Administration of dexamethasone (which normally suppresses the release of ACTH and production of cortisol) does not affect cortisol production by the adenoma.
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Functional adrenal masses
Clinical featuresHormone levels
Cortisol-producing adenoma
(most common)
  • Central obesity, moon facies, enlarged dorsocervical fat pad
  • Hypertension
  • Proximal muscle weakness
  • Hyperglycemia, hypokalemia
  • Elevated cortisol (urine, salivary)
  • Decreased ACTH & DHEAS
  • No suppression by dexamethasone
Aldosterone-producing adenoma
  • Hypertension
  • Hypokalemia (muscle cramps, weakness)
  • Elevated plasma aldosterone-to-plasma renin activity ratio
Pheochromocytoma
  • Paroxysmal tachycardia, headache, tremor
  • Hypertension
  • Elevated urine metanephrines & catecholamines
  • Elevated plasma metanephrines
DHEAS = dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate.

Adrenal masses can be functional (ie, metabolically active) or nonfunctional.  Among functional tumors, cortisol-producing adenomas are the most common.  This patient has several signs of hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome), including hypertension, hyperglycemia, obesity, facial plethora, striae, and dorsocervical fat accumulation (buffalo hump).  In light of her CT scan findings, these clinical features are most likely due to a cortisol-producing adrenal adenoma.

A cortisol-producing adenoma causes elevated levels of cortisol in urine and (late-night) saliva.  Pituitary ACTH secretion is suppressed due to feedback inhibition.  Because adrenal production of dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) is ACTH dependent, low ACTH levels lead to low DHEAS levels.  Finally, as cortisol production by such tumors is autonomous (ACTH independent), cortisol levels are not suppressed following low-dose dexamethasone administration.

wrongAnswers.A: (Choice A)  ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome is characterized by an elevated (or inappropriately normal) ACTH level, cortisol production that is nonsuppressible following low-dose dexamethasone administration, and a high DHEAS level.  Most cases are due to pituitary ACTH secretion (eg, pituitary adenoma), which would be suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone administration; some cases are due to ectopic ACTH production (eg, ACTH-producing small cell lung cancer), which would not be suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone administration.
wrongAnswers.C: (Choice C)  A normal hormonal profile would be characterized by normal ACTH and DHEAS levels with suppressible cortisol following low-dose dexamethasone administration.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Elevated DHEAS levels with normal ACTH and cortisol profiles can be seen in patients with androgen-secreting tumors and certain subtypes of congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Dexamethasone-suppressible cortisol production with low ACTH and DHEAS occur in Cushing syndrome due to exogenous corticosteroid administration.

questions.explanation: Esophageal perforation Etiology Instrumentation (eg, endoscopy), trauma Effort rupture (Boerhaave syndrome) Esophagitis (infectious/drug-induced/caustic) Clinical presentation Chest/back &/or epigastric pain, systemic signs (eg, fever) Crepitus, Hamman sign (crunching sound on auscultation) Pleural effusion with atypical (eg, green) fluid Diagnosis X-ray or CT scan of chest: widened mediastinum, pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax, pleural effusion CT scan: esophageal wall thickening, mediastinal fluid collection Esophagography with water-soluble contrast: leak from perforation Management NPO, IV antibiotics & proton pump inhibitors Emergency surgical consultation IV = intravenous. This patient has chest pain, fever, and pneumomediastinum on chest x-ray, concerning for esophageal perforation (EP). EP is most commonly caused by instrumentation (eg, endoscopy) but can occur due to effort rupture (eg, protracted vomiting) or trauma, or in the setting of underlying esophagitis. This patient with a recent history of low-grade chest pain and epigastric burning likely had medication-induced esophagitis (from potassium chloride pills, which cause local tissue injury) that progressed to perforation. EP typically presents with severe pain (chest, back, and/or abdomen given the location of the esophagus) and a systemic inflammatory response (eg, fever, tachycardia) due to spillage of inflammatory gastrointestinal contents through the perforation. Efflux of esophageal air into the mediastinum (pneumomediastinum, widened mediastinum) may be visible on chest x-ray; some patients have a crunching sound heard in the precordium with each heartbeat (Hamman sign) or neck/precordial crepitus (subcutaneous emphysema). Esophagography or CT scan with water-soluble contrast can visualize the location of contrast leakage and confirm the diagnosis. Emergent surgical consultation is warranted because EP can quickly progress to mediastinitis, septic shock, and death. (Choice A) Acute-onset chest pain in a patient with cardiomyopathy is concerning for acute coronary syndrome. However, given this patient's lack of concerning ECG findings (eg, ST changes) and chest x-ray findings of a widened mediastinum/pneumomediastinum, EP is a more likely diagnosis. (Choice B) Omeprazole and antacids may be part of the treatment for reflux or esophagitis. However, in the setting of EP, all oral intake should be restricted and intravenous (not oral) medications administered. (Choice C) Transesophageal echocardiography can be used to evaluate some cases of aortic dissection, which can cause severe chest pain accompanied by a widened mediastinum. However, pneumomediastinum and fever make EP a more likely diagnosis. In addition, in patients with suspected EP, esophageal instrumentation (eg, transesophageal echocardiogram) should be avoided because it may worsen the perforation. (Choice D) Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy has a limited role in diagnosing EP because insufflation of air into the esophagus can exacerbate pneumomediastinum and instrumentation can worsen the esophageal injury. Educational objective: Esophageal perforation may occur due to underlying esophagitis (eg, medication-induced). Patients typically have severe chest pain and may have pneumomediastinum from leaked esophageal air. Confirmation with esophagography or CT scan using water-soluble contrast should prompt emergent surgical consultation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to severe, retrosternal chest pain that suddenly started a few hours ago. For the past few days, the patient had some mild chest pain and epigastric burning, but he says that the current pain is different. Other medical history includes nonischemic cardiomyopathy, for which he takes furosemide, carvedilol, spironolactone, lisinopril, and potassium chloride pills. Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F), blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 22/min. The patient is in obvious distress due to pain. Lungs are clear to auscultation. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Chest x-ray reveals a widened mediastinum and some mediastinal air. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: For relative risks (RR) and odds ratios (OR), values >1 indicate a positive association (eg, increased risk, higher odds) and values <1 indicate a negative association (eg, decreased risk, lower odds). Confidence intervals (CIs) containing the null value (= 1 in the case of RRs and ORs) indicate that the result is not statistically significant. For cigarette smoking, 0.81 indicates decreased risk of endometrial cancer among smokers; as the CI of 0.74-0.88 does not contain 1, the result is considered statistically significant. Multiple studies (including meta-analyses) have suggested that cigarette smoking is protective against endometrial cancer, possibly due to cigarette smoking-induced hepatic metabolism of estrogens. This clearly does not outweigh the risks of cigarette smoking. (Choice B) A RR = 2 indicates that the risk is twice as high (ie, 100% higher), not 20% as high. OR = 2 indicates odds being twice as high. (Choice C) Effect modification results when an external variable positively or negatively impacts the observed effect of a risk factor on disease status. For instance, aspirin use is associated with Reye syndrome in children but not adults; therefore, age modifies the effect of aspirin on Reye syndrome development. Stratification (eg, analyzing the data by age) can help detect effect modification. The risk calculations given alone do not provide enough information about effect modification. (Choice D) Caffeine consumption does not appear to be significantly associated with breast cancer as the CI of 0.84-1.22 contains the null value of 1. By contrast, caffeine consumption is associated with a statistically significant decreased risk of endometrial cancer with a CI of 0.48-0.86. It is difficult to draw additional comparisons between the risks of these 2 types of cancer among caffeine consumers based on the data provided. A lack of overlap in the CIs of similar parameters (eg, means in 2 populations) means that there is a statistically significant difference between these parameters; however, the converse is not necessarily true: if CIs of similar parameters overlap (eg, over the interval 0.84-0.86), there may or may not be a statistically significant difference between these parameters. (Choice E) Because the CI of 0.39-1.09 contains the null value of 1, the association between calcium/vitamin D supplementation and endometrial cancer is not statistically significant. Educational objective: For relative risks and odds ratios, values >1 indicate a positive association and values <1 indicate a negative association. Confidence intervals containing the null value indicate that the result is not statistically significant.

questions.explanation: Maternal thyroid testing in pregnancy, 1st trimester Hormone Change Mechanism Total T4 Increased hCG stimulates thyroid hormone production in 1st trimester Estrogen stimulates TBG; thyroid increases hormone production to maintain steady free T4 level Free T4 Unchanged or mildly increased TSH Decreased Increased hCG & thyroid hormone suppress TSH secretion TBG = thyroxine-binding globulin. Compared to prepregnancy, this patient has experienced a decrease in serum TSH and a concomitant increase in free T4 (but still within normal range). These findings represent physiologic changes of normal pregnancy. Pregnancy requires increased thyroid hormone production to meet metabolic demands. Alterations to thyroid hormone levels occur through 2 primary mechanisms: Estrogen stimulates the synthesis of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) and decreases TBG clearance, leading to higher circulating TBG levels and an increased pool of bound thyroid hormone. In patients with normal thyroid reserves, T4 production subsequently increases to maintain free hormone levels. hCG (which shares a common alpha subunit with TSH and a similar beta subunit) directly stimulates thyrotropin receptors on thyroid follicular cells, resulting in increased T4 production. TSH levels typically fall due to negative feedback of thyroid hormone on pituitary TSH release. In patients with normal thyroid function, the net effect can resemble subclinical hyperthyroidism with increased total T3 and T4, normal (or mildly elevated) free T4, and suppressed TSH, although the patient's state remains clinically euthyroid. In addition, high levels of hCG during pregnancy can lead to hyperemesis gravidarum (as in this patient), which can be associated with a transient hyperthyroid phase. (Choices A and D) Anti–thyroid peroxidase antibodies are associated with autoimmune thyroid disease, especially chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis. Iodine requirements increase during pregnancy, and iodine deficiency may lead to impaired thyroid hormone synthesis. These conditions typically present with primary hypothyroidism with low thyroid hormone levels and elevated TSH. (Choice B) In pregnancy, TBG levels are generally increased (due to estrogen) rather than decreased. (Choice E) TSH receptor–stimulating autoantibody is responsible for Graves disease, which is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in pregnant patients. However, Graves disease often improves during pregnancy due to immune modulation. In addition, this patient has no goiter or other signs of Graves disease. (Choice F) Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis typically follows a viral infection and is characterized by diffuse, tender enlargement of the thyroid gland and a transient hyperthyroid phase. Educational objective: Thyroid hormone production increases during pregnancy to cope with metabolic demands. Estrogen increases thyroxine-binding globulin, leading to increased total, but not free, thyroid hormone levels. hCG directly stimulates TSH receptors, causing increased production of thyroid hormones.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 11 weeks gestation comes to the office for follow-up due to severe nausea and vomiting with difficulty maintaining oral intake. The patient has regularly attended appointments at the antenatal clinic, and weight gain and blood pressure have been normal. She has no long-standing medical conditions, and the only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Her mother and maternal aunt have hypothyroidism; the patient had her thyroid function checked 6 months ago, prior to attempting to conceive. She has a 5-pack-year history but quit as soon as she found out that she was pregnant. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min, and respirations are 16/min. The thyroid gland is normal on palpation and is nontender. The rest of the physical examination is unremarkable. Thyroid function test results are as follows: 6 months ago Today TSH 2.5 μU/mL 0.2 μU/mL Free T4 1.1 ng/dL 1.7 ng/dL (normal in first trimester: 0.9-2.0) Which of the following is most likely responsible for the temporal change in this patient's laboratory findings?

questions.explanation: Paget disease of bone Clinical features Most patients are asymptomatic Bone pain & deformity Skull: headache, hearing loss Spine: spinal stenosis, radiculopathy Long bones: bowing, fracture, arthritis of adjacent joints Giant cell tumor, osteosarcoma Pathogenesis Osteoclast dysfunction Increased bone turnover Laboratory testing Elevated alkaline phosphatase Elevated bone turnover markers (eg, PINP, urine hydroxyproline) Calcium & phosphorus: usually normal Imaging X-ray: osteolytic or mixed lytic/sclerotic lesions Bone scan: focal increase in uptake Treatment Bisphosphonates PINP = procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide. Paget disease of bone is characterized by osteoclast dysfunction with increased bone turnover and disordered bone remodeling. It is most common after age 40 and can involve the axial skeleton and long bones of the lower extremities. Paget disease often presents as an asymptomatic elevation in alkaline phosphatase. However, it can cause symptoms due to focal enlargement, weakness, or fracture of bone. Bowing of long bones, bone pain, and arthritis in adjacent joints are common. Skull involvement may cause headaches, increased hat size, or cranial nerve palsies. Hearing loss may occur due to enlargement of the temporal bone and encroachment on the cochlea. Imaging findings include cortical thickening and osteolytic or mixed lytic/sclerotic lesions on x-ray or CT scan and focal uptake of radiotracer on bone scan. Symptomatic patients are treated with bisphosphonates (eg, alendronate). (Choice A) Periosteal reaction is excess mineralization of the periosteum in response to irritation. Common causes include osteomyelitis, benign or malignant tumors, and excess intake of vitamin A. (Choice B) Primary hyperparathyroidism can cause loss of cortical bone. Most patients have asymptomatic hypercalcemia, although bone pain, abdominal pain, or kidney stones may occur. Focal osteolytic lesions would not be seen. (Choice D) Fibrous dysplasia (bone portions replaced by fibrous connective tissue) primarily affects children. It is often asymptomatic and involves a single bone (monostotic). The polyostotic form (McCune-Albright syndrome) is commonly associated with precocious puberty and café-au-lait spots. (Choice E) Osteomalacia is characterized by defective mineralization of osteoid, most commonly due to vitamin D deficiency. Symptoms include fractures, bone pain, and muscle weakness. X-rays reveal diffuse (not focal) thinning of bone. (Choice F) Acromegaly can cause headaches and increased hat size. Increased bone turnover can occur, but focal osteolytic or sclerotic lesions are not seen. (Choice G) Multiple myeloma can cause lytic bone lesions or diffuse osteopenia due to osteoclastic activation. Most patients have systemic symptoms, and increased head size is not a feature. Educational objective: Paget disease of bone is characterized by osteoclast dysfunction with disordered bone remodeling. It is often asymptomatic, but can cause symptoms due to focal enlargement, weakness, or fracture of bone. X-rays reveal osteolytic or lytic/sclerotic lesions, and bone scan shows focal uptake. Treatment is with bisphosphonates.

Paget disease of bone is characterized by osteoclast dysfunction with increased bone turnover and disordered bone remodeling.  It is most common after age 40 and can involve the axial skeleton and long bones of the lower extremities.

Paget disease often presents as an asymptomatic elevation in alkaline phosphatase.  However, it can cause symptoms due to focal enlargement, weakness, or fracture of bone.  Bowing of long bones, bone pain, and arthritis in adjacent joints are common.  Skull involvement may cause headaches, increased hat size, or cranial nerve palsies.  Hearing loss may occur due to enlargement of the temporal bone and encroachment on the cochlea.  Imaging findings include cortical thickening and osteolytic or mixed lytic/sclerotic lesions on x-ray or CT scan and focal uptake of radiotracer on bone scan.  Symptomatic patients are treated with bisphosphonates (eg, alendronate).

wrongAnswers.A: (Choice A)  Periosteal reaction is excess mineralization of the periosteum in response to irritation.  Common causes include osteomyelitis, benign or malignant tumors, and excess intake of vitamin A.
wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  Primary hyperparathyroidism can cause loss of cortical bone.  Most patients have asymptomatic hypercalcemia, although bone pain, abdominal pain, or kidney stones may occur.  Focal osteolytic lesions would not be seen.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Fibrous dysplasia (bone portions replaced by fibrous connective tissue) primarily affects children.  It is often asymptomatic and involves a single bone (monostotic).  The polyostotic form (McCune-Albright syndrome) is commonly associated with precocious puberty and café-au-lait spots.
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Osteomalacia is characterized by defective mineralization of osteoid, most commonly due to vitamin D deficiency.  Symptoms include fractures, bone pain, and muscle weakness.  X-rays reveal diffuse (not focal) thinning of bone.
wrongAnswers.F: (Choice F)  Acromegaly can cause headaches and increased hat size.  Increased bone turnover can occur, but focal osteolytic or sclerotic lesions are not seen.
wrongAnswers.G: (Choice G)  Multiple myeloma can cause lytic bone lesions or diffuse osteopenia due to osteoclastic activation.  Most patients have systemic symptoms, and increased head size is not a feature.

questions.explanation: This patient's presentation - nausea, vomiting, and constant epigastric abdominal pain partially relieved by leaning forward - indicates acute pancreatitis. Activated pancreatic enzymes (eg, phospholipase, trypsin) and cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor) released from the inflamed pancreas into the circulation can lead to systemic inflammation. As a result, similar to sepsis, the most appropriate next step in management is aggressive volume resuscitation. Patients have significantly lower morbidity and mortality rates when appropriate volume replacement occurs in the first 48 hours as it helps to minimize hypotension, end-organ damage, acute tubular necrosis, and necrotizing pancreatitis. In addition to aggressive volume resuscitation, the initial management of acute pancreatitis involves pain management and close monitoring for complications (ie, infection, renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome). (Choice A) Antiplatelet agents are appropriate in a patient having a myocardial infarction. These patients can sometimes present atypically with nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain (especially an inferior myocardial infarction). However, fever and pain that improves while sitting up or leaning forward would not be typical. (Choice B) Patients with acute pancreatitis can be febrile and have a leukocytosis, so an infectious workup (eg, blood cultures, chest x-ray) should be considered; however, broad-spectrum antibiotics are generally not given empirically unless there is evidence of infected pancreatic necrosis (eg, on CT scan) or an extrapancreatic infection (eg, pneumonia). (Choice C) Patients with pancreatitis often have hypocalcemia, possibly due to calcium binding to free fatty acid complexes, calcium saponification, or cellular shifts. Hypocalcemia usually resolves with the management of pancreatitis and should be corrected only if it is severe (eg, low ionized calcium) or symptomatic (eg, Chvostek or Trousseau sign). Aggressive correction can actually worsen calcium saponification. (Choice D) A perforated viscus can cause severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and leukocytosis and may require an exploratory laparotomy; however, peritoneal signs (eg, involuntary guarding, rebound tenderness, rigidity) would be more typical. (Choice E) Patients with acute pancreatitis can develop severe hyperglycemia requiring an insulin infusion, but the initial management is aggressive volume resuscitation, which also helps to lower the blood glucose. (Choice G) A proton pump inhibitor would be appropriate in a patient with peptic ulcer disease, which would not usually cause fever, hemoconcentration (elevated leukocyte count and hematocrit), or hyperglycemia. Educational objective: Acute pancreatitis classically causes constant epigastric abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting. Patients initially require aggressive fluid rehydration, pain control, and close monitoring for any evidence of secondary complications (ie, infection, renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome).

questions.explanation: Clinical manifestations of hereditary hemochromatosis Skin Hyperpigmentation (bronze diabetes) Musculoskeletal Arthralgia, arthropathy & chondrocalcinosis Gastrointestinal Elevated hepatic enzymes with hepatomegaly (early), cirrhosis (later) & increased risk for hepatocellular carcinoma Endocrine Diabetes mellitus, secondary hypogonadism & hypothyroidism Cardiac Restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy & conduction abnormalities Infections Increased susceptibility to Listeria, Vibrio vulnificus & Yersinia enterocolitica This patient's fatigue, hypogonadism (eg, decreased sexual drive, erectile dysfunction), arthropathy, and hepatomegaly suggest hereditary hemochromatosis (HH). HH is an autosomal recessive disorder most commonly due to HFE gene mutations, which cause increased intestinal iron absorption and iron deposition in the tissues, resulting in multisystem end-organ damage. Most patients with HH are asymptomatic and diagnosed early in the disease by elevated liver enzymes on routine laboratory studies. Disease progression with further iron deposition can cause hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, arthropathy (associated with calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition disease), skin pigmentation, and hypogonadism (diminished libido, erectile dysfunction) in men (due to iron deposition in the pituitary). Iron deposition within the cardiac myocardium can also cause dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy, and conduction defects (eg, sick sinus syndrome) may occur due to deposition interfering with the conduction pathways. Only a small percentage of patients present with the classic triad of cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus with skin pigmentation ("bronze diabetes"), which is seen in later stages of the disease. Diagnosis can be confirmed in patients with evidence of iron overload by genetic analysis of HFE mutations. The mainstay of treatment is serial phlebotomy to deplete excess iron stores. (Choice A) Chronic alcoholism may lead to symptoms of fatigue and hepatomegaly, but hypogonadism develops as a consequence of cirrhosis. This patient's limited alcohol consumption and lack of other findings seen in cirrhosis (eg, ascites, splenomegaly) make cirrhosis unlikely. (Choices B and C) Both chronic fatigue syndrome and depression may present with fatigue and decreased libido. However, these would not explain the other abnormalities on physical examination (eg, hepatomegaly, arthritis). (Choice D) Hypothyroidism can cause fatigue and hypogonadism, but the lack of weight or appetite change and of bradycardia makes this less likely. Arthropathy is uncommon and hepatomegaly is quite rare in hypothyroidism. (Choice F) Primary biliary cholangitis (formerly primary biliary cirrhosis) commonly presents with fatigue and hepatomegaly; however, the absence of pruritus and icterus should suggest other diagnoses. Educational objective: Hereditary hemochromatosis causes abnormal iron deposition and commonly presents with fatigue, arthropathy, and hypogonadism. The classic triad of cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, and skin pigmentation is rare. Diagnosis can be confirmed by genetic analysis of HFE mutations.

questions.explanation: If the severity of a patient's condition leads to a provider's decision to choose a different treatment plan (eg, medical management versus early percutaneous intervention [PCI]), then results of studies comparing these treatment plans will be biased. This particular type of selection bias is called "susceptibility bias." In this example, patients who underwent early PCI were older (mean age of 69.5 versus 64.1 with a statistically significant P value [<0.05]) and, most importantly, were more likely to be on vasopressors on admission (15% versus 8% with a statistically significant P value), likely reflecting a more severe condition. It may be that patients who were sicker on admission were more likely to receive early PCI as compared to medical therapy; therefore, the worse outcomes that these patients experienced (1.6 times more likely to die in-hospital) may be due to (or at least confounded by) the severity of their condition on admission rather than the early PCI itself. In order to draw valid conclusions from the study results, differences between the 2 treatment groups in terms of baseline severity of illness must be taken into account. (Choice A) Ascertainment bias occurs when the results from an atypical population are extrapolated into the entire population. It is also a type of selection bias. These study results have not been extrapolated to the population. (Choice B) The Hawthorne effect refers to a change in behavior that occurs if study participants know they are being studied. (Choice C) Observer bias is a type of measurement bias in which the investigator unconsciously influences the outcome of the study by knowing the exposure status of each participant. (Choice D) Recall bias is an example of a measurement bias that results from a misclassification of exposure due to over- or under-reporting of the exposure by the study subjects. Educational objective: Patients in whom a treatment plan is selected based on the severity of their condition may have a worse outcome due to selection bias rather than due to the treatment itself.

questions.explanation: This patient has painless loss of peripheral vision associated with normal visual acuity. In an older adult, these findings are most consistent with chronic open-angle glaucoma (OAG). OAG is a type of optic neuropathy characterized by bilateral atrophy of the optic nerve head. It is more common with advancing age and is especially common in certain ethnicities (eg, African Americans). OAG is usually associated with elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) due to increased production or decreased outflow of aqueous humor. Diagnostic features of OAG include elevated IOP and decreased vision in the peripheral visual fields. Funduscopic examination reveals enlargement of the optic cup ("cupping") with an increased cup/disc ratio due to loss of ganglion cell axons. The goal of treatment in OAG is to decrease IOP with medications that either decrease the production of aqueous humor or increase its outflow. (Choice A) Signs of hypertensive retinopathy include arteriovenous nicking, arteriolar narrowing, and cotton-wool spots. Most patients are asymptomatic, although retinal hemorrhage can cause acute, painless monocular vision loss (not bilateral loss of peripheral vision). (Choice B) Cholesterol embolization to the retina from the carotid artery system or aortic arch can cause acute, transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax). These emboli can sometimes be seen as yellowish refractile plaques at arterial bifurcations (ie, Hollenhorst plaques). (Choice C) Central retinal artery occlusion is most commonly due to atherosclerosis, cardioembolic disease, or vasculitis (eg, giant cell arteritis) and presents as sudden monocular vision loss. Examination findings include retinal pallor with a cherry-red fovea. (Choice E) Diabetic retinopathy is seen in patients with poor glycemic control over a long period and manifests with vascular proliferation with or without vitreous hemorrhage. Symptoms are a late finding and may include floaters, decreased visual acuity, focal visual field defects, and acute monocular vision loss. Bilateral loss of peripheral vision is not typical and is more consistent with OAG. Educational objective: Chronic open-angle glaucoma is a type of optic neuropathy characterized by elevated intraocular pressure and atrophy of the optic nerve head. It presents with progressive loss of peripheral vision. Examination shows enlargement of the optic cup with an increased cup/disc ratio.

questions.explanation: Management of hypercalcemia Severe (calcium >14 mg/dL) or symptomatic Short-term (immediate) treatment Normal saline hydration plus calcitonin Avoid loop diuretics unless volume overload (heart failure) exists Long-term treatment Bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid) Moderate (calcium 12-14 mg/dL) Usually no immediate treatment required unless symptomatic Treatment is similar to that for severe hypercalcemia Asymptomatic or mild (calcium <12 mg/dL) No immediate treatment required Avoid thiazide diuretics, lithium, volume depletion & prolonged bed rest This patient has severe symptomatic hypercalcemia. Considering his smoking history and the mass in his lung, this likely represents humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy due to secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein. Severe hypercalcemia (serum calcium >14 mg/dL), especially with a rapid rise in serum calcium, can cause weakness, gastrointestinal distress, and neuropsychiatric symptoms (eg, confusion). Patients are typically volume-depleted due to polyuria (hypercalcemia-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) and decreased oral intake. Severe hypercalcemia requires aggressive hydration with normal (0.9%) saline to restore intravascular volume and promote urinary calcium excretion. By inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, calcitonin quickly reduces serum calcium and can be administered concurrently with saline. Bisphosphonates (eg, pamidronate, zoledronic acid) also inhibit bone resorption and provide a sustained reduction in calcium levels. However, the effect of bisphosphonates is delayed, usually occurring over 2-4 days, and they are typically given after initial hydration. (Choices B and E) Hypertonic saline is used in the treatment of acute, severe (ie, <120 mEq/L), symptomatic hyponatremia. Fluid restriction is used in hyponatremia due to the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) in euvolemic patients. However, this patient's tachycardia and dry mucous membranes suggest dehydration rather than SIADH, and his confusion is more likely due to severe hypercalcemia than to mild (ie, 130-135 mEq/L) hyponatremia. (Choice C) Hypotonic fluids are not as effective as isotonic fluids in restoring intravascular volume and can worsen hyponatremia. (Choice D) Glucocorticoids are effective for hypercalcemia due to extrarenal calcitriol production, which occurs in certain lymphomas and granulomatous diseases (eg, sarcoidosis). (Choice F) Loop diuretics are used to treat hypercalcemia with significant fluid overload (eg, congestive heart failure). They are otherwise not recommended as they can worsen volume depletion. This patient's mild edema is likely due to his calcium channel blocker, and his other clinical features suggest hypovolemia. (Choice G) This patient's potassium is within normal limits. (Choice H) Insulin increases cellular uptake of potassium (and glucose) and can be used for severe hyperkalemia. It does not have a significant effect on hypercalcemia, and this patient's mild hyperglycemia will likely improve with hydration. (Choice I) Infusion of bicarbonate is used in severe metabolic acidosis or hyperkalemia; this patient's bicarbonate and potassium levels are normal. Educational objective: Severe hypercalcemia can cause weakness, gastrointestinal distress, and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Patients are typically volume-depleted due to polyuria and decreased oral intake. Initial treatment includes saline hydration to restore intravascular volume and calcitonin to inhibit bone resorption. Bisphosphonates further reduce calcium levels and are given after initial hydration.

  • Avoid thiazide diuretics, lithium, volume depletion & prolonged bed rest

This patient has severe symptomatic hypercalcemia.  Considering his smoking history and the mass in his lung, this likely represents humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy due to secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein.  Severe hypercalcemia (serum calcium >14 mg/dL), especially with a rapid rise in serum calcium, can cause weakness, gastrointestinal distress, and neuropsychiatric symptoms (eg, confusion).  Patients are typically volume-depleted due to polyuria (hypercalcemia-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) and decreased oral intake.

Severe hypercalcemia requires aggressive hydration with normal (0.9%) saline to restore intravascular volume and promote urinary calcium excretion.  By inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, calcitonin quickly reduces serum calcium and can be administered concurrently with saline.  Bisphosphonates (eg, pamidronate, zoledronic acid) also inhibit bone resorption and provide a sustained reduction in calcium levels.  However, the effect of bisphosphonates is delayed, usually occurring over 2-4 days, and they are typically given after initial hydration.

wrongAnswers.B: (Choices B and E)  Hypertonic saline is used in the treatment of acute, severe (ie, <120 mEq/L), symptomatic hyponatremia.  Fluid restriction is used in hyponatremia due to the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) in euvolemic patients.  However, this patient's tachycardia and dry mucous membranes suggest dehydration rather than SIADH, and his confusion is more likely due to severe hypercalcemia than to mild (ie, 130-135 mEq/L) hyponatremia.
wrongAnswers.C: (Choice C)  Hypotonic fluids are not as effective as isotonic fluids in restoring intravascular volume and can worsen hyponatremia.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Glucocorticoids are effective for hypercalcemia due to extrarenal calcitriol production, which occurs in certain lymphomas and granulomatous diseases (eg, sarcoidosis).
wrongAnswers.E: See the shared discussion for choice B.
wrongAnswers.F: (Choice F)  Loop diuretics are used to treat hypercalcemia with significant fluid overload (eg, congestive heart failure).  They are otherwise not recommended as they can worsen volume depletion.  This patient's mild edema is likely due to his calcium channel blocker, and his other clinical features suggest hypovolemia.
wrongAnswers.G: (Choice G)  This patient's potassium is within normal limits.
wrongAnswers.H: (Choice H)  Insulin increases cellular uptake of potassium (and glucose) and can be used for severe hyperkalemia.  It does not have a significant effect on hypercalcemia, and this patient's mild hyperglycemia will likely improve with hydration.
wrongAnswers.I: (Choice I)  Infusion of bicarbonate is used in severe metabolic acidosis or hyperkalemia; this patient's bicarbonate and potassium levels are normal.

questions.explanation: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone Etiologies CNS disturbance (eg, stroke, hemorrhage, trauma) Medications (eg, carbamazepine, SSRIs, NSAIDs) Lung disease (eg, pneumonia) Ectopic ADH secretion (eg, small cell lung cancer) Pain &/or nausea Clinical features Mild/moderate hyponatremia: nausea, forgetfulness Severe hyponatremia: seizures, coma Euvolemia (eg, moist mucous membranes, no edema, no JVD) Laboratory findings Hyponatremia Serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg H2O (hypotonic) Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg H2O Urine sodium >40 mEq/L Management Fluid restriction ± salt tablets Hypertonic (3%) saline for severe hyponatremia ADH = antidiuretic hormone; JVD = jugular venous distension; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; SSRIs = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Carbamazepine is a frequent cause of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). It is thought to cause SIADH by sensitizing the kidneys to antidiuretic hormone, possibly through an increase in the number of vasopressin-2 receptors in the collecting tubules. SIADH leads to an inability of the kidneys to excrete adequately dilute urine to maintain normal blood tonicity. Hyponatremia due to SIADH is characterized by serum hypotonicity (<275 mOsm/kg H2O), inappropriately high urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/kg H2O), and euvolemia (eg, moist mucous membranes, absence of peripheral edema). The urine sodium concentration is typically high (>40 mEq/L) as the kidneys do not aggressively retain sodium in the setting of euvolemia. The risk of developing drug-induced SIADH is increased in elderly patients as well as patients on multiple medications associated with SIADH (eg, carbamazepine, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs). Patients who experience mild decreases in serum sodium or decreases that develop relatively slowly (over >48 hours) may be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms (eg, nausea, forgetfulness). More profound or rapid decreases in serum sodium may lead to severe symptoms (eg, seizures, coma) and can be fatal. (Choice A) Low serum osmolality with low urine osmolality occurs in primary polydipsia. The kidneys are able to excrete dilute urine but become overwhelmed by excess free water intake, resulting in hypotonic hyponatremia. Patients are euvolemic, so the kidneys are not aggressively retaining sodium (eg, urine sodium >40 mEq/L). (Choice C) Low serum osmolality and low urine sodium may occur in patients with hyponatremia due to hypovolemia as the kidneys attempt to retain sodium in an effort to increase blood volume. Urine is concentrated, increasing urine osmolality. Clinical evidence of hypovolemia (eg, dry mucous membranes, orthostasis) would be expected. (Choices D and E) High serum osmolality in the setting of hyponatremia may be due to the presence of osmotically active compounds other than sodium; examples include hyperglycemia and infusion of exogenous solute (eg, mannitol, radiocontrast). Urine electrolytes can be variable. Educational objective: The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is characterized by serum hypotonicity, inappropriately high urine osmolality, and high urine sodium concentration in a patient with euvolemia. Drug-induced SIADH can occur with a number of commonly used medications (eg, carbamazepine, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).

questions.explanation: Clinical features of subarachnoid hemorrhage Risk factors Hypertension Smoking, moderate to heavy alcohol use Family history Sympathomimetic drug use Clinical presentation Ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm (most common) Severe & sudden onset of headache different from previous pattern or described as "worst headache of my life" Nausea, vomiting, brief LOC, focal neurologic deficits, or meningismus Diagnosis Noncontrast CT scan of the head: performed initially due to high sensitivity early in SAH Lumbar puncture: required to exclude SAH definitively if CT scan is negative; xanthochromia confirms the diagnosis (~2 hr after onset) Cerebral angiography: used to identify bleeding source LOC = loss of consciousness; SAH = subarachnoid hemorrhage. Although this patient has a history of migraines, they typically present as severe, pulsatile, left-sided headaches with nausea and vomiting. In contrast, her current headache is different in character, raising concern for a serious intracranial process. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), which is typically due to a ruptured arterial berry (saccular) aneurysm, should be considered given that her headache: quickly (eg, within seconds) became unbearable (described by some as "the worst headache of my life") is generalized (unlike her left-sided migraines) and associated with neurologic symptoms (eg, blurry vision) began while she was running (possible aneurysm rupture with exertion) Patients with symptoms concerning for SAH should undergo urgent noncontrast CT scan of the head, which may show blood in the basal cistern and cerebral sulci from the ruptured aneurysm. If the noncontrast CT scan is negative and high suspicion for SAH remains, lumbar puncture should be performed (Choice E). With SAH, lumbar puncture shows an elevated opening pressure with cerebrospinal fluid xanthochromia (yellow or pink discoloration due to hemoglobin breakdown) and continued high levels of red blood cells from the first collection tube to the fourth. (Choice A) Administration of 100% oxygen by face mask is the acute treatment for cluster headaches, which are short attacks of unilateral, severe orbital and temporal pain. Patients typically have associated autonomic findings (eg, ptosis, miosis) on the same side as the pain, features not present in this patient. (Choice B) Sumatriptan and metoclopramide are used to treat migraine headaches; these medications, especially when administered together, may be beneficial to this patient if SAH is ruled out. However, she has several concerning findings that require further urgent evaluation prior to administration of medications for migraine. (Choice C) CT angiography of the neck should be performed when there is concern for a dissection or narrowing of the major vessels of the neck (eg, carotids) that could cause a stroke. This study focuses on the vasculature of the neck rather than that of the head and therefore would not help elucidate whether the patient has SAH. Educational objective: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) typically presents with sudden-onset, severe headache that is different from the patient's prior headaches. Noncontrast CT scan of the head should be obtained urgently; if the scan result is negative and there is still a high suspicion for SAH, lumbar puncture should be performed.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to a severe headache. Medical history includes migraine headaches; they typically present acutely with severe pulsatile pain on the left side of her head accompanied by nausea and vomiting. The patient had been treated in the emergency department for migraines twice before but did not require migraine prophylaxis. Earlier this afternoon, she was running in the park when she experienced a severe, sudden-onset, generalized headache that became unbearable in seconds. Her vision became blurry, which caused her to stumble and almost fall. The patient continues to have a severe headache and feels nauseated. Blood pressure is 148/86 mm Hg and pulse is 94/min and regular. Pupils are symmetric and reactive. Funduscopic examination is unremarkable. Deep tendon reflexes and sensation are normal and bilaterally symmetric. Plantar reflexes are bilaterally flexor. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Rett syndrome Pathophysiology & epidemiology Rare, progressive neurologic disorder MECP2 mutation on X chromosome Affects mostly girls Development Normal development until age 6-18 months followed by regression: Loss of speech Loss of purposeful hand use (stereotypical hand movements [eg, wringing] common) Other neurologic findings Head growth deceleration Seizures Autistic features Gait abnormalities Sleep disturbances Breathing abnormalities Diagnosis DNA analysis for MECP2 mutation This patient's presentation is most suggestive of Rett syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder that occurs almost exclusively in females. Affected individuals typically have normal development for the first few months. Subsequently, at age 12-18 months, loss of communicative and fine motor skills follows and may be sudden or slow in onset. In addition to stereotypical hand movements (eg, hand rubbing, clapping), sleep disturbances (eg, waking up screaming), and autistic features (eg, lack of eye contact and social reciprocity), other characteristics of Rett syndrome include gait disturbance, deceleration in head growth, seizures, and breathing abnormalities. Diagnostic evaluation for suspected Rett syndrome should include MECP2 gene analysis because most cases are caused by de novo mutations in the MECP2 gene, located on the X chromosome. The mutations are virtually always on paternal genes. Females are almost exclusively affected. A diagnosis is made if an MECP2 mutation is found in a patient with characteristic clinical features. (Choice A) FMR1 DNA analysis is indicated when fragile X syndrome (FXS) is suspected. FXS is more common in males, and diagnosis is based on detection of an alteration in the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) gene. Clinical features include intellectual disability; a long, narrow face; large, protruding ears; macrocephaly; and macroorchidism. (Choice C) Not pursuing further testing would be inappropriate because this patient has characteristic signs of Rett syndrome in addition to autistic features. It is especially important to pursue genetic testing in patients with developmental regression or dysmorphic features because these patients are more likely to have a genetic abnormality. (Choice D) Serum hexosaminidase A levels are indicated in suspected cases of Tay-Sachs disease, a neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disease predominantly found in the Ashkenazi Jewish population. Development is generally normal until age 6 months. Findings include macrocephaly and a characteristic cherry-red spot on the macula. (Choice E) Elevated serum concentrations of phenylalanine are found in classic phenylketonuria (PKU), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. PKU affects both sexes and may present with intellectual disability, musty odor, seizures, skin diseases, and microcephaly. Educational objective: Rett syndrome is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder that mostly affects females. Key features include loss of speech, stereotypical hand movements, and gait abnormalities after a period of normal development. Autistic features are common. Most cases are caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene.

questions.explanation: 22q11.2 deletion syndromes Phenotypes DiGeorge syndrome, velocardiofacial syndrome* Pathogenesis Loss of genes that control embryonic tissue template transformation (eg, pharyngeal apparatus, secondary heart field) & migration of neural crest cells Clinical features (CATCH) Cardiac outflow tract anomalies (eg, tetralogy of Fallot, persistent truncus arteriosus) Anomalous face (eg, prominent nasal bridge, low-set ears, micrognathia/retrognathia) Thymic hypoplasia/aplasia → decreased T-cell immunity Cleft palate Hypoparathyroidism (hypoplastic/aplastic parathyroids) → hypocalcemia *DiGeorge syndrome requires thymic involvement (CD3+ T-cell count <500/mm3); velocardiofacial syndrome requires facial abnormalities. DiGeorge syndrome is a genetic disorder due to a deletion in chromosome 22q11, resulting in abnormal development of the pharyngeal pouches. Facial deformities such as cleft lip and palate are common. Patients often have conotruncal defects, resulting in cardiac murmurs. The recurrent muscle spasms and generalized tonic-clonic seizures are most likely due to hypocalcemia, which occurs commonly in DiGeorge syndrome due to abnormal development of the parathyroid glands. Immune function is frequently abnormal in patients with DiGeorge syndrome. The thymus, which develops from the pharyngeal pouches, is hypoplastic to absent. This results in the abnormal production and development of T cells, leading to cellular immune deficiency and increased risk of viral and fungal infections. The B-cell count is usually normal, but humoral immunodeficiency (ie, increased susceptibility to bacterial infection) can result from defective T-cell help in B-cell activation for antibody production. Therefore, all patients with DiGeorge syndrome should receive routine killed or subcomponent vaccines. The safety of live vaccines (eg, rotavirus, measles-mumps-rubella) for these patients depends on the degree of immunodeficiency. (Choice B) Complement deficiency may occur as an isolated inherited immunodeficiency or in association with certain autoimmune disorders (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus). It is not associated with specific disorders of chromosomal deletion such as DiGeorge syndrome. (Choice C) Hypogammaglobulinemia is associated with disorders such as Bruton agammaglobulinemia and severe combined immunodeficiency. The B-cell count is generally normal in DiGeorge syndrome, although function may be abnormal. (Choice D) Neutrophils arise from the bone marrow rather than the pharyngeal pouches, so phagocyte dysfunction is not seen in DiGeorge syndrome. Phagocyte dysfunction may be encountered in disorders such as leukocyte adhesion deficiency and chronic granulomatous disease. (Choice E) Splenic dysfunction is not characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome. Hyposplenism may develop in disorders such as sickle cell anemia and autoimmune disease. Educational objective: DiGeorge syndrome is due to a deletion in chromosome 22q11, which leads to abnormal development of the pharyngeal pouches. Common findings include facial abnormalities such as cleft lip and palate, hypocalcemia due to abnormal development of the parathyroid glands, cardiac anomalies, and impaired cellular immunity due to abnormal thymic development with abnormal production and development of T cells.

Educational objective:
DiGeorge syndrome is due to a deletion in chromosome 22q11, which leads to abnormal development of the pharyngeal pouches.  Common findings include facial abnormalities such as cleft lip and palate, hypocalcemia due to abnormal development of the parathyroid glands, cardiac anomalies, and impaired cellular immunity due to abnormal thymic development with abnormal production and development of T cells.
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
22q11.2 deletion syndromes
Phenotypes
  • DiGeorge syndrome, velocardiofacial syndrome*
Pathogenesis
  • Loss of genes that control embryonic tissue template transformation (eg, pharyngeal apparatus, secondary heart field) & migration of neural crest cells
Clinical features (CATCH)
  • Cardiac outflow tract anomalies (eg, tetralogy of Fallot, persistent truncus arteriosus)
  • Anomalous face (eg, prominent nasal bridge, low-set ears, micrognathia/retrognathia)
  • Thymic hypoplasia/aplasia → decreased T-cell immunity
  • Cleft palate
  • Hypoparathyroidism (hypoplastic/aplastic parathyroids) → hypocalcemia
*DiGeorge syndrome requires thymic involvement (CD3+ T-cell count <500/mm3); velocardiofacial syndrome requires facial abnormalities.

DiGeorge syndrome is a genetic disorder due to a deletion in chromosome 22q11, resulting in abnormal development of the pharyngeal pouches.  Facial deformities such as cleft lip and palate are common.  Patients often have conotruncal defects, resulting in cardiac murmurs.  The recurrent muscle spasms and generalized tonic-clonic seizures are most likely due to hypocalcemia, which occurs commonly in DiGeorge syndrome due to abnormal development of the parathyroid glands.

Immune function is frequently abnormal in patients with DiGeorge syndrome.  The thymus, which develops from the pharyngeal pouches, is hypoplastic to absent.  This results in the abnormal production and development of T cells, leading to cellular immune deficiency and increased risk of viral and fungal infections.  The B-cell count is usually normal, but humoral immunodeficiency (ie, increased susceptibility to bacterial infection) can result from defective T-cell help in B-cell activation for antibody production.  Therefore, all patients with DiGeorge syndrome should receive routine killed or subcomponent vaccines.  The safety of live vaccines (eg, rotavirus, measles-mumps-rubella) for these patients depends on the degree of immunodeficiency.

wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  Complement deficiency may occur as an isolated inherited immunodeficiency or in association with certain autoimmune disorders (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus).  It is not associated with specific disorders of chromosomal deletion such as DiGeorge syndrome.
wrongAnswers.C: (Choice C)  Hypogammaglobulinemia is associated with disorders such as Bruton agammaglobulinemia and severe combined immunodeficiency.  The B-cell count is generally normal in DiGeorge syndrome, although function may be abnormal.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Neutrophils arise from the bone marrow rather than the pharyngeal pouches, so phagocyte dysfunction is not seen in DiGeorge syndrome.  Phagocyte dysfunction may be encountered in disorders such as leukocyte adhesion deficiency and chronic granulomatous disease.
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Splenic dysfunction is not characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome.  Hyposplenism may develop in disorders such as sickle cell anemia and autoimmune disease.

questions.stem: A 14-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department after an episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He has had no fever, runny nose, cough, or emesis but has had extremity muscle spasms. The patient was born at full term after a normal pregnancy and delivery. A cleft palate was identified at birth, and the family was advised to follow up with a specialist after discharge. Physical examination today demonstrates a jittery neonate with jerking of the extremities. The anterior fontanelle is open and flat. Pupils are equal and reactive; the fundi are normal. The ears are low set, but the tympanic membranes are clear. The lower jaw is small and a cleft palate is present; there is no erythema of the pharynx. Cardiac auscultation reveals a harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, which was not present at birth. The lungs fields are clear to auscultation. The abdomen is soft with no organomegaly. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?

questions.explanation: This patient has multiple risk factors for a deep venous thrombosis (DVT), including pregnancy (a hypercoagulable state due to elevated endogenous hormones and increased stasis of blood in the lower extremities from pressure on the inferior vena cava) and sickle cell trait (2- to 4-fold increased incidence of DVT). Heparin is the anticoagulant of choice for pregnant patients due to its safety profile. Daily low molecular weight heparin injections are used for long-term therapy. So-called vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin (inhibits coagulation factor carboxylation) are not used because they are teratogenic between 6 to 12 weeks and can cause fetal bleeding through placental transfer at any stage of pregnancy (Choice G). Treatment of DVT during pregnancy is continued for at least 3 months (throughout the remainder of the pregnancy and the first few weeks postpartum). Before stopping treatment, repeat duplex ultrasound should be performed to assess if the thrombus remains as this would extend treatment length. (Choice A) Compression stockings would be appropriate if the patient only had edema and not a DVT. (Choice B) Exchange blood transfusions are used in sickle cell crisis for patients with acute chest syndrome. Patients with sickle cell trait are typically unaffected carriers. (Choice C) An inferior vena cava filter can be considered when there is a high risk for bleeding from anticoagulation (eg, recent surgery, hemorrhage). Temporary filters are sometimes difficult to retrieve due to filter tilt. In the absence of contraindications to anticoagulation, heparin is recommended. (Choice D) Low-dose aspirin has no role in the treatment of acute DVT as it is a platelet inhibitor and does not work on the coagulation cascade. (Choice F) Thrombolysis is reserved for situations in which there is a large burden of thrombus (eg, phlegmasia cerulea dolens) and/or hemodynamic compromise. There is a risk of maternal bleeding and fetal loss. Educational objective: Pregnancy increases the risk of deep venous thrombosis (DVT) due to hypercoagulability and blood stasis in the lower extremities. If there are no bleeding concerns, the treatment of choice for DVT in pregnant patients is either unfractionated heparin or low molecular weight heparin. Warfarin is teratogenic and generally avoided unless absolutely necessary.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida at 26 weeks gestation comes to the office due to right leg pain. Her pregnancy was complicated by nausea and vomiting in the first trimester but has otherwise been normal. Medical history is significant for sickle cell trait. The patient takes daily prenatal multivitamins. She does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. An older sister who had sickle cell anemia died of a severe pulmonary infection at age 34. Blood pressure is 135/80 mm Hg and pulse is 100/min. Chest examination is unremarkable. There is swelling and tenderness of her right ankle and calf. The patient's hemoglobin level is 10.5 g/dL and platelet count is 190,000/mm3. Duplex ultrasound shows non-compressible right popliteal and distal femoral veins. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
