questions.explanation: Uric acid kidney stones Risk factors Low urine pH: chronic diarrhea (GI bicarbonate loss), metabolic syndrome/ diabetes mellitus Increased uric acid excretion: gout, myeloproliferative disorders Increased urine concentration: hot, arid climates; dehydration Pathophysiology Acidic urine favors formation of uric acid (insoluble) over urate (soluble) Supersaturation of urine with uric acid precipitates crystal formation Clinical characteristics Radiolucent stones (not visible on x-ray) Uric acid crystals on urine microscopy (diamond/rhomboid shaped) Urine pH usually <5.5 Treatment Alkalinization of urine (eg, potassium citrate) Reduction of uric acid production (eg, low-purine diet, allopurinol) GI = gastrointestinal. This patient has uric acid stones, a relatively uncommon cause of nephrolithiasis that accounts for about 5%-10% of cases. Acidic urine pH, increased urine concentration, and elevated urine uric acid level are factors that promote formation of uric acid stones. This patient has chronic diarrhea, which leads to gastrointestinal (GI) losses of bicarbonate and water with resultant acidic, hyperconcentrated urine. Dehydration (due to working in a hot environment) may have further exacerbated the condition. The solubility of uric acid declines as urine becomes more acidic (especially with urine pH <5.5). Therefore, management of uric acid stones involves urine alkalinization (to goal pH of 6-7) with potassium bicarbonate or potassium citrate; these medications can both promote dissolution of existing stones and prevent precipitation of new stones. (Choice B) Urinary tract infection, particularly due to urease-producing bacteria (eg, Proteus), is associated with formation of magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) kidney stones (not uric acid stones). These stones are usually large and irregular and often fill the renal pelvis. (Choice C) Decreased urine-concentrating ability leads to excretion of a large amount of dilute urine. However, uric acid stones are more likely to form when the urine is overly concentrated. (Choice D) Uric acid is produced when purines are degraded; it is not absorbed through the GI tract. For patients predisposed to uric acid stones, a diet that avoids high-purine foods (eg, red meat, seafood, alcohol) may be recommended. Intestinal oxalate (vs uric acid) absorption can be increased in patients with small bowel resection (eg, Crohn disease) or gastric bypass surgery, leading to calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis. (Choice E) A diet that is low in salt (which promotes urinary sodium and calcium reabsorption) and high in calcium (which decreases GI absorption of oxalate) can actually decrease the risk of calcium oxalate stone development but has little effect on uric acid stone development. Educational objective: Chronic diarrhea can cause urine to be hyperconcentrated and abnormally acidic due to ongoing gastrointestinal bicarbonate and water losses. Such urine predisposes to uric acid kidney stone formation. Urine alkalinization increases solubility of uric acid, helping to both dissolve existing stones and prevent precipitation of new stones.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to sudden-onset flank pain and hematuria. She came to the emergency department with similar symptoms 6 months ago. Medical history is significant for ulcerative colitis for which she underwent partial colon resection. The patient has 3 or 4 loose stools daily. She has had 2 urinary tract infections in her lifetime. There is no family history of kidney stones or kidney disease. The patient is a cook at a local restaurant and spends a lot of time near the grill. Blood pressure is 110/71 mm Hg and pulse is 75/min. Physical examination is unremarkable. Abdominal imaging reveals 2 ureteral stones, which subsequently pass with conservative management. Stone analysis is consistent with pure uric acid stones. Which of the following factors most strongly predisposed this patient to develop kidney stones?

questions.explanation: Pediatric septic arthritis Pathogenesis Age <3 months: Staphylococcus aureus, group B Streptococcus, gram-negative bacilli Age ≥3 months: Staphylococcus aureus, group A Streptococcus Clinical features Acute-onset joint pain, swelling, limited motion Refusal to bear weight Fever ≥38.5 C (101.3 F) Diagnosis ↑ WBC, ESR, CRP Blood culture Joint aspiration (synovial WBC count of >50,000/mm3) Effusion on ultrasonography/MRI Treatment Joint drainage & debridement Intravenous antibiotics CRP = C-reactive protein; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; WBC = white blood cell. This patient has fever, refusal to bear weight, leukocytosis, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate consistent with septic arthritis of the hip. Children prefer to keep the affected hip externally rotated because of painful pus accumulation in the joint space. Septic arthritis can follow an upper respiratory tract or skin infection in which there may be intermittent bacteremia, allowing for hematogenous spread of bacteria into the joint space. The most common offending organisms in children are Staphylococcus aureus and group A streptococci. Immediate evaluation and treatment are required because delays can result in permanent joint destruction. An interval of even 4-6 hours can lead to avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Because bacteremia is the most common cause of joint infection, blood cultures should be obtained. Arthrocentesis shows purulent synovial fluid with >50,000/mm3 leukocytes. Prompt surgical drainage is necessary to decompress the joint space and remove inflammatory debris. Empiric intravenous antibiotics should be administered immediately after cultures of the synovial fluid and blood have been obtained. (Choice A) Slipped capital femoral epiphysis typically causes insidious hip pain and limp in obese adolescents, not acute symptoms in toddlers, as in this patient. (Choice B) Developmental dysplasia of the hip (dysplastic development of the acetabulum and femur) is a chronic condition that may present with limp (Trendelenburg gait) in a child learning to walk. These patients do not have acute fever, pain, and refusal to walk. (Choice D) Idiopathic osteonecrosis of the femoral head describes Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, which presents with gradual onset of hip pain and limp. Infection is more likely in this patient with acute fever. (Choice E) Transient synovitis is a common, mild, self-limiting hip disorder that often follows a viral infection. High fever, leukocytosis, and elevated inflammatory markers can help distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis. Educational objective: Septic arthritis in children typically presents with fever, refusal to bear weight, leukocytosis, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. It usually results from hematogenous spread of bacteria into the joint space.

questions.stem: A 15-month-old boy is brought to the clinic because he has been refusing to walk. When the patient woke up this morning, he did not want to get out of bed. He has been asking his mother to carry him and cries when he attempts to move his right leg. A week ago, he had a low-grade fever and rhinorrhea, but the symptoms spontaneously resolved after 2 days. The patient was born via cesarean delivery for breech presentation and has no chronic medical conditions. Temperature is 39.2 C (102.6 F), blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg, pulse is 118/min, and respirations are 18/min. The patient appears anxious. The right hip is abducted and externally rotated. The patient cries with any movement of the right hip and refuses to stand or walk. Skin examination reveals no erythema or rashes. Laboratory studies reveal a leukocyte count of 19,800/mm3 and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 55 mm/hr. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for this patient's condition?

questions.explanation: Error disclosure to patients Describe the error "Unfortunately, the biopsy sample was lost, and a repeat procedure is necessary." Explain why the error occurred "The laboratory never received the sample, possibly due to a tracking or staffing error." Express regret or apologize for error "I apologize on behalf of our team." Describe steps to minimize consequences "We will waive all charges associated with the repeat procedure." Outline actions to prevent future recurrences "I will notify our administrators now of this error, and we will change our procedure so this does not happen again." This incident is a preventable medical error that could have caused serious harm to the patient if the guidewire had travelled up the inferior vena cava and into the pulmonary vasculature. The code of ethics of many professional associations, including the American Medical Association, requires that physicians inform patients and families of medical errors. Full disclosure is recommended, regardless of whether or not the patient suffers any harm. Patients should be fully informed of the facts and any unanticipated outcomes. Physicians should not wait for the error to be discovered by the patient, family, or other physicians. Several barriers prevent physicians from disclosing medical errors, such as lack of training in disclosure or fear of a malpractice claim, losing patients' trust, or damage to professional reputation. However, disclosure of an error also has significant potential benefits, including: Maintaining ethical and moral standards of professionalism Facilitating continued care for the patient Regaining trust of the patient and the patient's family Prevention of lawsuits (disclosure also establishes the physician as credible and sincere, which may aid in the defense of a suit) (Choice B) This statement acknowledges the difficulty inherent in medicine, but does not clearly reveal that an error occurred. No details were provided as to what the error was and how it happened. (Choice C) This statement involves using medical jargon that is not readily understood by a lay person. Physicians should use simple non-medical terms to disclose medical error details. (Choice D) This statement does not recognize that an error occurred and does not allow the physician to assume responsibility for it or apologize for any potential harm it may have caused. (Choice E) This statement is not truthful. Interventional radiology was consulted to remove the guidewire as a result of the error, not simply because of their expertise with catheter placement. Physicians should not distort facts and should be precise when disclosing a medical error. Educational objective: Physicians should disclose medical errors completely and promptly. A sincere apology by the physician helps to facilitate continued care, regain patient trust, and minimize the risk of lawsuits. Assuring efforts to prevent recurrence of an error can satisfy patient expectations.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is intubated in the emergency department due to pulmonary edema resulting from acute kidney injury. He requires urgent hemodialysis to remove excess fluid. Before placing the dialysis catheter, the physician calls the patient's wife to obtain verbal consent and explain the risks and benefits of the procedure. After inserting the catheter into the right femoral vein, the physician realizes that the metal wire to guide catheter placement is missing. Bedside x-ray reveals that the entire length of the guidewire is in the lumen of the femoral vein. The physician then consults interventional radiology to have the guidewire removed. After this is done, dialysis is initiated and the patient is soon extubated. The medical team meets with the patient the next day. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement to the patient?

This patient's clinical presentation is consistent with acute limb ischemia, most likely due to embolization of a mural thrombus formed within a left ventricular (LV) aneurysm. (Choice A) Aortic dissection presents with sudden-onset, severe chest pain with radiation to the back, usually in the setting of severe hypertension. Dissection involving the descending aorta can lead to lower extremity ischemia, but this patient's recent MI and ECG abnormalities suggest arterial embolus from LV thrombus. It is a life-threatening complication and causes acute, severe mitral regurgitation, leading to hypotension and pulmonary edema. questions.stem: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to sudden-onset, severe pain in the right leg that began 5 hours ago. He also states that the leg feels numb. The patient has had no chest pain, shortness of breath, syncope, cough, or lower extremity edema. Two months ago, he was hospitalized with anterior wall myocardial infarction but was not revascularized due to late presentation. The patient was discharged home with aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. He quit smoking last year but previously smoked a pack of cigarettes per day for 40 years. Temperature is 36.6 C (97.9 F), blood pressure is 110/67 mm Hg, and pulse is 87/min and regular. Lungs are clear to auscultation. The apical impulse is displaced to the left. There is a 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex with radiation to the axilla. The right leg is cold to the touch. There is a palpable femoral pulse but no popliteal, posterior tibial, or dorsalis pedis pulses palpable on the right. The pulses on the left are full. ECG reveals normal sinus rhythm and deep Q waves in leads I, aVL, and V2-V5 with 4-mm ST-segment elevation, which is unchanged from readings at discharge 2 months ago. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

questions.explanation: Borderline personality disorder Key features Pervasive pattern of unstable mood, relationships & self-image Frantic efforts to avoid abandonment Recurrent suicidal behaviors or threats of self-mutilation (eg, cutting) Impulsivity in ≥2 areas that are potentially self-damaging (eg, substance abuse, sex) Chronic feelings of emptiness; intense, inappropriate anger Transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation Differential diagnosis Bipolar disorder (distinct hypo/manic & major depressive episodes of longer duration) Major depressive disorder (sustained depression ≥2 weeks, marked neurovegetative symptoms) Other personality disorders: Histrionic (attention seeking but less intense anger, no self-destructive behavior) Narcissistic (grandiose self-image, less impulsive/self-destructive) Paranoid (more pervasive suspiciousness, stable self-image) Treatment Primary treatment is psychotherapy (best evidence for dialectical behavior therapy) Adjunctive pharmacotherapy to target mood instability & transient psychosis (second-generation antipsychotics, mood stabilizers) Antidepressants if comorbid mood or anxiety disorder This patient's pattern of unstable mood, inappropriate and intense anger, and frantic efforts to avoid abandonment are suggestive of borderline personality disorder (BPD). As seen in this patient, recurrent suicidal threats/history of multiple suicide attempts and feelings of numbness or emptiness are other key features of the disorder. Psychotherapy, not pharmacotherapy, is the first-line treatment for BPD. Dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) is a type of cognitive behavioral psychotherapy specifically developed to treat BPD that emphasizes management of self-injurious behaviors. Strategies include skills training to target impulses to self-harm and mindfulness to target emotional dysregulation. Medications are used adjunctively to target specific symptom clusters associated with BPD but are not typically part of the initial treatment because they do not address the core borderline pathology. Second-generation antipsychotics (eg, aripiprazole) and mood stabilizers (eg, lithium) target mood instability, inappropriate anger, dysphoria, impulsivity, aggression, and transient paranoid psychosis (Choices A and E). Antidepressants (eg, citalopram, venlafaxine) are generally reserved for patients with persistent comorbid depression or anxiety but is not currently indicated in this patient who does not have persistent symptoms (started a few days ago) and who did not have a response to a prior trial of fluoxetine (Choices B and F). (Choice D) Interpersonal psychotherapy focuses on the role of current relationships and adverse life events in depression. It is indicated for mild to moderate depression, not BPD. Educational objective: Psychotherapy (eg, dialectical behavioral therapy) is the first-line treatment for borderline personality disorder. Psychotropic medications are used as adjuncts to psychotherapy to target specific symptom clusters.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is brought to the office by her daughter for evaluation of irritability. The daughter moved out of her mother's house a few days ago to live with her boyfriend and says, "She's been calling me constantly. If I don't pick up, she'll leave an angry voicemail or send me texts about how I don't love her anymore. She did the same thing when I left home for college a few years ago." The daughter was hesitant to move out and fears that her mother "might do something she regrets" now that she's living alone. The patient has a history of 3 suicide attempts. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no medications. A past trial of fluoxetine prescribed for mood symptoms was ineffective. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, the patient appears dysthymic and says, "I couldn't cry or yell even if I wanted to. I'm just completely numb." Which of the following is the best initial treatment for this patient?

questions.explanation: Brief psychotic disorder Key features Acute onset, typically associated with severe stressor Psychotic symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior Duration: ≥1 days & ≤1 month Full return to premorbid functioning Differential diagnosis Mood disorders with psychotic features Substance-induced psychotic disorder Psychosis due to general medical conditions Other psychotic disorders: Delusional disorder (≥1 months of delusions, no other psychotic symptoms) Schizophreniform disorder (≥1 months & <6 months) Schizophrenia (≥6 months, functional decline) Management Hospitalization if safety issue &/or inability to care for self Supportive care Low-dose antipsychotic if necessary; discontinue once remitted This patient's sudden onset of psychotic symptoms (ie, paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations) of short duration is consistent with brief psychotic disorder. Brief psychotic disorder typically occurs abruptly, often in response to an extreme life stressor, as seen in this patient. Psychotic symptoms last ≥1 days and ≤1 month, with rapid return to normal functioning. Diagnosis requires ruling out psychotic disorders due to medical conditions, substances, and other psychiatric disorders. Although brief hospitalization may be necessary, symptoms typically resolve rapidly, often without antipsychotic medication. (Choice A) Acute stress disorder is characterized by intrusive reexperiencing (eg, nightmares, flashbacks) of a traumatic event, accompanied by symptoms of hyperarousal, dissociation, and avoidance. It is not characterized by psychotic symptoms. (Choice B) Although this patient's symptoms occurred in response to an identifiable stressor, adjustment disorder would not explain psychotic symptoms. It should not be diagnosed when criteria are met for a more specific disorder, such as brief psychotic disorder in this patient. (Choice C) A manic or depressive episode of bipolar disorder may include psychotic features; however, this patient does not have concurrent mood symptoms of sufficient duration (ie, 2 weeks for a major depressive episode, 1 week for a manic episode) to make this diagnosis. (Choice D) Although patients with borderline personality disorder may experience transient stress-related psychoses, there is no evidence suggesting other features of this disorder (eg, long-standing pattern of identity disturbance, mood lability, recurrent suicidal and self-mutilating behavior, abandonment fears). Personality disorders involve long-standing patterns of maladaptive behavior and would not explain this patient's acute onset and rapid return to functioning. (Choice F) Delusional disorder is characterized by persistent delusions lasting ≥1 months and no other prominent psychotic symptoms. The shorter duration and presence of auditory hallucinations in this patient rule out this disorder. Educational objective: Brief psychotic disorder is characterized by a sudden onset of psychotic symptoms lasting ≥1 days and ≤1 month, typically in response to a severe stressor. It is associated with a full return to the previous level of functioning.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the office for evaluation of anxiety symptoms. The patient's boyfriend of 3 years broke up with her a week ago. The night of the break-up, she could not fall asleep, so she watched television. While flipping through the channels, she came across horror movies only and became frightened that her ex was "trying to send a message." The patient unplugged the television and disconnected all the electronics. She stayed up the rest of the night, pacing in the living room and monitoring the front door. The patient remained awake the next day and, at times, heard her ex whispering that she is "worthless" and "horrible." That night, the patient regularly looked out the window to check if her ex's car was parked on the street. She eventually fell asleep early in the morning and woke up feeling less anxious. She returned to work that day and resumed her regular activities. The patient drinks alcohol occasionally and does not use illicit drugs. Medical history is unremarkable. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. The patient is fully oriented, and her thoughts are organized. She does not appear to be internally preoccupied. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Patients having emotional difficulties frequently demonstrate a combination of anxiety and depressive symptoms, making it difficult to differentiate anxiety from depressive disorders. In addition, anxiety is frequently an associated symptom of depression; depressed patients often feel overwhelmed and ruminate over life stressors. This patient has insomnia, anxiety about multiple stressors, and muscle tension, findings suggestive of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). However, further examination reveals that she meets the criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD), including depressed mood, anhedonia (eg, not socializing with friends, no interest in cooking or exercising), early morning awakening, weight loss, fatigue, and low self-worth (eg, "I am a total failure as a mother") lasting ≥2 weeks. Somatic symptoms (eg, headaches, neck pain) may also accompany MDD. There is significant symptom overlap between MDD and GAD (eg, fatigue, insomnia, impaired concentration). However, a diagnosis of GAD requires a duration of 6 months, and most GAD patients describe lifelong anxiety (Choice B). This patient's lack of psychiatric history, 2-month symptom duration, and prominent depressive symptoms make MDD more likely. (Choice A) MDD can occur with or without precipitants. Adjustment disorder cannot be diagnosed when the patient meets the criteria for a more specific disorder. (Choice C) Insomnia disorder is diagnosed when recurrent sleep disturbance is a predominant symptom for ≥3 months and is not explained by a coexisting psychiatric or medical condition. This patient's insomnia is a symptom of her MDD. (Choice E) Persistent complex bereavement disorder (PCBD) is characterized by extreme and persistent yearning for the deceased that causes functional impairment and inability to resume normal life. This woman's loss of her father a year ago is only one of multiple stressors, and her depressive symptoms only began 2 months ago, making PCBD less likely. Educational objective: Insomnia and anxiety are often presenting symptoms in patients with major depressive disorder, which should be suspected in patients who also have prominent depressive symptoms and no previous history of anxiety.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman comes to the office due to nightly insomnia for the past 2 months. She also reports frequent tension headaches, neck pain, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating at work. The patient describes feeling anxious and overwhelmed by multiple stressors in her life, including having a high-pressure job, grieving over her father's death a year ago, caring for her elderly mother, and coping with a teenage son who uses cocaine. At night she lies in bed worrying about her mother, son, and problems at work. She has difficulty falling asleep and often wakes at 4 AM and is up for the rest of the night. The patient has avoided socializing with her friends and says, "Every time I am around them, I feel they must know I am a total failure as a mother." She has lost 2.3 kg (5 lb) and reports that she now has no interest in cooking and exercising. The patient has no prior psychiatric history. She drinks a glass of wine at night to "help me relax and get a few hours of sleep" but does not use illicit drugs. Physical examination and laboratory evaluation are unremarkable. The patient bursts into tears when speaking about how she misses her father. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: In the vast majority of patients, headaches with no danger signs (ie, no systemic symptoms; no neurologic signs; no change in frequency, severity, or clinical features) do not have a secondary cause of their headache. Brain imaging may be reasonable to rule out remote etiologies and provide reassurance at first. However, repeated scans are not indicated because they expose patients to unnecessary risks (eg, distress from a false-positive result, incidental findings leading to invasive workup, radiation exposure) and are unlikely to provide lasting reassurance. When declining to perform an unnecessary test, it is important to discuss the request in a nonjudgmental fashion, accompanied by education about risks and benefits and an explanation of why the requested test is not in the patient's best interest. This should be followed by discussion of alternate approaches to address the patient's concern about her symptoms (eg, stress reduction techniques, biofeedback or counseling for associated anxiety). (Choice A) Physicians should not order testing that is not medically indicated. Any reassuring effect from a negative result is likely to be temporary and lead to requests for further testing. (Choice B) This response focuses on the low probability of a positive test result. It is unlikely to reassure this patient and also fails to address the risks of repeated testing. (Choice C) This response does not offer to explain why the test is not indicated. It is likely to be perceived as judgmental and negatively impact the physician-patient relationship. (Choice E) This response attempts to decrease the patient's anxiety but avoids responding directly to the request or explaining the rationale for declining the requested test. Educational objective: Physicians should not feel pressured to order tests that are not medically indicated. Requests for additional testing should be declined in a nonjudgmental manner, accompanied by an explanation of why the test is not in the patient's best interest.

Patients and families may value nonmaleficence ("do no harm") over autonomy (eg, right to be informed) due to cultural or personal factors (eg, perceiving disclosure of a serious illness to a family elder as causing unnecessary distress). Although physicians have a presumed obligation to disclose medical information to patients, patients have the right to decline information about their diagnosis and prognosis (Choice D). This patient's preference has been communicated indirectly (ie, by the patient's son). Before withholding results, the physician must confirm that the decision to decline information originates from her (rather than from her son). Given this patient's LEP, the physician should first communicate directly with her, using a certified interpreter, to understand her preferences (and explore the reasoning for her preference). If this patient ultimately provides informed consent declining her results and further interpretation services (which she is also entitled to decline), the physician can subsequently communicate directly in English with her son (Choice C). (Choice A) Although the physician can recommend that this patient receive her results, she is entitled to decline her results if she wishes. Furthermore, this discussion should take place directly with the patient (rather than with the son) using a trained interpreter. (Choice E) As a durable health care power of attorney, the son's ability to make medical decisions on the patient's behalf applies only if she cannot make such decisions (eg, comatose state, severe cognitive impairment). There is no indication that this patient lacks decision-making capacity; therefore, her preferences should first be directly ascertained and followed. questions.explanation: Adolescence is a developmental period in which individuals strive to solidify their identities, separate from parental figures, and discover their own place in society. This is often accompanied by rebellion against parental and authority figures, pushing of limits, and an intense desire to fit in with a peer group. All of these issues can contribute to poor adherence with both preventive measures and treatment. A contributing factor is that the prefrontal cortex (center of executive functioning) is not fully developed until the third decade of life. Compared to adults, adolescents are less able to weigh the risks and benefits of interventions or to consider that negative consequences could occur. Factors associated with better adherence rates include close peers with complementary behavioral practices (eg, condom use by friends in this case), positive family functioning, physician empathy, and immediate benefits of treatment. (Choice A) Ease of acquiring condoms is certainly important once the patient has decided to use protection, but her initial motivation will be more strongly influenced by peer behavior. (Choices B and C) Adolescents have difficulty conceiving of possibilities outside of their immediate experience. They discount the possibility of negative things happening to them (ie, "Not me"), and therefore the possibility of pregnancy or sexually transmitted disease is unlikely to be a major deterrent. (Choice D) Written and online educational resources can be helpful but are not as influential as peer behavior. (Choice E) Adolescents are striving for autonomy and naturally rebel against parental and authority figures. Aligning with the mother is unlikely to improve adherence. Educational objective: Adolescents have low treatment adherence rates due to issues with autonomy, rebellion against authority figures, and lack of judgment regarding potential risks. Peer behavior has a major influence on adherence due to adolescents' desire to fit in.

questions.explanation: This patient's acute onset of manic-type symptoms (ie, irritability, decreased sleep, hyperactivity, pressured speech, grandiosity) during cocaine intoxication is consistent with substance-induced mood disorder. The essential feature of substance-induced disorders is that the behavioral changes are due to the physiologic effects of the substance (intoxication or withdrawal) on the central nervous system. Diagnosis requires that the involved substance/medication be capable of producing the symptoms (ie, cocaine and other stimulants are known to cause manic-type symptoms) and that the disturbance is not better explained by a primary psychiatric disorder. This patient's lack of prior history of hypomania or mania, the temporal relationship of symptoms to cocaine intoxication, and the resolution of mania soon after intoxication make substance-induced mood disorder more likely than bipolar disorder (Choice B). Depressed mood and fatigue are common during cocaine withdrawal. (Choice A) Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder is characterized by symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that begin in childhood and may last through adulthood. The symptoms are chronic and would not explain this patient's acute onset. (Choice C) Major depressive disorder with psychotic features is characterized by severe depression accompanied by delusions and/or hallucinations. The timing of this patient's depression is consistent with cocaine withdrawal. (Choice E) This patient's symptoms suggest grandiosity, which is common in mania. He has no frank delusions, hallucinations, or psychotic disorganization. Educational objective: Substance-induced mood disorder occurs when mood symptoms are produced as a direct result of substance intoxication or withdrawal. Cocaine can produce manic-type symptoms during intoxication and depression during withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife due to behavioral changes after snorting large amounts of cocaine for the past 3 days. The patient has been irritable, talking fast, not sleeping, and beginning multiple projects at home that he does not complete. He is easily distracted and moves from one topic to another. At night, he sits at the kitchen table and draws large geometric shapes, saying that he has "great ideas for designing the city of the future." The patient has a history of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, major depression, and hypertension, but takes no medications. In the emergency department, he talks fast and is difficult to interrupt but is oriented and answers cognitive questions rapidly and correctly. The patient is afebrile, blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg, pulse is 112/min, and respirations are 20/min. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable, and laboratory results are normal except for a urine toxicology screen that is positive for THC and cocaine. The patient is transferred to a psychiatric unit, where he initially has residual irritability for a couple of days and then feels depressed and tired for the subsequent few days. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

questions.explanation: Intimate partner violence Risk factors for escalating violence Perpetrator Increasing threats or controlling behavior Violence outside the home/to children Threatening homicide and/or suicide Drug use History of injuring partner/pregnant partner Access to firearms Victim Admitting fear for life Attempting to leave Seeking outside help Threatening or attempting suicide Management Ensure privacy Do not confront perpetrator Provide nonjudgmental support & validation without pressure Assess for safety & create a safety plan Offer assistance (counseling, resources) Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a serious public health concern that affects both men and women but is more common in women, with lifetime estimates at 40% in the United States. It includes not only actual abuse (physical, emotional, or sexual), but threatened abuse as well. The most important first step for a physician to take when assessing IPV is to be supportive of the patient's courage and struggle to talk about the violence. This should be accompanied by validation that any threatening and abusive behavior is wrong and undeserved. The next step is to assess for safety and help to refer or assist in establishing a safety plan. This patient's willingness to accept and pursue referrals will depend on her stage of acceptance and may only happen after subsequent visits. It is important not to pressure her to take a specific action (Choice B) and to assure her that she will not be abandoned no matter what her choice. (Choices A and C) IPV is associated with a risk for abuse and even death at the hands of the perpetrator. Risk factors for increasing violence include attempts by the victim to leave the relationship and any confrontations experienced by the perpetrator. Neither of these actions should be taken without a safety plan in place. (Choice E) This patient has already expressed fears of being hurt. Threats often turn into action and should not be ignored. (Choice F) The patient has just divulged what is happening (precontemplative stage) and is ambivalent (alternately expressing concern, then denial). The first step is for the physician to encourage discussion, rather than make a referral that the patient most likely would not pursue at this time. Educational objective: When a patient divulges intimate partner violence, the physician's most important first step is to provide support, validation, and assurance that the patient will not be abandoned. This is followed by assessing the patient's safety and making a safety plan.

questions.explanation: Eating disorders Diagnosis Clinical features Treatment Anorexia nervosa BMI <18.5 kg/m2 Intense fear of weight gain Distorted views of body weight & shape Cognitive-behavioral therapy Nutritional rehabilitation Olanzapine if no response to above Bulimia nervosa Recurrent episodes of binge eating Binge eating & inappropriate compensatory behavior to prevent weight gain Excess worrying about body shape & weight Cognitive-behavioral therapy Nutritional rehabilitation SSRI (fluoxetine), often in combination with above Binge-eating disorder Recurrent episodes of binge eating No inappropriate compensatory behaviors Lack of control during eating Cognitive-behavioral therapy Behavioral weight loss therapy SSRI Lisdexamfetamine SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. A history of bingeing, restrictive dieting, excessive preoccupation with weight, dental carries, and halitosis in an otherwise healthy young female with a normal weight suggests bulimia nervosa (BN). Other signs of self-induced vomiting can include parotid gland enlargement, abrasions on the dorsum of hands (Russell sign), hypokalemia, hypochloremia, hyperamylasemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Pharmacotherapy is effective for BN when combined with nutritional rehabilitation (ie, establishing a structured and consistent meal pattern) and cognitive behavioral psychotherapy (CBT). Fluoxetine, the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, is considered first-line treatment. It effectively targets the behavioral and cognitive symptoms of BN and is better tolerated than other medications. Although it can be used alone when therapy is unavailable, fluoxetine in combination with CBT has shown the greatest efficacy (Choice F). (Choices A and G) The second-generation antipsychotics aripiprazole and olanzapine are not indicated for the treatment of BN. Olanzapine, an antipsychotic associated with weight gain, has been used as adjunctive treatment to psychotherapy for anorexia nervosa. (Choice B) The antidepressant bupropion is a norepinephrine dopamine reuptake inhibitor that carries less risk of weight gain and sexual side effects than other antidepressants. It is contraindicated for use in eating disorders due to increased risk of seizures. (Choice D) Lithium, a mood stabilizer primarily used to treat bipolar disorder, has no role in treating BN. A history of bingeing, restrictive dieting, excessive preoccupation with weight, dental carries, and halitosis in an otherwise healthy young female with a normal weight suggests bulimia nervosa (BN).  Other signs of self-induced vomiting can include parotid gland enlargement, abrasions on the dorsum of hands (Russell sign), hypokalemia, hypochloremia, hyperamylasemia, and metabolic alkalosis.

Pharmacotherapy is effective for BN when combined with nutritional rehabilitation (ie, establishing a structured and consistent meal pattern) and cognitive behavioral psychotherapy (CBT).  Fluoxetine, the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, is considered first-line treatment.  It effectively targets the behavioral and cognitive symptoms of BN and is better tolerated than other medications.

questions.explanation: The birth of a new baby often causes older siblings to feel displaced, unwanted, jealous, or angry as they are no longer the center of attention. Behavioral regression (eg, loss of toilet training, loss of acquired words, increased separation anxiety, and/or increased tantrums) as well as aggressive behavior toward the newborn can occur. The parents are understandably stressed by the dual demands of caring for a newborn and managing their toddler's aggressive behavior. When a child is not receiving adequate attention, he/she will seek it out from a parent even in negative ways, as this child is doing. The best initial approach is to encourage parents to spend one-on-one time with the daughter so that she feels special and wanted. If the parents are not available, another family member could also provide that one-on-one time. At age 3, the daughter is too young to understand that a baby requires more attention (Choice B) or to empathize with the baby's pain (Choice A). The ability to understand others' perspectives does not develop until approximately age 4 or 5. Other behavioral strategies to manage sibling rivalry include rewarding positive interactions and giving the toddler some supervised responsibility, such as bringing things for the baby. If these strategies are ineffective or the daughter's behavior worsens, a child psychological assessment along with parent management counseling should be considered. (Choice C) Although parents must intervene when there is risk of imminent harm, it is unrealistic to keep the children separated and does not address the primary issue of why the daughter is acting aggressively. (Choice E) Although the daughter's behavior is within the range of normal behavior for a toddler, it is not appropriate to simply dismiss the parents' concerns and assure them that the situation will improve without any intervention. In fact, if the parent's frustrations increase and negative interactions escalate, their toddler's behavior is likely to worsen. Educational objective: Older siblings often react to the birth of a baby with regressive behavior and sometimes aggression toward the infant. Parents should be counseled to spend one-on-one time with their older children to reinforce their importance and sense of security.

questions.explanation: Medication nonadherence Patient/disease characteristics Asymptomatic or chronic condition Denial of illness/chronicity No immediate harm from stopping Psychiatric illness (eg, depression, psychosis, cognitive impairment) Illness/cultural beliefs against medication Inadequate understanding of illness/risks of nonadherence Treatment/management characteristics Adverse effects Incomplete medication efficacy Complicated regimen Medication cost Impaired physician-patient communication, lack of follow-up Nonadherence with antihypertensive medication is a common reason for poor blood pressure control in hypertensive patients. Motivation is particularly difficult in chronic, silent illnesses, in which many patients are initially asymptomatic and have no immediate, perceived benefit to adherence. This patient's nonadherence is most likely due to being asymptomatic. She feels well and knows that there is no immediate consequence for stopping medication. Many other reasons may contribute to poor medication adherence, including patient characteristics, incomplete medication efficacy, side effect issues, and difficulties in the patient-physician relationship. Strategies to improve adherence include educating a patient about an illness, correcting misperceptions of benefits and risks of treatment, using the simplest and least costly medications possible, and following up closely. (Choices A and B) The patient acknowledges that she has hypertension and has received education about the illness. (Choice C) This patient has no apparent side effects from hydrochlorothiazide. Patients are often willing to tolerate mild side effects if the medication is beneficial (as in this patient's willingness to continue her antidepressant despite feeling slightly tired). (Choice E) Comorbid depression is a common cause of nonadherence because it can contribute to low motivation and hopelessness about treatment. The patient's depression has improved and is an unlikely cause of her nonadherence. Educational objective: Chronic, silent illnesses have particularly high rates of medication nonadherence. Strategies to improve adherence include targeted patient education, simple and inexpensive regimens, and close follow-up.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman comes to the office for follow-up. The patient was prescribed citalopram 8 weeks ago for treatment of major depression. She is feeling much better and states, "I feel that the antidepressant has finally kicked in. My concentration at work is improving. I am sleeping well and have even started exercising at the gym. I do feel a little bit tired after I take the medicine, but that passes quite quickly and overall my energy is better." The patient has a history of depression, hypertension, and seasonal allergies. She also takes hydrochlorothiazide. Blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 14/min. The patient admittedly does not take her antihypertensive medication consistently. She says, "I know I have high blood pressure, and during many of my visits with you, we have gone over how not taking medications can have complications in the long run, but it's hard to remember to take medications every day." Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's poor adherence to her antihypertensive medication?

questions.explanation: Posttraumatic stress disorder Clinical features Exposure to life-threatening trauma Nightmares, flashbacks, intrusive memories Avoidance of reminders, dissociation Emotional detachment, negative mood, decreased interest in activities Sleep disturbance, hypervigilance, irritability Duration >1 month Treatment Trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy Antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs) SNRIs = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors; SSRIs = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. This patient's anger, irritability, emotional detachment, and hyperarousal symptoms (eg, sleep disturbance, hypervigilance) are consistent with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), likely related to the trauma of his brother's drowning death 6 months ago. His reluctance to go to the lake, a reminder of the trauma, is an example of avoidance that is characteristic of the disorder. The full spectrum of symptoms required to diagnose PTSD do not always develop immediately following a trauma and may build up over time, such as in this patient. Effective treatment for PTSD includes trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy and pharmacotherapy with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (eg, sertraline) or a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (eg, venlafaxine). These medications have been shown to decrease hyperarousal and mood symptoms, including irritability, anger, and depression. (Choices A, D, and F) There is insufficient evidence to support the use of other classes of antidepressants in the treatment of PTSD. Bupropion, a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor, is a stimulating antidepressant. Mirtazapine and trazodone are sedating antidepressants, but they have not demonstrated efficacy in PTSD. (Choice B) Although benzodiazepines such as clonazepam have a role in the treatment of severe anxiety, they are not effective for PTSD. They should particularly be avoided when there is a history of comorbid substance use disorder. (Choice C) The mood stabilizer lithium is primarily used in bipolar disorder. Although irritability and anger can also be seen in a manic episode, this patient lacks other concurrent symptoms of mania (eg, grandiosity, goal-directed activity, pressured speech, flight of ideas). His poor sleep and hyperarousal are related to PTSD; patients with mania have a decreased need for sleep due to increased energy. (Choice E) Antipsychotics (eg, quetiapine) are not first-line treatments for PTSD but have been used as augmentation strategies in treatment-resistant cases. Educational objective: Treatment for posttraumatic stress disorder includes trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy and pharmacotherapy. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors are first-line treatments.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is brought to the office by his wife for evaluation of behavioral changes. Over the past few months, the patient has become uncharacteristically moody and has lashed out at his family several times. His wife says, "I've never seen him like this before—even after his brother died. Sometimes he is very quiet and withdrawn, but other times he is very hyper, nervous, and tense. Yesterday, he broke a few dishes and yelled at the kids because they were making too much noise." The patient explains that he has been "on edge" and is sleeping poorly due to frequent nightmares. The wife shares that they had planned to attend the annual family reunion at the lake this weekend, but the patient cancelled last-minute because he felt the kids would have more fun hiking instead. He does not use alcohol or recreational substances, saying he always prefers to be alert, "in case something happens." Family history is significant for a brother with bipolar disorder, who died 6 months ago after drowning in a lake. Vital signs are within normal limits. The patient appears restless and exhausted. Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient?

questions.explanation: Adolescent nonsuicidal self-injury Features Deliberate injury with no intent to die Methods: cutting, burning, scratching Typical onset: age 12-14 Function/purpose Regulate distressing emotions Punish self Elicit support or allow for avoidance (eg, missing school) Management Psychotherapy Psychiatric evaluation, medications for comorbid conditions Confidentiality vs safety Consider informing parents if any of the following are present: Suicidal ideation Impairment, distress Multiple episodes, escalating frequency Single episode with serious medical risks (eg, use of razor, sutures) This patient has engaged in superficial scratching behavior, a form of nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) that is often used to cope with distressing affective states. It typically begins in early adolescence and is common in teens and young adults. NSSI is seen in a wide range of disorders (eg, personality, eating, dissociative) as well as in patients with developmental disabilities. It may also occur in patients who do not meet criteria for a major psychiatric disorder. NSSI is associated with short-term relief of emotional distress and is not performed with suicidal intent. However, because there is the potential for escalation of self-harm in patients with NSSI, a complete psychiatric assessment and safety evaluation should be performed. When it comes to confidentiality, patient autonomy and rapport should be weighed against safety concerns and beneficence. Concerning signs, which would warrant parental involvement, include suicidal ideation, comorbid psychiatric disorders, impairment in other areas of functioning (eg, academic or social decline), and frequent or dangerous cutting. In this case, the patient has engaged in minor superficial scratching behavior, which is unlikely to cause serious harm, and is interested in pursuing psychotherapeutic assessment. The patient's autonomy can be respected and her request for confidentiality maintained (Choice A). However, she should receive regular follow-up to assess for any signs of escalation and the recommendation for further assessment and treatment shared with her mother. (Choice B) Although cutting behavior is frequently associated with borderline personality disorder, it is not pathognomonic. This patient does not exhibit sufficient symptoms to diagnose borderline personality disorder (eg, unstable self-image, affects, and relationships; fear of abandonment). (Choices D and E) These statements violate the patient's request for confidentiality and could be destructive to the physician-patient relationship. If the patient's NSSI presented a reasonable risk to her physical health (such as cutting rather than superficial scratching) or was associated with suicidal ideation, then it would be appropriate to break confidentiality. Educational objective: Nonsuicidal self-injury is a nonspecific psychiatric symptom commonly seen in adolescents that is used to relieve distressing, negative emotions. The benefits of confidentiality should be carefully weighed against the concern for safety. Psychotherapeutic assessment with close follow-up should be arranged.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother for an annual physical examination. The patient has no significant medical history and says she feels "fine." During the examination, the physician notes a few superficial scratches on her left forearm. The patient explains, "Oh, it's nothing. I scratch my skin with my nails sometimes when I feel stressed. Some of my friends do it, but it doesn't seem to be helping me." The patient says she often feels bored and hates her parents, who do not understand her, but denies any persistently depressed mood, appetite or sleep disturbance, or psychotic symptoms. She has no wish to be dead or active suicidal ideation, intent, or plan. The patient has used alcohol at parties but has no other substance use. She is not sexually active. questions.explanation: An impaired physician is one who has a medical, psychiatric, or substance use condition that affects ability to practice according to accepted and safe standards. This physician's increasing forgetfulness has already resulted in a prescribing mistake that could have caused patient harm (Choice B). Although this physician may be uncomfortable reporting her mentor, physicians are ethically and legally obligated to report impaired colleagues (Choice C). Most hospitals have a designated hospital committee, commonly called a physician health program (PHP). It is this committee's responsibility to gather all the facts and arrange for a comprehensive assessment with intervention and treatment if necessary. With treatment, many impaired physicians are able to return to either full or modified practice. If such a body does not exist or if the physician does not accept the PHP's recommendations, then the state licensing board should be contacted (Choice G). (Choice A) The colleague's forgetfulness is already causing problems. The physician should not wait any longer to report the issue as patient care is at risk. (Choice D) It is inappropriate to recommend retirement as the colleague's cognitive condition may be reversible or improve with treatment. It would be more appropriate to inform the PHP. (Choice E) The physician has already recommended that her colleague get help, but he has denied having a problem. Repeatedly asking the colleague to have an assessment could be seen as confrontational, and he may become more defensive. Educational objective: Physicians are obligated to report impaired colleagues. Reporting protects patient safety and can assist the impaired physician in receiving appropriate evaluation and treatment.

questions.explanation: Livedo reticularis (LR) is a transient red or purplish, blotchy or latticelike rash that primarily affects the lower extremities. It is caused by obstruction, vasospasm, or sluggish flow in the superficial venules. LR is often a benign finding and can frequently be seen in otherwise healthy women during cold weather. However, LR can also be a sign of vasculitic (eg, polyarteritis nodosa, systemic lupus erythematosus) or vasoocclusive (eg, cholesterol embolization, antiphospholipid syndrome, cryoglobulinemia) disorders. This patient has LR with acute leg swelling (likely due to deep venous thrombosis) and a history of recurrent miscarriages. In this context, LR is likely due to antiphospholipid (APL) syndrome. LR is the most common dermal sign of APL syndrome and is associated with an increased risk of arterial occlusive complications (eg, stroke, retinal artery occlusion). However, although APL is associated with thrombosis, the partial thromboplastin time – but not prothrombin time (Choice D) – will be prolonged, likely due to binding of phospholipid reagents in the assay by the antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant). Mixing of patient plasma containing lupus anticoagulant with normal plasma will not correct the partial thromboplastin time in contrast to patients with clotting factor deficiencies in which the addition of normal plasma will supply the necessary factors to normalize the assay. (Choice A) Specific antiphospholipid antibodies can be used to confirm the diagnosis of APL syndrome. These include anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I, antiphosphatidylserine, and anticardiolipin antibodies. Beta-2 microglobulin is elevated in lymphoproliferative disorders (eg, multiple myeloma) and other conditions with increased cell turnover. (Choice B) Serum iron, transferrin saturation, and ferritin are elevated in hemochromatosis due to increased intestinal absorption of iron. (Choice E) LR is commonly seen in myeloproliferative disorders (eg, polycythemia vera). By contrast, vitamin B12 deficiency typically presents with anemia, often with associated neurologic symptoms. Educational objective: Livedo reticularis (LR) is a transient, latticelike rash caused by impaired blood flow in the superficial venules. LR is often a benign finding but can be a sign of a vasculitic or vasoocclusive disorder. It is also the most common dermal manifestation of antiphospholipid syndrome.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the office due to a 3-day history of pain and swelling in the left leg. The pain is moderate in intensity and feels like a "toothache." The patient also has a purplish, blotchy rash on her hands, thighs, and legs that has been present for several months and worsens on exposure to cold temperatures. Medical history is significant for migraine headaches, irritable bowel syndrome, and recurrent miscarriages. She does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. On examination, vital signs are normal. The left calf and ankle appear swollen, and palpation of the left thigh and calf elicits tenderness. The rash is shown in the image below. Which of the following is most likely to be found on additional evaluation?

questions.explanation: This patient has a soft, rounded, well-demarcated swelling at the point of the elbow consistent with chronic olecranon bursitis. Chronic bursitis is caused by pressure, friction, overuse, or autoimmune disease (eg, rheumatoid arthritis). Overproduction of bursa fluid over time produces an enlarged, soft bursal sac, which can be easily visible in superficial bursae such as the olecranon bursa. Olecranon bursitis is common in individuals who work or drive for extended periods with their elbows weighted on a hard surface. Bursitis can be differentiated from true joint pathology as the joint will have relatively normal, pain-free range of motion (Choice E). Uncomplicated chronic bursitis causes mild, if any, pain. However, bacterial seeding of bursa fluid can lead to septic bursitis, with fever, erythema, and significant local pain and tenderness. Acute bursitis due to trauma or crystalline arthropathy can also generate significant pain. (Choice A) Chondrosarcoma is an uncommon tumor occurring in the 5th or 6th decade of life. It usually presents with symptoms in the axial (eg, back pain), rather than appendicular, skeleton. (Choice B) Distal biceps tendon rupture is caused by sudden loading against a contracted muscle. Findings include acute anterior elbow swelling, ecchymosis, weakness, and a visible defect where the biceps has retracted from its attachment at the radius. (Choice C) Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) causes lateral elbow pain without swelling. Patients have tenderness over the lateral epicondyle at the origin of the forearm extensor muscles and reproduction of pain when extending the wrist against resistance. (Choice F) Tophi are macroscopic deposits of uric acid crystals in subcutaneous tissues, joints, or other locations. They are usually seen in chronic, untreated gout, and most patients will have had recurrent episodes of acute gouty arthritis. Educational objective: Chronic bursitis is caused by pressure, friction, or overuse. Chronic bursitis can be differentiated from true joint pathology as the joint will have normal, pain-free range of motion.

Examination shows a soft, fluctuant swelling at his left elbow, as shown in the figure below, with minimal tenderness and no warmth. Pain or discomfort is not elicited on flexion or extension of the elbow, supination or pronation of the forearm, or resisted extension of the wrist. Examination of all other joints is normal. questions.explanation: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) should be considered in the diagnostic workup of any patient age >40 with a history of significant tobacco use (>30 pack years), chronic cough (often with sputum production), and progressive dyspnea on exertion. Spirometry is necessary for establishing the diagnosis; characteristic findings are a decreased FEV1 and a relatively normal FVC, resulting in an FEV1/FVC ratio <0.70. The degree of decrease in the FEV1 is used to gauge the severity of disease; an FEV1 <50% of predicted is consistent with the diagnosis of severe COPD. Spirometry is also helpful in monitoring disease progression as FEV1 declines over time with normal aging but usually at a faster rate in patients with COPD. Severe COPD may lead to pulmonary hypertension, resulting in right ventricular hypertrophy and a right-sided fourth heart sound, as observed in this patient. (Choice A) D-dimer testing is useful in ruling out pulmonary embolism (PE) in patients with suspected PE and a low probability of venous thromboembolic disease. This patient's progressive (rather than sudden-onset) dyspnea, productive cough, and absence of chest pain are consistent with COPD and create minimal suspicion for PE. (Choice B) Exercise stress testing is used to assess for myocardial ischemia in patients with symptoms suggestive of stable angina (eg, chest pain with exertion that resolves with rest). This patient has coronary artery disease (CAD), but his progressive dyspnea and productive cough are more consistent with COPD than stable angina. (Choice C) Metoprolol is a cardioselective beta blocker that may cause slight bronchoconstriction and worsening of symptoms of obstructive lung disease. However, metoprolol is indicated to decrease myocardial oxygen demand in this patient with CAD and should not be discontinued before evaluating for COPD and assessing the risks and benefits of discontinuing the drug. (Choice D) A low-dose, noncontrast chest CT scan is indicated for lung cancer screening in patients age 50-80 with a ≥20-pack-year history and active smoking in the last 15 years (such as this patient). However, spirometry is the best next step in evaluating the cause of this patient's dyspnea and productive cough. Educational objective: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease should be considered in any patient age >40 with a significant smoking history who has a chronic cough (productive or nonproductive) and progressive dyspnea on exertion. The spirometry finding of an FEV1/FVC ratio <0.70 is needed for the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the office due to slowly progressive shortness of breath for the past year. He is an avid golfer and increasingly finds himself using the golf cart to get around. He also has some dyspnea when walking up hills. The patient has a mild morning cough productive of whitish sputum but has no chest pain, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. He has coronary artery disease and had a drug-eluting stent placed 2 years ago. He also has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. The patient, a retired truck driver, stopped smoking 12 years ago, but before then, he smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 20 years. Medications include aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, and metoprolol. Blood pressure is 134/85 mm Hg, pulse is 62/min, respirations are 14/min, and pulse oximetry is 95% on room air. BMI is 27 kg/m2. Estimated jugular venous pressure is 6 cm H2O. The patient's lungs are clear to auscultation, and heart examination demonstrates a regular rate and rhythm with a fourth heart sound. There is no lower extremity swelling. Chest x-ray reveals no cardiomegaly or lung infiltrates. Which of the following is the best next step in evaluating this patient?

questions.explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome Etiology X-linked recessive defect in WAS protein gene Impaired cytoskeleton changes in leukocytes, platelets Clinical features Eczema Microthrombocytopenia (small platelets, low platelet count) Recurrent infections Treatment Stem cell transplant Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is caused by an X-linked recessive defect in the WAS gene that causes cytoskeletal defects in platelets and leukocytes (eg, T cells). As a result, patients have microthrombocytopenia (reduced size and number of platelets), recurrent infections, and eczema, as seen in this patient. Clinical findings of microthrombocytopenia range from petechiae or purpura to severe bleeding such as hematuria, hematochezia, or intracranial hemorrhage. T cell number and function may be normal in infancy but decrease in childhood. Affected patients are at increased risk for recurrent viral and fungal infections, as well as bacterial sinopulmonary infections, as seen in this patient with recurrent acute otitis media and pneumonia. In addition, eczema is often present in patients with WAS, as in this patient with dry cheeks. The diagnosis can be made clinically, but genetic screening of family members is recommended. Definitive treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. (Choice A) Ataxia-telangiectasia is a rare, progressive neurodegenerative disease that can present with recurrent sinopulmonary infections. However, patients also have ataxia, abnormal eye movements, and facial telangiectasias. Thrombocytopenia is not characteristic. (Choice B) Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by a lysosomal defect, leading to impaired phagocytosis. Affected patients have albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and recurrent skin and soft-tissue pyogenic infections, none of which are present in this patient. (Choice C) Hemolytic-uremic syndrome is a sequela of Shiga toxin-producing enteric pathogens such as Escherichia coli O157:H7 or Shigella. The condition is characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure; this patient does not have anemia or signs of renal failure (eg, poor urine output). (Choice D) Henoch-Schönlein purpura can present with renal disease (eg, hematuria) and rash. However, the rash is purpuric, and thrombocytopenia is not typical. In addition, these patients often have arthralgias and abdominal pain, neither of which is present in this case. (Choice E) Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by autoantibodies acting against platelet antigens and usually occurs after a viral illness. Platelet size is normal or enlarged. (Choice F) Job syndrome (hyper-IgE syndrome) is a rare immunodeficiency that causes recurrent skin and lung infections in addition to a pruritic rash similar to eczema. However, thrombocytopenia is not seen in Job syndrome. Educational objective: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder that presents with the classic triad of eczema, microthrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections.

questions.stem: A 21-month-old boy is brought to the clinic due to bright red blood in his urine that his parents first noticed when changing his diaper 2 days ago. The patient has not had any previous bleeding and has been eating and drinking normally. He recently had a week of cough and nasal congestion that has since resolved. Medical history is notable for recurrent otitis media and 2 episodes of pneumonia, 1 of which required hospitalization. Topical petrolatum is applied daily for dry skin on his cheeks, and immunizations are up to date. Vital signs are normal. The patient is at the 50th percentile for weight and height. Examination reveals scattered petechiae on his lower extremities but is otherwise unremarkable. Complete blood count results are as follows: Hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL Platelets 20,000/mm3 Leukocytes 8400/mm3 Peripheral smear is notable for small platelet size. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.stemHtml:

questions.explanation: This patient has clinical features suggesting osteoarthritis (OA), including age >40, pain that is worse with activity and relieved with rest, and crepitus on examination. The risk of OA is increased in patients with prior joint injury or abnormal alignment (eg, varus deformity). X-ray characteristically shows joint space narrowing and periarticular osteophytes but may be unnecessary prior to initial management. Management of OA of the knee should include weight loss and regular low-impact aerobic exercise (eg, walking, cycling). In addition, a dedicated exercise program (often with the assistance of a physical therapist) to strengthen the quadriceps muscles can improve function and protect the articular cartilage from further stress. Quadriceps strength typically declines with age, and the pain of OA may induce patients to decrease activity, leading to atrophy of the quadriceps complex. This can cause abnormal loading of the articular cartilage and accelerate degeneration of the joint. (Choice A) Although this patient has a history of anterior cruciate ligament injury, the Lachman test (anterior laxity) is negative, indicating normal integrity of the ligament. (Choice B) Arthroscopic lavage is often used in septic arthritis. However, lavage, with or without debridement, is ineffective for knee OA. (Choice D) Pes anserinus pain syndrome (often called anserine bursitis) is characterized by point tenderness over the medial aspect of the knee joint just distal to the joint line. The pain is typically exacerbated by pressure from the contralateral knee while lying on the side. (Choice E) Meniscal injuries are most common following twisting trauma to the knee. They are characterized by acute to subacute symptoms, medial joint line tenderness, and a catching sensation during extension. Educational objective: Initial management of osteoarthritis of the knee should include weight loss, regular low-impact aerobic activity, and simple analgesics. Exercises to strengthen the quadriceps muscles can reduce abnormal loading on the joint and protect the articular cartilage from further stress.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the clinic for evaluation of right knee pain. For the past 2 years, he has had pain after prolonged weight-bearing activity, with relief during rest and knee extension. The knee also becomes stiff after prolonged periods of sitting, such as during long-distance travel. The patient sustained an anterior cruciate ligament injury while playing football in college, requiring surgery at that time. He has no other medical history. On examination, the patient has an antalgic gait favoring his right knee and a varus deformity of both knee joints. There is no focal tenderness or palpable joint effusion, but crepitus is felt when the right knee is flexed and extended. When the right knee is held in 30-degree flexion and the thigh stabilized on the examination table, anterior traction on the proximal tibia elicits no significant laxity of the knee joint. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with nonvolitional weight loss, primarily affecting lean muscle mass (eg, thin extremities, temporalis wasting). This presentation is concerning for pulmonary cachexia, a form of malnutrition that occurs in 20-40% of patients with chronic lung disease. Mechanisms of pulmonary cachexia are related to an energy-calorie imbalance: Caloric intake is decreased due to poor appetite in the setting of systemic inflammation that accompanies COPD (eg, TNF-α is a potent anorexigen). Intake also tends to be restricted by meal-related dyspnea. Caloric expenditure is increased by high work of breathing (eg, accessory muscle use), along with a hypermetabolic state related to persistent inflammation or infections. Pulmonary cachexia is suggested in patients with BMI <20 kg/m2 and/or unplanned weight loss of >5% in a year. It is a poor prognostic sign, contributing to reduced lung function (respiratory muscle weakness), further deconditioning, greater fall risk, and increased mortality. Treatment of pulmonary cachexia involves reducing the work of breathing (eg, nocturnal noninvasive ventilation), increasing caloric intake (eg, small, frequent meals with high fat content), and structured exercise (eg, pulmonary rehabilitation) to maintain muscle viability. (Choice A) Adrenal insufficiency (AI) can produce fatigue, weight loss, and a small cardiac silhouette (due to chronic volume depletion). This patient is at risk for iatrogenic AI due to intermittent prednisone use, but significant adrenal axis suppression is unlikely after only 2 weeks of glucocorticoid exposure. In addition, AI is less likely in the absence of laboratory abnormalities such as hypoglycemia and hyponatremia. (Choice C) COPD is a strong risk factor for lung cancer, which can produce uncontrolled weight loss. Chest x-ray is insensitive for detection of early-stage tumors; however, cancer cachexia requires a significant tumor volume, which is unlikely in this patient without a large, locally advanced mass grossly visible on chest x-ray. (Choice D) Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection can complicate COPD. It classically presents with weight loss in lean and elderly females ("Lady Windermere syndrome") but is typically accompanied by increased sputum production and other constitutional symptoms (eg, fever, night sweats). Multifocal nodules and bronchiectasis are expected on chest imaging. (Choice E) Severe COPD can cause pulmonary hypertension and lead to right ventricular failure. Advanced heart failure can induce muscle wasting (ie, cardiac cachexia) but weight gain (due to accumulation of fluid) and elevated jugulovenous pressure are expected. Educational objective: Advanced chronic lung disease can be complicated by pulmonary cachexia, an indicator of poor prognosis characterized by loss of lean muscle mass due to energy-calorie imbalance and systemic inflammation.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman comes to the office for follow-up for severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). She uses 2 L/min of supplemental home oxygen and has had no recent changes in her respiratory symptoms. The patient's exercise capacity is limited due to shortness of breath, and her appetite has been poor. She has had no heat intolerance, polyuria, fevers, increased sputum, or hemoptysis. The patient was hospitalized with an acute exacerbation of COPD 3 months ago, and she received a tapered dose of oral prednisone over 2 weeks. Current medications include fluticasone/salmeterol, tiotropium, and albuterol, which she uses 4 or 5 times daily. The patient is a former smoker with a 50-pack-year history. Blood pressure is 139/72 mm Hg, pulse is 94/min, and respirations are 18/min. Pulse oximetry shows 92% on 2 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula. BMI is 17.4 kg/m2, and the patient has lost 9 kg (20 lb) over the last year. Physical examination reveals a thin woman with mild temporal wasting. Pulmonary examination reveals purse-lipped breathing and mild accessory muscle use. Cardiovascular examination is unremarkable. No hepatosplenomegaly is present on abdominal examination. The extremities are thin with decreased muscle mass and trace edema. Complete blood count and serum electrolytes are within normal limits. Chest x-ray reveals marked hyperinflation and a small cardiac silhouette. What is the most likely cause of this patient's weight loss?

questions.explanation: Acute gouty arthritis Signs & symptoms Usually involves first metatarsophalangeal joint or knee Swelling, erythema & exquisite tenderness Symptoms develop rapidly over 24 hr Diagnosis Joint aspiration shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals Treatment Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (eg, naproxen, indomethacin) preferred if no contraindications Colchicine used as second-line therapy This patient has abrupt onset of painful monoarthritis with inflammatory synovial fluid and needle-shaped uric acid crystals, consistent with gout. Gout is commonly triggered by thiazide and loop diuretics due to decreased clearance of urate. Other potential triggers include surgery, trauma, and volume depletion as well as lifestyle factors, including excessive intake of alcohol and a high-urate diet. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs ([NSAIDs] eg, indomethacin) are commonly used to treat gout. However, they may increase the risk of bleeding in patients on anticoagulants (eg, aspirin, clopidogrel, apixaban) and can acutely worsen heart failure (Choice D). In patients with contraindications to NSAIDs, colchicine can be used and usually results in resolution of symptoms. Colchicine inhibits polymerization of beta-tubulin into microtubules, preventing migration and activation of neutrophils. Important adverse effects include nausea, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Colchicine should not be used in elderly patients or those with severe renal dysfunction. This patient could also be considered for systemic or intra-articular glucocorticoids, although these agents may complicate his diabetic management. (Choices A, C, and E) Allopurinol and febuxostat reduce serum uric acid levels by inhibiting uric acid production. Probenecid promotes the renal excretion of uric acid and is used as a second-line agent if allopurinol or febuxostat is ineffective. These medications are used in chronic management to prevent recurrent attacks but should not be started until the gout is quiescent as they can trigger an attack if started acutely. Educational objective: Gout can be triggered by thiazide and loop diuretics due to decreased clearance of urate. Treatment options for acute gout include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), colchicine, and glucocorticoids. Colchicine and glucocorticoids are preferred in patients taking anticoagulants due to the risk of bleeding with NSAIDs.
