questions.stem: A 65-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for acute decompensated congestive heart failure and is treated with intravenous furosemide and supplemental oxygen. On the 3rd hospital day, he is awakened by sudden-onset right knee pain. The pain is severe, and the patient has never had similar symptoms. Medical history is notable for an acute myocardial infarction 3 months earlier that required drug-eluting stent placement to the left anterior descending artery. His other medical problems include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, persistent atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertension. Concurrent medications include long-acting insulin, metformin, lisinopril, aspirin, carvedilol, clopidogrel, rosuvastatin, apixaban, and furosemide. The patient quit smoking after the myocardial infarction and does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. Temperature is 38 C (100.4 F), blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min and irregular, and respirations are 16/min. Pulse oximetry is 94% on room air. On examination, there are a few crackles audible at the lung bases bilaterally. The right knee is swollen, erythematous, and tender, with moderate restriction of movement due to pain; 1+ peripheral edema is present in both ankles. Laboratory results are as follows: Hemoglobin 12 g/dL Platelets 180,000/mm3 Leukocytes 11,100/mm3 Blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL Synovial fluid analysis shows numerous inflammatory cells and scattered needle-shaped crystals. No bacteria are seen on Gram stain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient's clinical presentation – palpable thrill accompanied by a loud, harsh holosystolic murmur in the fourth left intercostal space – is typical for ventricular septal defect (VSD). VSD is one of the most common congenital heart defects, with spontaneous closure occurring during early childhood in 40%-60% of patients. A small (restrictive) VSD is associated with a loud murmur as there is high resistance to flow; a large (unrestrictive) VSD is associated with a soft murmur (little resistance to flow), which is prominent in early systole (due to the early equalization of right and left ventricular pressures during systole). Adult patients with a persistent, small restrictive VSD with left-to-right shunting usually have favorable hemodynamics and normal right-sided heart pressures. Such patients remain asymptomatic, and the VSD is usually detected during routine clinical evaluation when cardiac auscultation reveals a typical harsh holosystolic murmur with maximal intensity over the third and fourth intercostal spaces along the left sternal border. (Choice A) Cardiac auscultation in patients with an atrial septal defect reveals a characteristic wide and fixed splitting of the second heart sound (S2). Patients may also have a midsystolic ejection murmur (flow increase across the pulmonic valve) and a middiastolic rumble (flow increase across the tricuspid valve). (Choice B) Patients with bicuspid aortic valve and aortic stenosis (AS) typically have an ejection click followed by a midsystolic murmur with maximal intensity over the right second intercostal space. As the aortic valve becomes thickened and calcified with severe AS, the ejection click disappears and S2 becomes soft and single. (Choice C) Coarctation of the aorta typically leads to diminished or delayed femoral pulses (brachial-femoral delay), upper extremity hypertension, and a continuous "rumbling" murmur in the back over the interscapular area. (Choice D) Patients with a flail posterior mitral leaflet (or mitral valve prolapse) typically have single or multiple nonejection clicks followed by the mid- to late systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation (best heard at the cardiac apex). (Choice E) Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (left ventricular outflow obstruction) have a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur best heard at apex and the lower left sternal border. The murmur increases in intensity with Valsalva maneuvers and with standing from a sitting or squatting position. (Choice F) Patent ductus arteriosus causes a characteristic, continuous "machinery" murmur best heard in the left infraclavicular area. Educational objective: Patients with a ventricular septal defect typically have a harsh holosystolic murmur, with maximal intensity over the left third and fourth intercostal spaces, accompanied by a palpable thrill.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man is evaluated for a cardiac murmur. He states he has had a murmur since childhood but does not remember any details. He has had no symptoms and reports good exercise tolerance. Family history is unremarkable. The patient's blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg and pulse is 78/min and regular. In both upper and lower extremities, pulses are strong with a normal rate of rise and descent. On chest auscultation, a loud holosystolic murmur is present; it is best heard in the fourth intercostal space along the left sternal border and is accompanied by a thrill. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Abdominal examination is unremarkable with no palpable masses, organomegaly, or bruits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) Clinical features Heavy, prolonged menses Pressure symptoms Pelvic pain Constipation Urinary frequency Obstetric complications Impaired fertility Pregnancy loss Preterm labor Enlarged, irregular uterus Work-up Ultrasonography Treatment Asymptomatic: observation Symptomatic: hormonal contraception, surgery A copper-containing intrauterine device (IUD) commonly increases menstrual bleeding, an adverse effect that should resolve on removal. This patient's continued heavy menstrual bleeding despite IUD removal and an irregularly enlarged uterus make uterine fibroids (ie, leiomyomata uteri) the likely cause of bleeding symptoms. Uterine fibroids are benign, smooth muscle tumors that develop within the uterine myometrium. Although most fibroids are asymptomatic, symptoms can develop based on fibroid size and location: Submucosal fibroids are located directly beneath the endometrium and can protrude into the uterine cavity. They distend the endometrial lining and increase the endometrial surface area and therefore the amount of endometrial tissue shed with menses (ie, heavy menstrual bleeding). Intramural fibroids (within the uterine wall) can also cause heavy menses due to uterine enlargement and increased endometrial surface area. Subserosal fibroids, which protrude from the uterine surface, can create an irregular uterine contour. These fibroids can also compress adjacent pelvic structures, resulting in bulk symptoms (eg, pelvic pressure). (Choice A) Abnormal ovarian follicle development, seen in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), can be associated with heavy menses. Unlike this patient with monthly menses, those with PMOS have chronic anovulation resulting in heavy, irregular menses due to uncontrolled endometrial thickening and irregular endometrial shedding. (Choice B) Dysplastic overgrowth in the cervical transformation zone can lead to cervical cancer, which can cause vaginal bleeding (eg, postcoital bleeding) due to a friable, malignant tumor. However, there is no association with irregular uterine enlargement. (Choice C) Adenomyosis, caused by the abnormal presence of endometrial tissue within the myometrium, is a common cause of heavy menses and uterine enlargement. However, patients typically have a tender, globular (ie, uniformly shaped) uterus. (Choice D) Endometrial hyperplasia, the overproliferation of atypical endometrial tissue, can progress to cancer. In premenopausal patients, hyperplasia presents with heavy but irregular menses (ie, anovulatory bleeding) due to risk factors (eg, obesity, chronic anovulation, nulliparity) that increase unopposed estrogen levels. This patient has regular menses and a normal BMI. (Choice E) β-hCG–secreting trophoblastic tissue proliferates abnormally in gestational trophoblastic disease (eg, hydatidiform mole). Patients can have uterine enlargement and heavy bleeding; however, this diagnosis is unlikely in this patient with a negative pregnancy test (ie, no β-hCG). Educational objective: Uterine fibroids are benign proliferations of smooth muscle that develop within the uterine myometrium. Common clinical features are heavy menstrual bleeding and irregular uterine enlargement.

Educational objective:
Uterine fibroids are benign proliferations of smooth muscle that develop within the uterine myometrium.  Common clinical features are heavy menstrual bleeding and irregular uterine enlargement.
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids)
Clinical features
  • Heavy, prolonged menses
  • Pressure symptoms
    • Pelvic pain
    • Constipation
    • Urinary frequency
  • Obstetric complications
    • Impaired fertility
    • Pregnancy loss
    • Preterm labor
  • Enlarged, irregular uterus
Work-up
  • Ultrasonography
Treatment
  • Asymptomatic: observation
  • Symptomatic: hormonal contraception, surgery

A copper-containing intrauterine device (IUD) commonly increases menstrual bleeding, an adverse effect that should resolve on removal.  This patient's continued heavy menstrual bleeding despite IUD removal and an irregularly enlarged uterus make uterine fibroids (ie, leiomyomata uteri) the likely cause of bleeding symptoms.

Uterine fibroids are benign, smooth muscle tumors that develop within the uterine myometrium.  Although most fibroids are asymptomatic, symptoms can develop based on fibroid size and location:

  • Submucosal fibroids are located directly beneath the endometrium and can protrude into the uterine cavity.  They distend the endometrial lining and increase the endometrial surface area and therefore the amount of endometrial tissue shed with menses (ie, heavy menstrual bleeding).
  • Intramural fibroids (within the uterine wall) can also cause heavy menses due to uterine enlargement and increased endometrial surface area.
  • Subserosal fibroids, which protrude from the uterine surface, can create an irregular uterine contour.  These fibroids can also compress adjacent pelvic structures, resulting in bulk symptoms (eg, pelvic pressure).

wrongAnswers.A: (Choice A)  Abnormal ovarian follicle development, seen in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), can be associated with heavy menses.  Unlike this patient with monthly menses, those with PMOS have chronic anovulation resulting in heavy, irregular menses due to uncontrolled endometrial thickening and irregular endometrial shedding.
wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  Dysplastic overgrowth in the cervical transformation zone can lead to cervical cancer, which can cause vaginal bleeding (eg, postcoital bleeding) due to a friable, malignant tumor.  However, there is no association with irregular uterine enlargement.
wrongAnswers.C: (Choice C)  Adenomyosis, caused by the abnormal presence of endometrial tissue within the myometrium, is a common cause of heavy menses and uterine enlargement.  However, patients typically have a tender, globular (ie, uniformly shaped) uterus.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Endometrial hyperplasia, the overproliferation of atypical endometrial tissue, can progress to cancer.  In premenopausal patients, hyperplasia presents with heavy but irregular menses (ie, anovulatory bleeding) due to risk factors (eg, obesity, chronic anovulation, nulliparity) that increase unopposed estrogen levels.  This patient has regular menses and a normal BMI.
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  β-hCG–secreting trophoblastic tissue proliferates abnormally in gestational trophoblastic disease (eg, hydatidiform mole).  Patients can have uterine enlargement and heavy bleeding; however, this diagnosis is unlikely in this patient with a negative pregnancy test (ie, no β-hCG).

questions.sharedStimulusHtml: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, comes to the office due to heavy menstrual bleeding.  The patient's menses occur every 30 days and last 7 days, with 4 days of heavy bleeding that require a superabsorbent pad every hour.  She is sexually active with a new partner and has had 6 lifetime partners.  Two years ago, the patient had a copper intrauterine device (IUD) placed for contraception because she felt bloated on oral contraceptives.  The IUD was removed 6 months ago in an effort to decrease menstrual bleeding, but there has been no improvement.  Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 126/84 mm Hg, and pulse is 80/min.  BMI is 22 kg/m2.  Pelvic examination shows a nontender, slightly enlarged uterus with an irregular contour.  Urine pregnancy test is negative.

questions.explanation: This patient's heavy menstrual bleeding in the setting of an irregularly shaped, enlarged uterus is most likely due to uterine fibroids (leiomyomas). Fibroids are benign, smooth muscle tumors that can distort uterine anatomy. Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVUS) is the preferred imaging modality for diagnosing most types of fibroids because it is widely available, noninvasive (eg, no radiation exposure), and highly sensitive for female reproductive tract pathology (Choice B). However, intrauterine masses such as submucosal fibroids may go undetected on TVUS alone because they distort the uterine cavity, which is normally empty and collapsed (ie, a potential space). A more sensitive test for detecting submucosal fibroids and other intrauterine pathology (eg, polyps) is sonohysterography, a form of TVUS that infuses saline into the uterine cavity. Filling the uterus with fluid allows for better visualization of the intrauterine cavity by creating the space to identify structures that protrude into or distort the uterine cavity. (Choice A) Colposcopy examines the cervix for malignant transformation, which typically presents with an abnormal Pap test or postcoital spotting rather than heavy menstrual bleeding and an irregularly enlarged uterus. (Choice C) Laparoscopy is not used to diagnose uterine fibroids because they are readily visualized on noninvasive imaging (eg, sonohysterography). Laparoscopy is more commonly used to diagnose endometriosis, which is typically associated with dysmenorrhea. In addition, endometriosis does not cause irregular uterine enlargement. (Choice D) Endometrial biopsy is used to evaluate endometrial hyperplasia/cancer. In premenopausal women, endometrial cancer causes abnormal uterine bleeding in patients with risk factors (eg, obesity, chronic anovulation). Because this patient is young (age <45) and has no risk factors, endometrial biopsy is not indicated. Educational objective: Submucosal fibroids can protrude into the uterine cavity and distort the endometrial lining. A highly sensitive test for the evaluation of submucosal fibroids is sonohysterography, a form of transvaginal ultrasonography that infuses saline into the uterine cavity for improved detection of intrauterine pathology (eg, fibroid, polyp).

questions.explanation: Retained placenta Definition No placental expulsion within 30 min of fetal delivery Risk factors Retained placenta in prior delivery Uterine abnormality (eg, bicornuate uterus) Placenta accreta spectrum disorder Extreme preterm delivery Intraamniotic infection Intrauterine fetal demise Complications Postpartum hemorrhage Endometritis Management Manual placental extraction Dilation & curettage The third stage of labor (ie, fetal delivery until placental delivery) typically lasts <30 minutes. Signs of placental separation include a gush of blood, umbilical cord lengthening, increased uterine tone, and rising of the fundus in the abdomen. Following placental separation, uterine contractions typically cause placental expulsion. In contrast, delayed placental delivery occurs when the placenta does not deliver within 30 minutes, as in this patient. A common risk factor is extreme preterm delivery (eg, <26 weeks gestation) because these deliveries typically require prolonged oxytocin administration and are often complicated by intraamniotic infection, stillbirth, and placental disorders (eg, preeclampsia, placenta accreta). In addition, the prolonged oxytocin administration can cause a paradoxical decrease in myometrial contractility, thereby inhibiting placental expulsion. Intrauterine inflammation (eg, from intrauterine fetal demise) can also increase placental adhesion to the uterine wall. Patients with a retained placenta usually have profuse postpartum bleeding, which may be immediate or delayed. Initial management includes gentle downward cord traction and oxytocin administration to promote placental separation and expulsion. If the placenta does not deliver with these measures, manual placental extraction or dilation and curettage are indicated. (Choice A) Abruptio placentae can cause vaginal bleeding and fetal demise due to premature placental separation. However, patients typically have antepartum (not postpartum) bleeding and premature (not delayed) placental detachment. (Choice B) Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) can occur with severe postpartum bleeding. Patients typically have bleeding from mucosal surfaces and intravenous lines. This patient's vaginal bleeding has clotted, making DIC unlikely. (Choice D) Uterine inversion, typically caused by excessive umbilical cord traction and an adherent placenta, can cause postpartum hemorrhage. However, patients typically have a smooth mass (ie, the inverted uterus) protruding from the cervix or vagina. (Choice E) Uterine rupture is a full-thickness disruption of the myometrium. Although it can cause vaginal bleeding and fetal demise, patients typically have intense abdominal pain and antepartum bleeding. In addition, uterine rupture is unlikely in patients with no prior uterine surgery. (Choice F) A vaginal hematoma typically occurs in patients with fetal macrosomia or forceps-assisted vaginal delivery and causes bleeding in the paravaginal space. Patients typically have a vaginal mass and concealed bleeding. Educational objective: A retained placenta, or lack of placental delivery within 30 minutes of fetal delivery, can present with immediate or delayed vaginal bleeding and increase maternal morbidity due to postpartum hemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 24 weeks gestation comes to the emergency department due to not feeling fetal movement for 2 days. An ultrasound at 18 weeks gestation revealed a fetus with multiple anomalies and a posterior placenta. The patient's first pregnancy was uncomplicated, and the infant was delivered vaginally. An ultrasound confirms the absence of fetal heart movement. The patient is admitted to labor and delivery and delivers a 275 g (9.7 oz), stillborn infant vaginally after induction with multiple doses of misoprostol. After 30 minutes, the placenta has not delivered, and an oxytocin infusion is initiated. Ninety minutes after delivery of the infant, the patient has profuse bleeding that soaks the sheets. Current temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min. Examination shows a large volume of clotted blood in the vaginal vault. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's bleeding?

questions.explanation: This patient likely has urgency incontinence, which is the sense of urinary urgency followed by immediate loss of urine. It occurs due to involuntary detrusor contractions and is often associated with overactive bladder, a syndrome of disruptive urgency (eg, leaving work meetings, urinating every hour), frequency, and nocturia (eg, leaking at night). The resulting recurrent loss of urine may cause patients to wear pads daily, change clothes frequently due to soaked undergarments, and endure constant wetness that can result in vulvar rash and irritation (eg, diffusely erythematous vulva), as seen in this patient. First-line treatment of urgency incontinence includes bladder training and pelvic floor muscle (Kegel) exercises. Bladder training involves resisting the urge to void for longer durations to increase bladder capacity. Antimuscarinics (eg, oxybutynin, tolterodine) inhibit detrusor contractions and may be added if symptoms persist despite behavioral therapy. (Choices A, B, and E) Bladder outlet obstruction (eg, due to large fibroids blocking the urethra), detrusor underactivity, and peripheral neuropathy are causes of urinary retention. These patients eventually leak urine due to increased intravesical pressure (ie, overflow incontinence). Diagnosis is with a postvoid residual urine volume of ≥150 mL in women. In contrast, this patient's postvoid residual is normal, making bladder outlet obstruction unlikely. (Choice C) Postmenopausal women (median age 51) are at risk for genitourinary syndrome of menopause (vulvovaginal atrophy) and associated urinary incontinence due to estrogen deficiency. Although this patient is age 53, her vagina is well rugated, which is consistent with adequate estrogen levels. (Choice F) Urethral hypermobility causes stress urinary incontinence (SUI), which is urine leakage with increased intraabdominal pressure (eg, cough, laugh, sneeze). Although this patient's urine leaks with running, her 20-minute delay in symptoms is inconsistent with SUI, which typically occurs immediately with a precipitating event. In addition, she has no leakage with the Valsalva maneuver (ie, bearing down), making SUI unlikely. Educational objective: Urgency incontinence, the sense of urinary urgency followed by an immediate loss of urine, occurs due to involuntary detrusor contractions. Treatment is with bladder training and pelvic floor muscle (Kegel) exercises; antimuscarinics may be added if symptoms persist.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 3, comes to the office due to vulvar irritation. The patient has had a vulvar rash for the last week, with no relief using over-the-counter ointments. She developed the rash after wearing pads daily for the past month. The patient wears the pads for leakage of urine, which soaks through her undergarments at night and during the day. She also feels the need to urinate every hour, often requiring her to leave work meetings. The patient used to run for 45 minutes but now can run only 20 minutes without leaking. She has no pain with urination. Pelvic examination shows a diffusely erythematous vulva and a well rugated vagina. The patient has a 12-week, irregularly contoured uterus. When she bears down, no leakage of urine occurs. Postvoid residual and urinalysis are normal. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for this patient's incontinence?

questions.explanation: This patient's clinical signs and symptoms along with the presence of basophilic stippling on peripheral blood smear are most likely the result of lead poisoning. Clinical manifestations of lead poisoning may include neurologic deficits (eg, peripheral neuropathy resulting in foot or wrist drop, cognitive dysfunction), gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, abdominal pain, constipation), and musculoskeletal symptoms (eg, joint pains, muscle aches). Patients can have fatigue or exertional dyspnea due to microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Basophilic stippling on peripheral smear is not diagnostic of lead poisoning as it may be seen in other conditions (eg, thalassemias, alcohol abuse), but in the appropriate clinical scenario its presence can aid in diagnosis. Lead poisoning in adults is commonly the result of occupational exposure (eg, plumbing, smelting, battery manufacturing and recycling) with respiratory tract absorption representing the most significant route of entry. This is in contrast to children, in whom the most common entry route is gastrointestinal absorption (eg, chips from lead-painted surfaces). (Choice A) Patients with acute myeloid leukemia often have constitutional symptoms (eg, fever, weight loss) in addition to fatigue (anemia) and easy bruising (thrombocytopenia). On peripheral smear, identification of Auer rods (needle-shaped collections of granular material) in the cytoplasm of leukemic cells aids in the diagnosis. (Choice B) Intravascular hemolysis is a form of hemolytic anemia in which red blood cells are destroyed inside blood vessels due to various causes (eg, autoimmune, G6PD deficiency, mechanical trauma). Schistocytes (fragmented red blood cells) can be seen on peripheral smear. Patients usually have an elevated reticulocyte count and low haptoglobin levels as free hemoglobin released into the bloodstream is taken up by haptoglobin. (Choice C) Iron overload may occur as a result of primary (eg, hereditary hemochromatosis) or secondary (eg, numerous blood transfusions) causes. Iron overload predominately affects the liver (cirrhosis), heart (cardiomyopathy), pancreas (diabetes), and skin (hyperpigmentation). (Choice E) Vitamin B12 deficiency typically causes neurologic abnormalities (eg, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive dysfunction, subacute combined degeneration) and megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils (>6 lobes). Educational objective: Adult lead poisoning is often the result of occupational inhalation exposure (eg, plumbing, smelting) and typically presents with neurologic deficits (eg, peripheral neuropathy with foot drop, cognitive dysfunction), gastrointestinal distress, and arthralgias/myalgias. Hematologic findings include microcytic, hypochromic anemia with basophilic stippling on peripheral smear.

questions.explanation: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is defined by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) >20 mm Hg at rest. PH can result from a direct change to the pulmonary arteries, which can be idiopathic (often hereditary) or due to HIV, drugs (eg, methamphetamines), or connective tissue disease; this type of PH is referred to as pulmonary arterial hypertension (group 1 PH). Alternately, PH can develop secondary to other disease processes, including the following: Left-sided heart disease (group 2 PH) Chronic lung disease with hypoxia (group 3 PH) Chronic thromboembolic disease (group 4 PH) Other (eg, sarcoidosis, hematologic disorders, metabolic disorders) (group 5 pH) This patient with concentric left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, severe left atrial enlargement, and lung crackles in the setting of normal LV ejection fraction likely has heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), and her PH is most likely secondary to left-sided heart failure (group 2 PH). In such patients, PH develops due to pulmonary venous hypertension that reflects backward to increase mPAP and, over time, leads to irreversible vascular remodeling and increased pulmonary vascular resistance. In addition to LV systolic or diastolic dysfunction, mitral or aortic valve disease is a common cause of group 2 PH. The management of group 2 PH is directed at treating the underlying left-sided heart disorder. (Choices A and B) Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension is frequently due to an underlying gene mutation and is most commonly seen in relatively young women (eg, age 30-50). It involves direct vascular proliferation and intimal hyperplasia of the pulmonary arterioles. Connective tissue diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic sclerosis can directly narrow and obliterate the pulmonary arterioles. This patient's left atrial enlargement and pulmonary crackles (signs of pulmonary venous hypertension) make group 2 PH more likely than group 1. (Choices C and E) Group 3 PH typically results from hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in the setting of chronic hypoxia from chronic lung disease (eg, interstitial lung disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). Group 4 PH occurs due to recurrent and chronic thromboembolic occlusion of the pulmonary arteries. As with group 1 PH, evidence of pulmonary venous hypertension is not expected with these causes of PH. Educational objective: Pulmonary hypertension in patients with left-sided heart disease (group 2) is secondary to elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures. Common causes include left ventricular systolic or diastolic dysfunction and mitral or aortic valve disease.

In addition to LV systolic or diastolic dysfunction, mitral or aortic valve disease is a common cause of group 2 PH.  The management of group 2 PH is directed at treating the underlying left-sided heart disorder.

wrongAnswers.B: See the shared discussion for choice A.
wrongAnswers.C: (Choices C and E)  Group 3 PH typically results from hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in the setting of chronic hypoxia from chronic lung disease (eg, interstitial lung disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease).  Group 4 PH occurs due to recurrent and chronic thromboembolic occlusion of the pulmonary arteries.  As with group 1 PH, evidence of pulmonary venous hypertension is not expected with these causes of PH.

questions.explanation: This patient with diabetes mellitus has new-onset peripheral edema and heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), suggesting nephrotic syndrome. Diabetic nephropathy is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in adults, and patients with long-standing diabetes mellitus who develop nephrotic range proteinuria can often be presumed to have diabetic nephropathy without having to undergo kidney biopsy. However, this patient has several features suggestive of a diagnosis other than diabetic nephropathy. Rapid development of overt diabetic nephropathy would be rare in a patient who had normal renal function (eg, serum creatinine of 1.0) 3 months ago, especially in the setting of relatively well-controlled blood glucose (eg, hemoglobin A1c of 7.2%). In addition, hematuria and red blood cell casts are uncommonly seen in diabetic nephropathy and are suggestive of glomerulonephritis. Such features reflecting a mixed nephrotic-nephritic syndrome are often seen in membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, both of which are immune-mediated. In addition, glomerulonephritis (eg, IgA nephropathy) may occasionally develop with diabetic nephropathy, creating a mixed picture. Because the diagnosis is unclear in this patient, further evaluation with kidney biopsy is needed to guide appropriate treatment. (Choice A) Angiotensin II receptor blocker and ACE inhibitor (eg, lisinopril) monotherapy decreases the rate of progression of nephropathy in patients with diabetes mellitus. However, combination therapy is not recommended due to an increased risk for complications (eg, hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury). (Choices B and C) CT scan of the abdomen (or CT urography) and cystoscopy are useful in ruling out genitourinary malignancy (eg, bladder carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma) in patients age >40 with hematuria. However, this patient's presentation of red blood cell casts and worsening renal function is suggestive of a glomerular source of bleeding, and kidney biopsy is indicated prior to other diagnostic testing for hematuria. (Choice E) The initiation of corticosteroids is important in slowing the progression of some etiologies of nephrotic syndrome (eg, minimal change disease), nephritic syndrome (eg, IgA nephropathy), and mixed nephrotic-nephritic syndrome. However, corticosteroids are not helpful in treating diabetic nephropathy and should not be initiated until a steroid-responsive disorder is proved via kidney biopsy. Educational objective: Diabetic nephropathy is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome, but a diagnosis of diabetic nephropathy cannot be assumed in the presence of atypical features (eg, hematuria, red blood cell casts) that suggest glomerulonephritis. In such cases of mixed nephrotic-nephritic syndrome, kidney biopsy is needed to establish a clear diagnosis and guide treatment.

questions.explanation: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) Clinical features Age <45 Ongoing or recent smoking history Distal limb ischemia, gangrene, ulceration due to nonatherosclerotic occlusion, thrombosis Evaluation Ischemia on vascular studies (eg, digital plethysmography) Segmental occlusion of small- & medium-sized vessels on angiography Treatment Smoking cessation This patient, a young smoker with gangrene and painful ulceration involving the distal lower extremity, has typical features of thromboangiitis obliterans (TAO, Buerger disease). TAO is usually seen in heavy smokers but has also been noted in individuals who use smokeless tobacco or marijuana. It is more common in men, but the prevalence in women may be increasing. TAO is characterized by nonatherosclerotic, inflammatory thrombosis, ischemia, and fibrosis affecting small and medium-sized vessels. Peripheral pulses may be diminished, but patients frequently have normal pulses and a normal ankle-brachial index. TAO is often considered a diagnosis of exclusion, and inflammatory markers (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate), autoimmune serologies (eg, antinuclear antibody), and coagulation studies are normal. Vascular studies (eg, digital plethysmography) will show impeded digital blood flow, and angiography will confirm segmental occlusion of small and medium-sized arteries. Complete smoking cessation is the only definitive treatment, and even low-level smoking or nicotine replacement therapy can cause progression of the disease. (Choice A) Acrocyanosis is a painless, bluish discoloration of extremities, often triggered by cold. It can be seen with smoking, other medical conditions, and the use of certain medications. It is not associated with ulcers or gangrene. (Choice B) Antiphospholipid syndrome can cause unexplained peripheral arterial thrombosis; however, lower extremity deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, pregnancy complications (eg, miscarriages), and transient ischemic attacks or strokes are much more common manifestations. (Choice C) Arteriography may be needed to distinguish TAO from atherosclerotic occlusion, and both may occur in the same individual. However, clinically significant atherosclerosis is unlikely in a young woman, and this patient's vascular examination is not consistent with atherosclerotic disease. (Choices D and E) Raynaud phenomenon (RP) is characterized by intermittent digital vasoconstriction associated with sharply demarcated color changes. It may occur in isolation (primary RP) or in association with an underlying disorder (eg, CREST syndrome/limited scleroderma). This patient has no skin thickening or sclerodactyly suggestive of CREST syndrome. In addition, although painful digital ulcers may occur with RP, symmetric upper extremity involvement is more common. Educational objective: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is a nonatherosclerotic, inflammatory, vaso-occlusive disorder of small and medium-sized vessels leading to ischemic ulcers and gangrene. It is usually seen in heavy smokers, and complete smoking cessation is the only effective treatment.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the office due to a month of tingling, numbness, discoloration, and pain in the first and second toes of her right foot. She had similar symptoms 6 months ago during winter but attributed her symptoms to the cold temperatures and did not seek medical attention. There is no associated fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, or urinary symptoms. Medical history is unremarkable. The patient works as a prison guard. She smokes a pack of cigarettes daily but does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. Vital signs are normal, and BMI is 24 kg/m2. Chest and abdominal examinations are normal. The toes of the right foot appear dusky, with areas of dry gangrene at the first and second toes and a tender superficial ulcer at the tip of the third toe. The remainder of the skin examination is normal. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are normal in both feet. Lower extremity motor strength and deep tendon reflexes are normal and symmetric. Laboratory studies show normal blood counts and renal and liver function tests. Fasting blood glucose is 78 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 15 mm/h. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis Clinical features Pathophysiology: airway insult (eg, infection, inhalation) with impaired clearance (eg, mucostasis, immunodeficiency) Chronic: daily production of voluminous, thick ± blood-tinged mucus Acute exacerbations: recurrent infections with mucopurulent sputum ± frank hemoptysis Etiologies/contributory conditions Airway obstruction (eg, cancer, foreign body) & mucostasis (eg, CF, ABPA) Immunodeficiency (eg, ↓Ig) & autoinflammatory disease (eg, Sjögren syndrome) Chronic/past infection (eg, mycobacteria) or toxic inhalation Evaluation High-resolution CT scan of the chest (needed for diagnosis): airway dilation Pulmonary function testing: obstructive pattern Investigation of etiologies (eg, Ig levels, respiratory cultures, bronchial obstruction) Treatment Address underlying disorders (eg, Ig replacement) Airway clearance (eg, chest physiotherapy), mucolytics Antibiotics to suppress bacterial overgrowth & treat exacerbations ABPA = allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis; CF = cystic fibrosis; Ig = immunoglobulin; RA = rheumatoid arthritis. This patient likely has bronchiectasis due to a recurrent cycle of infection, inflammation, and tissue damage that ultimately leads to bronchial dilation and airway destruction. Development of bronchiectasis requires an infectious insult in combination with impaired bacterial clearance (eg, impaired immune defenses, structural airway defect). A single episode of severe (often necrotizing) pneumonia (suggested in this patient by pneumonia requiring treatment in the intensive care unit) can contribute to the development of bronchiectasis through massive tissue damage and permanent structural lung changes that result in impaired bacterial clearance. The most frequent symptom of bronchiectasis is a persistent cough with mucopurulent sputum that may be streaked with blood; dyspnea, fatigue, and weight loss are common. Exacerbations may be frequent, are marked by an increase in symptom severity and change in sputum quality/color, and typically require antibiotics. Chest x-ray may reveal bronchial dilation and irregular peripheral opacities, suggesting the diagnosis, but definitive diagnosis typically requires a high-resolution CT scan of the chest. (Choice A) Airway infiltration by eosinophils occurs in diseases such as asthma, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Churg-Strauss syndrome), drug-induced pneumonitis, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and parasitic lung infection (eg, ascariasis, strongyloidiasis). Airway infiltration of neutrophils plays an important role in bronchiectasis, but a significant infiltration of eosinophils does not occur. (Choices B and D) Interstitial lung fibrosis occurs in interstitial lung disease (ILD) due to excess collagen deposition and altered re-epithelialization in response to tissue damage. Permanent enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles describes the alveolar destruction that occurs in emphysema due to smoking (centriacinar) or alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (panacinar). Recurrent bacterial respiratory infection, as seen in this patient, is not a characteristic of ILD or emphysema. (Choice E) Squamous cell lung carcinoma has a strong association with tobacco exposure and would be very unlikely in this young patient with no smoking history. Educational objective: Bronchiectasis is a disease of bronchial damage and dilation that is typically triggered by an underlying impairment of host defense. Inability to clear bacteria from the airways results in a recurrent cycle of bacterial overgrowth, neutrophilic infiltration, inflammation, and tissue damage.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man comes to the office due to chronic cough. A year ago, he had a severe episode of pneumonia that required 4 days in the intensive care unit. questions.explanation: Primary versus secondary adrenal insufficiency Primary Secondary Mechanism Destruction of bilateral adrenal cortex Disruption of hypothalamic-pituitary axis Possible etiologies Autoimmune adrenalitis Infection, malignancy Chronic glucocorticoid therapy Infiltrative disease Ischemia of anterior pituitary gland Cortisol ↓ ↓ Aldosterone ↓ Normal ACTH ↑ ↓ Clinical features More severe symptoms Hypovolemia Hyperkalemia, hyponatremia Hyperpigmentation Less severe symptoms Euvolemia Minimal electrolyte disturbance No hyperpigmentation Primary adrenal insufficiency (PAI) is characterized by injury to all 3 layers of the adrenal cortex (ie, zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis). Patients with PAI can therefore have features of glucocorticoid (eg, fatigue, loss of appetite, weight loss) and mineralocorticoid deficiencies (eg, orthostatic hypotension). Women can also have symptoms of androgen deficiency (eg, low libido) as the adrenals are a major source of androgens in women. In contrast, patients with central adrenal insufficiency will have only glucocorticoid deficiency as aldosterone production is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system and is not affected. Patients with PAI require replacement of both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid. Hydrocortisone has partial mineralocorticoid activity, but physiologic doses do not provide adequate mineralocorticoid activity for most patients. Signs of relative mineralocorticoid deficiency include hypotension, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia (Choices C and D), and elevated plasma renin activity. Addition of fludrocortisone is advised to correct this deficiency. (Choice A) Adrenal androgens (eg, androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate) are secreted from the zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex and will be diminished in PAI. (Choice E) The adrenal medulla is not directly affected in PAI, and total catecholamine production is normal. Epinephrine levels may be low as the conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine is catalyzed by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase, which is normally upregulated by cortisol from the adrenal cortex; however, norepinephrine levels will be normal. Educational objective: Primary adrenal insufficiency is characterized by features of glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency. Hydrocortisone has partial mineralocorticoid activity, but most patients will require additional mineralocorticoid supplementation. In central adrenal insufficiency, mineralocorticoid production is normal.

questions.explanation: Acute liver failure Etiology Viral hepatitis (eg, HSV; CMV; hepatitis A, B, D, E) Drug toxicity (eg, acetaminophen overdose, idiosyncratic) Ischemia (eg, shock liver, Budd-Chiari syndrome) Autoimmune hepatitis Wilson disease Malignant infiltration Clinical presentation Generalized symptoms (eg, fatigue, lethargy, anorexia, nausea) Right upper quadrant abdominal pain Pruritus & jaundice due to hyperbilirubinemia Renal insufficiency Thrombocytopenia Hypoglycemia Diagnostic requirements Severe acute liver injury (ALT & AST often >1,000 U/L) Signs of hepatic encephalopathy (eg, confusion, asterixis) Synthetic liver dysfunction (INR ≥1.5) ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; CMV = cytomegalovirus; HSV = herpes simplex virus. Acute liver failure (ALF) (sometimes termed fulminant hepatic failure) is a syndrome characterized by severe hepatocellular injury in the absence of chronic liver disease (eg, cirrhosis). Likely etiologies in this patient include acetaminophen toxicity (frequent use for tension-type headache) and viral hepatitis (unprotected sex); however, many other causes (eg, idiosyncratic drug reaction, autoimmune hepatitis, liver ischemia, malignancy, Wilson disease) have been described. Diagnostic criteria for ALF are as follows: Severe, acute (<26 weeks) liver injury: Hepatic transaminases are often dramatically elevated (eg, >10 times the upper limit of normal) Liver synthetic dysfunction: A prolonged PT (ie, INR >1.5) is very sensitive because factor VII, which is produced by the liver, has a half-life of only 3-6 hours. In contrast, a decreased albumin level is less sensitive and occurs later due to albumin's longer half-life (~20 days) (Choice A). Hepatic encephalopathy: Common manifestations seen in this patient include somnolence, disorientation, and asterixis. Patients may also have fatigue, anorexia, nausea, pruritus, and edema. Tachycardia and relative hypotension are common due to intravascular volume depletion, and low-grade fever may occur. Physical examination may show right upper quadrant tenderness and jaundice. In addition to markedly elevated aminotransferases and evidence of coagulopathy, laboratory studies may also show anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypoglycemia, and electrolyte imbalances; however, these findings are not specific for ALF and are not part of the diagnostic criteria. ALF carries a grave prognosis and often prompts consideration for liver transplantation. (Choices B, D, and E) Serum alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, and bilirubin levels can be elevated in some cases of ALF but are characteristically more closely associated with biliary disease than with hepatocellular (eg, acetaminophen toxicity, viral hepatitis) disease. Levels are relatively variable and are not necessary for the diagnosis of ALF. (Choice C) Acute renal insufficiency, as evidenced by elevated serum creatinine levels, is common in ALF (up to 70% of cases) and is likely due to decreased renal perfusion (and direct renal tubular toxicity in the case of acetaminophen overdose). However, it is nonspecific and does not confirm the diagnosis of ALF. Educational objective: Acute liver failure is characterized by the triad of severe acute liver injury (elevated aminotransferase levels), hepatic encephalopathy, and impaired liver synthetic function (prolonged PT) in a patient without preexisting liver disease.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to a change in mental status. Symptoms started a week ago with low-grade fever, malaise, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia; he then developed progressive confusion and drowsiness. Medical history includes chronic tension-type headaches, for which the patient takes acetaminophen several times a week. He uses intravenous drugs and has frequently engaged in unprotected sex with anonymous men and women. Temperature is 37.9 C (100.2 F), blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg, and pulse is 112/min. The patient is somnolent and wakes to painful stimuli; he is disoriented but follows simple instructions. Physical examination shows jaundice, asterixis, and tender hepatomegaly. Acute liver failure is suspected. Which of the following laboratory findings is most useful to confirm the diagnosis in this patient?

questions.explanation: A galactocele is a benign milk retention cyst that typically occurs a few weeks to months after cessation of breastfeeding, when milk stagnates. Galactoceles may occur less commonly during lactation or, rarely, late in the third trimester. Dried, deposited proteins in the lactiferous duct cause blockage; milk accumulation behind the obstruction results in a soft, mobile, nontender subareolar mass as large as 5 cm. No intervention is required for an asymptomatic galactocele; symptomatic galactoceles may be needle aspirated. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality for diagnosis; aspiration confirms the diagnosis and is curative. Ice packs and a supportive, well-fitting bra provide symptomatic relief. (Choice A) Patients with a breast abscess typically have fever and a tender, fluctuant breast mass with surrounding erythema. (Choice B) Fat necrosis can present as a nontender breast mass; however, it is typically the result of trauma and is associated with ecchymosis, which is not seen in this patient. (Choice C) Fibroadenomas are a common benign (eg, mobile, nontender) breast mass in adolescents and young women. Fibroadenomas increase in size in response to estrogen, which is why they present during adolescence and involute in postmenopausal women; therefore, they are less likely to develop as new masses in recently breastfeeding (ie, estrogen-deficient) patients. (Choice D) Fibrocystic breast disease typically presents as diffuse, bilateral changes rather than a unilateral breast mass. (Choice F) An intraductal papilloma can present as a singular, nontender mass near the nipple; however, it is usually small (≤1 cm), solid, and irregularly shaped, with bloody nipple discharge. Educational objective: A galactocele may occur weeks to months after cessation of breastfeeding and is due to ductal blockage with resulting milk accumulation. Examination shows a soft, mobile, nontender mass in the subareolar region. Diagnosis is made with ultrasound and needle aspiration.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the office due to a right breast mass. The patient first noticed the mass several weeks ago and it has slowly increased in size. She had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery 7 months ago and exclusively breastfed her baby for 6 months. The patient has not had a breast mass before. She uses a progestin-releasing subcutaneous implant for contraception. Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F) and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination of the right breast shows a soft, mobile, nontender 4-cm subareolar mass. No skin changes, nipple discharge or retraction, or axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy is present. The left breast has no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

questions.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy Precipitating factors Drugs (eg, sedatives, narcotics) Hypovolemia (eg, diarrhea) Electrolyte changes (eg, hypokalemia) ↑ Nitrogen load (eg, GI bleeding) Infection (eg, pneumonia, UTI, SBP) Portosystemic shunting (eg, TIPS) Clinical presentation Sleep pattern changes Altered mental status Ataxia Asterixis Treatment Correct precipitating causes (eg, fluids, antibiotics) ↓ Blood ammonia concentration (eg, lactulose, rifaximin) GI = gastrointestinal; SBP = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; TIPS = transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt; UTI = urinary tract infection. This patient with cirrhosis has recurrent hepatic encephalopathy (HE) manifesting as mild confusion, slowed movements, asterixis (flapping hand tremor), and sleep disturbance. Given that she is already taking an appropriate amount of lactulose to reduce her serum ammonia levels (as she has 2 or 3 semiformed stools daily), a nonabsorbable antibiotic (eg, rifaximin) should be added. In HE, antibiotics are thought to act by decreasing ammonia-producing bacteria in the colon. In addition to the administration of medications to reduce the serum ammonia level, management of HE also includes determining any precipitating factors (eg, infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, electrolyte disturbances) and treating them. This patient is compliant with her medications, has no evidence of infection or gastrointestinal bleeding, and has normal electrolytes and renal function. HE may be due to progression of her cirrhosis, and the most appropriate next step would be adding a second agent to her drug regimen to lower serum ammonia level. (Choice A) Patients with cirrhosis tend to be malnourished; therefore, dietary protein restriction is generally not recommended. Protein-free diets can cause a negative nitrogen balance and increase mortality. Protein restriction is generally limited only to patients with cirrhosis who have required transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting (TIPS). (Choice B) Glucocorticoid therapy is used in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis (eg, discriminant function >32), not in those with HE unrelated to alcohol intake. (Choice C) Lorazepam would be used for alcohol withdrawal, which would be associated with tachycardia and hypertension. It is also sometimes used for management of insomnia; however, this patient's sleep pattern disturbances are likely due to HE. In patients with cirrhosis, benzodiazepines should be used judiciously as they are metabolized by the liver. (Choice E) TIPS is performed when a patient has ascites that does not respond to medical therapy (eg, diuretics) or ongoing active or recurrent bleeding from varices even after appropriate treatment with upper endoscopy. TIPS can worsen HE due to ammonia-rich blood being shunted past the liver. Educational objective: Patients with hepatic encephalopathy who have recurrent encephalopathy and are compliant with their medications should have a nonabsorbable antibiotic (eg, rifaximin) added to lactulose to prevent further episodes.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman is brought to the office by her husband for evaluation of confusion. She has a history of cirrhosis with ascites due to primary sclerosing cholangitis. The patient has had several hospitalizations for hepatic encephalopathy. Since yesterday, she has been mildly confused and her movements have "slowed." The patient also had trouble sleeping last night. She has 2 or 3 semiformed stools daily and has had no fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, or melena. The patient takes ursodeoxycholic acid, spironolactone, furosemide, and lactulose and is compliant with the medications. She does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 37.2 C (98.9 F), blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 78/min. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. The abdomen is nontender with moderate distension. Stool guaiac is negative. The patient has mild asterixis and incoordination. She is not able to spell "world" backwards. Laboratory testing shows normal electrolytes and creatinine. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment for this patient?

questions.explanation: Chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity Type I Associated with anthracyclines Myocyte necrosis & destruction (fibrosis) Progression to dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure More likely to be irreversible Type II Associated with trastuzumab Myocardial stunning/hibernation without myocyte destruction More likely to be reversible This clinical presentation - exertional dyspnea, displaced apical impulse, third heart sound, and cardiomegaly - is consistent with the development of dilated cardiomyopathy, most likely due to chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity. Anthracyclines (eg, doxorubicin, daunorubicin, epirubicin, idarubicin) are chemotherapy agents that are commonly implicated in chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity and can cause acute/subacute or chronic cardiotoxicity. Anthracycline cardiotoxicity usually presents with an asymptomatic decline in left ventricular systolic function that progresses to overt heart failure. It is thought to be due to oxidative damage of cellular membranes and to cardiac myocyte necrosis and death (induced by a topoisomerase II enzyme/anthracycline/DNA complex) with eventual replacement by fibrous tissue. Anthracycline cardiotoxicity is less likely to be reversible, and the risk of development is most strongly related to the total cumulative dose of chemotherapy. (Choice A) Cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and disarray are seen in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, an autosomal dominant condition that causes a systolic murmur due to left ventricular outflow obstruction. (Choice C) Ischemic myocardial necrosis leading to left ventricular systolic dysfunction is seen in patients with a prior myocardial infarction due to coronary heart disease. (Choice D) Trastuzumab-related cardiotoxicity is due to loss of myocardial contractility (myocardial stunning) and usually manifests as an asymptomatic decline in left ventricular ejection fraction. It is not related to the cumulative dose of trastuzumab received and is often reversible after discontinuation of trastuzumab therapy. Myocardial stunning can also occur with stress-induced cardiomyopathy, which tends to present acutely (often following an emotional trigger) and is transient. (Choice E) Radiation therapy to the chest for patients with Hodgkin lymphoma can lead to thickening and fibrosis of the pericardium. This patient has not received radiation therapy. Educational objective: Anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity is due to cardiac myocyte necrosis and death, and presents with an asymptomatic decline in left ventricular systolic function with progression to overt heart failure. It is less likely to be reversible, and the risk of development is related to the total cumulative dose of chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man comes to the office due to 2 months of progressive exertional shortness of breath and frequent nonproductive cough. Currently, he can hardly walk 3 blocks without stopping due to difficulty breathing. He has had no chest pain, lightheadedness, syncope, or lower extremity swelling. The patient has a history of Hodgkin lymphoma treated with combination chemotherapy a year ago. The chemotherapy regimen included doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine. He has no family history of heart or lung disease. The patient is afebrile. Blood pressure is 122/75 mm Hg and pulse is 88/min and regular. Lungs are clear to auscultation. The apical impulse is palpated at the anterior axillary line in the sixth intercostal space. A third heart sound is heard on cardiac auscultation. Chest x-ray reveals clear lung fields and cardiomegaly. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's current presentation?

questions.explanation: During thyroid surgery, the parathyroid glands can be inadvertently removed or injured by direct trauma or devascularization. This can lead to transient or permanent postoperative hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. Treatment of hypocalcemia requires supplementation with oral calcium and calcitriol (active form of vitamin D). Hyperphosphatemia is treated with avoidance of phosphate-rich foods and sometimes with oral phosphate binders. With permanent postoperative hypoparathyroidism, lifelong therapy and close monitoring are required to maintain normal serum calcium and phosphorus levels. A calcium-phosphorus product (serum calcium × serum phosphorus) >55 increases the risk of soft tissue calcification. This patient, who has not had consistent laboratory monitoring, has hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and an elevated calcium-phosphorus product (7.8 × 7.4 = 57.7). Deposition of calcium (possibly induced by hyperphosphatemia) in the basal ganglia, a complication associated with chronic hypoparathyroidism, has led to extrapyramidal manifestations (eg, movement disorders). Other potential complications of chronic hypoparathyroidism include nephrocalcinosis and cataracts. (Choice A) Chronic cannabis use can cause neurocognitive deficits and psychosis. Neuroimaging findings include atrophy of the medial temporal cortex, temporal pole, parahippocampal cortex, amygdala, and orbitofrontal cortex. Cannabis use would not cause basal ganglion calcification or explain this patient's electrolyte abnormalities. (Choice C) Recurrent cancer is uncommon in young patients with papillary thyroid cancer, especially after 10 years. In addition, elevated antithyroglobulin antibody and thyroglobulin levels are sometimes seen with recurrence. (Choice D) Excess intake of vitamin A can lead to dry skin and desquamation, cerebral edema, visual disturbances, fatigue, anorexia, and gastrointestinal upset. However, it would not explain the electrolyte abnormalities seen in this patient. In addition, extrapyramidal features are not typical with vitamin A toxicity, and this patient's skin findings can be explained by chronic hypocalcemia. (Choice E) Vitamin D toxicity would be associated with hyper- rather than hypocalcemia. Educational objective: Treatment of chronic hypoparathyroidism is with calcium and vitamin D, but calcium and phosphorus levels must be closely monitored. A calcium-phosphorus product (serum calcium × serum phosphorus) >55 increases the risk of soft tissue calcification. Calcification in the basal ganglia can cause extrapyramidal manifestations.

explanationPanel.html:
Educational objective:
Treatment of chronic hypoparathyroidism is with calcium and vitamin D, but calcium and phosphorus levels must be closely monitored.  A calcium-phosphorus product (serum calcium × serum phosphorus) >55 increases the risk of soft tissue calcification.  Calcification in the basal ganglia can cause extrapyramidal manifestations.

During thyroid surgery, the parathyroid glands can be inadvertently removed or injured by direct trauma or devascularization.  This can lead to transient or permanent postoperative hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia.  Treatment of hypocalcemia requires supplementation with oral calcium and calcitriol (active form of vitamin D).  Hyperphosphatemia is treated with avoidance of phosphate-rich foods and sometimes with oral phosphate binders.

With permanent postoperative hypoparathyroidism, lifelong therapy and close monitoring are required to maintain normal serum calcium and phosphorus levels.  A calcium-phosphorus product (serum calcium × serum phosphorus) >55 increases the risk of soft tissue calcification.  This patient, who has not had consistent laboratory monitoring, has hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and an elevated calcium-phosphorus product (7.8 × 7.4 = 57.7).  Deposition of calcium (possibly induced by hyperphosphatemia) in the basal ganglia, a complication associated with chronic hypoparathyroidism, has led to extrapyramidal manifestations (eg, movement disorders).  Other potential complications of chronic hypoparathyroidism include nephrocalcinosis and cataracts.

wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Vitamin D toxicity would be associated with hyper- rather than hypocalcemia.

questions.explanation: Several factors increase this patient's risk for postoperative pulmonary complications (eg, atelectasis, pneumonia, need for mechanical ventilation, exacerbation of underlying pulmonary disease), including: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) Active smoking Obesity Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) Age >65 Open thoracic surgery (eg, coronary artery bypass) Preoperative physical therapy (eg, aerobic exercise, inspiratory muscle training) significantly reduces the postoperative incidence of atelectasis and pneumonia and shortens the length of postoperative hospital stay in patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery. Smoking cessation is also helpful in reducing perioperative pulmonary risk, but that benefit may be present only when smoking is stopped >8 weeks prior to surgery. (Choice A) Use of preoperative antibiotics (eg, azithromycin) has not been shown to reduce pulmonary complications in patients without signs of active infection. (Choice B) Use of a perioperative cough suppressant may impair mucus clearance from the respiratory tract and increase the risk of postoperative pneumonia. (Choice C) Optimization of COPD prior to surgery may lead to better outcomes. However, inhaled corticosteroids increase the risk of pneumonia. Small studies have shown some benefit with the use of oral corticosteroids in patients with COPD throughout the perioperative period, but their use has not been widely adopted. (Choice D) The use of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is strongly advised in the postoperative period in patients with moderate to severe OSA. CPAP use is especially important as residual anesthetic effects may further impair the ability of patients with OSA to maintain a patent airway, and opiates (frequently used for postoperative pain control) reduce respiratory drive and increase the risk of a serious apneic event. CPAP likely significantly reduces the incidence of serious postoperative apneic events in patients with OSA. However, a reduction in the risk of postoperative pneumonia has not been well demonstrated. Educational objective: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, obstructive sleep apnea, active smoking, obesity, and advanced age are risk factors for postoperative pulmonary complications such as pneumonia. Preoperative physical therapy helps reduce the postoperative risk of pneumonia and shortens postoperative hospital stay.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is scheduled for elective coronary artery bypass grafting surgery in 2 weeks. questions.explanation: Viral pleuritis (viral pleurisy) Clinical presentation Viral prodrome (eg, cough, rhinorrhea) Pleuritic chest pain Shallowing breathing & dyspnea Pleural friction rub Absence of pleural effusion Treatment Supportive care & analgesia with NSAIDs NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. This patient most likely has viral pleuritis (viral pleurisy). Several viruses have been implicated in causing pleuritis, including parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and coxsackievirus. The parietal pleura is innervated by somatic pain receptors, and the inflammation of pleuritis causes friction and sharp pain as the parietal pleura moves against the visceral pleura (which is not innervated) during respiration. This pleuritic chest pain may radiate to the shoulder and may be severe, causing reduced lung expansion with a rapid and shallow respiratory pattern, resulting in dyspnea. Most patients have a viral prodrome (ie, preceding coldlike symptoms), and physical examination may demonstrate a pleural friction rub (ie, coarse grating sound). Chest x-ray is typically unremarkable, revealing no airspace disease or pleural effusion. The preferred treatment is with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which provide analgesia without suppressing respiratory drive. Other causes of pleuritis include bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis, malignancy, and autoimmune disease (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus), but viral infection is most common. (Choice A) Acute cholecystitis typically presents with fever and right upper quadrant abdominal pain that may radiate to the right shoulder. It is unlikely in the absence of abdominal tenderness. (Choice B) Pneumonia due to atypical bacterial organisms (eg, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae) usually presents with fever, fatigue, cough, and myalgias. Reticular interstitial markings are expected on chest x-ray. (Choice C) Costochondritis commonly causes sharp, centrally located chest pain that is worse with breathing or movement; however, the pain is unlikely to radiate to the shoulder. In addition, this patient's recent viral infection makes viral pleuritis more likely. (Choice D) Herpes zoster (shingles) can cause bandlike pain in a dermatomal distribution along the chest. However, the pain is not typically pleuritic, and a vesicular rash is usually present within 2 days of pain onset. (Choice E) Pulmonary embolism (PE) usually presents with pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea; however, significant PE is unlikely in the absence of tachycardia. In addition, this patient's viral prodrome and lack of risk factors for venous thromboembolism make viral pleuritis more likely. (Choice F) Reflux esophagitis typically causes burning, substernal chest discomfort that is exacerbated by lying down and is not worsened by breathing. Educational objective: Pleuritis (or pleurisy) is an inflammation of the parietal pleura that causes pleuritic chest pain, often with reduced lung expansion and dyspnea. It is usually caused by a viral infection and is characterized by a viral prodrome and the absence of pleural effusion.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to chest pain. The patient says, "I had a cold a few days ago, which subsided, but then 2 days ago I started having sharp pains under the right breast. It's hard to breathe or sit up straight, and I also feel pain in the right shoulder area." The patient has a history of a hiatal hernia and gastroesophageal reflux. She does not use tobacco but drinks alcohol occasionally. Temperature is 37.3 C (99.1 F), blood pressure is 120/74 mm Hg, pulse is 86/min, and respirations are 20/min. Lung percussion is resonant throughout, and auscultation reveals vesicular breath sounds bilaterally with no added sounds. The abdomen is nondistended, soft, and nontender. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Chest x-ray is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) History Asthma Cystic fibrosis Chest imaging Recurrent fleeting infiltrates Bronchiectasis Diagnosis Positive Aspergillus skin test &/or IgE Elevated serum IgE Eosinophilia Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is characterized by hypersensitivity to inhaled Aspergillus fumigatus and typically occurs in patients with underlying asthma or cystic fibrosis. The pathogenesis of ABPA is not completely understood, but the disease is likely due to a combination of impaired airway clearance and enhanced immune response to Aspergillus. Patients often present with symptoms of poorly controlled asthma with recurrent exacerbations; severe disease can manifest as recurrent infiltrates, fever, cough productive of brownish sputum, and hemoptysis. Central bronchiectasis commonly results from a recurrent cycle of inflammation. Peripheral eosinophilia is typically present, but ABPA is usually diagnosed using skin testing and Aspergillus-specific IgE levels. Treatment requires oral corticosteroids for several months in combination with the antifungal agent itraconazole. (Choice B) Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes early-onset, basilar-predominant emphysema. Dyspnea and chronic sputum production are common. Eosinophilia and an association with asthma are not characteristic. (Choice C) Along with asthma, cystic fibrosis (CF) is the other common underlying condition in patients with ABPA. However, in this adult patient with a history of asthma, concomitant undiagnosed CF would be highly unlikely. CF usually presents in childhood; adults are more likely to have an atypical initial presentation (eg, gastrointestinal manifestations). (Choices D and E) Patients with selective IgA deficiency are typically asymptomatic but may develop recurrent respiratory infections. Immotile cilia syndrome can cause recurrent respiratory infections due to impaired mucociliary clearance. Bronchiectasis can occur in both disorders, but neither is associated with eosinophilia or uncontrolled asthma. (Choices F and G) Legionella infection causes pneumonia that may be severe and is typically characterized by high fever and concomitant gastrointestinal symptoms. Acute tuberculosis typically presents with apical infiltrates and can rarely cause a lower lobe infiltrate. This patient's presentation with recurrent respiratory exacerbations, uncontrolled asthma symptoms, and eosinophilia is more consistent with ABPA than infection with either Legionella or M tuberculosis. (Choice H) Pulmonary sarcoidosis is characterized by reticular lung opacities and hilar adenopathy. Focal infiltrate and bronchiectasis are not typical. Educational objective: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus that usually occurs in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis. It typically presents with symptoms of uncontrolled asthma and can lead to recurrent pulmonary infiltrates and bronchiectasis. Treatment involves long-term oral corticosteroids and itraconazole.

questions.explanation: Small bowel obstruction Clinical presentation Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting Inability to pass flatus or stool if complete (no obstipation if partial) Hyperactive → absent bowel sounds Distended & tympanitic abdomen Diagnosis Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels on plain film or CT scan Partial: air in colon Complete: transition point (abrupt cutoff), no air in colon Complications Ischemia/necrosis (strangulation) Bowel perforation Management Bowel rest, nasogastric tube suction, intravenous fluids Surgical exploration for signs of complications This patient with intractable vomiting and dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels has a small bowel obstruction (SBO), a blockage that obstructs the flow of intestinal contents. In this patient with an adnexal mass, ascites, and omental caking, the SBO is likely due to advanced ovarian cancer, in which the omental metastases extrinsically compress the intestine. As the small bowel is compressed, the stomach becomes increasingly distended due to impaired food and water transit. With increasing intestinal compression, complete obstruction can occur, and patients develop intractable nausea and vomiting resulting in dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities (ie, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis), and air-fluid levels on abdominal x-ray. Distal to the obstruction, the lack of intestinal peristalsis leads to obstipation and absent bowel sounds. Most cases of SBO can be managed nonoperatively with electrolyte replacement, serial abdominal examinations, and decompression of the distended gastrointestinal (GI) tract with a nasogastric tube because the SBO can resolve spontaneously (Choice B). However, immediate surgery should be considered for patients who have an acute SBO with signs of bowel ischemia and necrosis, such as fever, leukocytosis, and elevated lactate (as in this patient). An exploratory laparotomy is performed to relieve the mechanical obstruction; resect necrotic bowel segments; and potentially treat the underlying cause (eg, tumor debulking), which nasogastric tube placement by itself would not. (Choice C) Paracentesis is performed for symptom relief (eg, abdominal distension) and histopathologic diagnosis (cytology) in patients with ascites due to advanced ovarian cancer. However, in this patient who has SBO with signs of ischemia requires immediate surgery rather than paracentesis. (Choice D) In patients with an SBO from adhesions, nonoperative management includes oral administration of Gastrografin, a hypertonic solution that stimulates intestinal movement and decreases bowel wall edema by pulling fluid into the lumen. In patients with concern for intestinal ischemia, Gastrografin is contraindicated due to the risk of intestinal perforation. (Choice E) An upper GI series with small bowel follow-through evaluates small intestine function and motility. It is contraindicated in a patient with signs of intestinal ischemia due to the risk of intestinal perforation with the increased pressure from barium swallow. Educational objective: Ovarian malignancy can manifest with acute small bowel obstruction and signs of bowel necrosis (eg, fever, leukocytosis). CT scan may show omental caking along with dilated loops of bowel and air-fluid levels. Exploratory laparotomy is required for treatment.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance due to intractable vomiting. The vomiting started suddenly a day ago and has been accompanied by worsening crampy abdominal pain. The patient has been unable to tolerate any oral intake and has neither passed gas nor had a bowel movement since the onset of her symptoms. questions.explanation: Genital warts (condylomata acuminata) Etiology HPV 6, 11 & other low-risk strains Clinical features Pink, skin-colored, hyperpigmented lesions Smooth or cauliflower-like papules/nodules Treatment Lesions <1 cm: imiquimod, cryotherapy, sinecatechins, podophyllotoxin, trichloroacetic acid Lesions >1 cm: excision, laser therapy, electrosurgery Screen for other STIs Recurrence is common Prevention Vaccination Barrier contraception HPV = human papillomavirus; STIs = sexually transmitted infections. This patient has condylomata acuminata (anogenital warts), which are caused by low-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11. Anogenital warts tend to increase in size and number during pregnancy due to physiologic, pregnancy-associated immunosuppression (ie, reduced cell-mediated immunity). They appear as fleshy, pedunculated, or sessile growths, sometimes coalescing into larger lesions. Treatment is based on patient preference, symptoms (eg, pruritis), and pregnancy status. First-line treatment in pregnancy is with topical trichloroacetic acid, which creates a chemical injury that induces wart regression. Imiquimod and podophyllin resin are contraindicated due to potential teratogenicity. Excisional biopsy is typically avoided during pregnancy due to increased anesthetic and surgical risks, but it may be performed for large, coalesced lesions in nonpregnant patients (Choice B). However, none of these therapies eliminates HPV presence or infectivity. Perinatal HPV transmission can result in juvenile-onset respiratory papillomatosis, a rare complication in which condylomata acuminata form on a child's larynx and/or vocal cords, resulting in stridor, chronic hoarseness, or cough. However, cesarean delivery does not reduce the risk of vertical transmission and is therefore reserved for large condylomata that block the introitus or pose a bleeding risk with vaginal delivery. (Choice A) Colposcopy is performed for abnormal cervical cancer screening (eg, high-grade intraepithelial lesions), typically due to high-risk HPV types 16 and 18. In this patient, recent cervical cancer screening was negative. (Choice C) Benzathine penicillin G treats condylomata lata (a complication of secondary syphilis), which are raised, gray or white lesions affecting mucous membranes (eg, mouth, perineum) that may be accompanied by a maculopapular rash on the palms and soles. (Choice D) Topical corticosteroids are used for inflammatory vulvar conditions such as lichen sclerosus (thin, pale, wrinkled skin and vulvar lichenification) and lichen planus (erosive, violet plaque–forming, vulvar lesions). (Choice F) Viral culture of genital ulcers is used to diagnose herpes simplex virus. Although anogenital warts are caused by low-risk HPV, viral culture is not performed as it does not change management. (Choice G) Wet mount microscopy differentiates common causes of vaginitis (eg, vulvovaginal erythema, vaginal discharge) such as trichomoniasis and vulvovaginal candidiasis. It is not indicated in evaluation of condyloma acuminata. Educational objective: Condylomata acuminata (anogenital warts) may worsen during pregnancy due to physiologic immunosuppression. Topical trichloroacetic acid is first-line therapy in pregnancy, although no treatment modality prevents vertical transmission.
