questions.explanation: This patient with painless, rapid, and transient monocular visual loss (<10 minutes) has amaurosis fugax. The most common etiology is retinal ischemia due to atherosclerotic emboli originating from plaques in the ipsilateral carotid artery. When an embolus occludes an artery supplying the retina (eg, ophthalmic or central retinal artery), hypoxia ensues and results in transient vision deficits. After the embolus is broken up or displaced, vision returns. Patients may experience mild blurring to complete monocular blindness involving all or part of the visual field. Funduscopic examination may show embolic plaques and retinal whitening (due to ischemia). Patients with amaurosis fugax and vascular risk factors (eg, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, smoking) should receive carotid imaging (eg, duplex ultrasound) to evaluate for atherosclerotic disease. Medical management includes smoking cessation, aspirin, and treatment of vascular comorbidities to reduce the risk of stroke. Surgical evaluation may be necessary in patients who are candidates for carotid endarterectomy. (Choice A) Diabetic retinopathy typically causes progressive bilateral vision loss and is characterized by dot and blot hemorrhages, exudates, and macular edema with or without neovascularization on funduscopy. This patient's recurrent, transient monocular vision loss is more concerning for atheroembolic carotid artery disease. (Choice B) Temporal arteritis is a systemic inflammatory disease that affects individuals age >50 and is characterized by inflammation of the large- and medium-size arteries of the head. Involvement of the ophthalmic artery may lead to transient monocular vision loss; however, associated features (eg, malaise, fever, polymyalgia rheumatica, jaw claudication) are not evident in this patient. (Choice C) In patients with atrial fibrillation, stasis of blood in the left atrium may lead to the formation of a thrombus that can dislodge and occlude the central retinal artery, resulting in amaurosis fugax. This patient has a normal heart rate and rhythm, making atrial fibrillation and cardioembolism less likely. (Choice D) Occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery can cause unilateral infarction of the primary visual cortex, resulting in contralateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparring (macula receives collateral circulation from the middle cerebral artery). (Choice E) Middle cerebral artery occlusion typically results in profound neurologic deficits, such as contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss, homonymous hemianopsia, and gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion. Educational objective: Amaurosis fugax is characterized by painless, rapid, and transient (<10 minutes) monocular vision loss. The most common etiology is retinal ischemia due to atherosclerotic emboli originating from plaques in the ipsilateral carotid artery.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to painless vision loss in his left eye. The patient states that he was watching television when suddenly everything became dark and he could not see out of his left eye. This resolved spontaneously after approximately 5 minutes and was not associated with headache, slurred speech, numbness, or weakness. He experienced a similar episode several months ago, at which time he did not seek medical attention. His medical history is significant for hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia; he admits that he is not compliant with his medication regimen. Two years ago, the patient was hospitalized for hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, and his HbA1c level 4 months ago was 9.5%. He has a 30-pack-year smoking history. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg, and pulse is 80/min and regular. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

questions.explanation: Diagnostic features of dementia with Lewy bodies Central (required) Progressive cognitive decline, dementia Core Fluctuating cognition Visual hallucinations (detailed, recurrent) Spontaneous parkinsonism features REM sleep behavior disorder (eg, dream enactment) Suggestive Severe antipsychotic sensitivity SPECT or PET showing low dopamine transporter uptake in basal ganglia Supportive Repeated falls Syncope or near-syncope Severe autonomic dysfunction Delusions Depression or anxiety Conflicting (make DLB less likely) Neuroimaging showing cerebrovascular disease Parkinsonism appearing first, with dementia later DLB = dementia with Lewy bodies; PET = positron emission tomography; SPECT = single-photon emission computed tomography. This patient likely has dementia with Lewy bodies, the second leading cause of dementia after Alzheimer disease, characterized pathologically by deposition of alpha-synuclein (Lewy bodies) in the brainstem (eg, substantia nigra), limbic system, and neocortical structures. Patients typically present with progressive dementia (usually before the onset of parkinsonism) with fluctuating cognition/attention (eg, "good days and bad days"), well-formed visual hallucinations, and motor manifestations of parkinsonism (eg, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability), which may lead to frequent falls. Deficits in attention and visual-spatial ability (eg, clock drawing, navigating through a familiar neighborhood) may be prominent early in the disease course; however, in contrast to Alzheimer dementia, memory is usually affected later. Other features can include rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, autonomic dysfunction (eg, orthostatic hypotension, constipation), and neuroleptic sensitivity. (Choice A) Babinski sign is characterized by an extensor plantar response ("upgoing toe") on cutaneous plantar stimulation and is indicative of an upper (pyramidal) motor neuron lesion. This may be seen in patients with vascular dementia due to cerebral infarction; however, dementia with Lewy bodies predominantly affects the extrapyramidal motor system, which does not result in upper motor neuron signs (eg, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign). (Choice B) Limb ataxia, dysmetria, and dysdiadochokinesia are suggestive of lesions in the cerebellar hemisphere, which is typically not affected in patients with dementia with Lewy bodies. (Choice D) Primitive reflexes (eg, rooting, sucking, glabellar) are frontal release signs that are generally more prevalent in frontally based dementias (eg, frontotemporal dementia). They are not commonly observed in patients with dementia with Lewy bodies. (Choice E) Startle myoclonus is a reflex myoclonus/body jerk that is elicited with a loud auditory stimulus and is more commonly seen in prion-related dementias such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Other features of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease include behavioral changes and very rapidly progressive dementia. Educational objective: Dementia with Lewy bodies is characterized by fluctuating cognition/attention, well-formed visual hallucinations, and motor manifestations of parkinsonism (eg, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability). Deficits in attention and visual-spatial ability may be prominent early in the disease course, but memory is usually affected later.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the office by her son due to cognitive decline and frequent falls. Over the last year, the patient has gotten lost multiple times while driving in a familiar neighborhood. According to her son, she has "good days and bad days" with occasional episodes of agitation and disorientation. Her movements and speech are slow. On mini-mental state examination, she recalls 3 out of 3 subjects after a minute but has significant difficulty with clock drawing. Which of the following would you expect most on this patient's physical examination?

questions.explanation: Adenoid hypertrophy is the most common etiology of persistent nasal obstruction during childhood. Affected patients have nasal congestion refractory to medical management. History may suggest chronic upper airway obstruction (eg, recurrent sinus and ear infections, mouth breathing, sleep disturbances/snoring due to apnea). Adenoids are not easily accessible and not easily visualized during physical examination. Mucopurulent nasal discharge, postnasal drip, and elongated/flattened facial features (due to changes in the structure of the palate, jaw, and teeth) may suggest the diagnosis. Concurrent tonsillar hypertrophy is common. (Choice B) Allergic rhinitis predisposes children to recurrent otitis and sinusitis. However, it typically improves with standard allergy treatments (eg, antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroids), varies with specific seasons, and is associated with erythematous or edematous nasal turbinates. (Choice C) Choanal atresia causes nasal obstruction. However, bilateral atresia would result in significant respiratory distress at birth, and unilateral atresia would result in symptoms only on the affected side. (Choices D and F) Children with cystic fibrosis (CF) often have recurrent otitis media, sinusitis, and pneumonias (due to impaired ciliary clearance and viscous respiratory secretions), but they also typically have failure to thrive (due to exocrine pancreas insufficiency). This patient has been consistently above the average percentiles for height and weight, making CF unlikely. Nasal polyps can cause chronic congestion and may be associated with recurrent upper respiratory infections; however, in children, they are typically associated with CF and may be visualized on examination. (Choice E) An intranasal foreign body is often seen in toddlers and younger children. It may present with nasal congestion, malodorous discharge, or purulent, bloody nasal secretions. If undetected (eg, unwitnessed object insertion), it may result in infection on the side of the object. Typically, symptoms are unilateral and would not persist for 4 years. (Choice G) Patients with selective IgA deficiency are often asymptomatic. Symptomatic children may experience frequent otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia, or gastrointestinal infections (typically after age 6 months, when maternal protective antibodies decrease). However, IgA deficiency is not associated with chronic nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, or disordered sleep. Educational objective: Adenoid hypertrophy is the most common etiology of persistent nasal obstruction in the pediatric population. It may present as chronic congestion refractory to medical management. Affected children are predisposed to recurrent otitis and sinusitis.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the office for evaluation of nasal congestion. He remains congested throughout the year despite the use of antihistamines and intranasal corticosteroids. Each year since age 2, the patient has had 3 or 4 episodes of otitis media and sinusitis, but has otherwise been healthy. He snores loudly at night and feels tired during the day. The boy frequently reports, "I can't breathe through my nose," but he has no shortness of breath or wheezing. He was born at 40 weeks' gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery and has been at the 75th percentile for height and weight since birth. Developmental milestones have been achieved on time. Immunizations are up to date. Vital signs are normal. Examination reveals an alert child in no acute distress who breathes loudly through his mouth. Nasal turbinates are not enlarged or erythematous. Tonsils are enlarged without erythema or exudate. Mucopurulent postnasal drip is present. Breath sounds are normal without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi. Which of the following underlying abnormalities is likely to be the cause of this patient's symptoms?

questions.explanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome Lambert-Eaton syndrome Myasthenia gravis Pathogenesis Antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels at NMJ Antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at NMJ Clinical features Proximal limb weakness (legs > arms) ↓ or absent reflexes Improvement in strength & reflexes following isometric contraction Autonomic dysfunction (eg, dry mouth) Muscle weakness: Ocular (ptosis, diplopia) Bulbar (dysphagia, dysarthria) Proximal limbs (arms > legs) Normal reflexes Weakness that worsens with activity Electrophysiologic studies ↑ Action potential amplitude with repetitive nerve stimulation ↓ Action potential amplitude with repetitive stimulation Associated neoplasm Small cell lung cancer Thymoma NMJ = neuromuscular junction. This patient's 40-pack-year smoking history, proximal muscle weakness, and absent deep tendon reflexes raise suspicion for Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). LEMS is caused by the formation of autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. Almost all cases are triggered by underlying small cell lung cancer because this tumor often expresses voltage-gated calcium channels on its surface, leading to autoantibody formation. Most cases present with proximal muscle weakness in the lower limbs, which results in difficulty rising from chairs and climbing stairs; weakness in the upper limbs typically develops later. questions.stem: A 58-year-old man comes to the office due to 10 weeks of progressive weakness. The patient has had difficulty climbing stairs and raising his arms above his head. He has also had trouble standing up from a seated position without pushing off with his arms. He has had no vision or swallowing problems or muscle aches. The patient has hypertension and a 40-pack-year smoking history. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 126/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 78/min. BMI is 19.5 kg/m2. There is moderate weakness of the proximal muscles of the upper and lower limbs, and deep tendon reflexes are absent throughout. Plantar reflexes are flexor. Sensory examination shows no abnormalities, and cranial nerve function is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Preventing neonatal group B Streptococcus infection Antenatal screening Rectovaginal culture at 36-38 weeks gestation Indications for intrapartum prophylaxis GBS bacteriuria or GBS urinary tract infection in current pregnancy (regardless of treatment) GBS-positive rectovaginal culture in current pregnancy Unknown GBS status PLUS any of the following: <37 weeks gestation Intrapartum fever Rupture of membranes for ≥18 hr Prior infant with early-onset neonatal GBS infection Intrapartum prophylaxis Intravenous penicillin GBS = group B Streptococcus. Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a frequent colonizer of the gastrointestinal and genital tracts in women. Maternal GBS is typically asymptomatic; however, GBS can be vertically transmitted to the neonate during vaginal delivery or with rupture of membranes, resulting in early-onset neonatal infection (eg, sepsis, pneumonia). Therefore, women are universally screened by rectovaginal culture at 36-38 weeks gestation and administered intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis if they test positive for GBS. Patients with an unknown GBS status, such as this patient, are administered intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis based on their risk factors. Patients delivering at <37 weeks gestation (eg, preterm rupture of membranes) have higher rates of GBS transmission and more severe neonatal infection (due to neonatal immune system immaturity); therefore, these patients require intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis with penicillin. (Choice A) Amnioinfusion is used during labor to decrease umbilical cord compression after rupture of membranes. Umbilical cord compression would be evidenced by variable decelerations; this patient's fetal heart tracing is normal. (Choice B) Cesarean delivery is indicated for fetal distress (eg, category III fetal heart rate tracing) or breech presentation, which are not seen in this patient. (Choice C) Magnesium sulfate is administered to patients at risk for delivery at <32 weeks gestation for fetal neuroprotection (eg, cerebral palsy prevention). This patient is at 35 weeks gestation. (Choices D and F) Nifedipine and terbutaline are tocolytics used to delay delivery in patients in preterm labor. However, patients with preterm rupture of membranes at ≥34 weeks gestation require delivery because the risk of complications (eg, intraamniotic infection) outweighs the benefit of further fetal development. Educational objective: Patients with an unknown group B Streptococcus (GBS) status who are delivering at <37 weeks gestation (eg, preterm rupture of membranes) require intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. These patients are at increased risk for vertical GBS transmission and severe neonatal infection due to neonatal immune system immaturity.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, comes to the hospital at 35 weeks gestation due to leakage of fluid and contractions for the past 3 hours. The patient was last seen in the office 2 weeks ago, and her prenatal care has been uncomplicated. She has no chronic medical conditions and no medication allergies. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg, and pulse is 84/min. Speculum examination shows a vaginal pool of nitrazine-positive, clear fluid and the cervix dilated to 1 cm. Transabdominal ultrasound reveals a fetus in vertex presentation, and the amniotic fluid has a deepest vertical pocket of 1.5 cm. The fetal heart rate tracing has moderate variability and no decelerations. The tocometer reveals contractions every 2-3 minutes. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient, an older man who has an acutely painful groin bulge and features of bowel obstruction (ie, vomiting, abdominal distension, hyperactive bowel sounds), most likely has a strangulated inguinal hernia. Direct inguinal hernias are common in older men and usually present with a chronic or slowly progressive bulge and dull discomfort that is worse with Valsalva. However, trapping of a loop of bowel within the hernia (incarceration) can disrupt blood flow to the involved bowel segment, leading to ischemic necrosis (strangulation). Strangulated hernias can be exquisitely tender on palpation, with associated fever and erythema of the overlying skin. Ultrasound or CT imaging can rapidly confirm the diagnosis but is not always necessary. Management of a strangulated hernia requires expedited surgical intervention. (Choice A) Arteriovenous fistula involving the femoral vessels is a potential complication of percutaneous coronary interventions. Early signs include a palpable thrill and distal ischemia. Late manifestations can include high-output heart failure. Delayed inflammatory complications are uncommon. (Choice B) An epidermoid cyst is a discrete nodule in the skin and is a result of epidermal keratin becoming lodged in the dermis. It may occasionally become inflamed or infected but would not cause bowel obstruction. (Choices C and D) A varicocele, a chronic disorder characterized by distension of the pampiniform plexus within the spermatic cord, can present with dull discomfort and a palpable bulge in the groin. Testicular torsion is most common in children and adolescents and is characterized by acute pain with a high-riding, horizontally oriented testis. These conditions would not cause bowel obstruction. (Choice F) Inguinal abscesses are uncommon but can occur due to complicated skin and soft tissue infections or an extension of an intra-abdominal abscess. Bowel sounds would be normal or hypoactive rather than hyperactive. (Choice G) Malignant inguinal adenopathy can be seen in melanoma and other skin neoplasms, lymphoma, and squamous cell carcinoma of the anus or genitalia. However, symptoms would be subacute to chronic rather than acute. Educational objective: Strangulated hernias are characterized by disruption of blood flow to the involved bowel segment, leading to ischemic necrosis. Clinical features include severe local pain and tenderness, fever, and signs of bowel obstruction. The diagnosis can be confirmed by imaging, and urgent surgical intervention is required.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to painful swelling in the right groin. He also has had nausea and 2 episodes of bilious vomiting since the onset of pain several hours ago. Medical history is notable for hypertension and a myocardial infarction treated with a coronary stent a year ago. The patient is a former smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. Temperature is 38.2 C (100.8 F), blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 110/min. On examination, the abdomen is soft and mildly distended with hyperactive bowel sounds. There is a 4-cm tender mass in the right inguinal region with erythema of the overlying skin. The patient subsequently undergoes urgent exploratory surgery of the right groin. Which of the following is most likely to be found during surgery?

questions.explanation: Groin hernias Type Classic presentation Pathophysiology Anatomy Indirect inguinal Male infants Patent processus vaginalis Originates lateral to inferior epigastric vessels Protrudes through the deep inguinal ring into inguinal canal May extend into the scrotum (following spermatic cord) Direct inguinal Older men Weakness of transversalis fascia Protrudes medial to the inferior epigastric vessels into Hesselbach's triangle May pass through superficial inguinal ring No direct route into the scrotum Femoral Women Widening of the femoral ring Emerges inferior to inguinal ligament Protrudes through the femoral ring into the femoral canal This patient has a direct inguinal hernia. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through the inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle, which is formed by the inguinal ligament inferiorly, the inferior epigastric vessels laterally, and the rectus abdominis muscle medially. The transversalis fascia forms the floor of the triangle, and defects or weakness in the fascia can lead to protrusion of abdominal contents through the triangle into the inguinal canal. Failure of this fascial layer is most often due to acquired connective tissue abnormalities or chronic abdominal wall injury. Direct inguinal hernias are most common in older men and present with a visible bulge at the groin and dull discomfort that is worse with Valsalva. These hernias are usually chronic or slowly progressive. Possible complications include incarceration (trapping of a loop of bowel within the hernia) and strangulation (disruption of blood flow to the involved bowel, leading to ischemic necrosis). The diagnosis is generally made on physical examination. Treatment is laparoscopic or open surgical repair. (Choice A) Varicocele is a chronic disorder characterized by distension of the pampiniform plexus within the spermatic cord. A varicocele can present with dull discomfort and a palpable bulge in the groin, but the peritoneum is not involved. (Choices B and C) Indirect inguinal hernias are due to a patent processus vaginalis, allowing passage of bowel through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. Indirect hernias may occasionally present in adulthood but are usually apparent in infancy or childhood. A patent processus vaginalis is also associated with the development of a hydrocele (fluid-filled sac around the testicle). (Choice E) Femoral hernias are characterized by defects in the femoral ring inferior to the inguinal ligament. They are much less common than inguinal hernias and occur predominantly in women. Educational objective: Direct inguinal hernias occur most commonly in older men and are due to weakness of the transversalis fascia in the inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle. They present with dull discomfort and a visible bulge in the groin. Complications include incarceration and strangulation, and treatment is surgical.

During the resulting surgical treatment, a peritoneal sac originating above the inguinal ligament and medial to the inferior epigastric vessels is seen. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

questions.explanation: Narcolepsy DSM-5 diagnostic criteria Recurrent lapses into sleep or naps (≥3 times/week for 3 months) ≥1 of the following: Cataplexy: brief loss of muscle tone precipitated by strong emotion (eg, laughter, excitement) Low cerebrospinal fluid levels of hypocretin-1 Shortened REM sleep latency Associated features Hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations Sleep paralysis Polysomnography is commonly used to aid in the differential diagnosis of excessive daytime sleepiness. It evaluates sleep architecture (including sleep latency and REM latency), monitors physiologic parameters during sleep, and can identify obstructive respiratory events (eg, apneas, hypopneas) and arousals associated with sleep apnea. This patient most likely has narcolepsy due to the presence of hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations and cataplexy (sudden muscle weakness in response to intense emotion). Narcolepsy is associated with decreased REM latency, with patients entering REM sleep within 15 minutes of sleep onset (normal is 90 minutes). The combination of an overnight polysomnogram followed by a multiple sleep latency test (patient given 5 opportunities to nap) to evaluate for sleep-onset REM periods can provide strong evidence of narcolepsy while excluding other sleep disorders. (Choice A) If obstructive sleep apnea were the cause of this patient's excessive daytime sleepiness, >15 obstructive respiratory events/hour would be expected. The lack of witnessed apneas by the bed partner makes this diagnosis less likely. (Choices B and E) Narcolepsy is associated with increased, not decreased, REM density (frequency of rapid eye movements during REM sleep) and decreased, not increased, sleep latency (time to sleep onset). (Choice D) Polysomnography can be used to identify seizures during sleep. A generalized spike-wave activity of 3 Hz is typical of absence seizures. These seizures, which begin in childhood (generally age 4-10), are characterized by brief and frequent episodes of impaired consciousness with intact muscle tone; patients typically appear to be staring. This man, however, describes loss of muscle tone when laughing, suggestive of cataplexy, not a seizure disorder. Educational objective: Narcolepsy is a common cause of excessive daytime sleepiness. Polysomnography can be used to rule out other sleep disorders and typically shows decreased REM latency.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man comes to the office due to persistent fatigue and sleepiness. He describes a long history of excessive daytime sleepiness that he previously managed by taking frequent naps in his office. questions.explanation: A nonhealing oral ulcer with indurated margins is concerning for malignancy, especially in patients who use tobacco. Immunosuppression (eg, HIV) is also an important risk factor, although the effect from tobacco exposure is much greater. Most cancers of the head and neck arise from squamous epithelial cells that undergo stepwise, premalignant changes (hyperplasia to dysplasia to carcinoma). This may manifest in the oral cavity as hyperplastic white (leukoplakia) or dysplastic red (erythroplakia) precancerous plaques that progress to ulceration and deeper tissue invasion. Regional metastatic spread to cervical lymph nodes is very common. This patient with suspected oral squamous cell carcinoma should undergo biopsy of the lesion. A CT scan of the neck with contrast should also be obtained to evaluate the extent of invasion and characterize the metastatic nodal spread to stage the disease and plan for treatment. (Choice A) Acyclovir is used to treat herpes simplex virus (HSV), which causes painful vesicular eruptions on the lips and oral mucosa (ie, gingivostomatitis). However, a single subacute ulcer on the tongue is not likely due to HSV. (Choice B) Benzathine penicillin is used to treat primary syphilis, which may cause a painless (not a painful) oral ulcer (chancre), and induration would not be expected. (Choice D) Fluconazole therapy can be used to treat oral candidiasis, a common opportunistic infection. Immunosuppression, xerostomia, use of antibiotics, and use of corticosteroid inhalers are common risk factors. Oral candidiasis typically presents with white patches or plaques on the tongue or buccal mucosal surfaces; however, ulceration would not be present. (Choices E and G) Topical glucocorticoids are sometimes used to treat aphthous ulcers, which tend to be multiple, painful, and short lasting (<2 weeks). Behcet syndrome is diagnosed by the pathergy test and often causes recurrent oral aphthous ulcers (and systemic symptoms). A single, persistent ulcer with raised margins in the setting of tobacco use makes cancer more likely. (Choice F) Glossitis may be caused by a deficiency in certain B vitamins (eg, riboflavin, B12) but usually presents as a smooth tongue with loss of papillae rather than a single, indurated ulcer. Educational objective: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity often manifests as a nonhealing ulcer with indurated edges. Tobacco exposure is an important risk factor. Biopsy is required for diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man comes to the office for evaluation of a tongue lesion. The patient first noticed a small, whitish lesion on the right edge of his tongue 1 month ago. questions.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica Risk factors Resource-limited regions (contaminated food/water) Clinical manifestations Most are asymptomatic Colitis: prolonged bloody/mucoid diarrhea Liver abscess: RUQ pain, fever Complications: pleural effusion, rupture into peritoneum/pleural space Diagnosis Stool PCR/antigen: preferred Stool microscopy: low sensitivity Serology:* useful for isolated liver abscess Treatment Metronidazole or tinidazole PLUS Intraluminal antibiotic (eg, paromomycin) *Does not distinguish between prior & current infection. RUQ = right upper quadrant. This patient's diarrhea after travel to a resource-limited country makes infectious gastroenteritis most likely. Prolonged (≥2 weeks) infectious diarrhea is more commonly due to parasites than to bacteria or viruses, and this patient's dysentery (blood/mucus in the stool) suggests infestation with Entamoeba histolytica. E histolytica is a protozoan acquired by consuming contaminated food or water. Patients are often asymptomatic, but those with amebic colitis have subacute diarrhea containing blood and mucus. Abdominal pain typically reflects areas of patchy colonic involvement (eg, right lower quadrant [cecal inflammation] as well as left upper quadrant in this patient), and weight loss is common. For patients with diarrhea, the preferred diagnostic modality is stool PCR (nucleic acid amplification) testing, which has >98% sensitivity and specificity and is usually performed as multiplex testing that broadly screens for multiple bacterial and parasitic organisms; stool E histolytica antigen is also diagnostic. Microscopic examination can identify trophozoites or cysts but has lower sensitivity (<50% with a single sample) and is not preferred. In contrast to infections by other invasive pathogens, E histolytica infestation often results in negative fecal leukocyte testing because the parasite destroys white blood cells in the gastrointestinal tract. (Choice A) Colonoscopy in the setting of active infection increases the risk for bowel perforation, and noninvasive diagnostic testing is preferred. If noninvasive testing is unrevealing, this patient with weight loss and bloody stools would likely warrant more invasive testing with colonoscopy to evaluate for inflammatory bowel disease. (Choice B) Because prolonged (≥2 weeks) infectious diarrhea is most commonly due to parasites, not bacteria, empiric antibiotics are not recommended. (Choice C) Acute watery diarrhea is often managed expectedly due to the high likelihood of self-resolution. In contrast, bloody or prolonged diarrhea warrants evaluation. Reassurance and observation are not recommended for suspected E histolytica infestation because invasive disease (eg, liver abscess) can occur without treatment (eg, metronidazole plus paromomycin). (Choice D) Strongyloides stercoralis can cause diarrhea in patients who have traveled to resource-limited regions. However, stools are not typically bloody, and skin (eg, pruritic streaking) and respiratory (eg, cough) manifestations would be expected. Educational objective: Entamoeba histolytica colitis presents with prolonged bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain after travel to a resource-limited country. The preferred diagnostic modality is stool PCR or E histolytica antigen testing.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man comes to the office due to diarrhea for the past 3 weeks. The symptoms began while he was traveling in the Philippines and have continued following his return home. The patient has had 4 or 5 daily episodes of diarrhea that contain blood and mucus. He also has intermittent abdominal cramping and nausea. The patient has been able to tolerate oral fluids and food but has lost 2 kg (4.4 lb) during this time. He has no other symptoms. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F), blood pressure is 117/76 mm Hg, pulse is 82/min, and respirations are 14/min. Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness of the right lower and left upper quadrant. The remainder of the examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Breast cancer is most common in postmenopausal patients because the risk of breast cancer increases with age. This postmenopausal patient has a new palpable breast mass in the setting of a recent screening mammogram. Although a normal mammogram from 6 months ago may seem reassuring, it does not exclude the interval development of breast cancer in patients with a new mass and high baseline risk for cancer. Therefore, despite recent normal breast imaging, this postmenopausal patient's new breast mass requires further evaluation. Mammography is the gold standard for evaluation of a new breast mass in women age ≥30. Unlike ultrasound, diagnostic mammography can better identify signs of malignancy (eg, calcifications); in addition, diagnostic mammography performed in this patient can be directly compared to her recent screening mammogram, which was performed prior to the discovery of the new mass. If the repeat mammogram is normal, breast ultrasound is also performed (Choice A). (Choice B) Combined estrogen/progestin menopausal hormonal therapy (MHT) is a risk factor for breast cancer, although the absolute risk is low; however, the use of estrogen-only MHT in patients with no uterus (eg, prior vaginal hysterectomy) does not appear to increase the risk of breast cancer and may even slightly decrease the risk. Therefore, there is no need to discontinue MHT in this patient while she is undergoing evaluation unless the breast mass proves malignant. (Choice C) Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration is indicated for symptomatic relief of painful breast cysts. However, it has no role in the initial evaluation of a new breast mass, which first requires breast imaging. In addition, breast cysts are less likely in this patient because they most commonly occur in premenopausal women (ie, age 30-50). (Choice E) Conservative management with observation and repeat breast examination in 1 month may be appropriate for adolescents with a new, palpable breast mass because their risk for cancer is low; however, this approach is inappropriate in adult women, particularly postmenopausal women, because their risk of cancer is high. Educational objective: Breast cancer is most common in postmenopausal patients because the risk of breast cancer increases with age. Therefore, a postmenopausal woman with a new, palpable breast mass requires breast imaging (ie, diagnostic mammography), even if her latest mammogram was recent and the results were normal.

questions.explanation: Contraception options Type Effectiveness with typical use Intrauterine device >99% Implant >99% Injection 94% Pills, patch, ring 91% Condom 80% Withdrawal 75% Adolescents have the highest rate of unintended pregnancy of any age group. Adolescent mothers are more likely to live below the poverty line and not complete a high school education. The ability to provide effective contraception can be challenging due to cost and limited awareness of birth control options and their safety profiles. Additional obstacles include misperceptions about pregnancy risk and access to confidential care. Adolescents with families and/or clinicians who support the use of contraception have much lower pregnancy rates with no associated increase in sexual partners. Adolescents have higher discrepancies between perfect and typical (imperfect) use rates with many forms of contraception due to inconsistent compliance compared to other age groups. As a result, long-acting, reversible contraceptive devices (LARCs) such as the levonorgestrel and copper intrauterine devices (IUDs) and subdermal progestin implant are first-line contraception options for adolescents. LARCs have the lowest failure rate in pregnancy prevention, with >99% effectiveness in typical use, and have the highest continuation rate. They can be placed in nulliparous and adolescent patients who have no evidence of an active pelvic infection. (Choices A, B, and C) Combination oral contraceptive pills and hormonal patches/vaginal rings have a lower efficacy than LARCs. This discrepancy is magnified in adolescents, who have high failure rates with typical use. (Choices D and F) Barrier methods, such as the condom and diaphragm, are not as effective as LARCs. Pregnancy rates with typical use are equivalent to average fecundity rates. Barrier methods should be used in addition to other contraceptives to help prevent sexually transmitted infections. (Choice G) Depo medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) is a long-acting contraceptive that requires an injection every 3 months. DMPA has a higher failure rate than LARCs. It is not recommended for long-term use (>2 years) in adolescents or young women due to significant risk for loss of bone mineral density. Educational objective: Copper and levonorgestrel intrauterine devices are long-acting, reversible contraceptives that have the lowest failure rates in pregnancy prevention. Intrauterine devices are a first-line option in adolescents and safe in nulliparous patients.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old nulligravid girl is brought to the office by her mother for contraceptive counseling. The patient recently became sexually active with one male partner and is interested in contraception. Her mother agrees with this plan. Next month, the patient will attend an out-of-state university and wants the most reliable option. She received a swimming scholarship and will have a busy training schedule in addition to her school work. Menarche was at age 13 and she has regular menses typically lasting 3-4 days. Her only medical problem is asthma, for which she uses albuterol prior to exercise. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Gonorrhea and chlamydia testing is negative. Which of the following is the best option for this patient?

questions.explanation: Resumption of postpartum menstruation Formula feeding 8-14 weeks postpartum Exclusively breastfeeding >6 months postpartum (variable) The postpartum period is the 6- to 8-week interval after delivery when pregnancy-related changes resolve and the patient returns to her prepregnancy state. The hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis normalizes and ovulation resumes. In patients who are not breastfeeding, ovulation typically resumes at 6-12 weeks and menses at 8-14 weeks postpartum. Because lactation suppresses ovulation, half the women who are exclusively breastfeeding resume ovulation at about 6 months postpartum, although there is great variation between patients. After delivery, the endometrium regenerates. This regeneration is evidenced by lochia, the normal shedding of uterine decidua and blood after delivery. Lochia may persist for as long as 2-3 months and has variations in color and consistency, transitioning from red/brown (lochia rubra) to serosanguinous (lochia serosa) to white (lochia alba). This patient is 8 weeks after delivery, near the end of the postpartum period. Her protracted pink discharge is lochia, and the episode of heavy bleeding is likely the resumption of her menses. Therefore, this patient should be provided reassurance and routine postpartum care, including contraception if desired. (Choice A) This patient's hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is returning to normal, as evidenced by the return of menses. Therefore, FSH, TSH, and prolactin tests are not indicated. (Choice B) Von Willebrand disease is typically diagnosed at menarche in patients with heavy, regular menses, but it can have a delayed presentation with an excessive postpartum hemorrhage. This patient had an uncomplicated delivery and has normal menses, making this diagnosis unlikely. In addition, von Willebrand disease is not associated with light, daily bleeding. (Choices C and D) Evaluation for abnormal uterine bleeding can include a pelvic ultrasound (to assess for a uterine structural anomaly) and an endometrial biopsy (to exclude endometrial neoplasia and/or hyperplasia). This patient's bleeding is normal and does not require further workup. (Choice E) Broad spectrum antibiotics may be prescribed for postpartum endometritis, which typically presents with purulent lochia, vaginal bleeding, and uterine tenderness. This patient's light pink discharge is consistent with lochia, and she has no signs of infection (eg, fever). Educational objective: Lochia, the normal shedding of blood and uterine decidua after delivery, is red/brown for several days and pink for several weeks. In nonlactating women, ovulation typically resumes 6-12 weeks postpartum, and menses resume 8-14 weeks postpartum.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, comes to the office for a routine 8-week postpartum examination and evaluation of vaginal bleeding. The patient had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with a second-degree perineal laceration. Since the delivery, she has had a persistent pink discharge and spotting that partially stained 1 pad a day. Six days ago, the bleeding became heavier and soaked 3 pads a day. Today, the bleeding is minimal. She is coping well and caring for her infant, although her husband was deployed for military duty 2 weeks after delivery. The patient switched to formula a few weeks ago due to ongoing difficulties with latching. Vital signs are normal. Speculum examination shows a closed cervix with minimal blood from the os. The perineum appears well healed, and the vagina has no lesions. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

IgM is the largest immunoglobulin and exists primarily in covalently bonded pentamers. High plasma concentrations of these large molecules may impede capillary circulation, resulting in hyperviscosity syndrome. Symptoms include vision changes, headaches, dizziness, confusion, and/or ataxia (due to impaired central nervous system microcirculation). Prompt removal of serum IgM with plasma exchange is required to reduce blood viscosity. Patients with WM often develop other clinical manifestations of high IgM levels (neuropathy, cryoglobulinemia, coagulopathy) as well as issues related to neoplastic infiltration of tissue (cytopenias, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly). WM is diagnosed using serum protein electrophoresis (M-spike) and bone marrow biopsy with cytogenetics (>10% clonal B cells with certain phenotypic features). (Choice A) A loop diuretic with an ACE inhibitor could be used to manage this patient's elevated blood pressure, lower extremity edema, and possible dilated cardiomyopathy (S3/displaced point of maximal impulse). However, hyperviscosity syndrome is a clinical emergency and must be addressed first. (Choice B) Packed red blood cells are not required; hemoglobin is >8g/dL and there is no evidence of acute bleeding, acute coronary ischemia, or symptomatic anemia. Symptomatic anemia typically manifests with dyspnea, fatigue, confusion, or chest pain (not dizziness, headaches, and blurry vision). (Choice D) This patient's ecchymoses are likely due to platelet and coagulation dysfunction from high IgM levels, not clinically active bleeding (platelet count is >50,000/mm3). Platelet transfusion is not required. (Choice E) Ultrafiltration is reserved primarily for those with massive volume overload whose condition does not respond adequately to aggressive diuretic medication. This patient has mild volume overload and would not require ultrafiltration. High levels of IgM may increase capillary viscosity, resulting in hyperviscosity syndrome. Symptoms include vision changes, headaches, dizziness, confusion, and/or ataxia (due to impaired central nervous system microcirculation). Patients require urgent plasma exchange to reduce serum IgM levels.

questions.explanation: This patient's presentation of chronic, watery diarrhea without any evidence of lactose intolerance or systemic symptoms likely indicates microscopic colitis (MC). MC is characterized by frequent watery bowel movements, fecal urgency, incontinence, and (classically) nocturnal diarrhea. Abdominal pain occurs only in half of patients. Risk factors include age >50, female sex, smoking, and possibly nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The exact pathogenesis of MC remains unclear, but it is likely a result of an abnormal mucosal immune response in genetically predisposed individuals. Stool studies should be performed to exclude other common causes of diarrhea, such as Clostridium difficile and other infectious agents. Colonoscopy is required to make the diagnosis and typically reveals inflammatory infiltrates with a mononuclear predominance. MC can be further subdivided into collagenous colitis (thickened subepithelial collagen layer) or lymphocytic colitis (more pronounced intraepithelial lymphocytic inflammatory infiltration). Management includes avoiding inciting agents such as NSAIDs and starting antidiarrheal agents. Corticosteroids (eg, budesonide) may be administered to patients with refractory disease. (Choices A and E) Inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis (characterized by crypt abscesses) and Crohn disease (characterized by noncaseating granulomas), is typically manifested by frank or occult bleeding, elevated inflammatory markers, and systemic symptoms (eg, fever, weight loss, fatigue). (Choice B) Patients with adenomatous polyps (low-grade dysplasia) are most commonly asymptomatic, although some may have evidence of rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy is not macroscopically normal. (Choice D) Mucosal atrophy and granulation tissue are not features of MC. These pathologic findings could be seen on biopsy in patients with chronic ischemic colitis, which typically presents with chronic abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, weight loss, and colonic strictures. Educational objective: Microscopic colitis is characterized by watery and nocturnal diarrhea, fecal urgency, and incontinence. Risk factors include age >50, female sex, smoking, and possibly nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Colonoscopy typically reveals inflammatory infiltrates with a monocytic predominance.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the office with a 6-month history of diarrhea. She describes 4-6 watery bowel movements a day that are not associated with any particular food type. The patient has tried a lactose-free diet without any relief. She has not lost any weight and has no nausea, vomiting, fevers, abdominal pain, back pain, blood in the stool, or melena. Her medical history is significant for hypertension treated with lisinopril and frequent migraines treated with ibuprofen. She does not smoke or use alcohol. Her family history is negative for inflammatory bowel disease or colon cancer. Blood pressure is 142/91 mm Hg and pulse is 78/min. BMI is 27 kg/m2. The abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended. questions.explanation: Urinary catheter placement is standard practice for most surgeries as it allows for bladder decompression, strict measurement of fluid intake and output, and a lower risk of postoperative urinary retention. However, potential complications of urinary catheterization include an increased risk of urinary tract infection (UTI) leading to increased antibiotic use and increased length of hospitalization. Removal of urinary catheters within 24-48 hours postoperatively has been shown to reduce the risk of UTI, allow for earlier discharge from the hospital, and reduce mortality compared to catheter continuation for more than 48 hours. In addition, early postoperative catheter removal has not been associated with higher rates of postoperative urinary retention. Therefore, early catheter removal should be performed in most surgical patients. (Choice A) High-dose (325 mg daily), but not low-dose, aspirin may provide adequate prophylaxis for deep venous thrombosis in patients who have recently undergone hip arthroplasty. However, other agents (eg, low-molecular-weight heparin, factor Xa inhibitors) are preferred for this purpose. (Choice B) Although morphine may cause respiratory depression, this patient is awake and alert and is not demonstrating any signs of respiratory failure (eg, dyspnea). Morphine is controlling this patient's pain and is a suitable agent for continued pain control. (Choice D) This patient is not currently agitated and there is no indication for prophylactic use of haloperidol. In addition, the use of haloperidol and other typical antipsychotics should be avoided in elderly patients with dementia due to adverse effects and possible increased mortality. If pharmacologic management of agitation is needed in these patients, atypical antipsychotics (eg, olanzapine, quetiapine) are preferred. (Choice E) There is no evidence to support packed red blood cell transfusion in patients with hemoglobin >7 g/dL and no symptoms of anemia (eg, chest pain, dyspnea). Unnecessary blood transfusions deplete resources and place patients at undue risk of transfusion-related complications (eg, volume overload, immunologic reaction). Educational objective: Discontinuation of urinary catheters within 24-48 hours postoperatively reduces the risk of urinary tract infection, shortens the length of hospital stay, and reduces mortality without increasing the risk of postoperative urinary retention.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman is evaluated in the hospital one day after having an elective right total hip arthroplasty for severe osteoarthritis. She has had no immediate operative complications, and her pain is well controlled by intravenous morphine. She has no chest pain or dyspnea. The patient has a history of hypertension and mild dementia. Her family reports that she had an episode of delirium with agitation several months ago during a previous hospitalization for a urinary tract infection. She has been living with her husband and was fairly active before the hip pain limited her daily activities. Today, she is afebrile. Blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 88/min and regular. The patient is awake, alert, and conversant. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. Right hip incision is clean and dry. She has an indwelling urinary catheter with clear urine. Cardiac monitor shows sinus rhythm. Her hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the patient at this time?

questions.explanation: Primary sclerosing cholangitis Clinical features Asymptomatic initially; fatigue & pruritus with progressive disease Associated with IBD, particularly ulcerative colitis Laboratory & imaging results Cholestasis (↑ ALP, GGT, bilirubin) Multifocal strictures/dilation of bile ducts on MRCP Complications Cholangitis, cholangiocarcinoma, colon cancer Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies ALP = alkaline phosphatase; GGT = γ-glutamyl transferase; IBD = inflammatory bowel disease; MRCP = MR cholangiopancreatography. This patient with fatigue and cholestatic liver injury (manifesting as pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, and acholic stool) has MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) findings consistent with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). PSC is a progressive disorder characterized by inflammation, fibrosis, and stricturing of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. It is more common in male patients; most (~90%) also have inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (with colonoscopy recommended in those found to have PSC without a history of IBD). PSC can be initially asymptomatic and manifest symptoms as biliary obstruction progresses (as seen here). Laboratory testing shows cholestatic liver injury pattern with dramatically elevated alkaline phosphatase levels, direct hyperbilirubinemia (in late stages of the disease), and normal or modestly increased serum aminotransferases (typically <300 U/L). MRCP is the preferred test for diagnosis and reveals multifocal intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile duct strictures with segmental dilation. Patients with nonspecific MRCP findings should undergo liver biopsy or endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography to confirm the diagnosis. (Choice A) Although intrahepatic bile duct destruction can also be seen in autoimmune hepatitis, this condition is characterized predominantly by hepatocellular injury with markedly elevated aminotransferases (eg, 10-20 times upper limit of normal), with hypergammaglobulinemia and anti–smooth muscle antibodies. (Choice B) Choledocholithiasis presents with a cholestatic pattern of liver injury accompanied by severe abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant (absent in this patient). MRCP would reveal gallstones instead of strictures in the common bile duct. (Choice C) Pancreatic head cancer can compress the common bile duct, leading to cholestatic jaundice and pruritus. However, MRCP would identify a pancreatic mass, not multifocal biliary strictures, which are more consistent with PSC. (Choice D) Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) occurs predominantly in women (~90%), affects only the intrahepatic biliary ducts, and typically causes significant bilirubin elevations only in late-stage disease, when cirrhosis is present (unlikely in this patient with normal albumin). PBC is usually diagnosed clinically if characteristic laboratory findings (eg, elevated antimitochondrial antibodies) are present or through percutaneous liver biopsy if the diagnosis is unclear. MRCP findings of segmental dilation and strictures in a male patient are not consistent with PBC and point to an alternate cause. Educational objective: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is characterized by biliary inflammation, fibrosis, and stricturing of the medium and large intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Manifestations are related to cholestasis and include pruritus, jaundice, hyperbilirubinemia, and elevated alkaline phosphatase levels. MR cholangiopancreatography demonstrates multifocal intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile duct strictures with segmental dilations.

questions.explanation: Solid liver masses Focal nodular hyperplasia Associated with anomalous arteries Arterial flow & central scar on imaging Hepatic adenoma Women on long-term oral contraceptives Possible hemorrhage or malignant transformation Regenerative nodules Acute or chronic liver injury (eg, cirrhosis) Hepatocellular carcinoma Systemic symptoms Chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis Elevated ɑ-fetoprotein Liver metastasis Single/multiple lesions Known extrahepatic malignancy This patient likely has focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH), the most common benign nonvascular liver lesion. It is normally asymptomatic, and most cases are discovered incidentally during evaluations for other causes of intraabdominal pathology (eg, gallstone disease, dyspepsia). Occasionally, patients may have abdominal symptoms due to the mass effect of the growing lesion. FNH is most commonly a small (<5 cm), solitary lesion and is due to a hyperplastic response to hyperperfusion that is caused by an inappropriately large artery typically found at the center of the lesion. The appearance of FNH on ultrasound is variable, although color Doppler may help distinguish the abnormal arterial flow. CT scan or MRI can be highly suggestive, demonstrating a hypo- or isodense lesion with arterial enhancement and a central stellate scar. FNH is more common in women than men. It is generally stable and does not normally result in complications. Management is conservative. Although FNH is not thought to be associated with oral contraceptives (unlike hepatic adenoma, the other most common solitary nonvascular lesion, which has a different radiographic appearance), some providers advise women to discontinue use of oral contraceptives and offer serial examinations for patients with larger masses (>8 cm). (Choice A) The liver lesions of Echinococcus appear as smooth, cystic masses on ultrasound and CT scan; they normally do not cause symptoms unless they become large (eg, >10 cm). (Choice B) Biopsy should be considered for a number of liver lesions (including hepatic adenoma) or for patients with nonclassical imaging of FNH. However, in patients with characteristic findings for FNH on CT scan, no further intervention is indicated. (Choice D) Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) can be helpful in distinguishing hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) from other types of liver lesions as AFP levels are elevated in HCC but normal in most other lesions, including FNH. In this patient with imaging findings consistent with FNH (eg, central stellate scar) and no risk factors for HCC (eg, chronic viral hepatitis, cirrhosis), AFP measurement is not required. (Choice E) Surgical resection should be considered for symptomatic, large (>8 cm) FNH but otherwise is not indicated as FNH does not undergo malignant transformation or have a high likelihood of complications (eg, hemorrhage). Management is generally conservative.

This patient likely has focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH), the most common benign nonvascular liver lesion.  It is normally asymptomatic, and most cases are discovered incidentally during evaluations for other causes of intraabdominal pathology (eg, gallstone disease, dyspepsia).  Occasionally, patients may have abdominal symptoms due to the mass effect of the growing lesion.

FNH is most commonly a small (<5 cm), solitary lesion and is due to a hyperplastic response to hyperperfusion that is caused by an inappropriately large artery typically found at the center of the lesion.  The appearance of FNH on ultrasound is variable, although color Doppler may help distinguish the abnormal arterial flow.  CT scan or MRI can be highly suggestive, demonstrating a hypo- or isodense lesion with arterial enhancement and a central stellate scar.

FNH is more common in women than men.  It is generally stable and does not normally result in complications.  Management is conservative.  Although FNH is not thought to be associated with oral contraceptives (unlike hepatic adenoma, the other most common solitary nonvascular lesion, which has a different radiographic appearance), some providers advise women to discontinue use of oral contraceptives and offer serial examinations for patients with larger masses (>8 cm).

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman is evaluated for dyspeptic symptoms. A year ago, the patient started using oral contraceptives and developed nausea and a bloating sensation. She stopped taking them after several months but continues to have episodic postprandial fullness, upper abdominal discomfort, and nausea. The patient has no other medical problems and takes no other medications, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. She does not use tobacco or recreational drugs and drinks alcohol occasionally. The patient is in a monogamous relationship with her husband and has no prior history of sexually transmitted infections. She traveled to Mexico 3 years ago. Blood pressure is 126/81 mm Hg and pulse is 68/min. Physical examination shows a soft and nontender abdomen. Bowel sounds are normal. Stool guaiac is negative. Abdominal ultrasonography reveals a 4-cm solitary lesion in the right hepatic lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrates enhancement of the mass during hepatic arterial phase and a central stellate scar. She is started on a proton pump inhibitor for her dyspepsia, with symptomatic improvement. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient's liver mass?

questions.explanation: Gestational diabetes mellitus causes potentially severe neonatal complications, including polycythemia due to both maternal and fetal factors. Persistent maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, which in turn leads to fetal hyperinsulinemia and increased fetal metabolism. In addition, diabetes in pregnancy can lead to placental vasculopathy with decreased uteroplacental blood flow and oxygen delivery to the fetus. The placenta is unable to meet the increased metabolic demands, which worsens fetal hypoxemia. In response to the fetal hypoxemia, fetal erythropoietin production increases to improve oxygen delivery to the tissues. Therefore, many infants of diabetic mothers have polycythemia (hematocrit of >65%). Patients are usually asymptomatic at birth but may appear plethoric. The viscous blood in polycythemic infants is at risk for vascular sludging, potentially causing tissue ischemia and thrombosis. (Choice A) Uncontrolled maternal hyperglycemia can cause macrosomia (birth weight >4 kg [8 lb 13 oz]), which is associated with increased risk of shoulder dystocia and its complications (eg, brachial plexus injuries), particularly with vaginal delivery. However, this infant was born via cesarean delivery, reducing the risk for birth injury. (Choice B) Maternal systemic lupus erythematosus can cause neonatal cardiac arrythmia, specifically heart block. Infants of diabetic mothers are at risk for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy but do not have increased rates of arrhythmia. (Choice C) Neonatal hypocalcemia is common in infants of diabetic mothers due to transient parathyroid hormone suppression. Neonates are usually asymptomatic but may develop signs of neuromuscular irritability (eg, seizures, tetany). Hypercalcemia is not seen. (Choice D) Although maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperglycemia, excessive maternal glucose delivery ends when the umbilical cord is clamped. The hyperinsulinemic state can last for several days in the newborn, resulting in profound neonatal hypoglycemia. (Choice E) Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy occurs when oxygen delivery to the fetal brain is interrupted before or during delivery. Causes include placental or cord injury (eg, abruption, vasa previa) or cord compression (eg, shoulder dystocia). Affected infants typically are born with poor tone and respiratory effort, weak cry, and decreased movement. This patient's delivery was uncomplicated, and his Apgar scores were normal. Educational objective: Uncontrolled maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperinsulinemia, increased fetal metabolic demands, and chronic hypoxemia. To compensate, fetal erythropoietin increases; therefore, infants of diabetic mothers are often polycythemic. Additional complications include hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia.

questions.stem: A newborn boy is evaluated in the operating room immediately after delivery. Due to suspected fetal macrosomia on ultrasound, the patient was delivered via uncomplicated, scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks gestation. The mother is a 28-year-old woman, gravida 1, who was diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus at 28 weeks gestation. She attempted dietary control of her glucose levels. At 31 weeks gestation, she was prescribed insulin due to persistent fasting blood glucose values of >110 mg/dL. However, the mother was inconsistent with medication administration and gained an additional 11.3 kg (24.9 lb) in the third trimester. The baby's birth weight is 5.4 kg (11.9 lb). Apgar scores are 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes respectively. Given his mother's medical condition, this newborn is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?

questions.explanation: Genital herpes Etiology Herpes simplex virus type 2 (most common) Clinical presentation Cluster of painful vesicles, pustules &/or ulcers on labia, penis, buttocks, or thigh ± Systemic symptoms in primary infection Treatment Acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir Genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) is transmitted via contact with infected mucosa or skin. Infectivity is highest when lesions or prodromal symptoms (eg, genital pain/itching, neuropathic pain in buttocks/legs) are present. However, transmission is most common during periods of asymptomatic viral shedding. Risk of transmission is reduced by limiting mucosal contact and viral shedding. Complete abstinence from vaginal, anal, and oral sex is the only practice that absolutely prevents transmission. For serodiscordant sexual partners (one partner is infected and the other is not), consistent use of barrier contraception with every sexual encounter is the single most effective strategy for preventing transmission (>95% effective). Because transmission may still occur due to contact with areas not covered by the condom, daily suppressive antiviral therapy (eg, valacyclovir) is often also recommended for the partner who is infected. (Choice A) Individuals with genital HSV are encouraged to disclose their status to their sexual partners and avoid sexual contact during outbreaks and when they experience prodromal symptoms. However, abstinence during outbreaks and prodromal symptoms reduces longitudinal risk of transmission by only ~50% due to viral shedding when no symptoms are present. (Choices B and D) Postexposure prophylaxis for the partner who is not infected and circumcision of the partner who is infected are effective strategies to reduce the risk of HIV transmission in serodiscordant sexual partners. However, neither of these strategies has been shown to significantly reduce genital HSV transmission. (Choice C) Long-term suppressive therapy with a daily antiviral medication (eg, valacyclovir) significantly reduces HSV outbreaks and the number of days each month that asymptomatic viral shedding occurs. This is the reason long-term suppressive therapy is generally recommended for the partner who is infected. In contrast, episodic antiviral therapy (ie, during outbreaks) is not nearly as effective as long-term suppressive therapy for preventing longitudinal transmission. Educational objective: Genital herpes can be transmitted when no lesions or prodromal symptoms are present due to subclinical viral shedding. Other than complete abstinence from oral, anal, and vaginal sex, the most effective strategy to prevent transmission is consistent use of condoms. Long-term daily suppressive therapy is also generally recommended for the partner who is infected when sexual partners are serodiscordant.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the office for routine gynecologic care. The patient is in a new relationship with a man. He recently informed her that he has a history of genital herpes and has outbreaks rarely. She is interested in starting a sexual relationship with him but is concerned about herpes transmission. The patient takes a combined estrogen/progestin oral contraceptive pill and no other medications. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. She has no significant medical history and no known drug allergies. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination shows no evidence of vaginal discharge, vesicular lesions, or other abnormalities. Urine pregnancy test is negative. Serologic testing detects no IgG against herpes simplex virus type 1 or type 2. Nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae is negative. Which of the following is the single most effective strategy to prevent this patient from acquiring herpes simplex virus infection?

choices: Calcific degeneration of the prosthetic valve
questions.explanation: Long-term antithrombotic therapy for mechanical prosthetic heart valves Valve position Other conditions increasing risk* Recommended therapy for modern bileaflet valve Aortic (or pulmonic) No Warfarin with target INR 2.5** Yes Warfarin with target INR 3 Mitral (or tricuspid) Not applicable Warfarin with target INR 3 *Including atrial fibrillation, reduced left ventricular systolic function, and previous thromboembolic disease. **A lower target INR of 1.5-2 is appropriate for the On-X valve. Daily low-dose aspirin is also recommended with the On-X valve, but it is not recommended with other valve types in the absence of a separate indication (eg, coronary artery disease). This patient most likely has prosthetic valve thrombosis (PVT) of a mechanical mitral valve. Due to relatively low flow velocity between the left atrium and left ventricle, PVT affects mechanical mitral valves twice as often as mechanical aortic valves. To minimize the risk of PVT, oral anticoagulation with warfarin (with a target INR of 3) along with daily aspirin therapy is recommended in all patients with a mechanical prosthetic mitral valve. Inadequate anticoagulation is the strongest risk factor for PVT; this patient's recent initiation of multivitamins (often containing vitamin K) may have decreased the efficacy of warfarin, leading to subtherapeutic INR. Mitral PVT typically causes valvular obstruction and has clinical manifestations similar to mitral valve stenosis. Patients may have minimal symptoms or may develop rapid onset of dyspnea, heart failure with pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic shock. Mitral PVT may also be complicated by systemic thromboembolism (eg, stroke, limb ischemia). The diagnosis is made by echocardiography. For patients with large valvular thrombus or severe heart failure, surgical valve replacement is needed. Patients with small valvular thrombus and mild heart failure can be managed with anticoagulation (eg, heparin) and close monitoring. (Choice A) Calcific degeneration can affect bioprosthetic valves 10-15 years after implantation. However, mechanical valves are more durable and rarely affected. (Choice B) Coronary artery disease is extremely unlikely in this young woman with no significant risk factors (eg, smoking, diabetes mellitus). (Choice C) Interstitial lung disease typically presents with gradually progressive dyspnea. This patient's history of a mechanical mitral valve, subtherapeutic INR, and rapid symptom development makes PVT more likely. (Choice D) Mechanical valves can lead to hemolytic anemia due to direct fragmentation of circulating red blood cells. This patient's normal hemoglobin makes fragmentation hemolysis unlikely. (Choice E) Left ventricular systolic dysfunction in a young patient is often due to viral myocarditis. Absence of viral prodrome (eg, fever, myalgias) makes viral myocarditis less likely. (Choice G) Pulmonary embolism typically presents with dyspnea; however, absence of chest pain and presence of crackles on lung auscultation make it less likely. Educational objective: Inadequate warfarin anticoagulation is the strongest risk factor for prosthetic valve thrombosis of a mechanical heart valve, and mechanical mitral valves are more commonly affected than mechanical aortic valves. Patients with prosthetic valve thrombosis typically present with symptoms of heart failure.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the clinic due to shortness of breath for the past 4 days. The patient describes her exercise tolerance as excellent but recently has had rapidly progressive breathlessness on exertion. She can hardly walk half a block without stopping. She has also noticed mild lightheadedness. The patient has no fevers, skin rash, chest pain, palpitations, or syncope. She has a history of rheumatic mitral valve stenosis and underwent mechanical mitral valve implantation 2 years ago. She takes warfarin and low-dose aspirin. The patient does not smoke cigarettes. She tries to follow a healthy lifestyle and started taking multivitamins several weeks ago to boost her immune system. Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and heart rate is 90/min and regular. Lung examination reveals bibasilar crackles. There is no peripheral edema. Laboratory results are as follows: Hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL Platelets 150,000/mm3 Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL INR 1.5 Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?

questions.explanation: Legionella pneumonia Epidemiology Contaminated water Hospital Travel (cruise, hotel) Clinical features Fever >38.8 C (101.8 F) Relative bradycardia Gastrointestinal: diarrhea, vomiting, cramps Pulmonary: delayed symptoms Diagnosis Hyponatremia Chest x-ray: lobar infiltrate Sputum Gram stain: PMNs, few/no organisms Urine Legionella antigen Treatment Respiratory fluoroquinolone or newer macrolide PMNs = polymorphonuclear leukocytes. This patient who recently returned from a trip has gastrointestinal symptoms, high fever with relative bradycardia, and likely pulmonary infiltrate (decreased breath sounds, crackles), raising suspicion for Legionella pneumophila pneumonia. Legionella is an aerobic, gram-negative bacillus that commonly causes community-acquired pneumonia. The organism is transmitted primarily via contaminated water, often in the hospital or travel setting (eg, hotel, cruise ship). Manifestations typically begin with headache, gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, watery diarrhea), and high fever (>38.8 C [101.8 F]). Respiratory symptoms develop a few days later. One characteristic sign of infection is fever with relative bradycardia (lower heart rate than expected with fever). Diagnosis is made with urine Legionella antigen testing and respiratory culture on specialized media. Because outcomes are improved with early treatment, patients often empirically receive pulmonary fluoroquinolones (eg, levofloxacin) or newer macrolides (eg, azithromycin). Fluoroquinolones are typically preferred due to excellent coverage against many community-acquired pneumonia pathogens (eg, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae). (Choices A, B, and F) Although beta-lactam antibiotics such as amoxicillin, ceftriaxone, and piperacillin-tazobactam are often used in the treatment of community- or hospital-acquired pneumonia, these agents are relatively ineffective for patients with Legionella (possibly due to low intracellular drug concentrations). (Choice C) Clindamycin is efficacious against many anaerobic and some aerobic organisms and is used primarily for dental and skin infections. It is not a common treatment for Legionella. (Choice D) Ertapenem is a carbapenem that treats many multidrug-resistant organisms, such as extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing pathogens (eg, ESBL Klebsiella). It is not an effective treatment for patients with Legionella. Educational objective: Legionella is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia and typically manifests with high fever and prominent gastrointestinal symptoms prior to the development of respiratory symptoms. Diagnosis is made with Legionella urine antigen and respiratory culture. Preferred treatment is a respiratory fluoroquinolone (eg, levofloxacin) or newer macrolide (eg, azithromycin).

wrongAnswers.C: (Choice C)  Clindamycin is efficacious against many anaerobic and some aerobic organisms and is used primarily for dental and skin infections.  It is not a common treatment for Legionella.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Ertapenem is a carbapenem that treats many multidrug-resistant organisms, such as extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing pathogens (eg, ESBL Klebsiella).  It is not an effective treatment for patients with Legionella.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to fever, mildly productive cough, and headache. He visited an urgent care center yesterday for lethargy, abdominal cramps, and watery diarrhea and was discharged after receiving intravenous fluids. The patient has no medical problems and takes no medications. He recently returned from a trip to Hawaii. He does not use tobacco and drinks alcohol only on social occasions. Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F), blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg, pulse is 74/min, and respirations are 20/min. The pharyngeal mucosa is not erythematous, and there is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Auscultation of the chest reveals reduced breath sounds and crackles in the right base. The abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended, with no organomegaly. Laboratory evaluation shows elevation of segmented neutrophils with band forms. Which of the following is the best initial treatment for this patient while confirmatory tests are pending?

questions.explanation: This patient with uncontrolled hypertension and cocaine use is at risk for hypertensive vasculopathy, the most common cause of spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage. Hypertensive cerebral vascular damage typically occurs near the branch points off of major intracerebral vessels. The basal ganglia is the most common (~50%) site of hemorrhage; it is located superiorly to the uncus. Several features of this patient's presentation are concerning for uncal herniation, including the following: Fixed and dilated right pupil due to ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III) dysfunction Left (contralateral) decerebrate posturing due to dysfunction of the rubrospinal tract below the red nucleus Comatose state with respiratory compromise due to midbrain dysfunction Uncal herniation occurs when the medial temporal lobe (uncus) becomes displaced under the tentorium cerebelli due to increased pressure (eg, mass effect from intracranial hemorrhage in the nearby basal ganglia). (Choice B) Hypertensive hemorrhages can occur in the cerebellum and may push the cerebellum through the foramen magnum, resulting in cerebellar tonsillar herniation. Manifestations typically include neck tilt, flaccid paralysis, coma, blood pressure instability, and respiratory arrest; extensor posturing and pupillary dysfunction are not typical. (Choice C) Because brainstem ischemic infarctions impact a small anatomic area, they are less likely to result in herniation. Instead, they typically result in contralateral hemiparesis with ipsilateral cranial nerve signs (ie, crossed signs), depending on which cranial nerve nuclei are impacted. Medullary infarcts often have dysfunction of the vagus nerve (CN X) (lateral medullary syndrome) or the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) (medial medullary syndrome). (Choice D) A midbrain ischemic stroke can lead to an ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil due to damage to CN III and contralateral hemiparesis. However, loss of consciousness and extensor posturing, as seen in this patient, is more characteristic of herniation. In addition, this patient has significant risk factors for hemorrhagic (rather than ischemic) stroke. (Choice E) Occipital cortex infarction can damage the primary visual cortex and lead to homonymous hemianopia if unilateral and cortical blindness if bilateral. However, pupillary responses are normal in patients with cortical blindness because the pupillary light reflex is mediated by cranial nerves, not the cortex. Consciousness would not be impacted. Educational objective: Uncal herniation may be caused by mass effect from basal ganglia hemorrhage. Symptoms of uncal herniation include a dilated, nonreactive ipsilateral pupil, contralateral extensor posturing, coma, and respiratory compromise.
