questions.stem: A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his family found him on the floor and unresponsive at home. The patient has a history of hypertension but is not adherent with medical treatment. He smokes cigarettes and uses cocaine. Temperature is 36.6 C (97.9 F), blood pressure is 176/98 mm Hg, pulse is 58/min, and respirations are 12/min and irregular. The patient is unresponsive to deep sternal rub. The right pupil is widely dilated and unresponsive to light. There is intermittent extended posturing of the left arm and leg. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ in the left extremities, and Babinski sign is present on the left side. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current condition?

questions.explanation: Complications at the site of vascular access are common in patients undergoing cardiac catheterization; the right common femoral artery is the most commonly used vascular access point. This patient has most likely developed a pseudoaneurysm of the right femoral artery. A pseudoaneurysm occurs when a defect in the arterial wall (eg, inadequately sealed arterial puncture site) causes bleeding that remains confined within the surrounding layer of periarterial connective tissue. The result is a contained hematoma that has ongoing communication with the arterial lumen. Diastolic pressure equalizes between the artery and the confined hematoma; therefore, as blood is forced through the arterial wall defect during systole, a systolic bruit is heard at the site of the pseudoaneurysm. A tender, pulsatile mass is also typically present. Inadequate post-procedural arterial compression is the strongest risk factor for pseudoaneurysm development. The diagnosis should be confirmed by ultrasound. (Choice A) An arteriovenous fistula can occur when inadequate hemostasis of an arterial puncture site allows blood to communicate with an inadvertently punctured adjacent vein. Patients may have localized swelling and tenderness, but no mass is present. A bruit is typically present, but it is continuous (arterial pressure exceeds venous pressure throughout the cardiac cycle) rather than systolic and is typically accompanied by a palpable thrill. (Choice B) Acute thrombosis of the femoral artery leads to acute arterial occlusion and limb ischemia. Patients typically present with the 5 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness (or reduced pulse), paresthesias, and paralysis of the involved lower extremity. (Choice D) Patients with femoral vein thrombosis usually have swelling, pain, or erythema of the involved lower extremity. A bruit is not typical. (Choice E) Post-procedural arterial bleeding that is not contained by periarterial connective tissue may lead to extravasation of blood into surrounding tissues (eg, thigh) and an expanding hematoma. Patients may have localized pain and bruising. A palpable mass may be present, but it is not typically pulsatile and there is no bruit. Such a hematoma can occasionally undergo massive extension into the retroperitoneal space, resulting in hypotension and flank pain. Educational objective: Vascular access site complications are common in patients undergoing cardiac catheterization. An arterial pseudoaneurysm occurs when an arterial wall defect leads to a hematoma contained within the periarterial connective tissue. Ongoing arterial communication of the contained hematoma leads to a pulsatile mass with an audible systolic bruit.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to persistent right groin pain after cardiac catheterization 3 days ago. Coronary angiography was performed to evaluate recurrent chest pains and revealed a left anterior descending artery stenosis; a drug-eluting stent was placed. The patient has had no chest pain since the procedure and no lightheadedness, weakness, or shortness of breath. He experienced mild discomfort at the arterial access site after the procedure, but the pain has since increased and swelling has developed at the right groin. His other medical problems include hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Temperature is 36.8 C (98.2 F), blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 86/min. Physical examination shows a pulsatile mass at the catheter insertion site in the right inguinal region. Auscultation over the mass reveals a systolic bruit. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: This patient's presentation raises concern for biliary leakage, a rare but serious complication of laparoscopic cholecystectomy that happens when incomplete/faulty clipping of the cystic duct or intraoperative bile duct injury leads to extravasation of bile into the abdominal cavity. It usually occurs 2-10 days after surgery with persistent abdominal pain, fever, nausea/vomiting, and anorexia. Right upper quadrant (RUQ) tenderness with localized peritoneal signs (eg, rebound tenderness) is often present due to inflammation triggered by the leaking bile acids. Leukocytosis is typical, and elevated liver function tests (eg, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, transaminases) are common due to perihepatic inflammation, with hyperbilirubinemia progressively worsening over time due to peritoneal reabsorption of leaked bile. On imaging, most patients have relatively normal-appearing bile ducts or only mild dilation, which can be from the postoperative state alone. An abnormal fluid collection in the gallbladder fossa or bilious ascites (in large leaks) may also be seen and, if present, supports the diagnosis. Early recognition and treatment are important for preventing acute complications such as biliary peritonitis, cholangitis, and sepsis. Although mild leaks may resolve spontaneously with appropriate drainage, more significant leaks may require endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with stent placement or open surgical repair. (Choice B) Drug-induced hepatotoxicity (eg, acetaminophen overdose) can manifest with nausea, vomiting, and RUQ pain. However, transaminase levels are usually markedly elevated (≥3,000 IU/L), and peritoneal signs (eg, rebound tenderness) are unlikely. (Choice C) Gilbert syndrome causes an isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that is typically asymptomatic (occasional jaundice). It would be unlikely to cause elevated alkaline phosphatase, fever, or abdominal pain. (Choice D) Ischemic hepatitis can occur after disruption in liver perfusion (eg, intraoperative hypotension) and presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. However, associated transaminase elevation in ischemic liver injury is generally quite significant (eg, 25×-250× the upper limit of normal). (Choice E) A retained gallstone within the biliary tree after cholecystectomy can cause symptoms mimicking biliary colic (eg, RUQ pain, nausea, vomiting) and elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. However, bile duct dilation would be expected on ultrasonography secondary to obstruction. (Choice F) Small bowel obstruction could present postoperatively as nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, but it is generally a long-term complication due to adhesions from prior surgeries. Small bowel obstruction is less likely to cause isolated RUQ tenderness and elevated liver function tests. Educational objective: Biliary leakage should be suspected in patients with persistent abdominal pain, fever, and right upper quadrant tenderness 2-10 days after laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Laboratory studies often demonstrate elevated liver function tests (especially bilirubin), with normal-appearing bile ducts (often with an intraabdominal fluid collection) on imaging.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman comes to the postoperative clinic due to persistent abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting after undergoing an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy 4 days ago. During the procedure, she had an episode of hypotension that resolved with intravenous fluids; there were no other intraoperative complications. The patient has no chronic medical conditions. She has been taking acetaminophen-hydrocodone for pain control. Temperature is 38.2 C (100.8 F), blood pressure is 122/84 mm Hg, and pulse is 92/min. Abdominal examination demonstrates mild abdominal distension with decreased bowel sounds and healing surgical incisions without erythema. Right upper quadrant tenderness with guarding and rebound tenderness is present. Laboratory results are as follows: Complete blood count Hematocrit 33% Leukocytes 13,000/mm3 Liver function studies Total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL Direct bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase 150 U/L Aspartate aminotransferase (SGOT) 62 U/L Alanine aminotransferase (SGPT) 74 U/L Right upper quadrant ultrasonography demonstrates normal-sized biliary ducts. questions.explanation: Classification of hyponatremia Serum osmolality ECV Urine findings Causes Hypotonic (<275 mOsm/kg) Hypovolemic UNa <40 mEq/L Nonrenal salt loss (eg, vomiting, diarrhea) UNa >40 mEq/L Renal salt loss (eg, diuretics, primary adrenal insufficiency) Euvolemic UOsm <100 mOsm/kg Primary polydipsia Malnutrition (eg, beer potomania) UOsm >100 mOsm/kg & UNa >40 mEq/L SIADH* Hypervolemic Variable Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome Isotonic Variable Pseudohyponatremia (eg, paraproteinemia, hyperlipidemia) Hypertonic (>295 mOsm/kg) Translocational hyponatremia (eg, hyperglycemia, exogenous solutes such as mannitol) *Hypothyroidism & secondary adrenal insufficiency should be ruled out. ECV = extracellular volume; SIADH = syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion; UNa = urine sodium; UOsm = urine osmolality. This patient with fever, toothache, and leukocytosis likely has a dental abscess, which, in combination with missed doses of antidiabetic medication, has led to severe hyperglycemia and a hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. An excess of osmotically active substance (eg, glucose) in the bloodstream draws intracellular water and dilutes extracellular fluid sodium, a process known as translocational hyponatremia (TH). The serum osmolality (estimated by 2 × serum sodium [mEq/L] + serum glucose [mg/dL]/18 + serum blood urea nitrogen [mg/dL]/2.8) will be elevated (315 mOsm/kg H2O in this patient), which may manifest clinically with dehydration (due to osmotic diuresis) and symptoms of neurologic dysfunction (eg, lethargy, myoclonic jerks). Hyperkalemia is typically present due to "solvent drag" of intracellular potassium by fluid shifting into the bloodstream. In patients with TH due to hyperglycemia, the serum sodium concentration drops by approximately 2 mEq/L for every 100 mg/dL increase in blood glucose over the normal value (eg, 100 mg/dL). Administration of insulin shuttles glucose intracellularly and water follows, restoring the extracellular fluid sodium concentration to normal. Other potential causes of TH include intravenous mannitol infusion (sometimes used to treat elevated intracranial pressure) and receipt of high volumes of intravenous immunoglobulin or iodinated contrast, especially in patients with impaired kidney function. (Choices B, D, and E) This patient's history (eg, poor oral intake, osmotic diuresis due to severe hyperglycemia) suggests volume depletion. In the setting of volume depletion, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system will be activated, leading to high aldosterone levels (secondary hyperaldosteronism) and sodium reabsorption. Hypovolemia also stimulates nonosmotic release of antidiuretic hormone, which can lead to excess free water retention and hyponatremia. However, the hyponatremia will be hypotonic (true hyponatremia) rather than hypertonic. Excess free water intake in the setting of volume depletion can further contribute to hypotonic hyponatremia. (Choice C) This patient's blood urea nitrogen/creatinine ratio >20 mg/dL and low urine sodium (<40 mEq/L) represent an appropriate renal tubular response to volume depletion, making renal tubular dysfunction unlikely. Educational objective: Translocational hyponatremia is caused by shifting of fluid from the intracellular to extracellular space due to an excess of osmotically active substance in the bloodstream (eg, glucose). Serum osmolality will be elevated (hypertonic hyponatremia).

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to lethargy. For the past 3 days, she has had a severe toothache and low-grade fever. According to her son, she is not able to eat and is mostly drinking fluids. The patient's medical history is significant for hypertension, gout, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She has not taken her antidiabetic medications for the past 3 days. On examination, the patient is lethargic. Temperature is 37.8 C (100 F), blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg, pulse is 100/min, and respirations are 20/min. Pulse oximetry shows 99% on room air. BMI is 34 kg/m2. Her neck is supple, pupils are equal and reactive to light, and strength is normal in all extremities. She has occasional myoclonic jerks. Laboratory results are as follows: Leukocytes 16,000/mm3 (7% bands) Hemoglobin 18.5 g/dL Sodium 125 mEq/L Potassium 5.5 mEq/L Blood urea nitrogen 30 mg/dL Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL Glucose 986 mg/dL Urinalysis shows no protein or blood and 4+ glucose. questions.explanation: This patient's postoperative, dark red, sanguineous drainage and increasing incisional pain are consistent with an incisional hematoma, an abnormal collection of blood at the incision site often due to inadequate surgical hemostasis. Risk factors include obesity and hypocoagulability (eg, due to anticoagulation medication, as in this patient). Patients with an incisional hematoma typically develop pain or a fluctuant mass at the incision site hours to days after surgery. As the collection of blood enlarges, the hematoma can reopen surgical potential spaces, as evidenced by this patient's 5-mm incisional defect. Treatment of large, symptomatic hematomas involves opening the incision, evacuating the clot, obtaining hemostasis, and reclosing the incision. (Choice A) Fascial dehiscence, the reopening of the fascial incision, is more likely to occur in patients with obesity; however, it typically presents with a "popping" sensation followed by an incisional bulge and copious, serous drainage, which are not seen in this patient. In addition, the resistance encountered during the probing of the patient's incision suggests that her rectus fascia is intact. (Choices B and E) Although wound cellulitis and abscess are potential complications of an incisional hematoma, this patient has no fever, erythema, or purulent discharge to suggest a surgical site infection. (Choice D) Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency that presents with bullae, crepitus, and rapidly spreading, severe pain that is out of proportion to examination findings. Patients with necrotizing fasciitis are typically acutely ill and have unstable vital signs, which are not seen in this patient. (Choice F) Dehiscence of the hysterotomy (ie, opening of the uterine incision) is rare after cesarean delivery and presents with severe abdominal pain, hemodynamic instability, and heavy vaginal bleeding. This patient's uterus is firm, and her lochia is moderate, making this diagnosis unlikely. Educational objective: An incisional hematoma can present with increasing incisional pain and sanguineous drainage at the surgical incision site. Risk factors include inadequate surgical hemostasis, obesity, and hypocoagulability.

questions.explanation: Postpartum endometritis Risk factors Cesarean delivery Intraamniotic infection Group B Streptococcus colonization Prolonged rupture of membranes Operative vaginal delivery Clinical features Fever >24 hr postpartum Uterine fundal tenderness Purulent lochia Etiology Polymicrobial infection Treatment Clindamycin & gentamicin Postpartum endometritis is an infection of the uterine decidua (the modified endometrium that forms during pregnancy) and the most common pathologic cause of postpartum fever. Even after delivery of the placenta and membranes, the superficial uterine decidua continues to shed up to a month after delivery (as lochia). Infection of this layer occurs due to the direct inoculation of the uterine cavity by vaginal flora during labor. Risk factors for infection include prolonged time of exposure to vaginal flora (ie, prolonged labor, prolonged rupture of membranes), cesarean delivery (due to presence of foreign material [eg, suture]), operative vaginal delivery, intraamniotic infection, and group B Streptococcus colonization. Postpartum endometritis is diagnosed by fever >24 hours postpartum, uterine tenderness, and sometimes purulent or malodorous lochia (depending on the predominant bacteria). The infected endometrium can delay uterine involution, which is clinically observed as a soft, tender uterus, and often with an increase in postpartum bleeding. It is treated empirically with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (eg, gentamicin and clindamycin) for polymicrobial coverage. (Choice A) Breast engorgement, due to milk accumulation, presents with swollen, warm, and tender breasts. Breast engorgement can cause a mildly elevated temperature but not fever or uterine fundal tenderness. (Choice C) Cystitis, an infection of the urinary bladder, typically presents with dysuria and suprapubic pain rather than uterine tenderness. The urinary retention seen in this patient is a normal postpartum finding likely due to labor anesthesia. (Choice D) During the normal postpartum course, fever during the first 24 hours is typically physiologic and resolves without treatment. After the initial 24 hours, fever is usually associated with an infection and should be further evaluated. Dependent (ie, lower extremity) edema is a normal finding in pregnancy and immediately postpartum because the expanded plasma volume associated with pregnancy does not return to prepregnancy levels for 6 weeks. (Choices E and F) A pelvic abscess (eg, purulent pelvic fluid collection) and septic thrombophlebitis (eg, septic thrombus of the pelvic veins) are uncommon causes of postpartum fever. These diagnoses should be considered in patients who remain febrile after 48 hours of treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics. This patient's uterine fundal tenderness makes postpartum endometritis more likely. Educational objective: Postpartum endometritis, the most common puerperal infection, presents with fever, uterine fundal tenderness, and ± purulent or malodorous lochia. Risk factors include cesarean delivery, operative vaginal delivery, prolonged rupture of membranes, and intraamniotic infection. Treatment is empiric with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, is evaluated for fevers and chills on postpartum day 2 after a forceps-assisted vaginal delivery. The patient initially came to the hospital at 41 weeks gestation for leakage of fluid. After a 2-day induction, during which the patient received penicillin for a positive group B Streptococcus rectovaginal culture, a forceps-assisted vaginal delivery was performed for maternal exhaustion and a nonreassuring fetal heart rate tracing. A second-degree perineal laceration was repaired. A urinary catheter was placed on the first postpartum day for urinary retention but was discontinued later that day. The patient reports no dysuria. Current temperature is 39.4 C (103 F), blood pressure is 120/56 mm Hg, and pulse is 112/min. Physical examination shows firm, enlarged breasts. Auscultation of the lungs reveals normal breath sounds bilaterally. Abdominal examination shows uterine fundal tenderness but no suprapubic tenderness. Pelvic examination shows an intact laceration repair with a moderate amount of lochia. The patient has pitting edema of the feet and calves bilaterally but no palpable cords. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's fever?

questions.explanation: Water-soluble vitamins Vitamin Source Deficiency B1 (thiamine) Whole grains, meat, fortified cereal, nuts, legumes Beriberi (peripheral neuropathy, heart failure) Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome B2 (riboflavin) Dairy, eggs, meat, green vegetables Angular cheilosis, stomatitis, glossitis Normocytic anemia Seborrheic dermatitis B3 (niacin) Meat, whole grains, legumes Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, delusions/dementia, glossitis) B6 (pyridoxine) Meat, whole grains, legumes, nuts Cheilosis, stomatitis, glossitis, Irritability, confusion, depression B9 (folate, folic acid) Green leafy vegetables, fruit, meat, fortified cereal/grains Megaloblastic anemia Neural tube defects (fetus) B12 (cobalamin) Meat, dairy Megaloblastic anemia Neurologic deficits (confusion, paresthesias, ataxia) C (ascorbic acid) Citrus fruits, strawberries, tomatoes, potatoes, broccoli Scurvy (punctate hemorrhage, gingivitis, corkscrew hair) This patient has coiled hairs and perifollicular hemorrhages consistent with vitamin C deficiency (scurvy). In the United States, scurvy is most often seen in severely malnourished individuals (eg, homelessness, alcohol or drug use disorder, eating disorders). Other common symptoms include petechial hemorrhages, mucosal bleeding, and periodontal disease. Symptoms of vitamin C deficiency are the result of decreased connective tissue strength. Vitamin C is necessary for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis. Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine are essential for cross-linking collagen molecules; in scurvy, collagen cross-linking is compromised, thereby reducing its tensile strength. This leads to fragility of capillary walls and poor wound healing. Scurvy is even more severe in children and manifests with hemorrhages, bony deformities, and subperiosteal and joint hematomas. (Choice B) Deficiency of vitamin B1 can cause beriberi, characterized by peripheral neuropathy and high-output heart failure. Central nervous system involvement is responsible for Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (ie, confusion, ataxia, oculomotor abnormalities, impaired memory). (Choice C) Vitamin K is necessary for the synthesis of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X. Deficiency causes bruising and hematomas, but coiled hairs and perifollicular hemorrhages are more consistent with scurvy. (Choice D) Deficiency of vitamin B12 causes megaloblastic anemia, peripheral neuropathy, and neurocognitive deficits. (Choice E) Impaired night vision is a characteristic symptom of vitamin A deficiency. (Choice F) Chronic deficiency of vitamin B3 leads to pellagra, characterized by the triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. (Choice G) Sideroblastic anemia is due to abnormal synthesis of heme and impaired incorporation of iron. Causes include certain inherited disorders, myelodysplastic syndromes, lead or isoniazid toxicity, and deficiency of vitamin B6 or copper. Educational objective: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) causes impaired collagen synthesis with decreased connective tissue strength. Symptoms include petechial and perifollicular hemorrhages, mucosal bleeding, and periodontal disease.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her neighbor, who found her on the bathroom floor. The patient says that she slipped on the wet floor and fell, landing on her left hip. The neighbor adds that the patient lives alone and that he found her house in very poor sanitary condition. His family occasionally provides the patient with dinner; otherwise she mostly eats breads and canned food products. She does not use tobacco or alcohol. Temperature is 36.5 C (97.7 F), blood pressure is 140/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/min. She appears thin and weak. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and poor dentition. The patient has left hip tenderness. Skin examination shows small, rough, papules at the hair follicles with surrounding hemorrhage, as shown in the image. X-ray reveals a left femoral neck fracture. The nutritional deficiency causing this patient's skin findings is most likely to be associated with which of the following?

questions.explanation: This patient has acute onset of ataxia with disturbances in coordination and gait. Symmetric involvement of the extremities, staggering gait, intention tremor, and nystagmus help localize symptoms to the cerebellum. Sensation and deep tendon reflexes are preserved. In an otherwise healthy child, the most common etiology of these findings is acute cerebellar ataxia (acute postinfectious cerebellar ataxia), which often follows viral illness (eg, coxsackievirus, some human herpesvirus infections). Symptoms occur approximately 1-3 weeks after infection and generally resolve spontaneously within 2 weeks. No specific diagnostic test exists. It is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion after other sources of cerebellar dysfunction (eg, toxins, metabolic disease) are ruled out. (Choice B) Ataxia-telangiectasia is a genetic disorder that can cause neurologic symptoms (eg, speech delays, dysarthria, ataxia, progressive gait disturbance). However, ataxia usually develops at age <2, and the condition is also characterized by immunoglobulin deficiency (eg, recurrent infections) and cutaneous lesions (telangiectasias on skin and conjunctivae). (Choice C) Friedreich ataxia is a genetic disorder characterized by progressive ataxia. Nystagmus and dysarthria are common features. However, onset of symptoms typically occurs during the teenage years, deep tendon reflexes are decreased or absent, and cardiac and endocrine dysfunction is typically present. (Choice D) Guillain-Barré syndrome may follow viral illness and present with gait disturbance due to progressive, severe weakness of the extremities. However, cerebellar ataxia is not common, deep tendon reflexes are usually absent, and nystagmus is not a typical finding. (Choice E) Neuroblastoma is a childhood malignancy. A possible presentation is opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome, which is characterized by irregular, jerking eye movements; myoclonus of the extremities; and, often, ataxia. This patient does not exhibit myoclonus and has nystagmus rather than opsoclonus. (Choice F) Sydenham chorea is a feature of acute rheumatic fever, a possible sequela of untreated group A Streptococcus infection. It is characterized by irregular, purposeless, jerking movements of the extremities and may involve the facial muscles. Ocular symptoms (eg, nystagmus) are not characteristic. Onset is generally weeks to months after infection. (Choice G) Transverse myelitis is a postinfectious condition that results in abnormal gait. Involvement of the spinal cord results in weakness and flaccidity rather than ataxia, and symptoms may progress to paraparesis. Paresthesias occur, often with a sensory level below which sensation is abnormal. Nystagmus is not characteristic. Educational objective: Acute postinfectious cerebellar ataxia is the most common etiology of ataxia in children and often follows viral illness. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents due to walking "like she's drunk" and frequently falling for the past several hours. The patient has no history of major illness or trauma and has never had similar symptoms. A week ago, she had a runny nose, sore throat, and low-grade fever, which spontaneously resolved after 2 days. Birth history is unremarkable and normal developmental milestones were achieved. The patient is up to date on immunizations. The parents keep no medications or alcohol in the house. The girl appears cranky but is alert and active. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F). The patient is sitting comfortably on a chair and moves all extremities freely, with normal strength and sensation. When she is asked to reach and handle a small object with either hand, a slight tremor is observed. The patient has horizontal nystagmus, but her pupils are equal and reactive to light and accommodation. When asked to ambulate, she consistently staggers and falls to the right. Deep tendon reflexes are normal and symmetric, and sensation is normal bilaterally. There is no neck stiffness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

questions.explanation: Identifying the etiology of sexual dysfunction requires careful assessment of medical and psychiatric disorders as well as the role of relationship issues and prescription and recreational drugs. This patient has a number of risk factors for sexual dysfunction, including hypertension, diabetes, and depression. However, these problems are well controlled, as evidenced by his normal vital signs, examination, and hemoglobin A1c. The most likely cause of his decreased libido and erectile difficulties is his exposure to sertraline, a member of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) class of antidepressants, medications known to cause especially high rates of sexual dysfunction. SSRI sexual side effects include decreased libido, decreased arousal with erectile dysfunction in men, anorgasmia in women, and increased ejaculation latency in men. If this patient remains on antidepressant therapy, options to address his sexual dysfunction include decreasing the dosage of the SSRI, adding a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, and switching to or augmenting therapy with a non-SSRI antidepressant such as bupropion. questions.explanation: This patient with a long history of smoking has cough, chest discomfort, hemoptysis, and weight loss, raising strong concern for lung cancer. The single, large, cavitary lesion on chest x-ray makes squamous cell carcinoma the most likely diagnosis. Squamous cell carcinoma can be associated with extensive necrosis and causes ~85% of malignant cavitary lesions of the lung. Although most cases occur in the central portion of the lung (proximal tracheobronchial tree), up to 40% arise in the periphery. The single greatest risk factor for lung cancer is long-term exposure to cigarette smoke. The risk is reduced with >5 years of smoking cessation and continues decreasing thereafter, although it never fully reaches that of nonsmokers. Therefore, lung cancer screening with yearly low-dose CT scan of the chest is recommended for certain patients based on age and smoking history. In addition, current or former smokers who develop symptoms concerning for lung cancer (eg, weight loss, chest pain, hemoptysis, chronic cough) require chest imaging to evaluate for lung malignancy. (Choice A) Although adenocarcinoma most likely arises in the lung periphery, it does not typically cause a cavitary lesion. Most cases appear as a nodule on chest x-ray. (Choice B) Hodgkin lymphoma can occur in older adults but usually presents with a mediastinal mass rather than a peripheral lung lesion. (Choice C) Mesothelioma usually causes a pleural opacity with a reduction in lung volume. Rib destruction may be present. An apical cavitary lesion would be uncommon. (Choice D) Small cell carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor that usually causes a central (hilar, perihilar) mass, often with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. An apical, cavitary lesion would be uncommon. Educational objective: Long-term exposure to cigarette smoke is the single greatest risk factor for lung malignancy. Current or former smokers with weight loss, chest pain, hemoptysis, or chronic cough should be evaluated for lung cancer with chest imaging. A large cavitary lesion in this population is highly suggestive of squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection Epidemiology Respiratory droplet transmission Incubation 2-3 weeks Outbreaks in young patients with close contacts (eg, school, military) Clinical presentation Asymptomatic Mild URI/bronchitis Pneumonia: nonproductive cough, subtle examination findings Extrapulmonary symptoms: maculopapular rash, erythema multiforme, diarrhea Diagnosis Hemolytic anemia, normal/mildly increased WBC count Negative sputum Gram stain Direct or multiplex PCR, serology CXR: patchy reticulonodular/interstitial infiltrate (pneumonia) Treatment URI/bronchitis: symptomatic treatment only Pneumonia: azithromycin, doxycycline, respiratory fluoroquinolone (eg, levofloxacin) CXR = chest x-ray; URI = upper respiratory infection; WBC = white blood cell. This patient has acute pneumonia, likely due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae. M pneumoniae is transmitted by aerosolized droplets and frequently affects young, otherwise healthy individuals. Pneumonia due to M pneumoniae is usually mild and indolent, with patients frequently presenting in the ambulatory setting with low-grade fever and nonproductive cough. Upper respiratory (eg, nonexudative pharyngitis), skin (eg, maculopapular rash), and gastrointestinal (eg, diarrhea) manifestations are also common, and asymptomatic cases are also seen. Examination findings (eg, pulmonary crackles, wheezes) may be subtle or absent. Pneumonia is confirmed on chest x-ray, which shows interstitial pulmonary infiltrates. Unlike in classic lobar bacterial pneumonia, leukocytosis is not prominent; however, patients often have mild hemolytic anemia due to the formation of antibodies that cross-react with red blood cells (cold agglutinins). Empiric treatment (eg, azithromycin, doxycycline) is recommended in most cases; supplemental laboratory tests may include Gram stain, culture, PCR, and M pneumoniae antigen test, but are not necessary to initiate treatment. (Choices A and C) Penicillins (eg, amoxicillin) and cephalosporins (eg, ceftriaxone) inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis. Because M pneumoniae does not have a cell wall, these antibiotics are ineffective. (Choice D) Clindamycin, either alone or in combination, is efficacious in some genitourinary infections caused by Mycoplasma species (eg, Mycoplasma hominis) and related organisms but does not have established efficacy against M pneumoniae. (Choice E) Pneumocystis pneumonia is treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Although this infection often causes patchy, bilateral infiltrates on chest x-ray, it is rare in an otherwise healthy, young individual without immunocompromise (eg, HIV infection). Educational objective: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a common cause of pneumonia in healthy, young individuals, and presents with mild, indolent symptoms (eg, low-grade fever, nonproductive cough). Chest x-ray typically shows interstitial pulmonary infiltrates. Leukocytosis is not prominent but mild hemolytic anemia may occur. Treatment includes empiric oral antibiotics (eg, azithromycin).

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the office due to a 2-week history of increasing cough, fever, malaise, and headache. She has been unable to perform her normal exercises for the past week due to fatigue and exertional dyspnea. The patient has no chronic medical conditions and takes no medications. Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg, pulse is 84/min, and respirations are 18/min. The neck is supple, and there is no pharyngeal erythema or cervical lymphadenopathy. Cardiopulmonary examination reveals normal heart sounds and scattered wheezes. Neurologic examination shows preserved muscle strength in all extremities and 2+ deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory results are as follows: Complete blood count Hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL Reticulocytes 2.2% Platelets 240,000/mm3 Leukocytes 8,000/mm3 Chest x-ray demonstrates diffuse reticulonodular opacities. Which of the following is likely to be the most effective treatment for this patient?

questions.explanation: Key features of congenital infections* Toxoplasmosis Chorioretinitis Hydrocephalus Diffuse intracranial calcifications Syphilis Rhinorrhea Skeletal anomalies Desquamating rash (palms/soles) Rubella Cataracts Heart defects (eg, PDA) Sensorineural hearing loss Cytomegalovirus Periventricular calcifications Microcephaly Sensorineural hearing loss Herpes simplex virus Vesicular/ulcerative rash *Nonspecific findings include growth restriction, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly & blueberry muffin rash. PDA = patent ductus arteriosus. This infant most likely has cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, the most common congenital infection worldwide. Transplacental transmission of the virus to the fetus typically occurs during a primary infection of the mother, who may experience a nonspecific febrile illness, as in this case, or be asymptomatic. Approximately 90% of infants with congenital CMV are asymptomatic. In symptomatic infants, typical features include petechiae, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and microcephaly, as seen in this patient, as well as periventricular calcifications on neuroimaging. Premature delivery (<37 weeks) may also occur due to intrauterine growth restriction. Both asymptomatic and symptomatic infants may subsequently develop neurodevelopmental abnormalities, such as sensorineural hearing loss. The diagnosis is typically established by urine or saliva PCR testing. Symptomatic infants are treated with antiviral therapy (eg, ganciclovir, valganciclovir). (Choices B and C) Infants with perinatal (as opposed to congenital) infections (eg, Escherichia coli, group B Streptococcus) acquire infection from the maternal genitourinary tract during delivery. These infants appear ill and commonly have respiratory distress, temperature instability, or hypotension. (Choice D) A transplacental herpes infection usually occurs after a primary maternal infection during pregnancy. Infants who survive typically have microcephaly with severe neurologic devastation, eye damage, and a vesicular/ulcerative rash. In contrast, this infant appears comfortable and has a petechial rash. (Choice E) Maternal Listeria monocytogenes infection typically occurs after consumption of unpasteurized dairy products. Transplacental transmission can result in fetal death, premature delivery, or an infant with multiple abscesses and granulomas (ie, granulomatosis infantiseptica). (Choice F) Congenital parvovirus B19 infection presents with severe neonatal anemia and hydrops fetalis, in which significant fluid accumulates in various compartments (eg, pleural effusions, pericardial effusion, ascites). (Choices G and H) Congenital rubella and congenital syphilis (Treponema pallidum) can present with growth restriction, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly. However, this mother's laboratory results at delivery confirm that she did not have syphilis (negative rapid plasma reagin [RPR] test). In addition, this mother is rubella nonimmune, meaning that she does not have IgG antibodies from rubella vaccination or previous infection. Although she was susceptible to rubella, she was not infected with it during pregnancy. Educational objective: Cytomegalovirus infection is the most common congenital infection and classically presents with jaundice, petechiae, and hepatosplenomegaly, as well as periventricular calcifications and microcephaly.

questions.stem: A 1-day-old girl is evaluated for petechiae and jaundice. She was born at 36 weeks gestation to a 24-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 3, who had no prenatal care. During the second trimester, the mother had a week of fever and sore throat, which resolved without treatment, but no other complications. Maternal laboratory studies obtained on admission include rapid plasma regain (RPR), negative; hepatitis B surface antigen, negative; HIV, negative; and rubella, nonimmune. The patient has been feeding normally and has normal urine and stool output. Weight and length are at the 10th percentile, and head circumference is <3rd percentile. Temperature is 36.9 C (98.4 F). Physical examination shows a comfortable-appearing infant with a diffuse petechial rash, jaundice of the face and trunk, and hepatosplenomegaly. Auscultation of the heart and lungs is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this infant's symptoms?

questions.explanation: This patient has acute fever, confusion, headache, neck stiffness, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evidence of neutrophilic pleocytosis, strongly suggesting bacterial meningitis. Streptococcus pneumoniae causes approximately 70% of community-acquired bacterial meningitis. However, patients age >50 or those who are immunocompromised (eg, hematologic malignancy) are also at risk for Listeria monocytogenes, a gram-positive bacillus. L monocytogenes is primarily a foodborne illness transmitted via raw meats/vegetables, unpasteurized milk products, and prepackaged meats (eg, hot dogs, deli meat). Healthy adults are rarely symptomatic but may develop self-limited, febrile gastroenteritis if large inoculation occurs. However, patients who are at the extremes of age (<2, >50), pregnant, or immunocompromised have a much greater risk of invasive disease (eg, bacteremia, meningoencephalitis), which can present shortly after the gastroenteritis (within hours to days of exposure) or can have a prolonged incubation period (up to months following exposure). (Choice A) Legionella is a gram-negative (not gram-positive) bacterium often found in contaminated water supplies; symptoms of infection include high fever, lethargy, headache, stupor, gastrointestinal manifestations (diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain), and the slow onset of CAP (cough, dyspnea, lobar infiltrate). Meningitis is atypical. (Choice B) Vibrio vulnificus is a gram-negative (not gram-positive) bacterium that causes foodborne illness from shellfish. Wound infections and septicemia (septic shock, bullous skin lesions, disseminated intravascular coagulation) are the two most common manifestations. (Choice D) Campylobacter is a gram-negative (not gram-positive) bacterium transmitted by undercooked poultry. Manifestations include systemic symptoms (fever, myalgias, dizziness), enteritis (abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloody stools), and late complications of reactive arthritis and Guillain-Barré syndrome. (Choice E) Influenza causes abrupt fever, headache, myalgia, malaise, and respiratory tract symptoms (cough, sore throat, rhinorrhea). Neutrophilic pleocytosis on CSF testing and a positive bacterial blood culture make this an unlikely diagnosis. S pneumoniae is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis, and risk is reduced with age-appropriate (usually >65) vaccination. However, S pneumoniae is a gram-positive cocci (not bacillus). Educational objective: Listeria monocytogenes is a foodborne illness commonly transmitted via raw meat/vegetables, unpasteurized milk products, and prepackaged food. Healthy adults rarely experience symptoms (occasionally self-limited, febrile gastroenteritis), but individuals who are at the extremes of age (<2, >50), pregnant, or immunocompromised (eg, hematologic malignancy) are at greater risk of bacteremia and/or meningoencephalitis.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to fever, confusion, and lethargy. The patient travelled to Cape Cod, Massachusetts, for summer vacation yesterday and began having nausea, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. She also has had myalgias, headache, and photophobia. questions.explanation: Preeclampsia Risk factors Nulliparity Obesity Preexisting medical condition (eg, SLE, chronic hypertension) Multiple gestation Advanced maternal age Definition New-onset hypertension* (SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 mm Hg) at ≥20 weeks AND Proteinuria OR signs/symptoms of other end-organ damage Severe features Severe-range hypertension (SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 mm Hg) Platelets <100,000/mm3 Creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or 2x normal Elevated transaminases >2x upper limit of normal Pulmonary edema Vision or cerebral symptoms (eg, headache) Management <37 weeks & no severe features: expectant ≥37 weeks (or ≥34 weeks with severe features): delivery Severe-range blood pressure: IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, PO nifedipine Seizure prophylaxis: magnesium sulfate *On 2 measurements ≥4 hr apart. DBP = diastolic blood pressure; IV = intravenous; PO = by mouth; SBP = systolic blood pressure; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus. Preeclampsia is new-onset hypertension (ie, systolic ≥140 mm Hg or diastolic ≥90 mm Hg during pregnancy) at ≥20 weeks gestation plus proteinuria and/or signs of end-organ damage. To stratify the patient's risk for maternal (eg, eclampsia, stroke) and fetal (eg, abruptio placentae, fetal demise) complications, preeclampsia is divided into the subcategories of with and without severe features. The risk of developing complications from continued pregnancy is then weighed against the risk of neonatal prematurity from preterm delivery; this guides pregnancy management and delivery timing. In patients who have preeclampsia without severe features (ie, blood pressure <160/110 mm Hg and no signs of severe end-organ damage), the maternal and fetal risks of complications are lower than the fetal risks of prematurity. Therefore, delivery is indicated at term (≥37 weeks gestation). In contrast, patients who have preeclampsia with severe features have either severe-range blood pressures (systolic ≥160 mm Hg or diastolic ≥110 mm Hg) or signs of severe end-organ damage (eg, scotoma, headache, thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, elevated creatinine level). In these patients, the risks of maternal-fetal complications with continued pregnancy are higher than the fetal risks of prematurity. Therefore, delivery is indicated in patients at ≥34 weeks gestation. Patients who develop severe complications (eg, eclampsia, fetal demise) require immediate delivery regardless of gestational age. This patient at 35 weeks gestation has preeclampsia with severe features based on the elevated creatinine level (>1.1 mg/dL), thrombocytopenia, and severe range blood pressures; therefore, the best next step is immediate delivery. (Choice A) A 24-hour urine protein collection can be used to differentiate gestational hypertension from preeclampsia. Proteinuria is not required for the diagnosis of preeclampsia if signs of end-organ damage (eg, elevated creatinine level) are present. (Choice B) A biophysical profile (BPP) is used to assess fetal well-being and is performed in patients with a nonreactive nonstress test. This patient has a reactive nonstress test but has a medical indication for immediate delivery. Therefore, a BPP would not change management and would unnecessarily delay delivery. (Choices C and E) Weekly follow-up visits and outpatient blood pressure monitoring may be appropriate in patients with gestational hypertension or preeclampsia without severe features, but they are not appropriate for this patient. Educational objective: Preeclampsia with severe features is diagnosed based on new-onset hypertension at ≥20 weeks gestation with either severe-range blood pressures (systolic ≥160 mm Hg or diastolic ≥110 mm Hg) or signs of severe end-organ damage (eg, elevated creatinine level). Patients who have preeclampsia with severe features at ≥34 weeks gestation are at increased risk for maternal-fetal complications and require delivery.

questions.explanation: Children under age 6 typically have an incomplete understanding of death. As they acquire a sense of bodily integrity, they often become preoccupied with the potential for physical harm and death. They may also be unable to understand the permanence of death, believe that beings can magically come back to life, and fill in logic gaps with fantasy elements often taken from the media. Children sometimes believe they have magically caused a death due to negative thoughts or feelings about the deceased. They may also not fully grasp the inevitability or universality of death. This girl has an age-appropriate understanding of death, and her recent preoccupation with it was likely triggered by the death of her pet and watching a movie involving the death of parents. Experiencing anxiety about her own or her parents' death is normal. Her reactions and behavior are developmentally appropriate and are not interfering with school or her ability to socialize. Leaving drawings and even talking to her pet are likely ways of remaining connected to him rather than symptoms of a mental illness. The parents should be reassured that this is normal behavior. They can help their daughter by supporting her expression of feelings about her pet, responding truthfully to questions about death in a concrete manner, and maintaining routines as much as possible. (Choice A) Adjustment disorders are characterized by emotional or behavioral disturbances, which are out of proportion to a precipitating stressor and result in impairment. This child's reaction is age appropriate and is not affecting her ability to function at school or at home. (Choices B, D, and E) This patient does not have persistent worries about multiple issues, as seen in generalized anxiety disorder. She lacks the intrusive reexperiencing of symptoms (eg, flashbacks, nightmares) and hyperarousal that are characteristic of post-traumatic stress disorder. Although separation anxiety disorder involves fears of harm or death to major attachment figures, the patient does not have excessive distress with separation. She has friends and no apparent difficulty separating from her parents to go to school, making separation anxiety disorder unlikely. Educational objective: Children under age 6 have magical thinking and an incomplete understanding of death (eg, may view death as temporary and reversible). They are also gaining a sense of bodily integrity and may become anxious about physical harm or death.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the office by her parents for assessment of anxiety. The parents report that the patient is learning to read, enjoying school, and playing with friends in the neighborhood. However, they have recently been concerned because she talks about death, asks them repeatedly if they are going to die, and insists on sleeping with a night-light on. The patient worries when her father comes home from work late and frequently mentions a movie she has seen in which the children were left alone when the parents died in a car crash. She also worries about her pet hamster who died 3 months ago and draws pictures of food for him "so he will not be hungry." Although the family buried the hamster in the backyard, she insists on keeping the cage in her room with the door open and talks to her pet as if he is still alive. Family history is significant for panic disorder in the patient's father. The girl is in the 60th percentile for height and weight. Blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 88/min. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. The patient insists on sitting on her father's lap during the evaluation. She is shy and reluctant to speak with the physician but responds to questions with her parents' encouragement. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's behavior?

questions.explanation: Although fatigue is common in ovarian cancer and may persist after completion of chemotherapy, this patient is showing other signs suggestive of depression (impaired concentration, sleep disturbance, loss of motivation to work). Her decision to send her young children away is also concerning as it may reflect that she has given up. The most important next step is to further assess the patient for depression and specifically ask if she has any suicidal thoughts. Patients with cancer experience high rates of psychological distress and comorbid major depression. Identifying depression in cancer patients is difficult as impairment in sleep, appetite, and energy level can also be explained by the cancer itself or treatment effects. Pervasive anhedonia (inability to experience pleasure), feelings of worthlessness, excessive guilt, loss of self-esteem, and suicidal ideation can be used as more reliable symptoms to diagnose depression in cancer patients. Proper diagnosis and treatment (eg, psychotherapy, antidepressants) have been associated with improved quality of life. (Choices A and D) Psychostimulants such as methylphenidate have a role in the treatment of cancer-related fatigue. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine are first-line treatment for major depression in patients with or without cancer. However, a suicide risk assessment is critical to acute management and should precede pharmacological interventions. (Choice B) The husband might discuss his concerns more openly if spoken to alone; however, it is important for the patient to be fully assessed first. (Choice E) Pain medication itself can result in fatigue, and decreasing the patient's dose may improve it. However, assessing her for depression and suicidal ideation should take precedence. (Choice F) This response offers inappropriate reassurance and does not address the need to assess the patient for depression. (Choice G) A cancer survivor support group (particularly one that addresses issues in younger patients) can be helpful but would not substitute for assessing the patient for depression and suicidality. Younger age is a risk factor for depression in cancer patients. Educational objective: Patients with cancer have high rates of psychiatric comorbidity and should be screened for depression and suicidal thoughts.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the office for follow-up accompanied by her husband. She was diagnosed with ovarian cancer a year ago. At that time, an adnexal mass was found on routine pelvic examination and confirmed by imaging. Surgery was performed and a diagnosis of epithelial ovarian carcinoma was made. Since a course of chemotherapy, the patient has had persistent sleep disturbance and fatigue. She has pain on some days but says that it is tolerable, rating it 1-3 on a 10-point scale. Although she initially returned to work after the surgery, at today's visit the patient says that she has decided to resign her position as a paralegal due to problems with fatigue and concentration. She also informs the physician that she has sent her 2 young children, ages 4 and 7, to live with her mother because she has "no energy" and doesn't want "the children to see me this way." Her husband is very concerned that his wife seems tired all the time. The patient's medications include oxycodone and zolpidem. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145.5 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m2. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min, and respirations are 12/min. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Although an unexpected pregnancy can be overwhelming, this patient's multiple depressive symptoms and associated difficulty functioning are concerning and should not be minimized. Antenatal maternal depression often goes unrecognized and is associated with risks to both the mother and fetus, including adverse pregnancy and neonatal outcomes (eg, preterm birth, low birth weight, difficulty bonding). This patient's several-week history of frequent tearfulness, anhedonia, lack of energy (eg, avoidance of friends and family, staying in bed), sleep disturbance, impaired concentration, excessive guilt (eg, "I can't do anything right"), and psychomotor retardation (increased response latency on questioning, low volume) on mental status examination are suggestive of major depressive disorder. Treatment with structured psychotherapy (eg, cognitive-behavioral therapy) and/or antidepressants (eg, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) is indicated. The most appropriate response by the physician is to empathize with the patient and explain that some of her difficulties may be due to depression and are treatable. (Choice A) It is inappropriate to suggest that this patient is experiencing a normal response to pregnancy. Although pregnancy can be overwhelming for anyone, this patient is displaying symptoms of a major depressive episode that requires treatment. Waiting a month for follow-up places this patient and her fetus at increased risk. (Choice B) This response minimizes the patient's symptoms and suggests that they will improve if she acquires more knowledge about pregnancy. It does not target her depression. (Choice C) It would be helpful for the patient to tell her husband, who can be an important source of support. However, this is not a substitute for appropriate diagnosis and treatment. (Choice E) This response offers inappropriate reassurance that the patient's symptoms will improve with time. This patient is likely suffering from a depressive episode, which should be treated. Educational objective: Antenatal maternal depression often goes unrecognized and is associated with risks to both the mother and the fetus. Treatment options include psychotherapy and/or antidepressants.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks gestation comes to the office for an initial prenatal visit. Since finding out she was pregnant 3 weeks ago, the patient has been feeling overwhelmed. She says, "I just got married 2 months ago and wasn't planning on getting pregnant for another few years. This was all my fault—I wasn't taking my birth control regularly. I can't do anything right, and I'm going to fail at being a mom." The patient states that she has not told her husband yet, even though he is supportive and worried about why she has been crying frequently. She has been avoiding friends and family due to concern they will find out about her pregnancy and think she was irresponsible. The patient stays up late at night thinking about how her body will change in the coming months and feels unfocused at work and home. Medical history is noncontributory. She takes a daily prenatal vitamin. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, the patient appears tired and pauses before answering questions in a low volume. She says, "I really want to have a baby. I just don't know why I'm reacting like this." questions.explanation: Prognostic factors in schizophrenia Good Poor Later onset Female sex Acute onset with precipitant Predominantly positive symptoms No family history Short duration of active symptoms Onset in childhood or adolescence Male sex Gradual onset (prodrome), no precipitant Predominantly negative symptoms Family history of psychotic illness Long duration of untreated psychosis This patient's history is consistent with a diagnosis of schizophrenia, a chronic psychotic illness with typical onset in late adolescence and early adulthood (peak age: men, early 20s; women, late 20s). The patient's course of illness is characterized by early onset at age 16, no clear precipitant, a prodromal phase (ie, idiosyncratic thinking and perceptual disturbances, deterioration in academic or occupational functioning, increasing social isolation), and a gradual onset of psychosis, all of which are negative prognostic factors (Choices A, C, and D). The patient's history of predominantly positive psychotic symptoms (eg, hallucinations, delusions), as opposed to negative symptoms (eg, flat affect, loss of motivation, anhedonia), is a favorable prognostic factor. Antipsychotic medications are more effective for treating positive psychotic symptoms than negative symptoms, and early intervention to decrease duration of active psychosis improves the course of illness (Choice F). (Choice B) A family history of schizophrenia is associated with a poor prognosis. (Choice E) Female gender (possibly related to later age of onset) is associated with a more favorable prognosis compared with male gender. Educational objective: Favorable prognostic factors in schizophrenia include acute onset (lack of prodrome), identifiable precipitant, older age at onset, and the presence of predominantly positive (as opposed to negative) psychotic symptoms.

questions.explanation: Early Lyme disease Epidemiology Endemic to northeastern United States Ixodes scapularis tick transmits Borrelia burgdorferi Manifestations Erythema migrans (80%) Systemic symptoms: malaise, fatigue, arthralgia Regional lymphadenopathy Neurologic: meningitis, cranial nerve palsy, radiculoneuritis Carditis: atrioventricular block Diagnosis Clinical (if erythema migrans) B burgdorferi serology (if neurologic or cardiac disease) Treatment Oral antibiotics (eg, doxycycline): skin or mild disease Intravenous antibiotics (eg, ceftriaxone): neurologic or cardiac disease Lyme disease is a spirochetal infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi after zoonotic transmission from the Ixodes scapularis tick. Patients in Lyme disease–endemic areas often develop symptoms without being aware of a previous tick bite. Most infections present 1-2 weeks after transmission with erythema migrans, a spreading, annular, erythematous rash with central clearing. However, early localized symptoms do not occur in approximately 20% of patients, leading to presentations at later stages of the disease. Neurologic manifestations of Lyme disease usually occur several weeks after transmission and may include lymphocytic meningitis, cranial nerve palsies, and/or radiculoneuritis. Facial nerve palsy is particularly common, occurring in ~8% of infected individuals. Patients develop rapid-onset unilateral or bilateral facial muscle weakness. Diagnosis is made with B burgdorferi serology (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, then Western blot). Most patients recover completely after treatment with oral antibiotics (eg, doxycycline); intravenous antibiotics (eg, ceftriaxone) are indicated for those with concurrent carditis or encephalitis. (Choice A) Multiple sclerosis causes demyelinating plaques in the CNS. Although cranial nerve palsy can occasionally occur, it is an uncommon presenting feature. In addition, fever is atypical and suggests a different diagnosis. (Choice B) Guillain-Barré syndrome may cause rapidly progressive bilateral symmetric weakness (including bilateral facial nerve palsies). However, most cases (~90%) are marked by ascending weakness that begins in the lower extremities and occur after a gastrointestinal (eg, Campylobacter) or respiratory tract infection. Fever is atypical. (Choice C) Babesia microti is also transmitted by I scapularis and can be identified on peripheral blood smear (ie. intraerythrocytic parasites). Patients are often asymptomatic, but symptoms can include high fever (>38 C [100.4 F]), fatigue, malaise, and weakness. Facial nerve palsy is not typical. (Choice E) Herpes encephalitis often affects the temporal lobe and may cause fever, headache, seizures, focal deficits (including cranial nerve palsy due to meningeal irritation), and altered mental status. Bilateral facial nerve palsy with mild flu-like symptoms is more likely to be a result of Lyme disease. (Choice F) Syphilis is caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum and may result in neurologic disease, including meningitis (early) and tabes dorsalis/general paresis (late). Meningeal irritation can occasionally result in cranial nerve palsies, but Lyme disease is much more likely to cause bilateral facial nerve palsy in a Lyme-endemic area. Educational objective: Facial nerve palsy is a common manifestation of early disseminated Lyme disease and may occur alone or in combination with multiple erythema migrans lesions, systemic flu-like symptoms, and/or cardiac manifestations.

questions.explanation: Intertrigo is an inflammatory condition involving occluded skin surfaces such as the axillae, groin, inframammary folds, or abdominal folds. It is most commonly due to Candida species (especially C albicans) but can also be caused by a variety of other organisms (eg, Staphylococcus aureus). Factors that increase the risk of intertrigo include: Disruption of skin barrier function due to friction (eg, obesity) Excessive moisture (eg, occlusive clothing, high heat/humidity) Impaired immune function (eg, HIV, glucocorticoid therapy) Local environment conducive to microbial growth (eg, diabetes with hyperglycemia) Intertrigo presents with erythematous plaques in a symmetric "kissing" or "mirror image" pattern across the skinfold. In addition, Candida intertrigo typically also forms satellite lesions (vesicles, papules, pustules) near the primary infection. The diagnosis is mainly based on clinical features, but potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation or fungal culture of skin scrapings can confirm the diagnosis if needed. Candida will appear as pseudohyphae with budding yeast forms (blastoconidia). Treatment includes topical antifungals (eg, nystatin, miconazole) with good skin hygiene and measures to keep the affected area dry. (Choice A) Inflammatory breast cancer presents as cutaneous thickening with a "peau d'orange" appearance (superficial dimpling and pitting). The affected breast is edematous, erythematous, and painful. This patient's bilateral lesions and reflection across skinfolds are not consistent with malignancy. (Choice B) Erythrasma is a superficial skin infection that also affects intertriginal areas. It is caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum and presents with well-demarcated, thin, red-brown plaques with wrinkling and a fine scale. It has a coral-red appearance under Wood's lamp. (Choice D) Herpes simplex causes clustered vesicles and ulcers on an erythematous base. It can occur anywhere on the skin but is most common around the mouth and anogenital area. Bilateral, symmetric lesions would be unusual. (Choice E) Tinea cruris presents as annular lesions with partial central clearing (may be absent) and a scaly, raised border. It can be caused by a number of dermatophytes, which appear on KOH preparation as septate hyphae rather than pseudohyphae with budding yeasts. Educational objective: Intertrigo is an inflammatory condition involving occluded skin surfaces such as the axillae, groin, inframammary folds, or abdominal folds and is most commonly due to Candida species. It presents with erythematous plaques with a symmetric "kissing" or "mirror image" pattern across the skinfold and may have satellite lesions.

questions.explanation: Constitutionally small infant Definition Genetically predisposed small infant Association Short maternal stature Low prepregnancy weight Female infant Antepartum course EFW <10% for gestational age Normal umbilical artery Doppler findings Appropriate interval growth Outcomes Normal Apgar scores, neonatal course Normal long-term outcome EFW = estimated fetal weight. A uterine size–dates discrepancy (eg, uterine fundal height in centimeters < gestational age in weeks) and an ultrasound-estimated fetal weight <10th percentile for gestational age can be due either to a constitutionally small fetus (eg, a reflection of genetic predisposition) or to fetal growth restriction (FGR) (eg, due to pathology such as placental insufficiency). It is difficult to distinguish between constitutional smallness and pathologic FGR during the prenatal period. Placental insufficiency is associated with changes in blood flow through the umbilical artery, and these changes can be evaluated by Doppler sonography. Therefore, all fetuses with an estimated fetal weight <10th percentile for gestational age require serial ultrasounds to assess growth and umbilical artery Doppler evaluation to assess placental function and prevent intrauterine fetal death. This newborn's presentation is consistent with a constitutionally small infant, which is common in female fetuses and mothers with short stature, Asian ethnicity, and low prepregnancy weight. Constitutionally small fetuses typically have normal umbilical artery Doppler findings and appropriate interval growth on ultrasound. Because the placenta of a constitutionally small fetus has normal function, there is no increased risk for abnormalities on fetal heart rate tracing during labor or for abnormal Apgar scores. Constitutionally small infants typically have a normal neonatal course and normal long-term outcomes. (Choices A, B, C, and D) FGR is associated with multiple neonatal and long-term complications. Long-term neurologic complications include delayed cognitive development and motor dysfunction, as well as behavioral issues (eg, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder). Children with FGR are also at increased risk for growth failure (ie, failure to thrive), childhood obesity, and metabolic syndrome. Constitutionally small infants are not at increased risk for chronic disorders or other comorbidities. Educational objective: Fetal constitutional smallness is associated with short maternal stature, low prepregnancy weight, and fetal female sex. Constitutional smallness presents with an ultrasound-estimated fetal weight <10% for gestational age, normal umbilical artery Doppler evaluation, and appropriate interval growth. Constitutionally small infants have normal long-term outcomes.

questions.explanation: Patients with chronic and/or severe migraines often take multiple medications for both prophylactic and acute treatment. This patient's inability to sit still is most likely akathisia, a side effect of prochlorperazine. Akathisia is characterized by inner restlessness, or an internal sense of unease, and the need to walk or pace. Patients may or may not experience anxiety or overt restlessness and instead may have difficulty articulating their subjective distress. Akathisia does not always manifest as obvious tremulousness or agitation. Akathisia is an extrapyramidal symptom (EPS) that can occur with dopamine antagonist medications, such as antipsychotics and antiemetics (eg, prochlorperazine, promethazine, metoclopramide). Other EPSs include acute dystonias, cogwheeling, and parkinsonism, all of which can occur after using a dopamine antagonist such as prochlorperazine. (Choices A, B, E, and G) Acetaminophen, used at high doses, may have adverse hepatic effects. Amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant, may cause orthostatic, anticholinergic, antihistaminic, and cardiac side effects. Sumatriptan may cause dizziness, flushing, chest tightness, or neck and throat discomfort. Valproate may cause dizziness, nausea, sedation, hepatic toxicity, and, infrequently, hepatic encephalopathy. However, none of these medications typically cause akathisia or other EPSs. (Choice C) Excess caffeine can cause restlessness, but this would not typically or primarily manifest as inability to sit and the need to walk. Tachycardia and tremulousness may occur with caffeine intoxication. (Choice F) Tetrahydrocannabinol may cause euphoria, lethargy, distorted sensory perceptions, conjunctival injection, and increased appetite. Educational objective: The antiemetics prochlorperazine, promethazine, and metoclopramide (and most antipsychotics) are dopamine antagonists that can cause extrapyramidal symptoms. These include akathisia, dystonias, cogwheeling, and parkinsonism.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man with a history of severe migraines and depression comes to the emergency department with an intractable headache. He has severe pain, photophobia, and nausea. Prior to arrival, he took his standing amitriptyline and valproate for migraine prophylaxis, as well as doses of an acetaminophen/caffeine combination, sumatriptan, and prochlorperazine in an effort to reduce his pain and nausea. He has no other medical illness but occasionally smokes marijuana. During the examination, the patient immediately stands up and begins to walk around the room. He is not otherwise agitated and denies being anxious, but he states, "I don't know why, I just need to walk." Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min, and respirations are 16/min. He is not tremulous. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's behavior?

questions.explanation: This patient's depressive symptoms characterized by fatigue, weight gain, impaired concentration, and decreased libido are possibly due to hypothyroidism, a potential complication of long-term lithium therapy. Lithium-induced hypothyroidism may occur in the presence or absence of goiter. Lithium can interfere with the formation and release of T3 and T4, producing a hypothyroid state and a compensatory increase in the release of serum TSH. Because some of the symptoms of hypothyroidism overlap with those of worsening depression, the most appropriate next step in this patient would be to rule out lithium-induced hypothyroidism before attributing the symptoms to a recurrent bipolar depressive episode. Obtaining thyroid function tests should precede any therapeutic interventions such as adjusting any of the patient's bipolar medications, adding psychotherapy, or treating sexual dysfunction. Lithium-induced hypothyroidism can be treated with thyroid hormone replacement in patients who continue lithium and is generally reversible with lithium discontinuation. (Choices A and B) This patient's recent onset of decreased libido may be related to hypothyroidism, depression, and/or a sexual adverse effect of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor escitalopram. Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor used in the treatment of erectile dysfunction. Bupropion is an antidepressant that does not cause sexual adverse effects. The first step is to rule out lithium-induced hypothyroidism as the cause of this patient's sexual dysfunction before considering these interventions. (Choices D and E) This patient's presentation is suggestive of hypothyroidism, and this condition must be ruled out before considering any changes to his bipolar medications or adding psychotherapy. Lurasidone is an antipsychotic medication that is used as a first-line medication for bipolar depression. Educational objective: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism is a potential adverse effect of chronic lithium therapy. Apparent worsening of mood symptoms in a patient taking lithium may be due to hypothyroidism rather than a recurrence of depression. Thyroid function should be monitored in patients on chronic lithium therapy.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man comes to the office due to depressive symptoms for the past 2 months. The patient has a history of bipolar disorder, which is currently treated with escitalopram and lithium. Although he has not had any affective episodes in the past 2 years, he has a history of multiple hospitalizations and a suicide attempt. The patient states he feels tired and has difficulty staying focused at work. He says, "I'm not even interested in sex anymore and that really bothers me. My wife thinks I don't find her attractive, but that's not true." The patient's lithium level from 2 weeks ago was 0.7 mmol/L (therapeutic range: 0.6-1.2). Medical history is otherwise noncontributory. Temperature is 36.3 C (97.3 F), blood pressure is 127/78 mm Hg, pulse is 64/min, and respirations are 14/min. His weight has increased 2 kg (4.4 lb) since his prior visit 10 weeks ago. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. The patient has no suicidal ideation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Prerenal acute kidney injury Etiology Decreased renal perfusion True volume depletion Decreased EABV (eg, heart failure, cirrhosis) Displacement of intravascular fluid (eg, sepsis, pancreatitis) Bilateral renal artery stenosis with ACE inhibition Afferent arteriole vasoconstriction (eg, NSAIDs) Clinical features Increase in serum creatinine (eg, 50% from baseline) Decreased urine output Blood urea nitrogen/creatinine ratio >20:1 Fractional excretion of sodium <1% Unremarkable (bland) urine sediment Treatment Restoration of renal perfusion EABV = effective arterial blood volume; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. This patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and evidence of pulmonary hypertension (eg, loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound) came to the hospital in decompensated right-sided heart failure. His initial response to furosemide (eg, high urine output on day 1) improved his cardiac function by decreasing right ventricular end-diastolic volume (preload); however, patients with right ventricular dysfunction are preload-dependent and therefore sensitive to excessive volume loss. Although this patient still has edema, he has likely developed acute kidney injury (AKI) due to intravascular volume depletion (eg, flat neck veins on repeat examination). Prerenal AKI occurs due to decreased renal perfusion. The kidneys increase tubular sodium and water reabsorption, leading to an increase in passive urea reabsorption and an elevated blood urea nitrogen/creatinine ratio >20:1. Urine output is typically decreased. There is no intrinsic kidney damage in prerenal AKI and urine studies are typically free of casts, protein, and cells. Restoration of renal perfusion corrects the AKI and prevents the development of acute tubular necrosis (which can occur from a prolonged prerenal state). (Choice A) In bilateral renal artery stenosis (RAS), glomerular filtration rate is often maintained by angiotensin II-induced constriction of the efferent arterioles. Severe AKI can occur if angiotensin II activity is removed by initiation of an ACE inhibitor (eg, lisinopril). This patient had normal renal function while taking lisinopril, making bilateral RAS unlikely. (Choice B) Bladder outlet obstruction due to benign prostatic hyperplasia is a common cause of postrenal AKI in elderly men; however, ongoing urine output rules out significant urinary obstruction. (Choice C) Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can cause prerenal AKI by blocking prostaglandin-induced dilation of the glomerular afferent arterioles. This patient has not been taking NSAIDs. (Choice E) Impaired cardiac contractility can lead to prerenal AKI due to decreased cardiac output. It is unlikely to be responsible for this patient's AKI as the initial response to diuresis indicates improved right ventricular contractility. (Choice F) Renal parenchymal inflammation occurs in intrinsic AKI due to interstitial nephritis (eg, medication-induced). Absence of leukocyte casts or protein in the urine makes interstitial nephritis unlikely. (Choice G) Splanchnic arterial dilation is the mechanism of hepatorenal syndrome in patients with cirrhosis. Ascites and lower extremity edema are typically present; however, this patient's history of COPD and a loud second heart sound on examination makes right-sided heart failure due to pulmonary hypertension more likely. Educational objective: Patients with right-sided heart failure are preload dependent and require careful diuresis. Prerenal acute kidney injury results from decreased renal perfusion and is typically characterized by an elevated blood urea nitrogen/creatinine ratio >20:1 and unremarkable urine sediment.
