questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease requiring home oxygen therapy came to the hospital 3 days ago due to worsening pedal edema, abdominal distension, and fatigue of several weeks duration. At the time of admission, his physical examination was notable for distended neck veins, loud second heart sound, bilateral lower extremity edema, and moderate ascites. The patient's clinical condition has gradually improved with intravenous furosemide, but he is found to have worsening renal function and decreasing urine output. His other medical problems include hypertension and hyperlipidemia. The patient has a 40-pack-year smoking history but quit 5 years ago. He takes atorvastatin, lisinopril, inhaled glucocorticoids, and bronchodilators at home, which have been continued in the hospital. Today, temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/min. Physical examination shows flat neck veins, 1+ bilateral lower extremity edema, and mild ascites. Breath sounds are diminished with no added sounds. Pulmonic component of the second heart sound is loud with no murmur. Rectal examination shows a slightly enlarged, smooth prostate. Urine output and renal function since admission are shown below. At admission Day 1 Day 2 Day 3 Urine output (L/24 hr) - 4.2 3.1 1.5 Blood urea nitrogen (mg/dL) 24 28 36 52 Serum creatinine (mg/dL) 1.0 1.2 1.5 2.1 Urinalysis shows no cells, casts, or protein. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current renal dysfunction?

questions.explanation: Hyperemesis gravidarum Risk factors Hydatidiform mole Multifetal gestation History of hyperemesis gravidarum Clinical features Severe, persistent vomiting >5% loss of prepregnancy weight Dehydration Orthostatic hypotension Laboratory abnormalities Ketonuria Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis Hypokalemia Hemoconcentration Treatment Admission to hospital Antiemetics & intravenous fluids This patient has hyperemesis gravidarum (HG), a severe form of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy that is characterized by dehydration (eg, dry mucous membranes, orthostatic hypotension, hemoconcentration, high urine specific gravity), hypoglycemia with ketonuria, serum electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia), and a loss of >5% of prepregnancy weight. Risk factors for HG include multifetal gestation and hydatidiform mole, both of which can present in the first trimester with a uterine size-greater-than-dates discrepancy (eg, 12-week-sized uterus at only 8 weeks gestation). The underlying etiology is likely elevated hCG levels: Multifetal gestations have increased placental volumes and therefore increased hCG production; hydatidiform moles are abnormal proliferations of trophoblastic tissue and therefore also produce markedly elevated hCG levels. To distinguish between these causes and to guide further management, a pelvic ultrasound is the most appropriate next step in evaluation of this patient (Choice C). (Choice A) Dilation and curettage (D&C) is a treatment option for hydatidiform moles, which can cause HG and an enlarged uterus. However, a pelvic ultrasound is required prior to the procedure to diagnose the hydatidiform mole and exclude a normal intrauterine pregnancy (eg, multifetal gestation). (Choice B) Insulin and C-peptide levels are indicated in patients with hypoglycemia due to suspected insulinoma or self-administration of insulin. This patient's nausea/vomiting, dehydration, and electrolyte abnormalities indicate that her hypoglycemia is more likely due to acute starvation than excessive endogenous or exogenous insulin. (Choice E) A right upper quadrant ultrasound is indicated for the evaluation of cholelithiasis or cholecystitis, which have a higher prevalence in pregnancy. This patient's normal aminotransferase level and lack of abdominal pain make these diagnoses less likely. Educational objective: Hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) is a severe form of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy characterized by dehydration, hypoglycemia with ketonuria, electrolyte abnormalities, and a loss of >5% of prepregnancy weight. Patients with a hydatidiform mole or multifetal gestation are at increased risk for HG. Therefore, a pelvic ultrasound should be performed in all patients with HG to evaluate for these causes.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to severe nausea and vomiting for the past 2 weeks. The patient has been unable to tolerate any oral intake for the past 12 hours and has become increasingly weak and lightheaded. She has no abdominal pain, hematemesis, diarrhea, or constipation. Her last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago. Temperature is 37.2 C (98.9 F). Blood pressure is 136/86 mm Hg and pulse is 98/min while supine, and 110/70 mm Hg and 115/min while standing. Weight is 56.7 kg (125 lb). BMI is 22 kg/m2. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and no thyromegaly. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. The abdomen is soft and nontender, and there is no hepatosplenomegaly. Capillary refill is approximately 3 seconds. Bimanual examination shows a 12-week-sized uterus. Laboratory results are as follows: Serum Sodium 135 mEq/L Potassium 3.1 mEq/L Chloride 85 mEq/L Bicarbonate 34 mEq/L Blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL Glucose 65 mg/dL Aspartate aminotransferase 26 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 82 (normal: 17-88) Lipase 52 units/L (normal: 21-76) Hemoglobin 14 g/dL Urine β-hCG positive Specific gravity 1.030 Ketones large Glucose negative Leukocyte esterase negative Nitrites negative Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

choices: Recurrent parasitic infection acquired after travel
questions.explanation: Major malaria species Plasmodium falciparum Plasmodium vivax Africa primarily Also India, East Asia, Oceania Americas primarily Also India, East Asia, Oceania Fever, chills, flu-like symptoms Often severe (eg, delirium, seizure, kidney/liver failure) No dormant phase Fever, chills, flu-like symptoms Lower severity Dormant hepatic hypnozoites can reactivate weeks/months later Chloroquine* or artemisinin-based combination therapy Chloroquine* or artemisinin-based combination therapy PLUS Primaquine to eliminate hepatic phase *Chloroquine is the preferred treatment in nonresistant areas. Malaria is a mosquito-borne parasitic infection that causes episodic fever, chills, and flu-like symptoms, sometimes with severe, life-threatening complications. Four species of Plasmodium cause malaria, but Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax account for the majority of infections worldwide. P vivax is the dominant species in Central and South America (eg, Panama) and, unlike P falciparum, has a dormant hepatic phase that may cause recurrent parasitemia weeks or months after the initial infection. Therefore, treatment of this species (and P ovale) requires the use of antimalarial drugs that targets both the erythrocyte phase (eg, chloroquine) and the dormant hepatic phase (eg, primaquine) to ensure eradication. When only the erythrocyte phase is treated (as in this case), infections usually relapse due to reactivation of hepatic hypnozoites. (Choice A) Malaria infection induces a T-cell and humoral response that may provide partial protection against severe malaria in the immediate future. This response wanes quickly when individuals leave an endemic area. An impaired immune response to malaria does not account for recurrence with P vivax; it is due to the activation of hepatic hypnozoites. (Choices B and C) Chloroquine resistance occurs in eastern Panama, but this patient had resolution of symptoms with chloroquine, making resistance and incorrect treatment duration unlikely. Approximately 80% of cases of P vivax relapse if the dormant hepatic phase is not also treated (with primaquine). (Choice E) Reinfection may occur in endemic regions, but infections usually cause symptoms within 1-4 weeks of transmission. This patient has been back in the United States (a nonendemic country) for several months and has not traveled again, making reexposure to the parasite unlikely. Educational objective: Plasmodium vivax is the most common strain of malaria in Central and South America. P vivax, unlike Plasmodium falciparum, is associated with a dormant hepatic infection that may reactivate weeks or months after initial illness. Therefore, treatment requires antimalarial drugs targeting the erythrocytic phase (eg, chloroquine) plus primaquine to eliminate hepatic hypnozoites.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to several days of episodic fever, chills, sweating, headache, malaise, and nausea. The patient developed similar symptoms 4 months ago during a visit to Panama and was diagnosed with malaria. After she took chloroquine for 3 days, her symptoms resolved completely. The patient used mosquito repellents and bed netting during the rest of her travels and has felt healthy since returning to the United States 3 months ago. She lives in Pennsylvania and, aside from the trip to Panama, has not traveled recently. The patient has no other medical conditions and takes no medications. Temperature is 39 C (102.2 F), blood pressure is 105/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min. The tip of the spleen is palpable on inspiration. Laboratory results are as follows: Hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL Platelets 105,000/mm3 Leukocytes 4,200/mm3 Plasma glucose 85 mg/dL Aspartate aminotransferase (SGOT) 58 U/L Alanine aminotransferase (SGPT) 64 U/L Total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL Peripheral smear shows intraerythrocytic parasites. questions.explanation: This patient's signs and symptoms are consistent with serotonin toxicity, a potentially dangerous condition associated with excess serotonergic activity in the central nervous system. It is usually caused by serotonergic medications alone or in combination, drug interactions (eg, serotonergic drugs and a monoamine oxidase inhibitor), or intentional overdose on serotonergic medications. This patient is taking 2 serotonergic medications: venlafaxine, an antidepressant that works as a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, and tramadol, an analgesic medication with serotonergic activity. Serotonin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis based on a classic triad of mental status changes (eg, anxiety, restlessness, agitated delirium), autonomic dysregulation (eg, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia), and neuromuscular hyperactivity (eg, hyperreflexia, tremor, rigidity, myoclonus, ocular clonus [slow, continuous, horizontal eye movements], bilateral Babinski signs). There are also serotonin receptors in the gut, resulting in hyperactive bowel sounds and diarrhea. Management includes discontinuation of all serotonergic agents, supportive care (eg, hydration), and sedation with benzodiazepines. Severe cases may require the use of a cyproheptadine, a serotonin antagonist. (Choice A) Anticholinergic toxicity involves exposure to anticholinergic medications and typically presents with hyperthermia, delirium, mydriasis, dry mucous membranes, urinary retention, and decreased bowel sounds. It would not cause diaphoresis, hyperreflexia, tremors, and clonus. (Choice B) Serotonin toxicity can be confused with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), a rare life-threatening adverse reaction to dopamine antagonists (eg, antipsychotics). This patient's recent exposure to a second serotonergic medication and prominent neuromuscular hyperreactivity (tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus) make serotonin toxicity more likely. NMS involves diffuse muscular rigidity and bradyreflexia. (Choices C and D) Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is an inhibitory neurotransmitter involved in the effects of benzodiazepines, alcohol, and some anticonvulsants. Excess GABA activation can result in sedation. Glutamate is an excitatory neurotransmitter. An imbalance in glutamate has been linked to neurodegenerative processes. (Choice E) Drugs that increase norepinephrine commonly produce hypertension and stimulating effects but would not explain this patient's neuromuscular hyperactivity. Although venlafaxine has both serotonergic and noradrenergic activity, it is the effects of excess serotonin from the addition of tramadol that are causing this patient's symptoms. Educational objective: Serotonin toxicity can result from the use of serotonergic medications, alone or in combination, or from intentional overdose. Co-administration of tramadol with commonly used serotonergic antidepressants (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors/serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) increases the risk of serotonin toxicity.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband for new-onset tremors and extreme restlessness. She feels nauseated and anxious. The patient works as a nursing aide; she recently injured her back lifting a patient and was prescribed tramadol. She has a history of major depression with psychotic features. Her other medications include venlafaxine and aripiprazole. Temperature is 38.3 C (101 F), blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg, pulse is 125/min, and respirations are 20/min. questions.explanation: Tricyclic antidepressant pharmacology Inhibitory effects Consequences Central & peripheral muscarinic acetylcholine receptors Tachycardia, delirium, dilated pupils, flushing, decreased sweating, hyperthermia, ileus, urinary retention Peripheral α1-adrenergic receptors Peripheral vasodilation (orthostatic hypotension) Cardiac fast sodium channels Conduction defects, arrhythmias Presynaptic (norepinephrine & serotonin) neurotransmitter reuptake Antidepressant & anxiolytic effects, seizures, tremors Histamine (H1) receptors Sedation, increased appetite This patient's new-onset seizure, signs of anticholinergic toxicity (ie, dilated pupils, hyperthermia, flushed skin, decreased bowel sounds), and QRS widening are most likely due to tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose. Although newer classes of antidepressants (eg, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) are commonly used as first-line therapy, TCAs continue to have a role in the treatment of major depression. TCAs have an inhibitory effect on multiple receptor types, thereby causing a variety of symptoms in the case of overdose: Mental status changes may include sedation (histamine [H1] receptors), seizures (GABA A receptors), and agitation or delirium (central muscarinic acetylcholine receptors). Because of the antagonism of central and peripheral muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, anticholinergic symptoms may include hyperthermia; dry, flushed skin; dilated pupils; tachycardia; and decreased bowel sounds. Cardiovascular toxicity may include QRS widening, associated with an increased risk for ventricular arrhythmia (with values >100 msec), due to inhibition of cardiac fast sodium channels. Hypotension can also occur due to blockade of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. Cardiovascular toxicity is the major cause of mortality in TCA overdose. (Choice A) Alcohol, a CNS depressant, binds to the GABA A receptor complex. Withdrawal can cause CNS excitation with seizures and autonomic hyperactivity, including tachycardia; however, hypertension (vs hypotension) is typical, and anticholinergic symptoms and QRS widening are not expected. (Choice B) Bupropion, a monocyclic antidepressant, inhibits reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine. Overdose can cause altered mental status, seizures, tachycardia, and prolongation of QTc intervals. However, bupropion does not cause anticholinergic symptoms, which are present in this patient. (Choice C) Cocaine overdose has sympathomimetic characteristics that can cause seizures, hyperthermia, tachycardia, myocardial infarctions, and cardiac arrhythmias. However, hypertension (vs hypotension) is also expected due to sympathetic stimulation. (Choice D) Opioid withdrawal can cause dilated pupils and rebound autonomic hyperactivity, resulting in hyperthermia and tachycardia. This typically causes hypertension (vs hypotension), and cardiac conduction delay is not expected. In addition, diarrhea and cramps (vs decreased bowel sounds) are common in opioid withdrawal. (Choice E) Serotonin syndrome can occur with overdose of serotonergic antidepressants or interaction between serotonergic medications. Serotonin syndrome can cause hyperthermia and tachycardia but also frequently presents with agitation (vs sedation), hypertension (vs hypotension), and neuromuscular hyperactivity (eg, hyperreflexia, clonus); it is not associated with QRS widening. Educational objective: Symptoms of tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose include seizures, anticholinergic toxicity, and cardiovascular toxicity (eg, QRS widening, hypotension). These varied symptoms are due to the interaction of TCAs with multiple different receptors.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his roommate 45 minutes after he was observed having a seizure. The patient has no known history of a seizure disorder. The roommate reports that the patient has been depressed since a serious motorcycle collision 5 years ago and recently completed a drug rehabilitation program for alcohol, cocaine, and prescription opioid abuse. He thinks the patient is taking an antidepressant but is unsure of which one. On examination, the patient is sedated, disoriented, and flushed. Temperature is 38.3 C (100.9 F), blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg, and pulse is 130/min. The pupils are dilated and bowel sounds are decreased. ECG reveals sinus tachycardia and a QRS duration of 130 msec. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

questions.explanation: Panic disorder Clinical features Recurrent & unexpected panic attacks with ≥4 of the following: Chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, choking Trembling, sweating, nausea, chills Dizziness, paresthesia Derealization, depersonalization Fear of losing control or of dying Worry about additional attacks, avoidance behavior Treatment First-line/maintenance: SSRI/SNRI &/or cognitive-behavioral therapy Acute distress: benzodiazepines SNRI = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. This patient's history of recurrent, unexpected anxiety attacks with classic physical symptoms (palpitations, shortness of breath, sweating, tremors, dizziness, paresthesias) is consistent with panic disorder. Her fear of another attack is also characteristic. Treatment of panic disorder includes cognitive-behavioral psychotherapy, antidepressants, and benzodiazepines. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as escitalopram, and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) are preferred first-line pharmacotherapy due to their relatively benign side-effect profile compared to older antidepressants (ie, tricyclics, monoamine oxidase inhibitors) and lack of the abuse potential and physiologic dependence seen with benzodiazepines. Benzodiazepines (eg, lorazepam, clonazepam) are typically limited to short-term therapy in acutely symptomatic patients who require rapid relief while waiting for SSRIs or SNRIs to take effect. They are also used for those who have poor response to or cannot tolerate antidepressants (Choices B and E). Benzodiazepines should be avoided in patients with a history of substance abuse. (Choice A) Buspirone is used in generalized anxiety disorder but is not effective in panic disorder. (Choice C) The alpha-2 noradrenergic agonist clonidine is not effective in panic disorder. (Choice F) Beta blockers are not used as monotherapy for panic disorder. Propranolol has a role in treating the performance-only subtype of social anxiety disorder. Educational objective: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors are first-line pharmacotherapy for panic disorder. Benzodiazepines are also effective but ideally should be used for short-term relief only and avoided in patients with a history of substance abuse.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the office due to recurrent episodes of anxiety, palpitations, shortness of breath, tremors, and numbness and tingling in her hands. The patient describes breaking into a sweat suddenly and feeling dizzy several times a week. The last time it happened she was terribly embarrassed as it occurred during a meeting at work. She says, "I had to run out of the room. My chest was pounding and I was shaking uncontrollably. I felt like I was choking and couldn't catch my breath." The patient now feels anxious all the time because she fears having another episode. She does not feel depressed and reports no change in her sleep pattern or appetite. She has no medical history. Physical examination, laboratory evaluation, and ECG are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient?

questions.explanation: Choriocarcinoma Risk factors Advanced maternal age Prior complete hydatidiform mole Presentation Amenorrhea or abnormal uterine bleeding Pelvic pain/pressure Symptoms from metastases (lung, vagina) Uterine mass Elevated β-hCG level Treatment Chemotherapy This patient presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pressure, a symmetrically enlarged uterus, and a friable (vascular) vaginal lesion, a presentation concerning for choriocarcinoma, a type of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). Choriocarcinoma is a malignancy that arises from placental trophoblastic tissue and secretes high levels of hCG. GTN most commonly develops after a complete hydatidiform mole but can follow any type of pregnancy (including a spontaneous abortion). Choriocarcinoma is the most aggressive type of GTN characterized by rapid metastases, most commonly to the lungs and vagina. Symptoms of vaginal metastases include bloody or purulent vaginal discharge. (Choice B) Condyloma acuminata are typically asymptomatic and present as white or pink, verrucous (warty), papilliform lesions. (Choice C) Endometriosis can spread to the vagina but is typically associated with dysmenorrhea and an immobile uterus. Endometriosis implants are described as blue/black "powder burn" lesions that are not friable. (Choice D) Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor that presents with friable mucocutaneous lesions but is typically associated with immunosuppression (eg, HIV, organ transplant). (Choice E) Sarcoma botryoides (eg, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) typically presents in infancy and early childhood as non-friable nodules protruding from the vagina that have an appearance resembling a cluster of grapes. (Choice F) A uterine leiomyoma presents with abnormal uterine bleeding; pelvic pressure; and an irregularly shaped, enlarged uterus. A prolapsed leiomyoma appears as a firm, nonfriable, round mass protruding through the cervix. Educational objective: Choriocarcinoma, an aggressive form of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, can follow any type of pregnancy (including a spontaneous abortion). Patients with choriocarcinoma present with abnormal vaginal bleeding, pelvic pressure, and an enlarged uterus. Metastases to the vagina present as red, friable lesions.

questions.explanation: This trauma patient with profuse and prolonged bleeding from an open fracture now has severe hypotension and tachycardia. This is consistent with hypovolemic shock from hemorrhage (ie, hemorrhagic shock) and should prompt rapid type O blood transfusion. Management of the trauma patient with hemorrhagic shock requires multiple simultaneous interventions: Control of external bleeding (eg, compressive bandage, direct pressure) Investigation (eg, Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma [FAST]) for sources of internal hemorrhage that may require emergency surgery Rapid resuscitation with replacement of intravascular volume, transitioning from crystalloid to blood products as soon as possible Unstable patients (eg, systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg) cannot wait for cross-matching and should receive type O blood, which decreases the risk of hemolytic transfusion reaction. If hemorrhage or hemodynamic instability continues despite initial resuscitation efforts, massive transfusion protocol (MTP) should be activated. MTP requires the administration of packed red blood cells, platelets, and fresh frozen plasma in a 1:1:1 ratio to avoid coagulopathy from dilution of platelets and clotting factors. (Choices A and D) Eventual workup of this patient may include abdominal CT scan to assess for intraabdominal injury (eg, tenderness to palpation) and retrograde urethrogram to assess for urethral injury (eg, pelvic fracture, blood at urethral meatus). However, resuscitation should be performed first to stabilize the patient prior to diagnostic testing that requires transport of the patient away from the trauma bay. (Choice B) Diagnostic peritoneal lavage is sometimes used to test for intraabdominal blood in patients with a high probability of intraabdominal hemorrhage (eg, abdominal distension, severe pain) but equivocal FAST results. This patient has mild abdominal tenderness and a negative FAST. (Choice C) Vasopressor therapy (eg, intravenous norepinephrine) is contraindicated in the setting of isolated hemorrhagic shock. Peripheral vascular tone is already increased to compensate for decreased blood volume; therefore, restoration of blood volume (eg, blood transfusion) is more appropriate. (Choice E) Tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic agent, may reduce mortality from bleeding when administered promptly following major trauma. However, in this patient with severe hypotension consistent with hemorrhagic shock, blood products should be administered first to restore intravascular volume and improve organ perfusion. Educational objective: Management of trauma patients with hemorrhagic shock includes rapid replacement of intravascular volume with type O blood transfusion. Ongoing hemorrhage or hemodynamic instability should activate a massive transfusion protocol, with administration of packed red blood cells, platelets, and fresh frozen plasma in a 1:1:1 ratio.

Unstable patients (eg, systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg) cannot wait for cross-matching and should receive type O blood, which decreases the risk of hemolytic transfusion reaction.  If hemorrhage or hemodynamic instability continues despite initial resuscitation efforts, massive transfusion protocol (MTP) should be activated.  MTP requires the administration of packed red blood cells, platelets, and fresh frozen plasma in a 1:1:1 ratio to avoid coagulopathy from dilution of platelets and clotting factors.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. After a prolonged extrication due to severe vehicular damage, the patient was found to have an open fracture of the left femur with profuse bleeding. The paramedics stabilized the fracture and applied a compressive bandage, and the patient received rapid administration of 2 L of normal saline on the way to the hospital. On arrival, blood pressure is 80/52 mm Hg, pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 22/min. The patient is alert and diaphoretic. On examination, breath sounds are symmetric bilaterally, and heart sounds are normal. The abdomen is soft and mildly tender to palpation, without guarding. Blood is present at the urethral meatus, and the left thigh is swollen with no active bleeding. Portable chest x-ray is normal. Focused assessment with sonography for trauma is negative for pericardial effusion and intraperitoneal free fluid. Pelvic x-ray reveals a displaced fracture of the left pubic ramus. Which of the following is the best immediate step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient's presentation of first-trimester vaginal bleeding, a closed cervix, and a fetus with a normal heart rate on ultrasound is consistent with a threatened abortion. The bleeding often results from disrupted decidual blood vessels, which can sometimes be seen on ultrasound as a subchorionic hematoma (abnormal collection of blood between the placenta and uterus). This collection of blood, as seen in this patient, can cause mild uterine tenderness on physical examination. Risk factors for spontaneous abortion include advanced maternal age and previous spontaneous abortion. Most often, patients with threatened abortions have uncomplicated pregnancies with normal outcomes. Therefore, management is expectant with outpatient observation. Serial ultrasounds can be performed until either the symptoms resolve or there is progression to complete abortion. (Choice A) Rho(D) immunoglobulin prevents alloimmunization due to Rh incompatibility in the setting of fetomaternal hemorrhage (eg, delivery, spontaneous abortion, abruptio placentae) in Rh-negative patients. This patient is Rh-positive. (Choices B and C) Misoprostol and suction curettage are management options for nonviable spontaneous abortions (eg, missed, inevitable, incomplete). Suction curettage is indicated when a patient's condition is anemic, hemodynamically unstable, or septic. This patient has a viable pregnancy, and her condition is stable. (Choice D) Although patients with threatened abortions are at increased risk for pregnancy complications (eg, complete spontaneous abortion, preterm delivery), bed rest and hospitalization do not improve outcomes and are not recommended. In fact, bed rest is associated with an increased risk for venous thromboembolism. (Choice F) Serial β-hCG measurements are helpful in distinguishing between an intrauterine and an ectopic pregnancy when patients have first-trimester pain and bleeding and when ultrasound is nondiagnostic (eg, empty uterus, no adnexal masses). Because this patient has a viable intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal cardiac activity, serial β-hCG levels are not indicated. Educational objective: Threatened abortions present with vaginal bleeding, a closed cervix, and a fetus with a normal heart rate on ultrasound. Management is expectant with observation and repeat ultrasounds.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 0 aborta 1, at 9 weeks gestation comes to the emergency department due to vaginal spotting and intermittent lower abdominal pain and pressure for the past 6 hours. The patient reports spotting of bright red blood but no passage of clots or tissue. Abdominal pain is mild and relieved with acetaminophen. The patient's first pregnancy, 5 years ago, ended in a first-trimester spontaneous abortion. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg, pulse is 76/min, and respirations are 14/min. Bimanual examination reveals a closed cervix, a slightly tender uterus with a size consistent with gestational age, and no adnexal tenderness or masses. Pelvic examination shows scant, bright red blood in the vaginal vault. A bedside ultrasound reveals a 9-week intrauterine gestation with normal fetal heart motion. Hemoglobin is 11.8 g/dL. Blood type is B, Rh-positive. Antibody screen is negative. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient with an enlarging pigmented nail lesion has a nail melanoma. Unlike dermal melanomas, which typically appear as asymmetric shapes with irregular borders, nail melanomas form longitudinal bands in the nail plate (longitudinal melanonychia) due to the presence of pigment in the nail as it grows outward. Unpigmented melanomas can also occur and present as nodules or irregularities in the nail plate. Longitudinal melanonychia that involves multiple nails, is stable over years, or is <3 mm wide is usually benign and may be observed with regular follow-up. However, lesions that are larger, have indistinct borders, change appearance over time, or extend into the nail folds suggest possible melanoma. (Choice A) Psoriasis is a T cell-mediated immune disorder characterized by keratinocyte hyperproliferation. It presents with erythematous plaques with a silvery scale over extensor surfaces (eg, knees, elbows) and the scalp. Associated nail findings include pitting, distal onycholysis, and hyperkeratosis. (Choice B) Impaired cellular proliferation in the nail matrix (eg, trauma, local or systemic illness, medications) leads to formation of horizontal ridges that move outward as the nail grows (Beau lines). (Choice D) Microemboli from infectious endocarditis can disrupt capillaries in the nail bed, leading to splinter hemorrhages, which appear as small linear or flame-shaped streaks under the nail. (Choice E) Digital clubbing is a thickening of the distal phalanges with a "drumstick" appearance, flattening of the nail folds, and shininess of the nail and distal finger. It is typically associated with pulmonary malignancy and chronic hypoxic pulmonary disease (eg, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis). (Choice F) Trauma to the nail bed can cause subungual hematoma. The appearance may resemble melanoma, but most patients recall a specific inciting injury. Given its prolonged duration, this patient's lesion is unlikely to be a simple hematoma. Educational objective: Nail melanomas present as longitudinal, pigmented bands in the nail plate (longitudinal melanonychia). Longitudinal melanonychia that involves multiple nails, is stable over years, or is <3 mm wide is usually benign. However, lesions that are larger, have indistinct borders, change appearance over time, or extend into the nail folds are suggestive of melanoma.

questions.explanation: Schizophrenia Diagnosis ≥2 of the following (at least 1 symptom from 1-3) Delusions Hallucinations Disorganized speech Disorganized or catatonic behavior Negative symptoms (eg, apathy, flat affect) Continuous impairment ≥6 months Significant functional decline Treatment Antipsychotic medication Adjunctive psychosocial interventions (eg, social skills training, cognitive-behavioral therapy, family intervention) This patient's onset of illness at age 23, evidence of paranoid delusions, and negative symptoms (eg, persistent social withdrawal) are most consistent with schizophrenia. Patients with schizophrenia have a typical age of onset in late adolescence or young adulthood (18-25 for men, 25-35 for women) and exhibit significant social and occupational dysfunction. Although the course of schizophrenia is variable, a history of intermittent acute psychotic episodes that often require hospitalization is characteristic. Although substance intoxication and withdrawal may also be associated with psychotic symptoms (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganization), they are less likely explanations for this patient's longstanding history of paranoia. In substance-induced psychotic disorders, the symptoms typically do not persist once the intoxication/withdrawal state has resolved. (Choice A) Although this patient has anxiety, benzodiazepine withdrawal is also associated with rebound insomnia, tremors, palpitations, diaphoresis, and perceptual disturbances that are not present in this case. Psychosis and seizures can occur in severe cases. (Choice B) Patients with delusional disorder can have persecutory type delusions (eg, paranoia about being watched and about enemy agents). However, they do not have the other psychotic symptoms characteristic of schizophrenia (eg, negative symptoms) and may function normally apart from the impact of the delusion. Recurrent hospitalizations and episodes of bizarre behavior make schizophrenia more likely. In addition, compared to schizophrenia, age of onset of delusional disorder is typically later. (Choice C) Paranoid personality disorder involves a lifelong pattern of paranoia and hypervigilance but would not explain this patient's paranoid delusions (eg, believes that he is being watched and that the interviewer is an "enemy agent"). (Choices D and F) Phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication may present with hallucinations, psychotic or violent behavior, and dissociation. It is classically associated with multidirectional nystagmus, not seen in this patient. In addition, although substance use (eg, PCP, stimulant) should always be considered in patients with psychosis, schizophrenia is a better explanation for this patient's persistent paranoia and recurrent psychosis-associated hospitalizations. Educational objective: Schizophrenia is characterized by onset in adolescence/young adulthood, psychosis (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganization), and persistent social and occupational impairment (ie, ≥6 months). Although substance intoxication and withdrawal may also cause psychotic symptoms, they typically do not persist once the intoxicated/withdrawal state has resolved.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his roommate due to unusual behavior. The roommate says, "I've lived with him for 3 years. He's a very private and anxious person who rarely leaves the apartment and often makes comments that people are watching him. Last night, he covered all the windows with newspaper and tried to hit me when I asked him to stop." The roommate adds that the patient has had similar episodes of paranoia in the past but has never become physically aggressive. Review of medical records indicate a history of 3 psychiatric hospitalizations beginning at age 23. Temperature is 36.6 C (97.9 F), blood pressure is 138/90 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 14/min. Physical examination is unremarkable. On mental status examination, the patient is hypervigilant, fearful, and physically restless. He declines to answer most questions saying, "I don't talk to enemy agents." Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: This patient has nail changes, including distal onycholysis (nail plate separation from nail bed) and pitting (small depressions in nails). In association with progressive skin rash, these findings are characteristic of psoriasis, an inflammatory condition caused by immune cell dysregulation resulting in epidermal cell hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation. Skin involvement includes erythematous plaques with silvery scales on the extensor surfaces (eg, knees, elbows). Other nail changes include oil drop discoloration and nail plate crumbling. Psoriasis is associated with an increased risk for inflammatory arthritis (up to 30% of patients), especially in those with nail changes and positivity for human leukocyte antigen B27. Psoriatic arthritis is typically symmetric, although other presentations may be seen (eg, spondylitis, sacroiliitis). Adequate and early disease control can delay onset of psoriatic arthritis. (Choice A) Patients with vitiligo are at higher risk for autoimmune thyroiditis. Although psoriasis may be associated with certain autoimmune conditions (eg, ulcerative colitis), the risk for arthritis, especially in patients with psoriatic nail changes, as in this patient, is substantially higher and well established. (Choice B) Esophageal dysmotility is seen in systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), a disorder involving fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. Associated skin, nail, and digital changes in these conditions include dilation of capillaries in the nail bed, ischemic fingertip ulcers caused by Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and calcinosis cutis (calcification of soft tissues of the hand); none of these are present in this patient. (Choice C) Sjögren syndrome is an autoimmune disorder involving exocrine gland dysfunction. Patients usually have dry mouth, dry eyes, and dysphagia. Associated nail changes are uncommon, although Raynaud phenomenon may be present. (Choice D) Patients with invasive candidiasis (eg, underlying immunosuppression) are at increased risk for fungal endophthalmitis; characteristic associated skin lesions (painless pustules or nodules on an erythematous base) can be present. This patient's nail pitting and onycholysis are not typical findings. (Choice F) Nail changes associated with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis include nail clubbing and digital cyanosis. Fibrotic lung disease is also a possible complication of sarcoidosis and a number of connective tissue diseases, but nail pitting is not a common finding. Educational objective: Patients with classic nail findings of psoriasis, which include onycholysis (nail plate separation), pitting, and oil spots, have a significantly higher chance of developing psoriatic arthritis. Psoriatic arthritis typically manifests as a symmetric polyarthritis, but other presentations (eg, spondylitis, sacroiliitis) may be seen.

questions.explanation: Coarctation of the aorta Etiology Congenital Acquired (rare) (eg, Takayasu arteritis) Clinical features Upper body Well developed Hypertension (headaches, epistaxis) Lower extremities Underdeveloped Claudication Brachial-femoral pulse delay Upper & lower extremity blood pressure differential Left interscapular systolic or continuous murmur Diagnostic studies ECG: Left ventricular hypertrophy Chest x-ray Inferior notching of the 3rd to 8th ribs "3" sign due to aortic indentation Echocardiography: diagnostic confirmation Treatment Balloon angioplasty ± stent placement Surgery This patient most likely has secondary hypertension due to coarctation of the aorta (CoA). CoA is characterized by narrowing of the descending aorta, usually just distal to the left subclavian artery. This causes hypertension in the systemic circulation proximal to the obstruction (eg, head, upper extremities) but decreased blood flow to the lower extremities. CoA is most commonly due to a congenital defect; depending on the degree of narrowing, it may present shortly after birth, in childhood, or in adulthood. Asymptomatic hypertension is the most common adult presentation, although patients may have headaches, epistaxis, lower extremity claudication, or heart failure. Examination findings include brachial-femoral pulse delay, a sustained apical impulse due to left ventricular hypertrophy, and a systolic or continuous murmur at the left interscapular area. The diagnosis of CoA is confirmed by echocardiography, which visualizes the aortic narrowing and can identify other commonly associated congenital heart defects (eg, bicuspid aortic valve). (Choice A) Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is sometimes used when the diagnosis of hypertension is uncertain. Hypertension does not need to be confirmed in this patient with several high blood pressure readings (eg, at prior immigration health assessment and current preemployment physical examination) and evidence of CoA (eg, brachial-femoral pulse delay). (Choice B) CT scan of the adrenal glands is useful in suspected secondary hypertension due to an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma (primary hyperaldosteronism). Older adults are typically affected, and equal pulses in all extremities would be expected. (Choice D) Lower extremity duplex imaging is used to diagnose peripheral arterial disease. Aortic or bilateral iliac artery atherosclerosis can cause diminished lower extremity pulses; however, atherosclerosis is extremely unlikely in this young patient and would not cause hypertension unless the renal arteries are affected (ie, renal artery stenosis). (Choice E) Measuring plasma and urine catecholamines is useful in diagnosing pheochromocytoma, which typically causes severe, paroxysmal hypertension associated with episodic headaches, flushing, sweating, and tachycardia. (Choice F) Renovascular imaging (eg, CT angiography) is used to diagnose fibromuscular dysplasia, a potential cause of secondary hypertension due to narrowing of the renal arteries. Delayed femoral pulses would be unusual because the aorta and iliac arteries are rarely affected. In addition, fibromuscular dysplasia more commonly affects women. Educational objective: Coarctation of the aorta is characterized by narrowing of the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, causing hypertension proximal to the obstruction but decreased blood flow distally. Possible symptoms include headaches, epistaxis, lower extremity claudication, and heart failure. explanationPanel.html:
Educational objective:
Coarctation of the aorta is characterized by narrowing of the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, causing hypertension proximal to the obstruction but decreased blood flow distally.  Possible symptoms include headaches, epistaxis, lower extremity claudication, and heart failure.  Examination findings include delayed femoral pulses, sustained apical impulse, and murmur at the left interscapular area.  The diagnosis is confirmed by echocardiography.
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Coarctation of the aorta
Etiology
  • Congenital
  • Acquired (rare) (eg, Takayasu arteritis)
Clinical features
  • Upper body
    • Well developed
    • Hypertension (headaches, epistaxis)
  • Lower extremities
    • Underdeveloped
    • Claudication
  • Brachial-femoral pulse delay
  • Upper & lower extremity blood pressure differential
  • Left interscapular systolic or continuous murmur
Diagnostic studies
  • ECG: Left ventricular hypertrophy
  • Chest x-ray
    • Inferior notching of the 3rd to 8th ribs
    • "3" sign due to aortic indentation
  • Echocardiography: diagnostic confirmation
Treatment
  • Balloon angioplasty ± stent placement
  • Surgery

This patient most likely has secondary hypertension due to coarctation of the aorta (CoA).  CoA is characterized by narrowing of the descending aorta, usually just distal to the left subclavian artery.  This causes hypertension in the systemic circulation proximal to the obstruction (eg, head, upper extremities) but decreased blood flow to the lower extremities.  CoA is most commonly due to a congenital defect; depending on the degree of narrowing, it may present shortly after birth, in childhood, or in adulthood.

Asymptomatic hypertension is the most common adult presentation, although patients may have headaches, epistaxis, lower extremity claudication, or heart failure.  Examination findings include brachial-femoral pulse delay, a sustained apical impulse due to left ventricular hypertrophy, and a systolic or continuous murmur at the left interscapular area.

The diagnosis of CoA is confirmed by echocardiography, which visualizes the aortic narrowing and can identify other commonly associated congenital heart defects (eg, bicuspid aortic valve).

wrongAnswers.A: (Choice A)  Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is sometimes used when the diagnosis of hypertension is uncertain.  Hypertension does not need to be confirmed in this patient with several high blood pressure readings (eg, at prior immigration health assessment and current preemployment physical examination) and evidence of CoA (eg, brachial-femoral pulse delay).
wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  CT scan of the adrenal glands is useful in suspected secondary hypertension due to an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma (primary hyperaldosteronism).  Older adults are typically affected, and equal pulses in all extremities would be expected.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Lower extremity duplex imaging is used to diagnose peripheral arterial disease.  Aortic or bilateral iliac artery atherosclerosis can cause diminished lower extremity pulses; however, atherosclerosis is extremely unlikely in this young patient and would not cause hypertension unless the renal arteries are affected (ie, renal artery stenosis).
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Measuring plasma and urine catecholamines is useful in diagnosing pheochromocytoma, which typically causes severe, paroxysmal hypertension associated with episodic headaches, flushing, sweating, and tachycardia.
wrongAnswers.F: (Choice F)  Renovascular imaging (eg, CT angiography) is used to diagnose fibromuscular dysplasia, a potential cause of secondary hypertension due to narrowing of the renal arteries.  Delayed femoral pulses would be unusual because the aorta and iliac arteries are rarely affected.  In addition, fibromuscular dysplasia more commonly affects women.

questions.explanation: Infantile hemangioma Natural history Appears days to weeks after birth Proliferation (age 0-12 months): growth of bright red, soft, raised plaque Involution (age >12 months): deep red/violet lesion that regresses in size Evaluation Clinical diagnosis Special considerations: ≥5 cutaneous lesions → liver ultrasonography Facial/segmental → echocardiography & MRI of the head (ie, PHACE) Cervicofacial (beard distribution) → laryngoscopy Lumbosacral → spinal ultrasonography Management Observation for most lesions Beta blocker therapy (eg, propranolol) for high-risk features: Large, facial, segmental, &/or rapidly growing (ulceration/scarring) Periorbital (visual impairment) Hepatic (high-output heart failure) Subglottic (airway obstruction) PHACE = Posterior fossa anomalies, Hemangioma, Arterial anomalies, Cardiac anomalies, Eye anomalies. Infantile hemangiomas are common, benign, vascular tumors that present days to weeks after birth. During the first 6 months of life, hemangiomas proliferate (due to vasculogenesis) into bright red, raised nodules or plaques that increase in size. Hemangiomas then typically involute and regress (due to increasing apoptosis) over subsequent years, during which time they may appear patchy and deeper red/violet in color. Diagnosis is clinical for hemangiomas with a classic history and appearance, as in this case. Due to the natural history of involution in early childhood, the management of such lesions is reassurance and serial observation. Beta-blocker therapy, which works via local vasoconstriction, should be considered for lesions with high-risk features, such as periorbital involvement that can lead to visual impairment or large (>5 cm) hemangiomas with increased risk of scarring. (Choices A and B) Biopsy is rarely required for diagnosis of a hemangioma but can be considered for atypical lesions with increased risk of malignancy, such as those that are present since birth or appear deep (ie, raised subcutaneous nodule with blue hue). Intralesional corticosteroids can also be considered for hemangiomas that extend deep into the subcutaneous tissue but are not indicated for simple superficial hemangiomas, as in this case. (Choice C) MRI of the head and echocardiogram should be performed for patients with a segmental hemangioma on the face/scalp due to an association of this subtype with PHACE syndrome (posterior fossa anomalies; hemangioma; arterial, cardiac, and eye anomalies). In contrast to this patient's single, well-circumscribed nodule, segmental hemangiomas have a geographic appearance with clusters of lesions extending over a large area. (Choice E) Excision of a cutaneous hemangioma is generally avoided due to risk of bleeding and scarring, and most hemangiomas involute without complications. Educational objective: Infantile hemangiomas are benign, vascular tumors that present as bright red, raised nodules that proliferate in early infancy and regress in early childhood. Management of uncomplicated hemangiomas is serial observation.

questions.explanation: Hemodynamic measurements in shock Parameter Hypovolemic shock Cardiogenic shock Obstructive shock Distributive shock CVP (right-sided preload) ↓ ↑ ↑ ↓ PCWP (left-sided preload) ↓ ↑ ↓* ↓ Cardiac index (LV output) ↓ ↓ ↓ ↑** SVR ↑ ↑ ↑ ↓ SvO2 ↓ ↓ ↓ ↑** *In tamponade, left-sided preload is decreased, but measured PCWP is paradoxically increased due to external compression by pericardial fluid. **Cardiac index & SvO2 are usually decreased in neurogenic shock due to impaired sympathetic reflexes. CVP = central venous pressure; LV = left ventricular; PCWP = pulmonary capillary wedge pressure; SvO2 = mixed venous oxygen saturation; SVR = systemic vascular resistance. This patient with numerous risk factors for coronary artery disease (eg, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, active smoking) has likely had an acute myocardial infarction (MI). Patients typically have substernal chest pain (sometimes intermittent) as well as dyspnea, fatigue, nausea, and/or diaphoresis. Low-grade fever may be present, and laboratory results can demonstrate mild leukocytosis. A new left bundle branch block on ECG is suggestive of an acute MI. Acute MI can lead to profound impairment in left ventricular (LV) contractility, decreased stroke volume, and cardiogenic shock. Cardiac output (stroke volume × heart rate) is low as tachycardia is unable to compensate for the decrease in stroke volume. LV end-diastolic volume, also known as LV preload, is high due to impaired ejection of blood from the left ventricle. Systemic vascular resistance (SVR), a major component of LV afterload, is high as well due to compensatory peripheral vasoconstriction in an effort to maintain blood pressure. Patients typically have hypotension, jugular venous distension, and respiratory distress (eg, dyspnea, tachypnea) due to pulmonary edema. Cold extremities are also present due to poor tissue perfusion. Laboratory results typically demonstrate elevated lactate, reflective of poor organ and tissue perfusion. (Choice A) High-output heart failure (eg, thyrotoxicosis, beriberi, arteriovenous fistula) is characterized by low SVR leading to high cardiac output. LV preload is high due to increased venous return. (Choice C) Hypovolemic shock involves low LV preload and, consequently, low cardiac output. SVR is high due to compensatory vasoconstriction. Pre-pulmonary obstructive shock (eg, due to pulmonary embolism) also demonstrates low LV preload, low cardiac output, and high SVR; although it can present with dyspnea, clear lungs are expected on auscultation. (Choices D and E) Distributive shock involves low SVR due to peripheral vasodilation. LV preload is also low. With distributive shock due to sepsis, increased sympathetic drive increases heart rate and LV contractility to cause high cardiac output (hyperdynamic state in the early stages of sepsis), whereas with neurogenic shock the sympathetic response is disrupted and cardiac output is low. Educational objective: Myocardial infarction can lead to left ventricular systolic dysfunction and cardiogenic shock. Low cardiac output leads to high left ventricular end-diastolic volume (preload) and a compensatory increase in systemic vascular resistance (a major component of afterload).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with shortness of breath and generalized weakness since yesterday. This morning he could not get out of bed. He has also had several episodes of midline chest pain but currently is chest pain free. Medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and peripheral vascular disease. The patient is an active smoker with a 20-pack-year history. He appears to be in respiratory distress, and his extremities are cold and clammy. Temperature is 37.5 C (99.5 F), blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg, pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 30/min. There is visible jugular venous distension with the patient in a sitting position. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral crackles. The abdomen is soft and nontender. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block. Initial laboratory results are as follows: Complete blood count Leukocytes 12,000/mm3 Hemoglobin 11 g/dL Platelets 240,000/mm3 Serum chemistry Blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL Lactate 3.5 mg/dL (normal <2 mg/dL) Which of the following sets of parameters is most likely to be seen in this patient?

questions.explanation: Sunburn Clinical manifestations Symptoms begin hours after exposure & resolve by day 3-7 Mild-moderate: erythema, tenderness Severe: as above + blistering, systemic symptoms (eg, fever, vomiting, headache) Treatment Mild-moderate Topical: cool compresses, calamine lotion, aloe vera Oral: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs Severe Hospitalization Intravenous fluids & analgesia Wound care This child has symptoms of a mild to moderate sunburn. Clinical manifestations of mild sunburn include erythema and tenderness of the exposed areas without blistering, whereas severe sunburn presents with significant blistering or signs of dehydration (eg, fever, vomiting). The erythema typically peaks by 24 hours after exposure and subsides within 7 days. Treatment of minor sunburn is supportive and includes topical application of cool compresses, calamine lotion, and aloe vera, as well as oral pain medications such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (eg, ibuprofren). These measures are aimed at reducing symptom severity as they do not decrease healing time. Management of severe sunburn includes intravenous fluids (Choice A) and analgesia with possible hospitalization for rehydration and wound care. Prevention of sunburn includes the use of protective clothing (eg, long sleeves, hats) and the application of sunscreen 30 minutes prior to sun exposure with frequent reapplication. (Choices B and D) Oral and topical corticosteroids are not recommended in the management of sunburn given lack of evidence of their benefit. (Choices E and F) The management of blisters secondary to sunburn includes prevention of bacterial superinfection with topical agents such as silver sulfadiazine or mupirocin. This patient does not have blisters. Educational objective: A minor sunburn presents within 24 hours of exposure with erythema and tenderness without blistering. Treatment is support and includes cool compresses and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.

questions.explanation: Isotretinoin Indications Severe inflammatory acne (eg, nodular) Moderate inflammatory acne that forms scars or is treatment resistant Mechanism of action Normalizes follicular epithelial proliferation & desquamation Decreases sebum production Inhibits Cutibacterium acnes proliferation & inflammation Adverse effects Teratogenic Pseudotumor cerebri Hypertriglyceridemia Transaminase elevation Dry skin or mucous membranes Acne fulminans (initial worsening of acne) Laboratory monitoring Pregnancy test Liver function test Lipid panel Isotretinoin is an oral vitamin A analogue that binds to intranuclear receptors and alters gene expression. It is used to treat severe nodulocystic acne or milder acne that produces scars or has failed less aggressive treatments (eg, topical therapy with oral antibiotics or hormone therapy). Isotretinoin inhibits comedogenesis by normalizing epithelial proliferation and desquamation. It also decreases sebum production, thereby inhibiting the proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes, which depends on sebum as a nutrient. Consequently, the C acnes–triggered inflammatory response also declines. Because it treats multiple pathogenic pathways, it is typically used as monotherapy. Because isotretinoin is a teratogen, it is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Exposure can cause spontaneous abortion and severe fetal anomalies. Patients and prescribers must comply with an online risk-management program. For female patients, 2 negative pregnancy tests (urine or serum) are required prior to initiation, and monthly pregnancy testing is required during treatment, which usually lasts several months. In addition, patients must commit to not having sexual contact with males or to using 2 forms of highly effective contraception while on isotretinoin; therefore, this patient taking oral contraceptives should also use barrier contraception. (Choice B) Ocular adverse effects of isotretinoin include dry eyes (due to meibomian gland dysfunction), decreased night vision, corneal opacities, and pseudotumor cerebri, which may lead to headache, vision changes, and papilledema. However, a baseline eye examination is not usually needed, unless the patient reports ocular symptoms. (Choice C) Despite concerns, there is no evidence that isotretinoin causes depression and suicide. A baseline psychiatric examination is not typically performed unless the patient reports a history of psychiatric illness, is symptomatic, or has a family history of depression or suicide. (Choice D) Tetracyclines (eg, doxycycline) should not be administered with isotretinoin due to the risk for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri). Isotretinoin is typically used as monotherapy because it targets every aspect of acne pathogenesis. (Choice E) Tuberculin skin testing is recommended prior to the initiation of certain immunosuppressive therapies (eg, biologic disease-modifying agents for rheumatoid arthritis). Isotretinoin is not an immunosuppressant, so testing is not necessary. Educational objective: Isotretinoin is indicated for severe nodulocystic acne or milder acne that produces scars or has failed less-aggressive treatments (eg, topical therapy with oral antibiotics or hormone therapy). It is teratogenic; therefore, female patients should have pregnancy testing prior to and periodically during therapy and use 2 forms of contraception.

Isotretinoin is an oral vitamin A analogue that binds to intranuclear receptors and alters gene expression.  It is used to treat severe nodulocystic acne or milder acne that produces scars or has failed less aggressive treatments (eg, topical therapy with oral antibiotics or hormone therapy).  Isotretinoin inhibits comedogenesis by normalizing epithelial proliferation and desquamation.  It also decreases sebum production, thereby inhibiting the proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes, which depends on sebum as a nutrient.  Consequently, the C acnes–triggered inflammatory response also declines.  Because it treats multiple pathogenic pathways, it is typically used as monotherapy.

wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  Ocular adverse effects of isotretinoin include dry eyes (due to meibomian gland dysfunction), decreased night vision, corneal opacities, and pseudotumor cerebri, which may lead to headache, vision changes, and papilledema.  However, a baseline eye examination is not usually needed, unless the patient reports ocular symptoms.
wrongAnswers.C: (Choice C)  Despite concerns, there is no evidence that isotretinoin causes depression and suicide.  A baseline psychiatric examination is not typically performed unless the patient reports a history of psychiatric illness, is symptomatic, or has a family history of depression or suicide.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Tetracyclines (eg, doxycycline) should not be administered with isotretinoin due to the risk for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri).  Isotretinoin is typically used as monotherapy because it targets every aspect of acne pathogenesis.
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Tuberculin skin testing is recommended prior to the initiation of certain immunosuppressive therapies (eg, biologic disease-modifying agents for rheumatoid arthritis).  Isotretinoin is not an immunosuppressant, so testing is not necessary.

questions.explanation: DRESS syndrome is a rare, potentially life-threatening drug reaction characterized by the following: Drug - most commonly allopurinol and antiepileptics (eg, phenytoin, carbamazepine) Reaction (rash) - morbilliform eruption that starts on the face or upper trunk and becomes diffuse (often >50% body surface area) and confluent; facial edema is common Eosinophilia Systemic symptoms - fever, malaise, and diffuse lymphadenopathy; approximately 90% of patients have involvement of >1 organ system (eg, liver [transaminitis], kidney, lung) DRESS syndrome, unlike other drug reactions, has an unusually long latency (2-8 weeks) between drug initiation and the manifestation of symptoms. The pathogenic mechanism remains unclear, but the majority of patients with this syndrome also have antibody evidence of human herpesvirus 6 reactivation. Some studies suggest cross-reactivity between herpesvirus lymphocytes and drug antigens. Diagnosis is largely clinical; treatment involves the immediate cessation of the inciting drug and supportive care (eg, fluid, electrolyte, nutrition support). Most patients recover completely within weeks or months, but relapses may occur. (Choice A) Trichinella is a nematode transmitted by undercooked meat (usually pork). Periorbital edema and eosinophilia may occur, but muscle symptoms (eg, pain, tenderness, weakness) are usually predominant. This patient with facial edema, widespread rash, lymphadenopathy, and recent initiation of allopurinol more likely has DRESS syndrome. (Choice B) Patients with scarlet fever (due to Streptococcus pyogenes) may develop a diffuse rash; however, the rash usually begins in the groin/armpits and is erythematous, blanching, and papular. Eosinophilia would be atypical. (Choice C) Infectious mononucleosis is diagnosed by heterophile antibodies and usually manifests with fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, fatigue, and lymphocytosis. Maculopapular rashes are common if patients receive ampicillin or amoxicillin. Eosinophilia is not a typical feature. (Choice E) Patients with chronic hepatitis C virus can develop mixed cryoglobulinemia with palpable purpura, fatigue, and arthralgia. Diffuse lymphadenopathy and eosinophilia are uncommon. (Choice F) Secondary syphilis can manifest with a diffuse macular/papular eruption of the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Constitutional symptoms and lymphadenopathy are common. This patient on allopurinol with significant eosinophilia, facial edema, and a confluent morbilliform rash more likely has DRESS syndrome. Educational objective: DRESS syndrome is a drug reaction most commonly associated with allopurinol and antiepileptics. Manifestations develop 2-8 weeks after drug initiation and usually include diffuse/confluent morbilliform rash, eosinophilia, and systemic symptoms (eg, fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy). The offending drug should be immediately discontinued; most patients recover completely.

questions.explanation: Cervical cancer Risk factors Immunosuppression (eg, HIV) Early onset of sexual activity Multiple or high-risk sexual partners Previous sexually transmitted infection History of vulvar or vaginal cancer Cigarette use Pathogenesis Human papillomavirus infection Clinical manifestations Asymptomatic Postcoital bleeding Intermenstrual bleeding Increased vaginal discharge Pelvic/low back pain Diagnosis Cervical biopsy on colposcopy This patient has lower back pain and a lower uterine segment mass with associated hydronephrosis concerning for advanced-stage cervical cancer. Early symptoms of cervical cancer include irregular vaginal bleeding and postcoital spotting due to bleeding from the cervical lesion itself. As the tumor extends laterally through the parametrium and pelvis (low back pain), it can lead to obstruction of the surrounding blood vessels and lymphatics (lymphedema) and ureters (hydronephrosis). Cervical cancer is clinically staged through physical examination. Intravenous pyelogram or CT scan can be used to evaluate for hydronephrosis. Cervical cancer is an AIDS-defining illness. Immunosuppressed patients have persistent human papillomavirus infection that results in neoplasia or malignancy. Due to this risk, Pap test screening recommendations are more frequent for this population in the years immediately following diagnosis. (Choices A, F, and G) Bladder, ureteral, and renal cell carcinoma can present with hydronephrosis. However, they also present with hematuria, which is not seen in this patient. (Choice C) Colorectal cancer typically presents with changes in bowel pattern or fecal incontinence. Imaging would reveal a colorectal, rather than uterine, mass. (Choice D) Diffuse large B cell lymphoma is an AIDS-defining malignancy that presents with fever, night sweats, and a rapidly enlarging mediastinal or abdominal mass. In addition, the most common site of extra-nodal disease is the gastrointestinal tract, not the cervix. (Choice E) Epithelial ovarian cancer presents with an adnexal mass and ascites, not a lower uterine segment mass. HIV does not increase the risk of epithelial ovarian cancer. (Choice H) A uterine leiomyoma can present with heavy irregular bleeding, a large uterine mass, and hydronephrosis. Leiomyomas are not associated with HIV and do not typically cause back pain or lower extremity edema. Educational objective: Advanced-stage cervical cancer can present with back pain, edema, a pelvic mass, and hydronephrosis. Cervical cancer is an AIDS-defining illness.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to persistent lower back pain that has worsened over the past week. The pain is now so severe that she is unable to ambulate. The patient has no weakness, loss of sensation, or new-onset urinary or fecal incontinence. She has had increased leg swelling. The patient was diagnosed with HIV infection 8 years ago, but has not seen a doctor in several years. She has no other medical problems and takes no medications. Menstrual periods are irregular with intermittent light spotting. The patient does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. There is no family history of any illness. Blood pressure is 145/90 mm Hg, pulse is 99/min, and respirations are 16/min. Abdominal examination reveals no palpable masses or hepatosplenomegaly. There is no paraspinal or vertebral tenderness. Bilateral lower extremities have 2+ edema; sensation and reflexes are intact. CD4 count is 198/mm3. Urinalysis is negative for blood and nitrites. CT scan reveals a lower uterine segment mass that extends laterally. Bilateral hydronephrosis is seen. Which of the following is the most likely underlying pathology in this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient's eye findings are consistent with a chalazion, a granulomatous reaction to a blocked meibomian tear gland. Chalazia occur more commonly in patients with rosacea or eyelid margin blepharitis and are somewhat more common on the upper eyelid due to the increased number and length of meibomian glands in the area. Patients typically develop eyelid swelling and erythema that progress to a solitary (usually painless), rubbery, nodular lesion. The lesions are best visualized with the eyelid everted. Chalazia often resolve spontaneously, but larger lesions may benefit from warm compresses to enhance drainage and speed healing. Persistent or severe lesions may require ophthalmology referral for resection or glucocorticoid injection. (Choice A) A hordeolum is an acute inflammatory nodule arising from an eyelash follicle (external hordeolum [stye]) or from a meibomian gland under the eyelid (internal hordeolum). It is typically due to infection with Staphylococcus aureus. Unlike a chalazion, a hordeolum is usually painful and tends to develop closer to the lid margin. (Choice B) Dacryocystitis is an acute infection of the lacrimal sac and is characterized by sudden-onset pain and redness at the medial canthal region. Some patients have purulent discharge from the lacrimal punctum. (Choice C) Orbital cellulitis is an infection posterior to the orbital septum. Typical features include an abrupt onset of fever, unilateral proptosis, restriction of extraocular movements, and swollen, red eyelids. (Choice E) Molluscum contagiosum is due to a poxvirus and typically presents as single or multiple small, dome-shaped, pearly papules with central umbilication. (Choice F) Dermoid cysts are uncommon cystic teratomas, most commonly seen at the lateral terminus of the eyebrow. They are typically present from birth. (Choice G) Xanthelasmas are cholesterol-filled lesions that appear as yellow-orange macules, papules, or plaques on the medial surface of the eyelids. Educational objective: A chalazion is a granulomatous reaction to a blocked meibomian tear gland. It is characterized by eyelid swelling and erythema that progress to a solitary (usually painless), rubbery, nodular lesion. Chalazia often resolve spontaneously, but warm compresses can enhance drainage and speed healing.

questions.explanation: Myelomeningocele (spina bifida), the most common type of neural tube defect (NTD), is due to the incomplete closure of the vertebral column and skin (eg, vertebral arch defect) resulting in an uncovered spinal cord and meninges (eg, neural tissue bulging into the amniotic cavity). Myelomeningoceles are typically isolated defects that are due to a variety of factors, but are commonly associated with folic acid deficiency. Folic acid is involved in the genetic regulation of the neural tube, and decreased levels result in failed neural tube closure. This patient is taking carbamazepine, an anticonvulsant with folic acid antagonist properties, placing her at increased risk for inadequate folic acid levels. High-risk patients (eg, NTD in a prior pregnancy, anticonvulsant medications) require additional folic acid supplementation (eg, 4 mg daily), rather than the 0.4 mg daily recommended for average-risk patients. (Choice A) Maternal age ≥35 is associated with an increased risk for chromosomal abnormalities, particularly aneuploidy. Aneuploidy typically results in multiple fetal anomalies (eg, trisomy 13 and 18). Advanced maternal age is not an independent risk factor for an isolated NTD. (Choice B) Cigarette use during pregnancy is associated with fetal growth restriction, intrauterine fetal demise, and cleft lip/palate; it is not associated with NTDs. (Choice C) Cocaine use during pregnancy is associated with fetal growth restriction and abruptio placentae. Cocaine is not a teratogen and is not associated with NTDs. (Choice D) There is no association between trisomy 21 and NTDs. Trisomy 21 is typically the result of a spontaneous mutation, and family history does not increase the risk of aneuploidy. (Choice E) Lithium use may be associated with congenital cardiac malformations (eg, Ebstein anomaly) but is not known to cause NTDs. Educational objective: Folic acid deficiency is associated with an increased risk of neural tube defects (eg, myelomeningocele). Anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine) can cause low folic acid levels; patients on these medications require higher doses (eg, 4 mg daily) of folic acid supplementation to decrease the risk for a neural tube defect.

questions.explanation: Vaccines during pregnancy Recommended Tdap Inactivated influenza Rho(D) immunoglobulin Indicated for high-risk patients Hepatitis B Hepatitis A Pneumococcus Haemophilus influenzae Meningococcus Varicella-zoster immunoglobulin Contraindicated HPV MMR Live attenuated influenza Varicella HPV = human papillomavirus; MMR = measles, mumps & rubella; Tdap = tetanus–reduced diphtheria–acellular pertussis vaccine. Pertussis (whooping cough) is an upper respiratory infection that in infants is associated with high rates of disease complications (eg, seizure, renal failure, pneumonia) and mortality. Because infant pertussis infection is so severe, Tdap vaccination (tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis) is recommended for women during each pregnancy regardless of vaccination history. Vaccination during the third trimester is preferred as it facilitates both the maternal antibody response and the transfer of maternal antibodies through the placenta, providing passive immunity to the fetus. Women who did not receive the Tdap vaccination during pregnancy should be vaccinated in the immediate postpartum period. Tdap vaccination is also recommended for family members who have not been recently vaccinated and will be in close contact with the newborn. This patient's hepatitis B surface antibody is positive, indicating immunity. (Choices B and F) The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine (MMR) and the varicella vaccine are indicated in this patient due to her nonimmune status. However, both are live attenuated vaccines, and their administration during pregnancy is associated with a theoretical risk of congenital infection. Vaccination should be postponed until the postpartum period. questions.explanation: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy Risk factors Asymptomatic bacteriuria Diabetes mellitus Age <20 Common pathogens Escherichia coli (most common) Klebsiella Enterobacter Group B Streptococcus Complications Preterm labor Low birth weight Acute respiratory distress syndrome Treatment Intravenous antibiotics Supportive therapy This patient's presentation of fever, flank pain, dyspnea, and hypoxia is consistent with acute pyelonephritis complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and preterm labor. During the second and third trimesters of pregnancy, elevations in progesterone cause urinary stasis and hydronephrosis, which predispose patients to the development of pyelonephritis. Risk factors include a history of asymptomatic bacteriuria, maternal age <20, tobacco use, and nulliparity. The most common pathogen is Escherichia coli. Pyelonephritis in pregnant women is associated with both obstetric and medical complications. Obstetric complications include preterm labor; fetal tachycardia is also commonly observed and typically resolves with treatment of the pyelonephritis and subsequent maternal defervescence. Medical complications include ARDS, as seen with this patient's dyspnea, hypoxia, diffuse crackles, and infiltrates on chest x-ray. Management is respiratory support and empiric intravenous antibiotics. (Choice B) Amniotic fluid embolism can cause dyspnea and hypoxia but also typically causes cardiorespiratory collapse (eg, hypotension, loss of consciousness) and disseminated intravascular coagulation. It is not associated with fever or flank pain. (Choice C) Influenza infection can cause pneumonia, which may present with fever, dyspnea, and hypoxia. Although patients may have diffuse muscle aches, focal flank tenderness is uncommon. (Choice D) Intraamniotic infection (IAI) is defined as maternal fever (without a clear source of infection) plus one of the following: maternal or fetal tachycardia, purulent amniotic fluid, or leukocytosis. However, although this patient has fever and maternal and fetal tachycardia, IAI does not cause focal flank tenderness. In addition, this patient's nontender uterus and intact membranes make IAI less likely. (Choice E) Peripartum cardiomyopathy typically presents with heart failure symptoms (eg, dyspnea, cough, pedal edema). Physical examination shows jugular venous distension and an S3. Fever and flank pain are not present. (Choice F) A posterior (ie, concealed) abruptio placentae can present with back pain; however, it typically causes fetal heart rate decelerations and uterine tenderness. Educational objective: Acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy typically presents with fever and flank pain and can be complicated by preterm labor and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Treatment includes intravenous antibiotics and supportive care (eg, supplemental oxygen).

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 0 aborta 1, at 31 weeks gestation comes to the emergency department due to fever, chills, and shortness of breath. The patient reports progressive dyspnea over the last few hours but has no cough, chest pain, or hemoptysis. Her symptoms began yesterday with fevers, chills, and back pain that radiates to the right flank. She has had no prenatal care and last saw a medical provider more than a year ago. Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F), blood pressure is 88/68 mm Hg, pulse is 115/min, and respirations are 24/min. Pulse oximetry is 90% on room air. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs and no jugular venous distension. Pulmonary examination reveals diffuse, bilateral crackles. There is tenderness over the right flank. The uterus is nontender, and the cervix is 1 cm dilated and 50% effaced, with intact amniotic membranes. Fetal monitoring shows a fetal heart rate baseline of 180/min with no decelerations; there are contractions every 4 minutes on the tocometer. Chest x-ray reveals bilateral infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
