questions.explanation: This patient has uncontrolled, severe cancer-related pain despite taking scheduled short-acting opioids (eg, morphine), resulting in breakthrough pain, disrupted sleep, and affective symptoms (eg, distress, frustration). Opioids are first-line therapy (alone or with acetaminophen or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) for moderate to severe cancer-related pain; when as-needed short-acting opioids are insufficient due to frequent or continuous pain, fixed-schedule dosing usually provides adequate relief. However, in patients with persistent breakthrough pain (eg, analgesia wears off) or inadequate overnight relief (eg, frequent awakening) despite taking scheduled short-acting opioids, adding long-acting opioids can improve convenience (eg, less frequent dosing) and help stabilize pain control (eg, steady drug levels). Typically, the total daily opioid requirement is split between the long- and the short-acting formulations. As such, even after transition to long-acting medications (eg, extended-release morphine, transdermal fentanyl), short-acting opioids should still be available as needed for the treatment of breakthrough pain. (Choice B) Fixed-schedule regimens of short-acting opioids at very short intervals (eg, every 2 hr) are unfeasible to maintain long-term, create an excessive pill burden, and are unlikely to provide relief throughout the night. (Choice C) Although cancer support groups can help patients with coping strategies, quality of life, and psychologic response to cancer-related pain, they would not address ongoing pain uncontrolled by the current opioid regimen. (Choice D) Antidepressants with analgesic properties (eg, duloxetine) are often used as adjuvant therapy for chronic cancer-related pain associated with depressed mood, and they should be considered for this patient with tearfulness and possible passive suicidality (eg, wondering "if it's worth living"). However, poorly controlled pain can cause many affective symptoms, and adequate pain control is an essential initial intervention for this patient that would not be immediately addressed by antidepressants, which would not take effect for weeks. (Choice E) Stimulant therapy (eg, modafinil) can be used for treatment-resistant depression and cancer-related fatigue. However, it may worsen this patient's weight loss and would not address the uncontrolled cancer-related pain. Educational objective: Opioids are first-line therapy for moderate to severe cancer-related pain; when as-needed, short-acting opioids are insufficient, fixed-schedule dosing usually provides adequate relief. However, in patients with persistent breakthrough pain or inadequate overnight relief despite scheduled dosing, adding long-acting opioids can improve convenience (eg, less frequent dosing) and help stabilize pain control.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer is evaluated due to poorly controlled chest, abdominal, and limb pain. The patient underwent a bilateral mastectomy 4 years ago but now has several skeletal and liver metastases that have not responded to chemotherapy. She takes an as-needed nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug and short-acting oral morphine every 4 hours. The dosing frequency of the morphine was increased 3 weeks ago, but the patient says the effects wear off before her next dose. She sleeps well but awakens frequently due to pain; she says, "I can't bear this. I'm frustrated and sometimes even wonder if it's worth living with this pain, but when I see all the support from my family, I know it is." The patient has lost 4.6 kg (10.1 lb) over the past 3 months. Blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg and pulse is 92/min. She appears tired and tearful. There is tenderness to palpation of several ribs. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention for this patient?

questions.explanation: Testicular torsion Epidemiology Most common in adolescents Clinical features Testicular, inguinal, or abdominal pain Nausea, vomiting Examination findings Tender, swollen, erythematous hemiscrotum Elevated, horizontally positioned testicle Absent cremasteric reflex Imaging No blood flow on scrotal ultrasound with Doppler Management Surgical detorsion & fixation with exploration of contralateral side Manual detorsion (if immediate surgery is not available) This patient has abrupt-onset scrotal pain associated with swelling and diffuse tenderness. In a young man, this is most likely due to testicular torsion. Testicular torsion is caused by twisting of the spermatic cord due to inadequate fixation of the lower pole of the testis to the tunica vaginalis. This twisting leads to compression of the pampiniform plexus and reduced venous outflow. Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency because irreversible testicular ischemia and necrosis can occur rapidly. Diagnosis is primarily clinical. Shortening of the spermatic cord can cause the testis to ride high in the scrotum with the long axis oriented horizontally (bell-clapper deformity). In addition, the cremasteric reflex (upward retraction of the testis on pinching or stroking the inner thigh) is absent in almost all patients. If uncertain, the diagnosis can be confirmed with Doppler ultrasound revealing a lack of blood flow in the affected testicle. (Choice A) Epididymoorchitis is characterized by gradual-onset pain, dysuria, and urethral discharge. Symptoms are often relieved with scrotal elevation, and cremasteric reflex is present. (Choice B) Scrotal hematocele is characterized by testicular rupture, with hemorrhage contained in the tunica vaginalis. It typically follows blunt trauma and presents with localized testicular swelling and focal tenderness. (Choice C) A testicular hydrocele is a collection of fluid between the parietal and visceral tunica vaginalis due to failure of closure (or reopening) of the processus vaginalis. It can cause testicular swelling but does not cause acute, severe pain. (Choice E) Torsion and ischemia of the vestigial appendix testis or appendix epididymis can cause acute pain similar to that in testicular torsion, although blood flow to the testicle itself is preserved. The associated tenderness is focal rather than diffuse, the cremasteric reflex is present, and the ischemic appendix may be visible as a dark area under the scrotal skin (blue-dot sign). Educational objective: Testicular torsion is characterized by acute scrotal pain, swelling and tenderness, bell-clapper deformity, and loss of the cremasteric reflex. Torsion is a surgical emergency due to the possibility of irreversible damage to the testis.

questions.explanation: Penile cancer Epidemiology Age >60 Risk factors: HPV, phimosis, cigarette smoking Most are squamous cell carcinoma Manifestations Painless ulcer/nodule Inguinal lymphadenopathy Distant spread rare until late Diagnosis Biopsy Lymph node assessment Treatment Excision Chemotherapy (depending on stage) HPV = human papillomavirus. This patient with a painless penile ulcer for several months likely has penile cancer. Penile cancer is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening malignancy that arises primarily in men age >60. Potent risk factors include human papillomavirus infection, phimosis, and cigarette smoking. The vast majority of cases are due to squamous cell carcinoma. Patients typically develop a painless nodule or ulcer on the distal penis (glans, coronal sulcus, or foreskin). Lymphatic spread (or inflammation) may lead to inguinal lymphadenopathy; distant metastases are not typically present until late in the course of illness. A biopsy is required for diagnosis. (Choice A) Behçet syndrome may cause genital aphthous ulcers that are recurrent and painful. Most occur on the scrotum and heal spontaneously within 1-3 weeks. This patient with a chronic, painless glans penis lesion is unlikely to have Behçet syndrome. (Choice B) Candida infections may cause balanitis or phimosis, especially in patients with diabetes mellitus. Symptoms usually include a painful or pruritic erythematous rash with foul-smelling, thick discharge. This patient has a painless, chronic ulcer and no discharge. (Choice C) Genital herpes usually causes a painful vesicular eruption that resolves spontaneously within 1-3 weeks. This patient has a single, chronic, painless ulcer. (Choice D) Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi and is quite rare in the United States. Manifestations typically include a painful genital papule that turns into a pustule and erodes into an ulcer. This patient with a chronic, painless genital ulcer is unlikely to have chancroid. (Choice F) Primary syphilis manifests with a painless papule that ulcerates over time (chancre). Syphilitic chancres are usually treated with antibiotics (penicillin) but otherwise resolve spontaneously within 3-6 weeks. This patient has had a penile ulcer for several months, making cancer more likely. Educational objective: Penile cancer develops primarily in older men with a history of human papillomavirus infection, phimosis, or cigarette smoking. Patients typically develop a painless nodule or ulcer on the distal penis (glans, coronal sulcus, or foreskin). Inguinal lymphadenopathy is common and may represent metastatic spread. A biopsy is required for diagnosis.

questions.explanation: Testicular cancer Epidemiology Age 15-35 Risk factors: family history, cryptorchidism Manifestations Unilateral, painless testicular nodule or swelling Sometimes presents with dull lower abdominal ache Metastatic symptoms (eg, dyspnea, neck mass, low back pain) Diagnosis Examination: firm, ovoid mass or unilateral swelling Scrotal ultrasonography Tumor markers (α-fetoprotein, β-hCG) Staging imaging (CT scan, chest x-ray) Treatment Radical orchiectomy Chemotherapy Cure rate ~95% This patient with a nontender nodule in the testis that does not transilluminate likely has testicular cancer, the most common solid organ malignancy in men age 15-35. The vast majority of cases (~95%) are due to malignant transformation of the seminiferous germinal epithelium (germ cell tumor); sex cord stromal tumors (eg, Leydig cell, Sertoli cell) can also occur but are much less common. Testicular tumors generally present with nontender, unilateral testicular swelling or a painless nodule, which is often first noticed after a groin injury or during sexual activity with a partner. Physical examination usually reveals an ovoid lesion within the tunica albuginea that is firm, hard, or fixed. Transillumination does not occur because light cannot penetrate solid tumors. Diagnostic workup includes bilateral scrotal ultrasound, serum tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein, β-hCG), and radical inguinal orchiectomy for histopathologic confirmation and initiation of treatment. Most cases require subsequent chemotherapy. Cure rates are >95%. (Choice A) Spermatoceles are cystic epididymal accumulations of sperm that form superiorly to (not within) the testicle. They are usually asymptomatic and do not require treatment. (Choice B) Varicoceles are due to pampiniform venous plexus dilation and typically feel like a "bag of worms" on examination. Most decompress with recumbency and increase in size with standing. (Choice C) Inguinal hernias usually cause a painless bulge in the groin, not a firm testicular mass. (Choice E) A hydrocele is a collection of serous fluid between layers of the tunica vaginalis (surrounding the testicle and spermatic cord). Most are asymptomatic and painless. Unlike testicular tumors, hydroceles transilluminate. (Choice F) Testicular trauma can cause blood accumulation in the tunica vaginalis (hematocele), leading to significant testicular pain. Although this patient initially had a traumatic testicular injury, the presence of a firm, nonpainful mass 2 months later strongly suggests testicular cancer. Testicular trauma sometimes alerts patients to an underlying testicular tumor. Educational objective: Germ cell tumors of the testicle are the most common solid malignancy in young men. Manifestations typically include a painless, ovoid, unilateral testicular mass that does not transilluminate. Scrotal ultrasound and serum tumor markers help support the diagnosis, but radical orchiectomy is required for tissue diagnosis and initiation of treatment.

questions.explanation: Comparison of benign prostatic hyperplasia & prostate cancer BPH Prostate cancer Risk factors Age >50 Age >40, African American & family history Affected part Central portion (transitional zone) Usually peripheral zone of prostate but can be anywhere Examination Symmetrically enlarged & smooth prostate Can have elevated PSA Asymmetrically enlarged, nodules & firm prostate Markedly elevated PSA BPH = benign prostatic hyperplasia; PSA = prostate-specific antigen. This patient has progressive lower urinary tract symptoms (eg, frequency, hesitancy, nocturia). In light of the palpable prostate nodule and elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level, this is most likely due to adenocarcinoma of the prostate. Prostate cancer can metastasize to the axial skeleton and proximal femurs but frequently follows an indolent course. Prostate biopsy is used for definitive diagnosis, most often with a transrectal approach under ultrasound guidance. Biopsy also can provide prognostic information based on pathologic grade (Gleason score). The 3 primary treatment options for early stage prostate cancer include active surveillance (watchful waiting), prostatectomy, and radiotherapy. (Choices A, D, and E) Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and mild lower urinary tract symptoms can often be managed with behavioral interventions (eg, reducing caffeine and fluid intake late in the day). Options for more significant symptoms include alpha-adrenergic blockers (eg, tamsulosin) and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride). Although BPH can be associated with a mild elevation in PSA, palpable nodules or gross asymmetry on prostate examination warrant biopsy to exclude prostate cancer. (Choice B) Thiazide diuretics are a common cause of erectile dysfunction but do not contribute to prostate cancer. Patients with nocturia may be advised to take their dose in the morning, but the medication can usually be continued. Educational objective: Adenocarcinoma of the prostate presents with firm, asymmetrical enlargement of the prostate or palpable nodules, usually with an elevated prostate-specific antigen level. Patients with signs of prostate cancer should undergo prostate biopsy for diagnosis and pathologic grade.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man comes to the office due to worsening urinary frequency, hesitancy, and nocturia for the past 2 months. The patient wakes up 2 or 3 times a night to urinate, causing him to be tired during the day. He has had no dysuria or hematuria. The patient has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Chlorthalidone was recently added to his antihypertensive regimen due to inadequate blood pressure control. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F), blood pressure is 120/84 mm Hg, and pulse is 80/min. The abdomen is soft and nontender to palpation and bowel sounds are normal. The bladder is not palpable and there is no flank tenderness. Rectal sphincter tone is normal, and the prostate is enlarged with a nodule on the right side. Laboratory results show a fasting blood glucose level of 130 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c of 7.2%. Prostate-specific antigen level is 7.4 ng/mL (age-adjusted reference value: <4.5 ng/mL). Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Common causes of erectile dysfunction Clinical features Vascular Cardiovascular risk factors (eg, hypertension, smoking, diabetes) Abnormal vascular examination (eg, bruits, decreased pulses) Neurologic Neurologic comorbidity (eg, diabetic neuropathy, multiple sclerosis, spinal injury/surgery) Gradual onset, loss of bulbocavernosus reflex Psychogenic Sudden onset Situational (eg, ED with partner, normal erection during masturbation) Normal nonsexual nocturnal erections Endocrine Additional symptoms due to underlying disorder Abnormal hormone levels (eg, TSH, prolactin) Medications Onset related to starting medication Antihypertensives, SSRIs, antiandrogenic medications Hypogonadism Gradual onset Decreased libido, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy Low serum testosterone ED = erectile dysfunction; SSRIs = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Normal male erectile function requires interplay between psychologic and physical stimulation and vascular, neurologic, and hormonal systems. Causes of erectile dysfunction (ED) can be categorized as organic (eg, hypogonadism, vascular, neurologic) or psychogenic. Organic ED is often initially intermittent or slowly progressive and is more common with advancing age. This patient has a significant smoking history and other risk factors for atherosclerotic vascular disease. ED is common in patients with cardiovascular disease due to decreased pelvic blood flow, endothelial dysfunction, and vasoactive medications. In men with neurologic or vascular dysfunction, both sexual and nonsexual (eg, nocturnal, early-morning) erections are affected, as seen in this patient. Testosterone deficiency must also be ruled out in this patient but is less likely given his normal libido. (Choice A) Chronic opioid use suppresses secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, leading to central hypogonadism and ED. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (eg, ibuprofen) inhibit testosterone production, but the compensatory rise in gonadotropins restores circulating testosterone levels to near normal; ED is uncommon. (Choice C) Autonomic control of erectile function is mediated by lower thoracic (T11-T12) sympathetic and sacral (S2-S4) parasympathetic fibers. Psychogenic stimuli (visual or imaginary) activate sympathetic-mediated erection. Tactile stimuli (touching genitalia) prompt erections by activating the sacral parasympathetic erection center. This patient's normal cremasteric reflex (or bulbocavernosus reflex [constriction of the anal sphincter following squeezing of the glans penis]) makes injury to the sacral erection center unlikely. (Choice D) Psychogenic ED can be due to interpersonal conflict, performance anxiety, or an underlying emotional disorder. Features suggesting a psychogenic etiology include sudden-onset, situational ED (eg, ED with a certain partner but normal erections during masturbation) and persistence of nonsexual nocturnal erections, unlike in this patient. (Choice E) The tunica albuginea is the fibrous tissue that immediately overlies the testicles and the corpora cavernosa of the penis. In Peyronie disease, excess collagen formation within the tunica albuginea can cause painful erections with curvature of the penis. Educational objective: Causes of erectile dysfunction can be categorized as organic (eg, hypogonadism, vascular, neurologic) or psychogenic. Organic erectile dysfunction is often slowly progressive and is more common with advancing age. In patients with neurologic or vascular dysfunction, both sexual and nonsexual (eg, nocturnal) erections are affected.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man comes to the office due to worsening sexual dysfunction for the past several months. The patient reports decreasing firmness of his erections, which are now inadequate for vaginal penetration. He also does not wake with early-morning erections as he did before, although he continues to have normal sexual desire. The patient has had chronic low back pain since a work-related injury 2 years ago, and he frequently takes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. questions.explanation: Mastoiditis Pathophysiology Infection of the mastoid air cells Complication of acute otitis media Most commonly due to Streptococcus pneumoniae Clinical findings Fever & otalgia Inflammation of mastoid Protrusion of the auricle Opacification of mastoid air cells on CT scan or MRI Management Intravenous antibiotics Drainage of purulent material (eg, tympanostomy, mastoidectomy) Complications Extracranial extension (subperiosteal abscess, facial nerve palsy, hearing loss, labyrinthitis) Intracranial extension (brain abscess, meningitis) This febrile child with a bulging tympanic membrane who has mastoid tenderness and displacement of the external ear likely has acute mastoiditis, the most common suppurative complication of acute otitis media (AOM). The mastoid air cells are in continuity with the middle ear, allowing spread of the infection. Infection of the mastoid classically causes tenderness (immediately posterior to the ear), erythema, and swelling, which can result in outward and/or vertical displacement of the auricle. Acute mastoiditis can often be diagnosed clinically, including in this patient. Treatment requires intravenous antibiotic therapy with activity against common upper respiratory pathogens (eg, Streptococcus pneumoniae), as well as Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus. Expanded coverage for Pseudomonas (eg, cefepime) should be provided if there is a history of recent antibiotic use. Drainage of the purulent material is also required. This can be achieved by tympanostomy (± ear tube placement) or mastoidectomy. Imaging is not required for diagnosis but is indicated if further complications (eg, meningitis, neurologic deficits) are suspected, if the child appears toxic, if there is no response to initial treatment, or if the diagnosis is unclear (eg, persistent otorrhea of unclear etiology). In these cases, CT scan of the temporal bones or MRI with contrast is preferred over plain radiographs (Choice D). (Choice A) The paranasal sinuses (ie, maxillary, ethmoid, sphenoid, frontal) drain into the nose, and CT scan of these structures is useful to diagnose complications of acute sinusitis (eg, Pott puffy tumor, orbital cellulitis). In contrast, the mastoid air cells are located behind the ear and are in continuity with the middle ear rather than the paranasal sinuses. (Choice C) Intracranial extension of mastoiditis can result in meningitis, which would require lumbar puncture and CSF analysis. Although meningitis can present as a complication of AOM, patients also have signs of meningeal irritation and increased intracranial pressure (eg, vomiting). (Choice E) Ototopical therapy is used to treat otitis externa, which presents with otalgia, edema and erythema of the external ear canal, and discharge from the ear canal but not ear displacement or mastoid tenderness. Educational objective: Acute mastoiditis, a complication of acute otitis media, is characterized by fever, otalgia, and mastoid process inflammation with displacement of the auricle. Treatment includes intravenous antibiotics and surgical drainage.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the office by her parents for fever, rhinorrhea, and fussiness for 2 days. She has been tugging at her left ear for a day but eating and drinking normally. The patient was treated for acute otitis media 2 weeks ago, but did not complete her oral antibiotic therapy because she recovered quickly. She takes no medications and has no drug allergies. Temperature is 38.5 C (101.3 F). Otoscopy of the left ear reveals an erythematous and mildly swollen external ear canal with an erythematous, bulging tympanic membrane that does not move with insufflation. questions.stemHtml: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the office by her parents for fever, rhinorrhea, and fussiness for 2 days.  She has been tugging at her left ear for a day but eating and drinking normally.  The patient was treated for acute otitis media 2 weeks ago, but did not complete her oral antibiotic therapy because she recovered quickly.  She takes no medications and has no drug allergies.  Temperature is 38.5 C (101.3 F).  Otoscopy of the left ear reveals an erythematous and mildly swollen external ear canal with an erythematous, bulging tympanic membrane that does not move with insufflation.  There are also erythema and tenderness to palpation immediately posterior to the left ear, which appears slightly lower than the right.  The lungs are clear to auscultation.  Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Although adolescents are frequently moody and this girl has been faced with major stressors of moving and changing to a new school, the severity of her mood symptoms and related academic and social impairment raise concern for clinical depression. Specifically, her persistent mood disturbance, loss of interest and motivation, fatigue, impaired concentration, hopelessness, marked hypersomnia, and significant weight loss lasting >2 weeks meet the criteria for major depressive disorder. Depressed children and adolescents may exhibit an irritable or cranky mood rather than a sad or dejected mood. Major depression can develop in response to a psychosocial stressor, and it is important for clinicians not to dismiss changes in behavior as a normal stress reaction. Identification and appropriate treatment are important to decrease the risk of suicide and minimize the impact of functional impairment during this critical developmental period. (Choice A) Although this patient's depressive symptoms were precipitated by stressful life events, adjustment disorder is not diagnosed if the symptoms are sufficiently severe to meet the criteria for major depressive disorder. (Choice B) Borderline personality disorder involves a persistent pattern of mood instability, unstable relationships, and suicidal threats and behavior. It would not explain this patient's marked fatigue, hypersomnia, and weight loss. (Choice C) Cyclothymic disorder involves fluctuating mood episodes that do not meet the full criteria for hypomanic or major depressive episodes. (Choice E) This patient's persistent mood symptoms causing marked functional impairment are not consistent with normal adolescent behavior. (Choice F) Parent-child relational problem is diagnosed when the main focus of clinical attention is the parent-child relationship. This patient's difficulties with her mother are more likely due to her depression. (Choice G) Chronic heavy marijuana use is associated with lethargy, mood symptoms, and academic decline. However, intermittent marijuana use is unlikely to be causing the severe and persistent depressive symptoms seen in this patient. Educational objective: Major depressive disorder precipitated by psychosocial stress can be differentiated from normal stress reactions and adjustment disorders by the severity of symptoms and related functional impairment. Patients who meet full diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder should be identified and offered appropriate treatment.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother, who is concerned about her adjustment to a new school. The family moved to a new home a few months ago, requiring the patient to transfer to a new school in her senior year. Her mother is worried as her daughter's grades have dropped and she has lost interest in applying to college. The girl says, "What does it matter? I can't focus on the work; it's just stupid. I won't get into a good college anyway." She has had difficulty making friends at the new school and explains that it is hard to fit in when social groups are already established. She does not participate in any afterschool activities because she is "too tired" and frequently gets into bed after coming home. The patient sleeps until 2:00 PM on weekends and has lost 6.8 kg (15 lb) since the start of the school year. She has not made any effort to stay in contact with her old friends. The mother says that her daughter is more moody than usual and overreacts to minor criticisms. The mother blames herself for her daughter's situation, as her job change was the reason for the move. The girl has used marijuana on several occasions but does not use alcohol or other drugs. Physical examination is normal. The patient has no suicidal thoughts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Myelodysplastic syndromes Epidemiology Hematopoietic stem cell neoplasm Risk ↑: Older age, previous chemotherapy/radiation May transform to acute leukemia Manifestations Cytopenias Anemia: Weakness, fatigue Leukopenia: Infections Thrombocytopenia: Bruising/bleeding Hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy are rare Diagnosis Dysplastic red & white blood cells* on peripheral smear Bone marrow biopsy (hypercellular marrow) Treatment Transfusions for symptomatic cytopenias Chemotherapy Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation *Dysplastic changes include ovalomacrocytosis & neutrophil hyposegmentation/hypogranulation. This elderly patient most likely has myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). MDS is a hematopoietic stem cell neoplasm that interferes with the production of functional blood cell lines and leads to dysplasia and cytopenias. Risk is increased in those with advanced age or a history of chemotherapy or radiation therapy. Patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis, but manifestations of anemia (weakness, fatigue), granulocytopenia (infection), or thrombocytopenia (bleeding, bruising) are common. Physical examination usually shows minimal findings other than conjunctival pallor; hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy are rarely present. Almost all patients have normocytic or macrocytic anemia with insufficient reticulocytosis. Leukopenia with immature neutrophil precursors and thrombocytopenia are also frequently present. Peripheral blood smear is notable for dysplastic erythrocytes (eg, ovalomacrocytosis) and granulocytes (eg, reduced segmentation [pseudo-Pelger-Huët]). Bone marrow biopsy is required for diagnosis. (Choice A) Aplastic anemia is a hematologic disorder due to a pluripotent stem cell injury that causes pancytopenia. Peripheral blood smear will show cells that are morphologically normal (not dysplastic). (Choice B) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a neoplastic disorder that results in absolute lymphocytosis (often >100,000/mm3). Lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are common. This patient has pancytopenia with no lymphocytosis and abnormal granulocytes (not lymphocytes) on peripheral smear. (Choice C) Chronic myeloid leukemia is associated with splenomegaly and massive leukocytosis (not leukopenia). (Choice D) Folate deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia with normal or low reticulocyte count; pancytopenia may occur in severe cases. However, peripheral blood smear shows hypersegmented (not hyposegmented) neutrophils. (Choice E) Hairy cell leukemia is a chronic B cell lymphoproliferative disorder usually associated with pancytopenia and splenomegaly (often massive). Peripheral blood smear typically shows abnormal lymphocytes with "hairy" cytoplasmic projections (not hyposegmented, hypogranulated neutrophils). (Choice G) Myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative disorder that is occasionally characterized by pancytopenia but is almost always associated with massive splenomegaly due to extramedullary hematopoiesis. Educational objective: Myelodysplastic syndrome is a clonal neoplasm of a hematopoietic progenitor cell that results in cytopenias and blood cell line dysplasias. Complete blood count typically shows normocytic or macrocytic anemia with insufficient reticulocytosis, leukopenia with immature neutrophil cells, and thrombocytopenia. Dysplasia of erythrocytes and granulocytes is present on peripheral blood smear.

The patient has a history of breast cancer treated with surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy 15 years ago. questions.explanation: Prophylactic ophthalmic erythromycin is recommended for newborns within 2 hours of birth to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum, an infectious conjunctivitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Administration of ophthalmic erythromycin is inexpensive, noninvasive, and safe. Therefore, because gonococcal conjunctivitis can lead to blindness, prophylaxis is advised for all newborns regardless of maternal history of sexually transmitted infections (Choice A). When patient hesitancy about or refusal of a medical intervention is encountered, the physician's responsibility is to convey all relevant information, including risks and benefits. This is best achieved by reflecting an empathic understanding of the patient's concerns (eg, "you want to make sure the baby is safe and healthy") followed by providing nonthreatening, nonjudgmental education (eg, "let's talk about why this medication is recommended, as well as its risks and benefits") to enhance patient knowledge and shared decision-making. (Choice B) This response initially expresses empathic understanding; however, following it with a comparison "to almost every baby" risks the patient feeling judged for her position. In addition, it is important to discuss the fact that chemical conjunctivitis can occur in a minority of cases. (Choices C and D) Neonatal prophylaxis against gonococcal conjunctivitis is required by most states regardless of consent, and the risks of not receiving it should be clearly discussed. However, immediately dismissing a patient's fears and focusing on the potential risks of not giving it and/or setting up a power struggle (eg "even if you do not provide consent") is likely to elicit patient resistance and frustration. Educational objective: Neonatal prophylaxis against gonococcal conjunctivitis is required by most states regardless of consent. Empathic, nonjudgmental discussion of patient concerns and the medication's risks and benefits is the first step in approaching hesitancy about or refusal of a necessary intervention.

questions.explanation: Phimosis, or the inability to retract the prepuce (foreskin) in an uncircumcised male patient, is usually considered physiologic in infants and young children. Forced manipulation of the prepuce (eg, the mother retracting the child's foreskin to clean the genitalia) may result in paraphimosis, the retraction and entrapment of the prepuce. Due to decreased lymphatic and venous blood flow to the distal penis, the presentation of paraphimosis includes edema and significant tenderness of the glans penis and prepuce. Initially, the glans may appear pink and soft. Without intervention, however, arterial blood flow may be compromised, leading to ischemia and penile tissue firmness and darkening (blue to black). Management of paraphimosis is emergency reduction, either manually or surgically, to maintain vascular flow to the glans penis. Circumcision is a definitive treatment option for preventing the recurrence of paraphimosis but may be unnecessary for an isolated episode that is easily resolved by reduction. (Choices A and D) Balanoposthitis, the likely diagnosis in this patient's history ("penis infection"), refers to inflammation of the glans penis and prepuce; it presents with penile pain, erythema, and discharge in uncircumcised male patients. Phimosis may also be present, so the prepuce would not be retracted or entrapped. Treatment of balanoposthitis includes sitz baths, emollients, and topical antibiotics. In contrast, these interventions would not be indicated in the setting of paraphimosis. (Choice B) Whereas a local lidocaine injection is often used for analgesia in the reduction of paraphimosis, phenylephrine should be avoided due to its vasoconstrictive effects and potential to worsen distal penile ischemia. (Choice E) Pathologic phimosis is the inability to retract the foreskin due to scarring and fibrosis (eg, secondary to balanoposthitis) of the prepuce. Topical corticosteroids are used in these cases but would not be the correct management of paraphimosis. (Choice F) Obtaining a urinalysis and urine culture would be indicated for detecting a urinary tract infection, which is more common in uncircumcised than circumcised infants. The presentation, however, would include dysuria, hematuria, frequency, and/or fever. Educational objective: Paraphimosis refers to the retraction and entrapment of the prepuce in an uncircumcised male patient. Management is urgent manual or surgical reduction of the prepuce.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents due to penile pain and swelling. A month ago, according to his mother, the patient had a "penis infection," which improved with warm baths and a topical ointment. Since then, she has been trying to keep his genitalia clean. Several hours ago, while bathing the child, she retracted the foreskin and was unable to return it to its normal position. The patient soon said he was in pain and has appeared progressively more uncomfortable. He was able to void at home with mild pain. The patient is otherwise healthy and is up to date with his vaccinations. Physical examination shows edema and tenderness of the retracted foreskin and glans penis, which is pink and soft. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Female sexual dysfunction Female sexual interest/arousal disorder Absent/reduced: Interest in sexual activity or erotic thoughts Sexual excitement during sexual encounters Response to sexual cues or attempts to initiate sexual activity Female orgasmic disorder Markedly reduced intensity of orgasm Delay, infrequency, or absence of orgasm Genitopelvic pain/ penetration disorder Persistent or recurrent difficulty with any of the following: Vaginal penetration during intercourse OR vulvovaginal pain during intercourse Fear or anxiety about pain from vaginal penetration Pelvic floor muscle tightening during vaginal penetration Genitourinary syndrome of menopause Normal sexual desire but pain due to vulvovaginal dryness, irritation This patient, who has both loss of libido (ie, loss of physiologic drive for sexual intimacy) and distress, most likely has female sexual interest/arousal disorder, a common sexual disorder in women characterized by significantly reduced or lack of sexual interest/arousal that is not caused by a medical disorder, medication adverse effect, or relationship issue. Although this patient has only low desire and decreased receptivity to her new partner's attempts to initiate intimacy, the diagnosis covers a wide spectrum of decreased interest, arousal, excitement, and pleasure. Common features include absent/reduced interest in sexual activity, thoughts, and fantasies; lack of initiation of sexual activity and/or receptivity to partner's attempts to initiate; and decreased arousal/excitement/pleasure in response to sexual cues and encounters. Diagnosis requires ruling out psychologic, medical, and medication- or substance-related issues that may affect sexuality (eg, depression, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors [SSRIs], alcohol). Although aging and menopause are associated with an increased risk for sexual dysfunction in general, their effects on sexual function vary considerably among women. This patient is distressed by her decreased interest, and it should not be assumed to be part of normal aging (Choice C). (Choice B) Although sexual dysfunction is a common adverse effect of serotonergic antidepressants, bupropion does not affect serotonin. It has been used to treat sexual dysfunction in women with or without associated depression and to treat SSRI-associated sexual dysfunction. (Choice D) Patients with performance anxiety desire to engage in sexual activity but fear that they will not perform well or will fail. This patient, however, has a lack of desire to engage in sexual activity in the first place. (Choice E) Sexual dysfunction is associated with several medical disorders, including diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, and cancer. Hypothyroidism can result in menstrual irregularities in premenopausal women and affect libido. However, this patient is receiving thyroid replacement medication, and her TSH level is within normal range, making hypothyroidism unlikely. Educational objective: Female sexual interest/arousal disorder is a sexual dysfunction commonly seen in postmenopausal women. It can cause significant distress and should not be assumed to be a normal consequence of aging. Substance-induced and medical causes must be ruled out when making the diagnosis.

This patient, who has both loss of libido (ie, loss of physiologic drive for sexual intimacy) and distress, most likely has female sexual interest/arousal disorder, a common sexual disorder in women characterized by significantly reduced or lack of sexual interest/arousal that is not caused by a medical disorder, medication adverse effect, or relationship issue.  Although this patient has only low desire and decreased receptivity to her new partner's attempts to initiate intimacy, the diagnosis covers a wide spectrum of decreased interest, arousal, excitement, and pleasure.

Common features include absent/reduced interest in sexual activity, thoughts, and fantasies; lack of initiation of sexual activity and/or receptivity to partner's attempts to initiate; and decreased arousal/excitement/pleasure in response to sexual cues and encounters.  Diagnosis requires ruling out psychologic, medical, and medication- or substance-related issues that may affect sexuality (eg, depression, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors [SSRIs], alcohol).

Although aging and menopause are associated with an increased risk for sexual dysfunction in general, their effects on sexual function vary considerably among women.

wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  Although sexual dysfunction is a common adverse effect of serotonergic antidepressants, bupropion does not affect serotonin.  It has been used to treat sexual dysfunction in women with or without associated depression and to treat SSRI-associated sexual dysfunction.
wrongAnswers.C: This patient is distressed by her decreased interest, and it should not be assumed to be part of normal aging (Choice C).
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Patients with performance anxiety desire to engage in sexual activity but fear that they will not perform well or will fail.  This patient, however, has a lack of desire to engage in sexual activity in the first place.
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Sexual dysfunction is associated with several medical disorders, including diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, and cancer.  Hypothyroidism can result in menstrual irregularities in premenopausal women and affect libido.  However, this patient is receiving thyroid replacement medication, and her TSH level is within normal range, making hypothyroidism unlikely.

questions.explanation: Aortic stenosis Causes Age-related calcification of normal valve (age >70)* Calcification of congenital bicuspid valve (younger patients) Rheumatic (common worldwide, rare in resource-rich countries) Clinical manifestations Prolonged asymptomatic period Symptoms progressively develop as stenosis becomes severe: Dyspnea on exertion, ↓ exercise tolerance Exertional angina Syncope or presyncope Decompensated heart failure Physical examination Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at RUSB Murmur radiates to carotids; S4 may be present (concentric LVH) Diminished & delayed pulses (pulsus parvus et tardus) Management Valve replacement for symptomatic severe aortic stenosis** *Most common cause in resource-rich countries. **Valve replacement is the only effective therapy. Medical therapy for severe aortic stenosis is limited. LVH = left ventricular hypertrophy; RUSB = right upper sternal border. Patients with aortic stenosis are usually asymptomatic for a prolonged period, and begin to develop symptoms once the stenosis becomes severe (aortic valve area usually <1 cm2). This patient's exertional fatigue and dyspnea are classic symptoms of restricted cardiac output from aortic stenosis; other classic manifestations include exertional angina, syncope/presyncope, and decompensated heart failure. In severe aortic stenosis, medical management is limited in improving hemodynamics; and mortality from aortic stenosis increases dramatically after the development of symptoms. Therefore, patients such as this one with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis should be referred for aortic valve replacement (AVR). (Choices A and B) Beta blockers reduce contractility and heart rate, which may destabilize forward blood flow in severe aortic stenosis. In addition, nitrates can reduce preload and cause profound hypotension in the preload-dependent state of severe aortic stenosis. Therefore, the addition of either of these medications to this patient's regimen is not appropriate; surgical valve replacement is the best next step. (Choice C) Exercise stress testing is recommended in asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis to assess tolerance and hemodynamic response with exercise (eg, fall in blood pressure with exercise). This patient has progressive symptoms, so further exercise testing is not recommended. Instead, coronary angiography is generally performed prior to AVR to evaluate for any coronary artery disease, as coronary artery bypass grafting (if indicated) could be completed concomitantly with AVR. (Choice D) Patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis should be monitored closely for the development of any new symptoms. In such patients, follow-up echocardiogram every 6-12 months is recommended to evaluate serial LV function. This symptomatic patient requires referral for AVR. His concentric LV hypertrophy is likely due to chronic pressure overload from severe aortic stenosis, which can also lead to left atrial enlargement. Educational objective: Patients with aortic stenosis that is severe (aortic valve area usually <1 cm2) and symptomatic (eg, exertional dyspnea, angina, presyncope/syncope) should be referred for aortic valve replacement. Medical management is of little benefit for severe aortic stenosis.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man comes to the office for follow-up of his hypertension. Since his last visit a year ago, the patient has had increasing fatigue and difficulty catching his breath when walking quickly. He says he is "getting old" and needs to adjust his lifestyle accordingly. He has not had any chest pain or palpitations. The patient's other medical problems include carpal tunnel syndrome, chronic neck pain, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He takes amlodipine and lisinopril for hypertension. He is a lifetime nonsmoker. Blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg and pulse is 70/min and regular. On examination, he has a 3/6 mid-systolic murmur best heard over the right upper sternal border and radiating to the neck. The lungs are clear to auscultation. There is no peripheral edema. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with T wave inversions in leads V5 and V6. Echocardiogram shows left atrial enlargement, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%. The aortic valve appears calcified with restricted opening; the estimated aortic valve area is 0.9 cm2. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

questions.explanation: This patient with a recent 20-kg (44.1-lb) weight loss, low BMI, and secondary amenorrhea most likely has functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA). This form of amenorrhea is caused by disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, with a decrease in GnRH leading to decreased levels of LH, FSH, and estrogen. Low estrogen level can be confirmed with a progesterone challenge test. In this test, progesterone is administered for several days and then discontinued. When progesterone is discontinued (which mimics the normal menstrual cycle), an endometrium exposed to estrogen will bleed. However, a patient with FHA lacks the estrogen required to induce endometrial proliferation; such a patient will have a thin endometrium and no withdrawal bleeding or endometrial shedding. Risk factors for FHA other than significant weight loss (eg, calorie deficiency) include strenuous exercise, chronic illness, and stress. In addition to amenorrhea, patients often have conditions secondary to hypoestrogenemia, including infertility and stress fractures. Treatment is first behavioral (eg, increased calorie intake) but should also include estrogen repletion for those who are unable or unwilling to treat the underlying cause (eg, unable to decrease stress levels, refuse to modify exercise patterns). (Choice A) Amenorrhea is a typical adverse effect of using a progestin-containing intrauterine device (IUD), but a patient using a copper IUD will still have regular menses. (Choice C) Lactational amenorrhea is a common finding in women who are breastfeeding. This patient stopped breastfeeding a year ago, so menses should have resumed. (Choice D) Postpartum thyroiditis occurs within a year of delivery with symptoms such as fatigue, heat intolerance, and tachycardia. This patient is asymptomatic and has a normal TSH level. (Choice E) A patient with primary ovarian insufficiency typically has amenorrhea and vasomotor symptoms. Unlike this patient, the patient with primary ovarian insufficiency would have a high serum FSH level. (Choice F) This patient has no risk factors for Sheehan syndrome, a pituitary infarction commonly associated with significant postpartum hemorrhage. This condition typically presents immediately postpartum with the inability to breastfeed and decreased anterior pituitary (eg, TSH, FSH) hormone levels. This patient was able to breastfeed and has a normal TSH level, making this diagnosis unlikely. Educational objective: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea should be suspected in a patient with significant weight loss and low BMI in addition to amenorrhea. Diagnosis is confirmed if a progesterone challenge test results in no withdrawal bleeding (due to low estrogen level).

questions.explanation: According to the ad, an 8-week treatment course of SALVOHEP in patients (such as this one) who: Have hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1a infection Do not have cirrhosis Have never been previously treated for HCV ("treatment-naïve") Have baseline HCV RNA levels <4 million IU/mL resulted in a 96% rate of sustained virologic response at 12 weeks (SVR12; virologic cure), which was the primary endpoint considered. The difference in SVR12 rate between 8 and 12 weeks of treatment was statistically nonsignificant as the confidence interval (−0.1% to 5.0%) crossed the null value (0%, in this case). In addition, prolonged exposure to SALVOHEP (eg, 12 versus 8 weeks) increased the risk of adverse reactions including fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, and headache. Therefore, this patient should receive 8 weeks of SALVOHEP, which would lead optimally to the maximal SVR12 with the lowest rate of adverse reactions. (Choices A and B) This patient has no medical problems other than chronic HCV, and his demographic (eg, age, BMI) and clinical (eg, HCV genotype, viral load, lack of cirrhosis, lack of prior treatment) features are similar to those of the patients in the study. He does not appear to fulfill any exclusion criteria that would make the results inapplicable to him. This patient's results are expected to be similar to those shown for the subgroup of patients with baseline HCV RNA <4 million IU/mL after 8 weeks of treatment, with no need for further subgroup analysis (ie, analysis of results of a subgroup of patients more similar to him). (Choice C) SVR12 should be measured to ensure virologic cure (primary endpoint). Absence of cirrhosis was not a primary endpoint of the study, and patients treated with SALVOHEP may have treatment failure (ie, elevated HCV RNA) with no evidence of cirrhosis. Educational objective: A confidence interval containing the null value reflects lack of statistical significance.

questions.explanation: Types of studies in the health sciences Experimental Randomized controlled trial Random allocation into treatment & placebo groups Can determine efficacy of the intervention Nonrandomized design Nonrandom allocation into treatment & placebo groups Can determine efficacy of the intervention Observational Cohort Data gathered from the same individuals over time (longitudinal) Can assess risk factors or outcomes Cross-sectional Data gathered at one point in time Can determine prevalence of an outcome in a population Case-control Data gathered from individuals with the condition of interest (cases) & compared to individuals without the condition (controls) Case Detailed information gathered about one individual (or a small group of individuals) Review Meta-analysis Data from multiple studies are statistically combined & analyzed Although the study design is not described, some details can be inferred: Based on the bar graphs and the sample sizes noted within each bar graph, at least 2 treatment arms were included in the trial (multiarm): an 8-week SALVOHEP treatment arm with N = 450 and a 12-week SALVOHEP treatment arm with N = 470. The baseline demographic (eg, age, BMI) and clinical (eg, HCV genotype) characteristics are given for all subjects in the trial, suggesting that these subjects were randomized to the different arms; without randomization, the characteristics of the patients in each group would likely have been given. According to the text below the bar graphs, results of "regimens including drug X are not shown" as no statistically significant difference in rates of virologic cure was found with the addition of drug X. This phrasing means that in addition to the SALVOHEP treatment arms, additional arms were included in which patients were treated with (SALVOHEP + drug X). In sum, this was likely a multiarm, randomized trial comparing SALVOHEP to (SALVOHEP + drug X). Comparing SALVOHEP to placebo among patients with HCV would be unethical (as a standard of care already exists) and provide limited information (Choice D). Trials comparing SALVOHEP to drug X could have been performed, but the drug ad mentions the "addition of drug X to SALVOHEP," which was likely done to determine if additive effects occur with combination therapy (Choice C). (Choices A and B) In case-control studies, researchers begin by selecting patients with the disease/outcome of interest (eg, HCV) as cases and patients without the disease/outcome of interest as controls. To minimize confounding, each case is matched with a control based on similar characteristics. These groups are then compared in terms of past exposure to risk factors. Educational objective: Multiarm, randomized trials can be used to study new drugs, particularly if a need exists to compare different treatment lengths or drug combinations.

questions.explanation: Among the 450 patients who received 8 weeks of SALVOHEP, subgroup analysis of the 235 patients with low baseline viral loads (<4 million IU/mL) showed an elevated (96%) SVR12 rate, comparable to that seen among all 450 patients (95%). No statistically significant difference was found when the SVR12 rates of these 450 patients were compared to those of the 470 patients who received 12 weeks of SALVOHEP. Therefore, although not explicitly stated in the ad, patients with low baseline viral loads who received 12 weeks of SALVOHEP likely also had a similar SVR12 that was not significantly different from the other groups. The additional bar graph depicting this result was probably omitted as it would not have provided clinically significant information, especially because the authors provided the SVR12 rate for patients with low baseline viral load after 8 weeks of treatment. Patients with low baseline viral loads should be distributed between those groups in approximately equal proportions. questions.explanation: Acute appendicitis Clinical presentation Nausea, vomiting, anorexia Initially: diffuse abdominal pain (visceral pain) Later: localized RLQ pain (somatic pain) Mild leukocytosis Examination McBurney point tenderness Psoas sign: pain with right hip extension Obturator sign: pain with right hip internal rotation Rovsing sign: RLQ pain with LLQ palpation Diagnosis Clinical presentation CT scan or ultrasound Treatment Surgical appendectomy LLQ = left lower quadrant; RLQ = right lower quadrant. This patient most likely has acute appendicitis. Luminal obstruction of the appendix (eg, fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia in the setting of infection) leads to appendiceal wall inflammation, decreased tissue perfusion, and necrosis. Perforation can occur, resulting in localized abscess or diffuse peritonitis. Appendicitis most commonly occurs in teenagers and young adults; patients typically present with abdominal pain, low-grade fever, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. The abdominal pain characteristically begins as diffuse (or mid-abdominal) due to the activation of poorly localizing visceral pain fibers and then localizes to the right lower quadrant due to peritoneal inflammation and the recruitment of somatic pain fibers. Physical examination typically reveals exquisite right lower quadrant tenderness as well as abdominal rigidity and guarding; however, tenderness in the right lower quadrant may be mild if the appendix is located retrocecally. Psoas sign (pain with right hip extension) may be present when the appendix is located retrocecally and is highly specific for appendicitis. Laboratory findings typically demonstrate mild leukocytosis. In addition, microscopic hematuria may be present, likely due to the proximity of the right ureter to appendiceal inflammation. (Choice A) Bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma describes pyelonephritis. Patients typically have high fever, flank pain, and urine studies consistent with infection (eg, nitrites, leukocytes, bacteria). The right lower quadrant location of this patient's pain and absence of bacteria on urine microscopy make pyelonephritis less likely. (Choice C) Fallopian tube rupture can occur in an ectopic pregnancy; patients typically have pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding. This patient's positive psoas sign and absence of vaginal bleeding on pelvic examination make appendicitis more likely. (Choice D) Small bowel twisting around an adhesion can lead to small bowel obstruction; patients typically have a history of prior abdominal surgery and present with nausea, vomiting, and colicky abdominal pain. This patient's diffuse abdominal pain localizing to the right lower quadrant and lack of prior abdominal surgery make appendicitis more likely. (Choice E) Ureteric passage of a renal calculus describes nephrolithiasis. Patients typically have hematuria and severe flank pain radiating to the groin. A positive psoas sign makes appendicitis far more likely. Educational objective: Acute appendicitis typically presents with nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and, initially, diffuse abdominal pain that later localizes to the right lower quadrant. When the appendix is located retrocecally, tenderness in the right lower quadrant may be milder than expected, and a positive psoas sign (highly specific for appendicitis) may be present.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to abdominal pain for the past several hours. The pain was initially mid-abdominal and crampy, and now the patient has constant pain in the right lower quadrant. She has had one episode of vomiting since the pain started. The patient has no prior medical problems and takes no medications. She is sexually active and her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. Temperature is 38 C (100.4 F), blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/min. The patient is supine on the bed with her hips flexed and reports worsening of the pain when her hips are extended. There is mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant, with guarding. Bowel sounds are decreased. Pelvic examination reveals tenderness in the right adnexal area. Her leukocyte count is 14,000/mm3 and urinalysis shows 10-20 leukocytes/hpf and 1+ blood. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current condition?

questions.explanation: Small bowel obstruction Clinical presentation Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting Inability to pass flatus or stool if complete (no obstipation if partial) Hyperactive → absent bowel sounds Distended & tympanitic abdomen Diagnosis Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels on plain film or CT scan Partial: air in colon Complete: transition point (abrupt cutoff), no air in colon Complications Ischemia/necrosis (strangulation) Bowel perforation Management Bowel rest, nasogastric tube suction, intravenous fluids Surgical exploration for signs of complications This patient with a history of abdominal surgery has subacute nausea, vomiting, crampy mid-abdominal pain, high-pitched bowel sounds, and radiographic evidence of distended small-bowel loops with air-fluid levels, concerning for a small-bowel obstruction (SBO). Given that this patient lacks obstipation and has gas in the rectum on plain film, she likely has a partial SBO. High-pitched bowel sounds suggest a narrowed intestinal lumen. A mildly elevated amylase can support the diagnosis but is neither sensitive nor specific for SBO. Diagnosis can be confirmed by plain film, as in this case; however, abdominal CT scan is more specific. Surgical adhesions are among the most common causes of SBO. They can cause a fixed, partial obstruction at one location (resulting in chronic nausea, vomiting, and postprandial pain) or a recurrent, intermittent obstruction with episodic symptoms. Either condition may progress to complete obstruction. (Choice A) Acute cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder, usually due to obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone. It typically presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and leukocytosis with a positive Murphy sign on examination. (Choice B) Acute pancreatitis is most commonly caused by alcohol or gallstones and results in severe epigastric pain that radiates to the back. Amylase and lipase are elevated at least 3 times the normal upper limit. (Choice C) Acute viral gastroenteritis is a common diarrheal illness associated with mild abdominal pain, significant diarrhea output, nausea, and vomiting. (Choice D) Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) is defined by obstipation, abdominal pain and distension, and colonic dilation without anatomic obstruction on imaging. Distended loops of small bowel alone with air in the rectum would not be expected. Ogilvie syndrome is associated with certain surgical and nonoperative (eg, trauma, severe infection) conditions. (Choice E) Gastric outlet obstruction usually leads to postprandial nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, and succussion splash (heard with the stethoscope over the upper abdomen and the patient rocked back and forth at the hips). It is often caused by peptic ulcer disease, strictures, and malignancies, (Choice F) Perforated peptic ulcers lead to acute, severe epigastric pain that soon becomes generalized as stomach and intestinal contents cause peritonitis. Plain films may detect free air under the diaphragm. Educational objective: Small-bowel obstruction (SBO) due to adhesions should be suspected in a patient with a history of abdominal surgery who has nausea, vomiting, and colicky mid-abdominal pain. In a partial SBO, obstipation may not be present. Abdominal plain films reveal dilated small-bowel loops with air-fluid levels, and gas may be seen in the colon if the SBO is partial.

The vomitus initially contained ingested food particles but now is mostly yellow liquid. Her last bowel movement 24 hours ago was normal, and she has been passing flatus. The patient has not consumed anything out of the ordinary and has had no fever. She takes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for osteoarthritic knee pain and had an abdominal hysterectomy 20 years ago due to dysfunctional uterine bleeding. The patient occasionally drinks alcohol but does not use tobacco or illicit drugs. Temperature is 37.0 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 98/min. BMI is 33 kg/m2. Bowel sounds are increased and high-pitched. Rectal examination reveals an empty rectal vault and no masses. There is air in the rectum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?

questions.explanation: Acute colonic pseudoobstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) Etiologies Major surgery, traumatic injury, severe infection Electrolyte derangement (↓ K, ↓ Mg, ↓ Ca) Medications (eg, opiates, anticholinergics) Neurologic disorders (eg, dementia, stroke) Clinical findings Abdominal distension, pain, obstipation, vomiting Tympanic to percussion, ↓ bowel sounds If perforation: guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness Imaging X-ray: colonic dilation, normal haustra, nondilated small bowel CT scan: colonic dilation without anatomic obstruction Management NPO, nasogastric/rectal tube decompression Neostigmine if no improvement within 48 hr This elderly patient who recently underwent a major orthopedic procedure now has abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and vomiting. A CT scan reveals colonic dilation with oral contrast visualized throughout the colon, suggesting no anatomic obstruction. This presentation is characteristic of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome). Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction more commonly occurs in men age >60. Predisposing conditions include nonoperative trauma, severe illness, and surgery, particularly in combination with metabolic abnormalities (eg, hypokalemia) or medication administration (eg, opioids). Postoperative Ogilvie syndrome tends to present 3-7 days after surgery. The underlying mechanism is likely related to interruption of the autonomic nervous system, possibly due to anesthesia, analgesia, or surgical trauma. As a result, colonic dilation occurs, usually involving the cecum and ascending colon, although the entire colon may be involved. Increasing colonic dilation increases the risk of colonic ischemia and perforation. Diagnosis is confirmed with an abdominal CT scan as plain abdominal radiographs lack specificity. (Choices A and G) Acute infectious colitis is likely to cause diarrhea, often with fever and leukocytosis, none of which are seen in this patient. Toxic megacolon is a potentially fatal complication of inflammatory or infectious (eg, Clostridium difficile) colitis that results in pathologic dilation of the colon. It is frequently marked by systemic toxicity (eg, fever, hypotension, leukocytosis) and preceded by manifestations of colitis (eg, diarrhea). (Choice B) Acute ischemic colitis can occur postoperatively but is more commonly associated with vascular surgeries. It presents with moderate abdominal cramping, hematochezia, and occasionally leukocytosis and lactic acidosis. (Choice C) Cecal volvulus is a mechanical obstruction from torsion of a mobile cecum and ascending colon. It can be easily visualized on an abdominal radiograph or CT scan. Most patients experience progressive abdominal pain with episodes of cramping. (Choices E and F) Opioid analgesia is a common culprit in postoperative constipation, but opioid-induced constipation is unlikely to cause asymmetric colonic dilation or an empty rectal vault. Postoperative ileus can occur following any operation and results in uncoordinated intestinal motility and obstipation. Although symptoms may be similar to those of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction, postoperative ileus would not cause severe colonic dilation and usually develops before a return of bowel function (making it unlikely in this patient who had bowel movements after surgery). Educational objective: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) is an uncommon postoperative complication characterized by abdominal pain, distension, and colonic dilation without radiographic evidence of an anatomic obstruction. Progressive colonic dilation can lead to colonic ischemia and perforation. Abdominal CT scan is the diagnostic test of choice.

questions.explanation: This patient has manifestations of obstructed intestinal flow (eg, constipation, abdominal distension, no stool in the rectal vault), with radiographs demonstrating colonic dilation and no air in the rectum, consistent with anatomic obstruction from sigmoid colon torsion (sigmoid volvulus). This condition is often seen in elderly patients who are institutionalized (eg, nursing home) and have an underlying neurologic disorder (eg, dementia). Colonic dysmotility and redundant sigmoid colon, likely from chronic constipation, increase the risk of torsion of the sigmoid colon around its mesentery. This can lead to mechanical obstruction and ischemia of the intestines, predisposing the colon to dilation, necrosis, and perforation. Clinical presentation is variable. The elderly are at risk for a delayed presentation due to milder initial symptoms, but necrosis and bowel perforation can result in a more acute presentation. Most patients have progressive abdominal pain, obstipation, abdominal distension, and subsequent nausea and vomiting. High-pitched bowel sounds imply active intestinal motility with severe narrowing or obstruction. Discomfort during rectal examination and no stool in the rectal vault may be present. On radiograph, the dilated colon (no haustra) appears as an inverted U shape (arrow); a transition point at the site of torsion leads to no air in the rectum. (Choice A) Small-bowel obstruction from adhesions occurs in those who, unlike this patient, had abdominal surgery and developed adhesive scar tissue. Radiographic findings include dilated loops of small bowel with multiple air-fluid levels and no air in the large intestine; an inverted U-shaped, ahaustral, dilated loop of bowel is more consistent with sigmoid volvulus. (Choice B) Gallstone ileus is a mechanical small intestine obstruction following passage of a gallstone through a biliary-enteric fistula. Patients classically have episodic symptoms of obstruction as the stone becomes transiently impacted and then travels in the small intestine until it becomes impacted again. X-rays may reveal pneumobilia (gas in the biliary system) and a gallstone. (Choice C) Obstructing rectal carcinoma could cause colonic dilation but would likely present as chronic symptoms (eg, change in bowel habits, rectal bleeding). It may be detected on a thorough rectal examination. (Choice D) Hernia strangulation is an incarceration of hernia contents in the hernia sac, with impedance of vascular flow resulting in ischemia. It would present as a warm, painful, and nonreducible hernia. questions.stem: An 82-year-old nursing home resident is brought to the emergency department due to 3 days of progressively worsening abdominal pain. He has had several episodes of vomiting during the past 24 hours. The patient usually has a bowel movement every 2-3 days, but his last bowel movement was 4 days ago. He has Alzheimer disease, hypertension, and osteoarthritis. The patient has had no prior abdominal surgery. Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 140/88 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/min. Physical examination shows a distended and tympanitic abdomen with tenderness to palpation. Peritoneal signs are absent. Bowel sounds are high pitched and increased. The patient has discomfort during rectal examination and no stool is present. Blood counts and serum electrolytes are within normal limits. Abdominal radiography reveals a markedly distended bowel loop, without any haustra, extending from the pelvis to the right upper quadrant in an inverted U shape. There are several dilated small-bowel loops with air-fluid levels. No air is present in the rectum. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's abdominal pain?

questions.explanation: This patient most likely has hemolytic anemia due to intravascular hemolysis. Mechanical prosthetic heart valves can cause mechanical trauma and destruction of circulating red blood cells. A normally functioning mechanical valve may cause a low level of red blood cell destruction, and patients may experience mild, asymptomatic anemia. However, patients with significant dysfunction of a mechanical prosthetic valve can develop marked anemia. Mechanical prosthetic valve dysfunction is typically accompanied by paravalvular regurgitation, which in this patient is evidenced by a holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex. Patients with significant intravascular hemolysis typically have signs and symptoms of anemia (eg, fatigue, dyspnea, tachycardia). Mild jaundice may be present and dark urine can occur due to the presence of hemoglobin in the urine. Serum laboratory tests show elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (due to its release from hemolyzed red blood cells), decreased haptoglobin (due to binding of hemoglobin released from hemolyzed red blood cells), and elevated indirect bilirubin (due to macrophage breakdown of heme). Thrombocytopenia may be present due to the mechanical destruction of platelets. Peripheral smear typically demonstrates red cell fragments and schistocytes. (Choice A) Interstitial nephritis typically occurs as an adverse medication effect (eg, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, beta-lactam antibiotics) and presents with worsening renal function. This patient's relatively normal serum creatinine makes interstitial nephritis unlikely. (Choice B) Myelodysplasia typically presents with pancytopenia due to impaired bone marrow production of all 3 blood cell lines (ie, leukocytes, red blood cells, platelets). The absence of leukopenia and an elevated LDH in this patient makes myelodysplasia unlikely. (Choice C) Occult bleeding (eg, microscopic gastrointestinal blood loss) can lead to anemia, but an elevated LDH level would not be expected. (Choice E) Ventricular tachycardia, a rapid abnormal heart rhythm (>120/min) that typically occurs in patients with myocardial ischemia or severe heart failure, often results in circulatory collapse. This patient's ECG findings of sinus tachycardia and laboratory evidence of anemia make ventricular tachycardia an unlikely cause of his progressive fatigue and dyspnea. Educational objective: Mechanical prosthetic heart valve dysfunction can lead to intravascular hemolysis and hemolytic anemia due to mechanical destruction of circulating red blood cells. Elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase helps differentiate anemia due to hemolysis from anemia due to impaired red blood cell production or excessive red blood cell loss.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the clinic due to fatigue for the last 4 weeks. He states that he feels "exhausted" by the end of the day and gets short of breath while climbing stairs or walking at a fast pace. The patient has no chest pain, lightheadedness, lower extremity swelling, fever, or weight loss. His urine turned dark recently. He has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. A year ago, the patient's mitral valve was replaced with a mechanical valve due to mitral valve prolapse. He takes warfarin. He is a lifetime nonsmoker. Blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg and pulse is 101/min and regular. A 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex. The lungs are clear on auscultation. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with occasional ventricular premature beats. Laboratory results are as follows: Leukocytes 7,000/mm3 Hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL Platelets 100,000/mm3 Lactate dehydrogenase 1,200 U/L Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL INR 3.0 Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

questions.explanation: This patient most likely had an acute pulmonary embolism (PE). PE typically presents with the acute onset of dyspnea, chest pain, and tachycardia. Low-grade fever and signs of deep vein thrombosis (eg, unilateral lower extremity edema) may be present, and large PE is typically accompanied by hypotension and hypoxemia. Approximately 10%-15% of cases present with syncope. Massive PE can lead to a sudden occlusion of >50% of the pulmonary arterial circulation, causing a rapid increase in pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular (RV) pressure load. This can result in acute RV dysfunction and sudden loss of cardiac output. Depending on the degree of compensation for these cardiovascular changes, patients can present with sudden cardiac death, syncope, or presyncope. Acute PE can also cause syncope due to cardiac arrhythmia induced by RV strain and ischemia, or due to a vasovagal response to PE. Obesity, smoking, and recent long-distance travel (eg, flight from China) increase the risk of PE. ECG most commonly shows sinus tachycardia and may show evidence of right heart strain (eg, T wave inversion in leads V1-V3). (Choice A) Acute left ventricular (LV) dysfunction can occur due to myocardial infarction. Pulmonary edema evidenced by crackles on lung auscultation and bibasilar infiltrates on chest x-ray would be expected. (Choice B) Pericardial effusion can cause syncope due to pericardial tamponade. Patients typically present with the triad of hypotension, distant heart sounds, and jugular venous distension, but hypoxemia is rare. This patient's hypoxemia and risk factors for PE make acute PE more likely. (Choice C) Marked reduction in RV preload occurs in severe hypovolemia (eg, massive hemorrhage). LV preload is markedly reduced in acute PE due to impaired delivery of blood through the pulmonary circulation, but RV preload remains normal. (Choices E and F) Profound peripheral vasodilation can occur in anaphylaxis (due to IgE-mediated hypersensitivity) and gram-negative sepsis (due to response to endotoxin). Syncope may rarely occur but is typically orthostatic (on standing from a supine or sitting position) or preceded by evidence of cerebral hypoperfusion (eg, somnolence, confusion) rather than sudden. Educational objective: Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) may present with syncope due to right ventricular dysfunction, cardiac arrhythmia, or vasovagal response to PE.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a brief syncopal episode. The event was not witnessed, but his wife came into the room immediately after she heard a thud and found him on the floor. She did not note seizure activity when she came in. The patient woke up almost immediately and was oriented but had shortness of breath. He had no dizziness or lightheadedness prior to the event. His past medical history is significant for hypertension. The patient smokes a pack of cigarettes a day. He recently traveled to China for business and returned 3 days ago. Temperature is 38 C (100.4 F), blood pressure is 85/65 mm Hg, pulse is 124/min, and respirations are 22/min. Oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. BMI is 32 kg/m2. The lungs are clear on auscultation and there are no audible murmurs. There is 2+ bilateral lower extremity edema, more pronounced on the left side. ECG shows sinus tachycardia and T wave inversion in leads V1 to V3. Chest x-ray reveals right basilar atelectasis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's syncope before admission?
