questions.explanation: This patient has eye symptoms associated with an erythematous, pustular rash affecting the central face, consistent with rosacea. The etiology of rosacea is unknown but may be due to a chronic inflammatory reaction to cutaneous microorganisms, ultraviolet light damage, or vasomotor dysfunction. Rosacea can present with 4 primary manifestations: Erythematotelangiectatic rosacea: erythema and facial flushing, telangiectasias, roughness or scaling, and burning discomfort Papulopustular rosacea: small papules and pustules resembling acne Phymatous rosacea: chronic, irregular thickening of the skin, usually involving the nose Ocular rosacea: involvement of the cornea, conjunctiva, and lids with burning or foreign body sensations, blepharitis, keratitis, conjunctivitis, corneal ulcers, and recurrent chalazia Ocular rosacea is seen in the majority of patients with rosacea, although symptoms are not always concurrent with skin findings. It can lead to vision loss, and most cases warrant ophthalmologic consultation. Mild symptoms are treated with lid scrubs, topical antibiotics (eg, metronidazole, erythromycin), and ocular lubricants. More severe cases may require systemic antibiotics and topical immunosuppressive agents (eg, glucocorticoids, cyclosporine). (Choices A and F) Allergic conjunctivitis can resemble ocular rosacea, but it is usually associated with pruritus and nasal symptoms and would not cause the characteristic skin rash. Viral conjunctivitis causes acute ocular discomfort with watery discharge and upper respiratory symptoms. (Choice B) Angle-closure glaucoma is characterized by increased intraocular pressure from impaired aqueous humor drainage. It causes acute headache, nausea, eye pain, vision loss, and an afferent pupillary defect. (Choice C) Herpes zoster can cause ocular symptoms along with a vesicular or pustular rash. However, symptoms would be acute and almost always unilateral. (Choice E) Uveitis is characterized by inflammation of the uveal tract (ie, iris, ciliary body, choroid) and typically presents with intense pain and photophobia in one eye. Educational objective: Ocular rosacea can involve the cornea, conjunctiva, and lids and causes burning or foreign body sensations, blepharitis, keratitis, conjunctivitis, corneal ulcers, and recurrent chalazia. Symptoms may not be concurrent with skin findings. Mild symptoms are treated with lid scrubs, topical antibiotics, and ocular lubricants.

questions.explanation: This patient with HIV has several months of anal pain and bleeding with evidence of an anal ulcer and painless lymphadenopathy, suggesting anal cancer. Anal cancer develops primarily from squamous epithelial cells due to human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Risk is greatest in men who have receptive anal intercourse and those with advanced HIV (due to immunosuppression and increased prevalence of multiple HPV serotypes). Rectal bleeding is the most common manifestation of anal cancer and may be falsely attributed to hemorrhoids if the tumor is located above the anal sphincter, hiding it from view. Patients also commonly have anal pain and/or a sensation of anal pressure. Examination may show a mass or an ulcerated anal lesion; spread via the lymphatic system may result in firm, nontender inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis requires a biopsy of the lesion. (Choice B) Anal fissures can cause pain with bowel movements and a small amount of rectal bleeding. However, lesions typically heal in <6 weeks, and a 3-cm ulcer would be uncommon. (Choice C) Chancroid (caused by Haemophilus ducreyi) typically causes large, painful genital ulcers with gray-yellow exudate and severe lymphadenitis that may suppurate; painless lymphadenopathy is not characteristic. (Choice D) HPV infections are also associated with condylomata acuminata (anogenital warts). Manifestations typically include asymptomatic, skin-colored verrucous papules, not a solitary ulcer. Less than 50% of patients with anal cancer have a history of condylomata acuminata, although HPV is associated with both conditions. (Choice E) Crohn disease can cause anal fissures, fistulas, abscesses, and stenosis; anal carcinoma is rarely associated with Crohn disease. (Choice F) Anal fistulas usually arise after anorectal abscess and manifest with chronic purulent perianal drainage and intermittent rectal pain. This patient has an ulcer and no purulent drainage. (Choice G) Gonococcal proctitis is usually asymptomatic but may cause tenesmus, anorectal pain, and mucopurulent discharge. A single ulcer and 6 months of intermittent bleeding would be atypical. (Choice H) Chlamydia trachomatis can cause lymphogranuloma venereum that manifests with an anogenital ulcer (primary), lymphadenitis (secondary), and fibrosis/strictures of the anogenital tract (tertiary). This patient with 6 months of symptoms, a friable ulcer, and painless lymphadenopathy is more likely to have cancer. (Choice I) Hemorrhoids can cause painless rectal bleeding and perianal itching; thrombosis may lead to acute (not chronic) pain and ulceration. A 3-cm anal ulcer and firm, nontender lymphadenopathy would be atypical. Educational objective: Anal cancer is usually caused by human papillomavirus and occurs most often in men who have receptive anal intercourse and/or HIV infection. Manifestations include anal bleeding, pain, sensation of fullness, and an anal mass or ulcerated lesion.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man comes to the office due to intermittent rectal pain and bleeding. Six months ago, the patient first noticed small amounts of blood on the toilet paper after wiping. He self-treated with laxatives and sitz baths, but the symptoms persisted. The patient was diagnosed with HIV a year ago and does not take antiretroviral medication consistently. He has had receptive anal intercourse in the past but not since the symptoms began. Vital signs are within normal limits. The abdomen is soft and nontender with no organomegaly. Anal examination shows a tender, 3-cm ulcer at the posterior anal verge with an indurated base that bleeds with light palpation. He has no genital lesions or urethral discharge. Two firm, nontender, 3-cm lymph nodes are present in the right groin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

As seen in this scenario, it is often proactively used in the development of new policies. FMEA incorporates human factors engineering (ie, systems design incorporating expected human behaviors, strengths, and limitations) and is used in high-risk industries (eg, aviation) to increase reliability (ie, limit harmful variations affecting outcomes) and safety. Steps of FMEA include: Formation of an interdisciplinary team (members from multiple disciplines, such as pharmacy and nursing) Definition of FMEA goals and process (eg, reduce infections due to central line catheter insertion) Process mapping, including construction of a flowchart outlining all steps of the process Identification of failure modes, or areas where errors can occur, in each step (eg, improper sterile precautions during central line insertion) Hazard analysis, where each failure mode's root causes (system-level causes), possible effects, and probability of occurrence are identified Action plan formation, outlining steps to address each failure mode In this scenario, team formation and definition of goals and process have already been completed. Therefore, the next step is to map the process of catheter insertion using a flowchart. (Choice A) Implementation of an action plan is the final step of FMEA; process mapping should be completed first. (Choices B and D) "Five Whys" analysis, an approach used in root cause analysis, can inform systematic assessment of safety culture (ie, organizational commitment and action toward safety). "Five Whys" involves iteratively asking why an error occurred or could occur (typically 5 times), until fundamental causes are identified. In this scenario, "Five Whys" and systematic safety culture assessment may help identify causes and effects of hypothetical failure modes for catheter insertion (eg, ascertaining why adherence to sterile precautions could be suboptimal). However, mapping of the catheter insertion process and identification of possible failure modes should be completed first. Educational objective: Failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA) is a prospective, systematic, team-based approach used to identify potential errors in a defined process. FMEA is often used to guide development of new protocols in order to proactively reduce risk of medical error. Initial steps of FMEA include interdisciplinary team formation, process definition, process mapping (eg, flowchart), and identification of major areas of risk (ie, failure modes).

Failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA) is a prospective, systematic analysis that seeks to identify and reduce potential errors in a process (eg, central line catheter insertion) before they occur.  As seen in this scenario, it is often proactively used in the development of new policies.  FMEA incorporates human factors engineering (ie, systems design incorporating expected human behaviors, strengths, and limitations) and is used in high-risk industries (eg, aviation) to increase reliability (ie, limit harmful variations affecting outcomes) and safety.

Steps of FMEA include:

  • Formation of an interdisciplinary team (members from multiple disciplines, such as pharmacy and nursing)
  • Definition of FMEA goals and process (eg, reduce infections due to central line catheter insertion)
  • Process mapping, including construction of a flowchart outlining all steps of the process
  • Identification of failure modes, or areas where errors can occur, in each step (eg, improper sterile precautions during central line insertion)
  • Hazard analysis, where each failure mode's root causes (system-level causes), possible effects, and probability of occurrence are identified
  • Action plan formation, outlining steps to address each failure mode

In this scenario, team formation and definition of goals and process have already been completed.  Therefore, the next step is to map the process of catheter insertion using a flowchart.

questions.explanation: Colorectal cancer (CRC) screening reduces cancer mortality; however, screening adherence in the United States remains suboptimal. Screening is affected by factors involving patients (eg, health care access, beliefs), providers (eg, heavy workload), and systems (eg, complex electronic medical record). At this busy primary care clinic, CRC screening gaps occur due to suboptimal provider follow-up (ie, colonoscopy referral) of abnormal fecal occult blood tests. Provider CRC screening metrics will likely improve with pay-for-performance (P4P) program implementation. P4P links financial reimbursement (eg, bonus payments) to desired provider actions (eg, ordering recommended screening tests). P4P programs target high-value health care (ie, evidence-based care that optimizes patient outcomes while avoiding unnecessary treatment). Major P4P programs in Medicare (ie, a federally funded public health insurance program that insures individuals age >65) and private insurers have improved provider metrics in cancer screening and chronic condition monitoring (eg, laboratory testing). However, P4P programs do not address factors outside provider control (eg, patient socioeconomic status, health care access) and have not yet improved health outcomes (eg, mortality). P4P programs are best used with other systems strategies promoting high-value care, including distributing feedback on performance metrics (eg, percent of a provider's patients completing screening compared to a benchmark), clinical decision support (eg, reminders prompting follow-up of abnormal results), and patient registries (ie, patient database tracking health care and outcomes for specific conditions). (Choice A) Educating patients is useful for increasing CRC screening awareness and health literacy, but it has a smaller impact on provider behaviors (eg, follow-up screening rates) compared to system-level strategies (ie, P4P programs). The fact that most patients who receive colonoscopy referrals complete these procedures further highlights that the screening gap is mostly due to provider factors rather than patient factors. (Choice C) Colonoscopy is an appropriate initial screening strategy for CRC. However, exclusively ordering this invasive test over noninvasive approaches (eg, fecal occult blood testing) is not recommended because noninvasive methods achieve similar mortality benefits with fewer risks (eg, perforation, infection). Moreover, offering patients a choice among multiple CRC screening options is associated with increased patient screening adherence. (Choice D) Annual wellness examinations offer opportunities to discuss preventive care and may increase initial CRC screening rates. However, they would not address this clinic's suboptimal metric, which involves provider follow-up of abnormal test results rather than initial CRC screening. Educational objective: Pay-for-performance programs link financial incentives to provider actions (eg, completing cancer screening). They can promote clinicians' delivery of evidence-based care and high-value health care (ie, care that optimizes patient outcomes and quality while avoiding unnecessary treatment).

questions.stem: The medical director of a large, busy primary care clinic is considering strategies to improve quality of screening for colorectal cancer. Most of the clinic's patients are insured individuals age >40. The director finds that, among 3,500 patients who underwent annual fecal occult blood testing in the previous year, the clinic providers placed follow-up colonoscopy referrals for only 55% of the patients who returned positive results. The majority of patients who received colonoscopy referrals completed the procedure. Which of the following strategic initiatives has the greatest potential to improve the percentage of follow-up colonoscopy referrals?
